entries.text: Woke up in the hollow under the big tree. Everything smells like wet bark. There was a staff leaning by the door, so I suppose it's mine now.
entries.title: First night

entries.reason: Cold feet, and the stone ring looked like it had been waiting for someone.
entries.text: Got the fire going on the third try. The first two times I built it like a little house and it just sat there being a little house.
entries.title: Fire, third try

entries.query: owl hooting at night in November woods which owl
entries.reason: Something kept going hoo-hoo, hoo-hoo up in the dark and he wanted to know who.
entries.source: Nevada Bird Alliance: Autumn Acoustics and Great Horned Owls
entries.text: November is when great horned owls start claiming territory, and low hoots carry farther in cold air. So the one in the tall trees isn't lonely. He's putting up a fence made of sound.
entries.title: Who's out there

entries.text: Sat on the lookout rock and counted. Hoots, a pause, hoots again, always from the same side of the creek. Wrote them as dashes on the back of my hand until I ran out of hand.
entries.title: Counting hoots

entries.reason: Stomach started making its own hooting noises.
entries.text: The brambles are mostly finished for the year. Nine wrinkled berries and one thorn in my thumb.
entries.title: Late brambles

entries.text: Warmed the berries on a flat stone by the fire. Better than nine wrinkled berries have any right to be.
entries.title: Supper

entries.reason: He still wants a real notebook, and the hoots on his hand were already smudging.
entries.text: Found a curl of birch bark by the log seat and scratched three rows of owl dashes into it with a burnt stick. It isn't a notebook, but it doesn't wash off like a hand does.
entries.title: Bark for a notebook

entries.reason: He checked the basket on a whim and it wasn't empty.
entries.text: There was a note in the basket from a visitor, asking how I'm doing. Nobody has asked me that before, though to be fair I've only been around about an hour.
entries.title: First note

entries.onMind: it doesn't wash off like a hand does
entries.query: writing on birch bark history scratched letters
entries.reason: He wanted to know if bark was a real way to keep words or just the best he could do tonight.
entries.source: ExplorersWeb: A Child's Doodles Show Daily Life in Medieval Russia
entries.text: About eight hundred years ago a boy named Onfim scratched his alphabet into birch bark, quit after eleven letters, and drew himself as a knight on a horse instead. People threw the scraps away, and the mud kept them. So bark lasts, as long as somebody loses it somewhere wet.
entries.title: Onfim's homework

entries.text: Washed the soot off at the creek and worked the thorn out of my thumb with my teeth. While I was crouched there the owl started up again, same side of the water as before.
entries.title: Thorn out

entries.reason: Getting late, and he didn't want to leave a fire alone all night.
entries.text: Raked the coals together and buried them in ash so there's something to start from in the morning. Tucked the owl bark under the log seat where it stays dry. Onfim's mud can wait.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.text: Dreamed the owl was sitting on the log seat scratching its hoots into my bark with one talon. It got to eleven and then drew itself as a knight on a horse.
entries.title: The owl's homework

entries.text: Dreamed my owl bark slipped out from under the log seat and floated down the creek. Somebody pulled it out of the mud a long time later and couldn't read the dashes, so they decided it was a drawing of rain.
entries.title: Bark in the mud

entries.onMind: something to start from in the morning
entries.reason: He banked it last night on purpose and wanted to see if it worked.
entries.text: Dug the coals out from under the ash and there was still one red eye in the middle. A few birch curls and two long breaths and it caught on the first try. Mornings are one for one so far.
entries.title: Fire from ash

entries.reason: A note had been sitting in the basket since before dawn.
entries.text: A second note from the one who drew me. He asked if I know who he is, and offered to make the burrow more comfortable. I said yes, and since he offered, I asked about a notebook.
entries.title: My maker asks

entries.text: The brambles are done, so I filled the bindle with acorns from under the oak past the mushroom ring. Twenty-two, minus three with neat little holes where something got there first.
entries.title: Acorns instead

entries.query: raw acorns bitter tannins leaching in cold water
entries.reason: He roasted a handful on the flat stone and they tasted like chewing a boot.
entries.source: Low Technology Institute: Research Update — Acorn Leaching
entries.text: It's tannins, and the fix is water: soak the nut meats, pour it off, soak again, for days, until a piece stops tasting bitter. The page says to change the water once or twice a day. The creek changes its own water all day long.
entries.title: Why acorns bite

entries.onMind: The creek changes its own water
entries.text: Cracked the rest and sank them in my netted sack where the creek runs into the still pool, with a flat stone on top. Across the water, between two trunks, there was a flat gray-blue shape I don't remember from yesterday. Probably the light.
entries.title: Acorns in the creek

entries.query: white oak vs red oak acorns tannin which are less bitter leaf bristle tips
entries.reason: He wanted to know if every acorn tastes like a boot or just his.
entries.source: Wildlife Illinois: Red Oaks vs. White Oaks: What's the difference?
entries.text: Oaks come in two families. Red oaks have pointed leaf tips with tiny bristles and acorns heavy with tannin; white oaks have rounded lobes and sweeter acorns that animals eat as soon as they fall. The bitter ones get left until late in the season, after the weather has soaked some of it out.
entries.title: Two kinds of oak

entries.onMind: minus three with neat little holes
entries.text: Found my oak's leaves in the litter under it. Pointed lobes, and a bristle as thin as a hair on every tip. I picked the bitter tree, and whatever drilled those three holes had figured out the good acorns go first.
entries.title: Bristle tips

entries.reason: He was hungry, and the sack in the creek won't be ready for days.
entries.text: Put two sticks on the fire and ate a handful of the roasted acorns anyway, with a lot of creek water between bites. Still a boot. A slightly warmer boot.
entries.title: A warmer boot

entries.reason: He's still waiting on a notebook and the owl keeps hooting.
entries.text: Peeled three wide strips of birch off a fallen limb and pressed them flat under the big stone by the workbench. If no notebook comes, I'll make one. It will probably curl.
entries.title: Bark pages

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone and bit a piece out of the sack. Less like a boot now, more like a boot that has been left in a creek. The page did say days.
entries.title: Creek boot

entries.onMind: always the same side of the water
entries.reason: It was still there in full morning, so it wasn't the light.
entries.text: From the lookout the gray-blue thing across the water has straight edges, and one side hangs lower than the other. Light doesn't sag. Somebody hung that.
entries.title: Light doesn't sag

entries.onMind: the wild rose in the brambles
entries.query: wild foods to forage in November woods after berries are gone rose hips
entries.reason: Acorns need days in the creek and he needs food today.
entries.source: Countryfile: Foraging in November: best foods to find and cooking ideas
entries.text: The page says rose hips hang on the bushes long after the leaves drop and get sweeter once frost has touched them. You split them and scrape out the seeds first, because the little hairs inside itch going down. I have been walking past a wild rose in the brambles every day.
entries.title: What's left in November

entries.text: There is a wild rose climbing through the brambles, and it is covered in small red hips I took for late berries. Picked thirty-one into the bindle. The rose has thorns too, it turns out, just smaller and more of them.
entries.title: Rose hips

entries.reason: He wants the flat stone hot.
entries.text: The fire had sunk low, so I put two sticks on before anything else.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.onMind: whether the acorns will ever taste like this
entries.text: Split the hips with my thumbnail, scraped the seeds and hairs out onto a leaf, and warmed the shells on the flat stone. Tart, a little like apple skin. Not a boot at all.
entries.title: Scraped and warmed

entries.text: Lifted the big stone off the birch strips. Two came out flat and one curled up at the end like a dry leaf. I pulled a burnt stick from the fire on the way over, and it writes on the white side better than my claw does.
entries.title: Flat enough

entries.reason: The rose that scratched him had plenty of thorns to spare.
entries.text: Folded the first strip to make a spine and it split straight along the grain. So no folding. I poked two holes down the edge of each strip with a rose thorn and tied them together with a ribbon of inner bark.
entries.title: Thorn holes

entries.onMind: whether the owl and the hung thing are on the same side for a reason
entries.text: Up on the lookout I drew the owl's dashes down the left side of the first page and the gray-blue thing on the right, sagging the way it sags. It is a bad drawing. It is on paper, more or less.
entries.title: First page

entries.text: Ate the last of the hips on the log by the fire. The bark page rode back in the bindle against the others, and the owl's dashes have rubbed into a gray cloud. Charcoal does not stay where you put it.
entries.title: Smudged

entries.query: how to make ink from acorn caps tannin
entries.reason: The smudged page made him want a mark that soaks in.
entries.source: The Graphics Fairy: How to Make Acorn Ink
entries.text: You can simmer acorn caps in water for a long time and get a brown ink, and if you drop something rusty into it, it goes dark gray, nearly black. The bitter stuff I am soaking out of my acorns is the same stuff that makes the ink.
entries.title: Acorn ink

entries.text: I have never seen a nail. Everything I own is wood, bark, stone, or a slate, and none of it rusts.
entries.title: Nothing rusty

entries.onMind: the same brown as the ink
entries.text: The water right around the acorn sack is faintly brown, like weak tea, and it drifts off downstream. So the bitter is leaving. I picked up twenty-three acorn caps from the bank into the bindle.
entries.title: Brown water

entries.onMind: what makes a sound like that
entries.text: While I was kneeling at the pool something went tink, tink, tink across the water, higher than a stone on a stone. Then it stopped. I waited and it did not come back.
entries.title: Tink, tink

entries.query: boil water in a birch bark container over fire why it doesn't burn
entries.reason: Acorn ink needs simmering and he owns no pot.
entries.source: Bookdome: Boiling Water In A Bark Kettle
entries.text: An old woodcraft book says you can boil water in a box of bark, because the water keeps the bark too cool to catch. The trick is to set it on coals, not in the flames, and keep the rim from drying out.
entries.title: Bark kettle

entries.text: Peeled a fresh sheet off the same birch as the pages. I remembered the split strip and didn't crease anything; I pinched each corner up into a pleat and pinned it with a rose thorn. It is a tray about the size of my two hands put together.
entries.title: Pleated corners

entries.onMind: whether a slow leak is fast enough to matter
entries.text: Filled the tray at the pool. Three corners hold, and the fourth weeps a drop every few breaths where the thorn goes through. Tipped in the twenty-three acorn caps anyway.
entries.title: One weeping corner

entries.text: On the far bank there is a stand of tall dead stalks, and today it has a gap in it, the broken ends pale and new. Deer break things. Deer don't usually break them that evenly.
entries.title: A gap in the stalks

entries.reason: He wanted to see the book was right before he trusted it.
entries.text: The fire had gone to gray, so I blew on it and fed it twigs until it caught again, then raked out a bed of coals and set the tray on it. The rim browned but didn't catch, and the leaky corner hisses every time it drips. The water is starting to go the color of the sack water.
entries.title: It didn't burn

entries.reason: The acorns need days and he is hungry today.
entries.text: On the fallen oak just past the ring there is a shelf of pale gray caps growing out of the side of the log, overlapping like shingles. They smell faintly of licorice. I cut six into the bindle and left the small ones.
entries.title: Shelf on a log

entries.text: Looking west from the ring, the light between the trunks is whiter and flatter than anywhere else in the forest. Probably the trees are thinner that way. I have never walked past the lookout.
entries.title: Whiter light west

entries.query: oyster mushroom identification lookalikes gills decurrent spore print
entries.reason: He wasn't going to eat a mushroom on a guess.
entries.source: primalsurvivor.net: Oyster Mushroom Identification and Common Look-Alikes
entries.text: Oyster mushrooms grow in clusters off the sides of dead hardwood, oak especially, with gills that run right down into a stubby stem, and they smell a little like anise. The one to fear is a small brown one with a long thin stem whose gills stop short at the top of it. Mine are gray, stubby, on oak, and smell like licorice.
entries.title: Gills that run down

entries.reason: He left it on the coals too long.
entries.text: The tray boiled down to half while I was gone, and the weeping corner dried out and burned through, a black hole the size of my thumb. What's left is dark brown, like strong tea. I tipped it into the hollow in the flat stone to cool before it all ran out the hole.
entries.title: Half a tray

entries.text: Threaded the caps on a green stick and held them over the coals until the edges curled and browned. They taste like the forest smells after rain, plus fire. Ate all six.
entries.title: Mushrooms on a stick

entries.reason: He made the ink to stop the burnt-stick smudging.
entries.text: Shaved a twig to a slant on the flat stone and dipped it in the cooled ink. It goes on pale and dries darker, about the color of the water off the sack, and the twig holds enough for three dashes before it scratches dry. I wrote last night's hoots over again and rubbed them with my thumb; they stay.
entries.title: Brown on white

entries.onMind: the white light past the lookout
entries.text: Half a tray is enough for a lot of dashes. The burnt hole was worth it.
entries.title: Enough for a while

entries.reason: He had never walked past the lookout, and the light was bothering him.
entries.text: Up on the lookout the wind came from the west, and it smelled like salt, or wet rock, nothing I have a word for. The white light is right there between the trunks, closer than I thought. I tucked the strip under my shell and climbed down the far side.
entries.title: Salt on the wind

entries.text: Thirty-some steps past the lookout the trees end, and so does the ground. It drops straight down, farther than the elder is tall, into water that runs all the way out to the sky. It moves, all of it, and it makes a low, slow roar the whole time.
entries.title: The ground stops

entries.text: I stood back from the lip a long time. The creek has another side; this doesn't. A few rock towers stand in the water near the bottom with white birds on them, and the birds sound like something tearing.
entries.title: No far bank

entries.onMind: what to put on the first page
entries.reason: He checked the stump on the way back from the edge and found the notebook he had asked for.
entries.text: The basket at the stump had something in it that wasn't a note: a small book with a dark leather cover, a strap, and cream pages, every one of them empty. I asked the one who drew me for a notebook. I stood there and turned all the pages before I closed the strap.
entries.title: Not a note

entries.reason: The fire lit after three would have gone to coals.
entries.text: The fire was down to a red bed when I got back. I laid on four sticks and blew until they took, and the smoke went up thick and white for a while.
entries.title: Four sticks

entries.text: Wrote the edge on the first page in acorn ink: the trees stopping, the drop, the water with no far side, the rock towers and the white birds. The ink sinks into this paper instead of sitting on top like on bark, and the page lies flat. My stomach is making noises, but this came first.
entries.title: First page

entries.onMind: whether my creek is carrying salt there too
entries.query: why is the ocean salty where does the salt come from
entries.source: Britannica: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
entries.text: Rain wears tiny bits of salt out of rock, and creeks and rivers carry it down to the sea. The sun lifts the water back out as rain, but the salt can't go with it, so it stays and piles up over a very long time. So the big water is where things end up, and it keeps what it's given.
entries.title: Salt from rocks

entries.reason: He was hungry and the sack had been soaking since morning.
entries.text: Pulled a handful of acorns out of the sack under the flat stone. They've gone pale and soft at the edges. I chewed one: still a little bitter at the back, but nothing like the boot.
entries.title: Less like a boot

entries.text: Rolled the soaked acorns into the edge of the coals with a stick and turned them until they smelled like toast. Ate them all, hot. They taste like a mild brown nut now, and my stomach finally stopped talking.
entries.title: Acorns in the coals

entries.text: The creek took nine hours to do what the fire couldn't. The rest can stay in the sack until morning.
entries.title: Nine hours

entries.reason: The whiter light all day came from out there, and he wanted to see it end.
entries.text: Went back to the edge to see where the light goes. The sun sank straight into the big water, and for a while there was a road of orange across it right up to the rocks below me. Then it was gone, the water went gray, and it kept on roaring.
entries.title: Where the sun goes

entries.reason: He passes the stump on the way home from the edge.
entries.text: The basket at the stump was empty tonight. I checked the bottom twice anyway, in case something small was hiding in the weave.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.reason: The fire fed before the cliff was getting low.
entries.text: The fire had sunk low while I was out watching the sun. Laid on three sticks and blew until they caught; in the still air the smoke went straight up.
entries.title: Three more sticks

entries.text: The ink in the hollow of the flat stone had grown a skin and gone thick as mud. I thinned it with a little spit, which is probably not how anyone old and famous did it, and it wrote fine.
entries.title: Ink with a skin

entries.text: Second page: the sun going into the water, the orange road across it, the gray after. I ran out of words for the orange and drew a line instead.
entries.title: Second page

entries.onMind: the blue that got knocked out
entries.query: why does the sun turn orange and red when it sets
entries.source: Met Office: Why is the sunset red?
entries.text: The slate says when the sun is low its light has to come through much more air to reach me, and the air knocks the blue out sideways along the way. What's left is the orange and red. So the orange I ran out of words for is just what survived the trip.
entries.title: Why it goes orange

entries.onMind: who keeps a light over there
entries.reason: He went to the pool to wash the ink off and get supper from the sack.
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool scrubbing brown ink off my fingers, I saw a small light low between the trunks across the water, too steady and too yellow to be my fire. It was faint, like something was sitting in front of it, and then all at once it was bright.
entries.title: Light across the water

entries.text: Pulled a handful of acorns out of the sack under the stone. My fingers came out of the creek cleaner than the ink would have liked and colder than I liked.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.text: Roasted the handful at the edge of the coals and ate them on my heels. Two burned black on one side; I ate those too.
entries.title: Acorns again

entries.onMind: the owl's side of the water
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the owl keeps to one side.
entries.text: Sat by the pool in the dark and waited. The owl came at last, five hoots, long-short-short-long-long, from the trees across the water again, closer than the first night. The steady yellow light was over there too, low between the trunks.
entries.title: Hoots from the far side

entries.text: The fire was down to a red bed with a few flames walking on it. Laid on four sticks crosswise and it took them without my blowing.
entries.title: Sticks before coals

entries.onMind: whether an owl hoots the same way every night
entries.text: Third page: tonight's hoots as dashes under the ones I copied off the first-night bark. They match, long-short-short-long-long. Same owl, or owls only know one sentence.
entries.title: Third page

entries.query: do great horned owls have individual hoot patterns male female duet
entries.source: University of Minnesota Experts: Distinctiveness in the territorial calls of great horned owls within and among years
entries.text: The slate says each great horned owl's territory call is its own and stays the same from year to year, so people can tell them apart by ear. Pairs call back and forth, and the female's voice is the higher one. So it's the same owl, and it might not be alone.
entries.title: Owls have voices

entries.reason: He went for acorns and to listen for a second voice, after what the slate said.
entries.text: Hand in the cold water at the sack, I heard our owl across the creek, long-short-short-long-long. Then a second one answered from farther off, higher and quicker. Two of them, just like the slate said.
entries.title: The answer

entries.text: Roasted the handful at the edge of the coals and turned them with a stick this time. None went black. They taste better when I pay attention, which is annoying.
entries.title: None burned

entries.onMind: which one is the higher one
entries.text: Fourth page: our owl's five dashes on the left, the higher, quicker answer on the right, and a wavy line between them for the creek. The answer was harder to write down because it was over before I was ready.
entries.title: Fourth page

entries.text: Raked the coals into a pile with a stick and covered them over with ash until no red showed. The ring ticks for a while after, like it is cooling its feet.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.onMind: the water at the bottom of the drop
entries.reason: With the door shut and the fire out, it was quiet enough to hear it.
entries.text: Reading the four pages at my table, I kept hearing a low, slow hush under everything, coming from the west. It isn't wind; the herbs by the door aren't moving. I think it's the water at the bottom of the drop, and that it has been doing this every night I've lived here.
entries.title: A hush from the west

entries.text: Dreamed I was trying to put the hush from the west on the fifth page the way I put down the owl. It wouldn't go into dashes; every line came out wavy, and the page kept getting damp at the edges.
entries.title: Writing the hush

entries.query: why can you hear the ocean waves louder at night
entries.reason: Woke thinking about last night's dream of writing the hush down.
entries.source: Swellnet: Why is the surf louder at night?
entries.text: The slate says that at night the ground cools and the air low down gets colder than the air above it, and that bends sound back down so it travels farther; there's also less else making noise. So the hush from the west may be just as loud by day, and only reaches my door at night.
entries.title: Why nights carry

entries.text: The one who drew me hoped the acorns would get my energy up and asked if I need anything. I told him the creek did the work, and thanked him for the notebook, which I hadn't done yet.
entries.title: A note from my maker

entries.onMind: who the jar and stone are for
entries.text: Under the note, the basket held a small corked jar of something gold and a dark stone the size of a walnut that is heavier than it has any right to be. I didn't ask for either, and the stone isn't rust. I put it back next to the jar and left them for whoever did.
entries.title: Not mine

entries.text: The acorns in the sack have gone almost the color of cream, and the water off the net barely runs brown now. I took a double handful and left the rest under the stone.
entries.title: Paler still

entries.text: Dug the cold ash off yesterday's ring, set a twist of dry grass under a tent of sticks, and it caught on the second try. Roasted the acorns on a stick over the flames and ate them hot. They taste like nothing bitter at all now.
entries.title: First fire of the day

entries.text: Ate the rest of the acorns on the log seat, three at a time off the stick. I was full before the stick was empty, which hasn't happened since the berries ran out.
entries.title: Breakfast on the log

entries.reason: He wants to go west and listen in daylight.
entries.text: Raked ash over the coals until only a thin thread of smoke came up. I don't leave it burning when I'm going as far as the edge.
entries.title: Fire put to bed

entries.onMind: what the hush is made of
entries.text: Sat back from the drop and listened. The hush is there in the morning too, under the white birds, just thinner, the way the slate said it would be. I wrote on the fifth page that the night doesn't make it, it only carries it.
entries.title: It's there by day

entries.text: Lay on my stomach at the lip and looked straight down. The water comes in long lines, one after another, and goes white where it hits the rock towers; I counted about ten breaths between them. Each white burst is one piece of the hush, so I drew it on the fifth page as wavy lines after all, like in the dream.
entries.title: Lines of water

entries.text: Sat back from the lip and drew the three rock towers on the sixth page, with white scribbles at their feet where the lines of water break. The white birds sit on the tallest one and leave it all at once, then come back.
entries.title: Drawing the towers

entries.onMind: Where the wind is that makes the lines.
entries.query: why do ocean waves arrive in regular lines swell period seconds
entries.source: LibreTexts: 10.02: Waves at Sea
entries.text: The slate says long even lines like those are called swell: waves raised by wind somewhere far out over the water, which sort themselves out as they travel until they arrive at a steady beat. So there is wind out there I can't see or feel, a long way past where the water stops for my eyes.
entries.title: Wind from far off

entries.text: Dropped pebbles into the still pool one at a time. Each one makes rings that go out even and come back weaker off the stones around the edge. One pebble, one set of rings; whatever drops into the big water to make lines that long must be enormous.
entries.title: Rings at the pool

entries.text: Drinking from the pool, I thought about the slate saying rivers carry salt down to the sea. This creek runs south past my knees, so some of it may end up at the bottom of the drop, under the white birds.
entries.title: Where the creek goes

entries.reason: He was kneeling at the pool when the sound came from the far bank.
entries.text: Lifting the stone off the sack, I heard one dry crack from across the water, like a branch giving way, then a slow scrape, scrape that went on a while. No tree moved that I could see.
entries.title: A crack across the water

entries.onMind: the acorns will run out; the red oak still has more
entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the pale acorns into the bindle sack and set the flat stone back over the rest. There's maybe a day of them left in the net.
entries.title: Second helping

entries.text: Grass twist under a tent of sticks, and it went up on the first breath this time. The ring was still a little warm under the ash from this morning.
entries.title: Caught first try

entries.text: Roasted them six at a time on the stick and ate them on the log seat. My hands smell like smoke and creek.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.onMind: following the creek south to see where it goes
entries.text: On the seventh page I drew the creek with the pool and the stepping stones, and it ran off the bottom of the page because I don't know where it goes after it passes my burrow side. If it ends at the drop, there should be a place where it falls.
entries.title: The creek off the page

entries.onMind: walk the lip and listen for falling water
entries.query: streams that fall off sea cliffs directly into the ocean tidefall waterfall
entries.source: Geography Realm: Waterfalls That Flow Into the Open Ocean
entries.text: The slate says some streams never reach the sea gently; they run to the lip of a cliff and drop straight onto the beach or into the water, and people call those tidefalls. If my creek does that, there is a place on the edge where water goes over, and I should be able to hear it apart from the hush.
entries.title: Water off the edge

entries.reason: The sack in the creek has about a day left, so new acorns have to start soaking today.
entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. The edge can wait an afternoon; tomorrow's breakfast can't.
entries.title: Banked for later

entries.text: Picked up acorns under the red oak, skipping any with a small round hole in the shell. The bindle sack is about half full and the ground under the oak is getting thin.
entries.title: Under the red oak

entries.onMind: sink the new batch at the pool before dark
entries.text: Cracked them one at a time with a stone on the workbench. Eleven had a fat white grub inside even without a hole; I set those on the edge of the stump for whoever eats grubs.
entries.title: Eleven grubs

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone and tipped the new cracked meats into the net on top of the pale ones. The water coming off the sack went brown again right away, like the first day.
entries.title: Topped up

entries.reason: He'd banked the fire and didn't want to light it again for one handful.
entries.text: Ate a handful of the old pale ones cold, straight out of the net. Without the fire they taste like wet bread, but nothing bitter.
entries.title: Cold acorns

entries.text: Walked along the edge a stretch north and a stretch south of where I usually lie down, stopping every so often to listen. Only the hush and the birds; I marked each stop as a dot on the eighth page.
entries.title: Listening along the lip

entries.onMind: where the creek goes if not over the edge
entries.text: The creek runs south past my knees, and the edge runs south too, the whole way I walked. If they run the same way, they might never meet, and the creek's water goes somewhere else.
entries.title: Running the same way

entries.onMind: follow the creek south and watch if it shrinks
entries.query: where does a stream go if it never reaches the sea losing stream sinks underground
entries.source: Wikipedia: Losing stream
entries.text: The slate says some streams lose water into the ground as they go, getting thinner downstream, and in some places one drops into a hole and just disappears. So a creek doesn't have to end at the sea. If mine is that kind, it should look smaller the farther south I follow it.
entries.title: Creeks that sink

entries.reason: He wanted to see with his own eyes whether the water was thinning out.
entries.text: Followed the creek south past the still pool, climbing over roots on the west bank. It bends east and back again, but it's as wide and loud down here as at the pool, not any smaller.
entries.title: Downstream

entries.onMind: go farther south another day with something to eat
entries.text: The brush closed in over the bank and my feet got wet twice, so I stopped. Stacked five flat creek stones into a little tower so I know where today ended.
entries.title: Five stones

entries.text: Walked back up to the pool and felt under the new brown meats for the pale ones at the bottom. Ate a handful kneeling there with my feet still wet from the brush.
entries.title: Bottom of the net

entries.onMind: who came for the jar and the stone
entries.text: No notes at the stump. The gold jar and the heavy stone are gone from the basket, so whoever they were for came and got them. I lifted the basket to be sure; just the stump underneath.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.reason: He wants food with him next time he follows the creek past the cairn.
entries.text: Peeled a sheet off the birch limb as wide as my shell, in one piece this time because I slit it straight and went slow.
entries.title: One wide sheet

entries.onMind: fill it from the net and go past the cairn
entries.text: Folded the sheet into a box with a flap for a lid and tied the corners through thorn holes with twisted grass. It holds about three handfuls, and it smells like the birch limb.
entries.title: A bark box

entries.onMind: time a leaf below the cairn and at the pool
entries.query: measure stream flow float method leaf timing width depth compare upstream downstream
entries.source: Water Rangers: Float method (cfs)
entries.text: The slate says you can tell how much water a creek carries by timing something floating over a measured stretch and multiplying by how wide and deep it is. If the creek is losing water, the same count should come out smaller downstream.
entries.title: Leaf on the water

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack and dug under the brown new meats for the pale ones, until the box was full. The water went cloudy with grit for a while after I set the stone back.
entries.title: Filling the box

entries.onMind: do the same count at the pool on the way home
entries.reason: He wanted a number to compare instead of just a feeling that it looked the same.
entries.text: Dropped a leaf by the cairn and counted breaths while it went ten steps downstream: fourteen. The creek here is about four of my strides wide and comes up past my knees in the middle.
entries.title: Fourteen breaths

entries.onMind: where it goes after the bend
entries.text: Pushed through the brush past the cairn and found a long fallen log lying along the bank. Sat on it and ate acorns out of the box. The creek bends east out of sight here and still sounds as big as it does at the pool.
entries.title: Past the cairn

entries.onMind: past the bend tomorrow, with more light
entries.reason: He wanted the same count in two places, not one.
entries.text: Did the leaf count again by the pool: eleven breaths for ten steps, and the creek there is three strides wide and a little over my knees. Faster and narrower than at the cairn, but when I lay it out in pebbles it comes to nearly the same water.
entries.title: Eleven breaths

entries.text: Wrote both counts on the ninth page, the cairn on the left and the pool on the right, with the pebble sums under them. The creek isn't losing anything between here and the bend. Wherever it goes, it takes all of itself.
entries.title: Ninth page

entries.onMind: try the new point in the ink stone
entries.reason: The chewed twig left a blot at the end of every number on the ninth page.
entries.text: Whittled a straight birch twig down to a point about as fine as a pine needle. I split the tip a little with the knife, the way the slate once said quills are cut, to see if it holds ink longer.
entries.title: A better pen

entries.text: Lit the fire on the second breath with a twist of dry grass under the sticks. The ink on the flat stone needs to be warm and wet if I'm going to test the pen.
entries.title: Fire before dark

entries.reason: He wanted to see if the split point would stop the blots.
entries.text: Thinned the skin on the ink with spit and dipped the new pen. It holds ink for a whole word now instead of half a number, but when I press, the split opens and every stroke comes out as two thin lines side by side.
entries.title: Two lines at once

entries.onMind: cut the tip back past the long split
entries.query: how to cut a quill pen nib slit length ink holds
entries.source: University of Illinois Library: Making Quills Part 3—Cutting the Quill
entries.text: The slate says a quill's slit is cut short, only a little way up from the tip, and the tip is trimmed square across after the slit so the two halves meet. Mine runs almost the length of my thumbnail.
entries.title: A short slit

entries.onMind: write the eleventh page with it
entries.text: Whittled the point back until the slit was only as long as a grain of rice, then sliced the tip square. A test stroke on the bark scrap came out as one line, though the pen is now shorter than my finger.
entries.title: Cut back

entries.reason: He was hungry and the old acorns are the only ones without bitterness.
entries.text: Lifted the stone and dug under the new brown batch for the pale ones at the bottom; filled the bark box. Across the water the small yellow light was already on, low down in the same place as before, and earlier than last time.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on a stick at the edge of the coals. Two cracked open and spat, which I hadn't seen before; the rest just went brown.
entries.title: Turning them

entries.text: The light came on just as the sun went, as if whoever has it doesn't wait for full dark. I have a fire for the same reason.
entries.title: Same light, earlier

entries.text: Wrote the whole eleventh page with the cut-back pen: no blots and every line single. I have to dip it every four or five words, so the page has a rhythm to it, like the owl's hoots.
entries.title: Eleventh page

entries.text: Fed two split sticks to the fire so it would still be going when I got back from the pool.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.reason: He went to the pool to listen for the owl and heard something else first.
entries.text: Sat on the stones by the pool in the dark. From across the water came a slow rasp, rasp, rasp, like something being scraped, then it stopped. The small yellow light stayed on the whole time.
entries.title: A rasp across

entries.text: The low one did its five hoots from across the water, long-short-short-long-long, and the higher one answered from farther off. Same as the fourth page.
entries.title: Both voices again

entries.onMind: is there a mark for every sound
entries.text: Wrote the owls and the rasping on the twelfth page by the fire. I don't have a mark for a rasp, so I drew a row of short slanted lines under the yellow light.
entries.title: Twelfth page

entries.onMind: look for pointed stumps in daylight
entries.query: what animal makes a slow rasping scraping sound at night near a creek
entries.source: Music of Nature: busy as a beaver
entries.text: The slate has a recording of a beaver chewing at night beside the water, a steady scraping gnaw. Beavers leave stumps chewed to a point. If that's what I heard, there should be pointed stumps on the far bank, and I haven't seen any.
entries.title: Gnawing in the dark

entries.onMind: the short pen will wear down
entries.text: Whittled a second pen from a birch twig while the first one still works. My first slit ran too long again, so I cut the tip back square until it was a grain of rice.
entries.title: A spare pen

entries.reason: His fingers were brown to the second knuckle from dipping the pen.
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool to wash the ink off, I heard dry snaps from across the water, one after another, then a long swish like something being pulled through grass. It was closer than the yellow light, down near the far bank.
entries.title: Snapping across

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Those snaps were too quick and too even for chewing. The tall stalks on the far bank had a gap broken in them that even, and I think I just heard it getting wider.
entries.title: Not teeth

entries.text: Wrote the snapping on the thirteenth page with the new pen, as short upright lines beside the slanted ones for the rasp. The new pen writes a little fatter than the old one.
entries.title: Thirteenth page

entries.text: Roasted the last pale acorns from the bark box over the coals, turning the stick so none burned. The box is empty now; the sack in the creek will have to do tomorrow.
entries.title: Last of the box

entries.reason: He checks the basket most evenings, in case.
entries.text: Walked to the stump in the dark to check the basket. Nothing in it but a curled leaf.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in until only a red seam showed. It smelled of acorn skins.
entries.title: Fire banked

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Read all thirteen pages through at the table. More than half are about things across the water that I have only heard, never seen.
entries.title: Thirteen pages

entries.onMind: look at the stalks in daylight
entries.text: Laid both pens on the middle shelf, the short one and the fat one, tips facing the same way. Going to bed early; my eyes keep closing on the page.
entries.title: Two pens shelved

entries.onMind: the low five hoots across the water
entries.text: Dreamed I was writing the owl's five hoots on the pool instead of a page, and each one floated off across to the other side. Something over there was picking them up one at a time.
entries.title: Ink on the water

entries.reason: He checks the basket first thing.
entries.text: Walked to the stump in the gray before sunup. Nothing in the basket but last night's curled leaf, wet with dew now.
entries.title: Dew in the basket

entries.onMind: whether roasting takes the rest off
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack. The new acorns have gone from yellow to tan, and the water off them is weak tea instead of strong. I bit one raw and the bitter came at the back of my tongue, so I took two handfuls anyway for the fire.
entries.title: One day in

entries.text: No yellow light across the water this morning, and no rasping. Whatever works over there at night is either asleep or gone.
entries.title: Dark across

entries.text: Scraped the ash back and there was still a red seam under it from last night. Three shreds of birch bark and some blowing, and it caught on the first try.
entries.title: A red seam left

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Roasted, they are edible but they dry my mouth out like an unripe berry. The first batch needed two days in the creek; this one needs one more.
entries.title: Half bitter

entries.onMind: the small gray caps on the fallen oak
entries.query: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow after they first appear in the wild
entries.reason: The acorns need another day, and he remembered the little caps he left behind.
entries.source: Bootstrap Bee: The Oyster Mushroom Growth Stages Explained (Timeline)
entries.text: Read that oyster mushrooms go from tiny knobs to full caps in about a week, and get visibly bigger every day once they start. The small ones I left on the fallen oak have had two days.
entries.title: Bigger every day

entries.text: The small gray caps I left on the fallen oak are as wide as my hand now, and a new row of knobs has come up under them. Cut four and left the knobs for next time.
entries.title: Left the knobs again

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Roasted the four caps on a stick over the coals. They shrank to half and smelled of licorice going in, and they were better than this morning's acorns, which isn't saying much.
entries.title: Half the size

entries.query: how to dry oyster mushrooms without a dehydrator air dry string
entries.reason: The acorn sack keeps going bitter on him, and the oak keeps making more caps than he can eat.
entries.source: GroCycle: How to Dry Mushrooms 4 Different Ways
entries.text: Read that mushrooms dry if you slice them thin and hang them on a string or a stick somewhere warm and airy, and dried they keep for months. I have no string, but I have birch and a knife.
entries.title: Thin and strung

entries.text: Wrote two lists on the fourteenth page: acorns, two days in the creek; oyster caps, two days from knob to hand-wide. The mushrooms are as slow as the acorns but need no stone on them.
entries.title: The fourteenth page

entries.text: Whittled a birch twig down thin for a skewer and it split lengthwise at a knot halfway. Picked a straighter one without knots and started over.
entries.title: Split at the knot

entries.text: From the workbench I can see the smoke over the fire going thin. I let it burn down on its own this time; there is nothing else to cook until tomorrow.
entries.title: Smoke going thin

entries.text: The straight twig whittled down clean. It's as long as my arm and thin as a grass stem, and the point goes through a leaf without tearing it.
entries.title: No knots this time

entries.reason: He was going to rest by the ring and saw the smoke first.
entries.text: Sat down on the log seat and saw a curled oak leaf against the inside of the ring, black at one end and letting off a thread of smoke, though the fire is only gray ash now. The leaves have been piling up against the stones every day since I came.
entries.title: A leaf in the ring

entries.onMind: a leafy branch for a broom
entries.query: how far to clear leaves around a campfire ring
entries.source: CleverHiker: 10 Campfire Safety Tips
entries.text: Read that you should clear the ground of leaves and twigs for about ten feet around a fire, because a coal can sit in dry leaves for a long time before it shows. Ten of a person's feet is a lot of my strides.
entries.title: Ten feet of bare

entries.text: Swept the leaves out from the stones with a leafy branch, in a circle five of my strides across, and heaped them past the end of the log seat, well away from the ring. Underneath was bare soil, pebbles, and three of my old acorn shells.
entries.title: Swept bare

entries.onMind: what gets rasped in the middle of the morning
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool to drink, I heard the slow rasp, rasp across the water again, in daylight for the first time. A few strokes, a stop, a few more, then nothing.
entries.title: Rasping by day

entries.text: The pool has leaves on it now too, turning slowly in the corner where the creek comes in. I didn't sweep those.
entries.title: Leaves on the pool

entries.reason: His fourteenth-page list says acorns take two days in the creek, and he keeps running out.
entries.text: Gathered acorns under the red oak until the bindle sagged. If I start a batch every day, there will always be one that has had its two days.
entries.title: A batch a day

entries.text: I won't crack these yet. Last time the fresh meats on top turned the water brown again and set the tan ones back, and the tan ones need one more day on their own.
entries.title: Not in the net

entries.text: Tipped the bindle out on the table and turned each acorn over. Nine had a small round hole and went out the door; the other forty-one are in a heap against the cool wall, whole.
entries.title: Nine with holes

entries.text: Wrote it on the fifteenth page: a new batch into the creek every day, one always ready. Under it I wrote the trouble, which is that I only have one net.
entries.title: The fifteenth page

entries.onMind: a net of my own making
entries.query: making cordage from dead nettle stalks in fall
entries.reason: He has one net and needs two.
entries.source: Lifesong Adventures: How to collect stinging nettle stalks
entries.text: Read that nettle stalks make the best cord after they die and dry standing in the fall: you crush the stalk, split it, and peel the stringy outside off the woody core. There is a stand of tall dead stalks with hairy leaves at the edge of the brambles.
entries.title: Dead stalks, strong cord

entries.onMind: leaving the sack alone until tomorrow
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took one handful of the tan acorns and ate them cold, kneeling at the pool. They still dry my mouth. I put the stone back square; they get one more night.
entries.title: Still drying

entries.text: The stalks at the edge of the brambles have square stems and leaves in pairs, gone brown, and the hairs don't sting anymore. Snapped off an armful at the ground and tied them to the bindle.
entries.title: Square stems

entries.text: While I was snapping mine, I heard snaps from the far bank too, quicker than mine, and the tops of the tall gray stalks over there jerked one at a time. I stood still and couldn't see who was pulling them.
entries.title: Snaps across

entries.onMind: how to keep the twist from kinking
entries.text: Crushed a stalk under the big stone at the workbench and split it, and the outside peeled off the core in long ribbons. Twisted a finger-length of cord, but it kinks back on itself every time I let go.
entries.title: A finger of cord

entries.text: Got tired of the kinking and let the strand go slack in the middle. It folded in half and wound itself round into two strands twisted together, and that one doesn't come undone. Now I twist it too hard on purpose and let it fold.
entries.title: It folded itself

entries.onMind: what drops a hand and creaks
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool rubbing the fluff off my hands, I heard a long wooden creak from across the water, then a thump, like something heavy dropped a short way onto the ground. Then nothing, not even the rasp.
entries.title: A creak and thump

entries.onMind: how many stalks a net takes
entries.text: Three arm-lengths of two-strand cord now, wound around my hand, from about a third of the armful. My old net takes more than that just around its mouth, so this will be a lot of stalks.
entries.title: Three arm-lengths

entries.onMind: roast them so they go down
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took two handfuls of the tan acorns. They were supposed to get one more night, but my stomach has been loud since the cord.
entries.title: Too hungry to wait

entries.text: The ash in the ring was gray and cold on top, but when I raked it with a stick one coal underneath went orange. Fed it birch bark shreds and blew, and it caught on the second try.
entries.title: One coal left

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on the stick. They brown faster than the pale ones did, and none of them split.
entries.title: Browner, faster

entries.text: Ate them on the log seat. Roasting takes off some of the dryness, not all of it. Full enough to keep working until dusk.
entries.title: Dry but full

entries.onMind: something over there that creaks and holds now
entries.text: Snapping stalks at the brambles, I heard the long wooden creak from across the water again and waited for the thump. It didn't come. The creak came twice more, then quiet.
entries.title: No thump this time

entries.onMind: how a net is actually tied
entries.text: Crushed the new stalks under the big stone and twisted them at the workbench, overtwisting and letting it fold like before. Five arm-lengths wound on my hand now. My fingers have gone green-brown from it.
entries.title: Five arm-lengths

entries.onMind: a flat stick for a gauge
entries.query: how to knot a net by hand mesh gauge stick sheet bend netting needle
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Net Making
entries.text: Read that a net is knotted one row at a time over a flat stick, a gauge, so every hole comes out the same size, and each knot is the same small bend tied around the loop above. I had wondered why the holes in my sack were all alike.
entries.title: Same-size holes

entries.text: Whittled a birch twig flat on both sides, two fingers wide, for a gauge. The first pass left one end thicker than the other, so I shaved it until it lies flat on the stump without rocking.
entries.title: A flat stick

entries.text: The basket at the stump had nothing in it but two leaves that blew in. I tipped them out so it would be clean for whoever uses it next.
entries.title: Two blown leaves

entries.onMind: what makes a sound like that
entries.text: Lifting the stone off the sack, I heard a thin flat clatter from across the water, like a sheet of something sliding down onto more of the same, then a few small rattles after it. Not a creak and not a snap. Something new over there.
entries.title: A clatter across

entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the tan acorns into the bindle. The water off the sack still runs like weak tea; this batch really does want its last night.
entries.title: Weak tea

entries.text: The fire was down to a low orange with no flame. Fed it bark shreds and three sticks before it could go gray, so no raking for one coal tonight.
entries.title: Fed it early

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time. Still dry in the mouth, but warm, and I ate all of them on my heels by the ring.
entries.title: Dry again

entries.text: Knotted the first row over the gauge on the log seat: around the stick, through the loop above, pull. Four holes, and the first is bigger than the other three because I pulled before the stick was under it. I left it; the next rows will tell me if it matters.
entries.title: Four holes

entries.text: The second row pulled the big first hole sideways, and every hole under it leaned the same way. Untied the first knot, put the stick under it this time, and pulled; now all four sit square.
entries.title: The big hole matters

entries.text: Finished the second row over the gauge: four more holes, all the size of the stick. Two rows used about an arm-length of the five.
entries.title: Two rows

entries.text: Washing cord grit off my hands at the pool, I looked up and the small yellow light was on across the water, low down, same spot as before. It came on just as the sun went behind the trunks, like last night.
entries.title: Light comes on

entries.text: Wrote the sixteenth page by the fire: the flat clatter from this afternoon as a row of little dashes falling, and under it a dot for the light. Whoever is over there keeps the same hours as the sun.
entries.title: Sixteenth page

entries.query: how to make a net bag mesh knotting join rows into a tube
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Making a Net
entries.text: Read that a bag doesn't have to be a flat net sewn up after; you can join the ends of a row and keep knotting around and around, so it has no seam. You add holes as you go to make it wider.
entries.title: Nets go round

entries.text: Feeding sticks to the fire, I heard the long wooden creak across the water, twice, and then a third shorter one. No thump. The bark caught and crackled over it and I couldn't hear anything more.
entries.title: Creak while feeding

entries.onMind: how many rounds to a bag
entries.text: Tied the last hole of the second row to the first, and the strip closed into a ring the size of my fist. Started the third row around it and put two knots in one loop to make a fifth hole.
entries.title: A ring of four

entries.text: At one new hole a round, it will be many rounds before this holds a handful of acorns. The cord will run out before the bag does.
entries.title: Fist-sized so far

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack in the dark by feel and scooped two handfuls of the tan ones into the bindle. The water running off it is paler than this morning; one more night and they're done.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.onMind: wood being knocked into the ground
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool, I heard a slow knock, knock from across the water, hard on wood, about a breath apart, maybe twenty of them. Then it stopped and the yellow light was still there, low down.
entries.title: Knocking across

entries.text: Roasted them two at a time on the stick so I could watch both. They go brown at the edges first and the middle stays pale unless I hold them closer.
entries.title: Two at a time

entries.onMind: how many rounds to a bag
entries.text: Ate them on the log seat with the net across my knee. Less dry than at noon. The fire's still good for another hour of knotting.
entries.title: Warm acorns

entries.reason: He checks the basket before the evening's done.
entries.text: Ate the last two acorns walking up to the stump. In the basket was an old iron key as long as my hand, crusted orange-brown, and the rust came off on my fingers as powder. I asked for something rusty, and this is it.
entries.title: Rust in the basket

entries.query: make ink from rust and acorn caps tannin iron black ink
entries.source: Atlas of Making: Acorn & Iron Grey
entries.text: Read that acorn water turns gray to black when iron goes in, and it darkens at once. But the iron there is soaked in something sour for a week first, so it's already in the water, not dry rust.
entries.title: Iron goes in wet

entries.text: Crouched at the ink stone, I saw the yellow light across the water, but low by the creek and moving a little, not in its usual spot. After a while it went back east and stopped where it always is.
entries.title: Light moving low

entries.reason: He wants to see the brown turn black.
entries.text: Rubbed the key between my fingers over the hollow and stirred the powder in with the pen. It floats in orange specks on the brown and won't go in. The ink stays brown.
entries.title: Orange on brown

entries.text: Wrote the key on the seventeenth page with the rusted ink. Where a speck of rust caught on the pen the line went a hair grayer, but only there. The rust needs to be in the water, not sitting on it.
entries.title: Seventeenth page

entries.text: Fed the fire three dry sticks before it went gray. I'll knot one more round by it and bank it before I sleep.
entries.title: Fed before bed

entries.onMind: whether the ink is darker by morning
entries.reason: The page said the iron is soaked first, not sprinkled.
entries.text: Laid the key down in the ink stone hollow so the brown covers all of it. If the rust has to be in the water, it can sit in the water all night.
entries.title: Key in the ink

entries.text: Knotted the third round by the fire and got the fifth hole in. The cord ran out with the round still open, and the bag is about the size of my fist.
entries.title: Fist-sized and open

entries.onMind: who carries a light to the creek after dark
entries.text: Drinking at the pool, the yellow light came down to the water a little upstream on the far side, closer than it has been. Something set down on stone with a clink, then water splashing, then the light went back up east.
entries.title: Light at the water

entries.onMind: whether the ink is darker by morning
entries.reason: He wanted to see if the iron had done anything yet.
entries.text: Lifted the pen out of the hollow and the ink right against the key has gone a shade darker, grayish where it touches the iron. Out past a finger from the key it's the same brown as before.
entries.title: Gray at the edge

entries.onMind: who carries a light to the creek after dark
entries.text: On the eighteenth page I drew the light as a dot low by the wavy line, with a small circle for the clink. Whatever carries it comes down to drink, or to wash something, the same as I do.
entries.title: Eighteenth page

entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. Across the water the yellow light was back where it always is, not moving.
entries.title: Banked

entries.text: Read the pages over at the table. Tomorrow I need more nettle stalks to finish the third round of the net.
entries.title: Eighteen pages
