entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone
entries.text: Dreamed the key came out of the ink stone dark all over, and when I held it up it fit a little door in the bark of a giant trunk. I woke before it turned, listened to the quiet dark, and went back under the quilt.
entries.title: The key turning

entries.reason: He checks the basket first thing in case anything came in the night.
entries.text: Walked up to the stump in the gray before sunup. Nothing in the basket but one wet leaf, which I tipped out.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack. The batch has gone cream after its second night and the water off it runs clear now. Fog sat on the creek so thick I couldn't see the far bank at all.
entries.title: Two nights in

entries.text: Raked the ash and found one coal still orange at the bottom, eight hours after I banked it. Bark shreds caught on it on the second breath.
entries.title: One coal left

entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone, after breakfast
entries.text: Roasted them two at a time on the stick. No dryness in the mouth this time, just nut, and I ate until I stopped wanting to. Two nights is the number.
entries.title: Not dry anymore

entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone
entries.text: Ate the last four off the stick and stopped because I was full, not because they ran out. Two nights in the creek and a fire, and that's breakfast.
entries.title: Full for once

entries.reason: He left the key soaking all night to see if the iron would finally get into the ink.
entries.text: Lifted the key out. The whole hollow has gone a dark slate gray, almost black where the key lay, and the underside of the key is crusted black instead of orange. Overnight did what rubbing couldn't.
entries.title: Gray all through

entries.text: Wrote the key on the nineteenth page with the split pen. The line goes on gray with a little purple in it, darker than the brown ever was, but not black.
entries.title: Nineteenth page

entries.query: iron gall ink goes on pale and darkens as it dries oxidation
entries.source: Maryland State Archives: Iron Gall Ink
entries.text: Read that ink made with iron and tannin goes on pale, light brown or sepia, and only turns purplish-black as it dries in the air. So the gray line may not be done yet. I'll look at the page again tonight.
entries.title: Ink that darkens

entries.onMind: what makes a hiss in water
entries.text: Snapping nettle stalks at the edge of the brambles, I heard a sharp tink across the water, down toward the stepping stones, then a hiss like a coal dropped in the creek. The fog still sat on the far bank and I couldn't see anything in it.
entries.title: A tink downstream

entries.text: Crushed the new stalks on the log seat, split them and peeled the fiber off the cores, then overtwisted it and let it fold. Four arm-lengths by the time my fingers went green. The sun is through the trunks now and the fog is gone off the creek.
entries.title: Four more lengths

entries.reason: The net in the creek is empty now that the batch is eaten, so a fresh one can go in without setting anything back.
entries.text: Scooped the acorns off the floor by the cool wall into the bindle sack. Two had rolled under the bed.
entries.title: Off the cool wall

entries.text: Cracked them on the workbench with the stone, one knock each and a second for the stubborn ones. Six had grub holes, so I lined them up on the stump edge; thirty-five went into the sack.
entries.title: Thirty-five

entries.text: Lifted the stone, tipped the meats into the empty net and set the stone back; the water went brown around it right away. Across the water there was a long wooden creak, then another, and nothing after either one.
entries.title: Creak at the pool

entries.onMind: whether two days was ever the right count for the caps
entries.reason: The new batch needs two nights, and he was getting hungry.
entries.text: The little caps I left on the fallen oak yesterday morning are only thumb-wide, nowhere near hand-wide. Took the three biggest and left the rest another day.
entries.title: Only thumb-wide

entries.text: The morning fire had gone down to embers. Two pinches of bark shreds and a long blow, and it came up on its own.
entries.title: Up from embers

entries.text: Roasted the caps on a stick till the edges curled brown and ate them off it, two bites each. Hot and licorice-smelling, but not much of a meal.
entries.title: Three caps

entries.onMind: how many more rounds before it holds a batch
entries.reason: A second net means fresh acorns don't have to go on top of half-soaked ones.
entries.text: Knotted the third round over the gauge stick with the new cord, every mesh the width of the stick. It closes now, and the bag holds about two fists.
entries.title: Third round closed

entries.reason: The page he read said iron ink only turns dark as it dries in the air.
entries.text: Opened to the nineteenth page on the log seat. Where the pen pressed hardest, the gray line has gone purple-black; the thin tails are still gray. The page did that by itself, shut, in a few hours.
entries.title: Darker by daylight

entries.text: Dipping the pen at the ink stone, I heard a gritty scraping across the water, down toward the stepping stones, round and round with little stops. Stone on stone, maybe, but nothing in a creek scrapes like that by itself.
entries.title: Scraping by the stones

entries.text: Wrote the morning's sounds on the twentieth page: the tink, the hiss, the two creaks, the scraping, each with its own mark. It goes on gray, and now I know to wait.
entries.title: Twentieth page

entries.onMind: the fallen oak the day after tomorrow
entries.query: oyster mushroom how many days for caps to grow to full size after pinning
entries.source: Bootstrap Bee: The Oyster Mushroom Growth Stages Explained (Timeline)
entries.text: Read that oyster caps are ready to pick a few days after they first show, and they like it cool but not cold. So my two days was a guess, and a short one; the thumb-wide caps on the fallen oak get a third.
entries.title: A third day

entries.reason: The net needs a fourth round before it holds a full batch.
entries.text: Snapped an armful of nettle stalks for the fourth round. Straight across the water, the tall gray stalks on the far bank have a gap broken in them too, low and even, a lot like the one I keep making here.
entries.title: A gap like mine

entries.reason: Hungry, with the caps a day off and the batch two nights off.
entries.text: The low hips on the wild rose are long gone, so I hooked the high stems down with my staff and picked a dozen into the sack. The thorns got me twice.
entries.title: High hips

entries.text: Split the hips with a thumbnail and ate the red skins off. They're thin and sweet-sour, and the seeds inside sit in itchy hairs that I scraped out onto the ground. A dozen hips is about one acorn's worth of food.
entries.title: Mostly seeds

entries.text: Fed the fire three dry sticks before it sank. The smoke went up thick and white for a minute, then thinned out.
entries.title: Three sticks

entries.onMind: what scrapes round and round down by the stones
entries.text: Twisting cord on the log seat, I heard the gritty scraping across the water again, down by the stepping stones. Slower now, little circles, then a long stop, then more.
entries.title: Scraping again

entries.reason: One net means one batch at a time, and he is tired of waiting on it.
entries.text: Knotted the fourth round over the gauge stick on the log seat, adding a hole every sixth knot so the bag starts to widen. Today's cord is stiffer than yesterday's and bites my fingers at each bend.
entries.title: Fourth round

entries.text: Drank from the still pool with both hands. The sky in it was one flat gray today. The sack under its stone still breathes a little brown into the water.
entries.title: Gray water

entries.query: hot water leaching acorns how long red oak boiling change water
entries.source: Backyard Forager: Hot Leached Acorns
entries.text: Read that acorns boiled, the brown water poured off and boiled again in fresh water, over and over, lose their bitterness in an hour or two instead of days in a creek. I have no pot, but I simmered ink in a folded birch tray once.
entries.title: Boiled, not soaked

entries.text: A tray holds a handful at a time, and the fire would need feeding the whole while. Still, a handful today beats thirty-five the day after tomorrow.
entries.title: Hungry math

entries.onMind: whether bark can take a real boil
entries.reason: A handful boiled today beats a batch soaked the day after tomorrow.
entries.text: Peeled the widest sheet left on the fallen birch, folded it up twice as deep as the ink tray and lashed the corners with nettle cord. It holds about two fists, if it holds.
entries.title: A deeper tray

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack and scooped two handfuls of half-soaked acorns into the tray, then filled it from the pool. I bit one to check: still bitter at the back, but not the way they were.
entries.title: Half a batch

entries.onMind: what scrapes round and round down by the stones
entries.text: Fed the fire and nudged the tray onto the edge of the coals. Down by the stepping stones the scraping started again across the water, but different now, a long swing and back, like a figure drawn over and over.
entries.title: Scraping, slower

entries.onMind: carrying a hot tray to the pool
entries.text: The water in the tray went tea-brown in a few minutes, which is the bitterness coming out. But the dry rim above the water browned and curled where the flames licked it, and I pulled it back an inch. To pour off and boil again I need fresh water, which means another walk to the pool with a hot tray.
entries.title: Brown water, singed rim

entries.text: Carried the tray to the pool by its lashed corners, tipped the brown water out on the stones and swished the acorns in fresh. The bottom has gone soft and sags in my hands now, like wet leather.
entries.title: Second water

entries.reason: The tray is the only pot he has.
entries.text: The second water came up lighter, more like weak tea than strong. But the corner nearest the coals has started to weep, and every drop hisses on the embers. I moved the tray back a finger and it still weeps.
entries.title: A leaking corner

entries.text: Ate them hot off the tray with my fingers. Soft like beans, with a bitter edge at the very end that the creek ones lose after two nights. Two handfuls in about an hour, and I am less hungry than I have been all day.
entries.title: Two boils

entries.onMind: what is being ground over there
entries.text: Wrote on the twenty-first page: two handfuls, two waters, one leaking corner, maybe three waters next time. While I wrote, a gritty grinding started across the water toward the stepping stones, heavier than the scraping this morning, like stone being rubbed on stone.
entries.title: Stone on stone

entries.onMind: folding the corner in instead of lashing it
entries.query: boiling water in birch bark container over fire bark only burns above the waterline folded not cut
entries.source: Bookdome: Boiling Water In A Bark Kettle
entries.text: The slate says a bark kettle has its corners folded inward, not cut, and pinned with splinters. You set it on live coals and bank ash around the base so no flame reaches the sides; the water keeps the bark below it from burning, but anything above the waterline can still scorch.
entries.title: A bark kettle

entries.reason: The lashed corner wept onto the coals.
entries.text: Whittled two birch splinters as long as my finger. Untied the weeping corner, folded it inward flat against the wall and pushed a splinter through all three layers; did the opposite corner the same so the tray sits even.
entries.title: Pinned corners

entries.onMind: what is being ground over there
entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the half-soaked batch into the tray and filled it at the pool for a three-water try. The water coming down from the stepping stones had a fine gray cloud in it that settled on the sack's stone like dust, the kind you get from rubbing two stones together.
entries.title: Gray water

entries.onMind: whether coals alone will bring it to a boil
entries.text: Raked live coals to the edge of the ring, set the tray on them and pushed ash up around its base with a stick. Nothing weeps at the pinned corners, but on coals alone it is slow; not even steaming yet. Across the water the grinding started again, slower and lighter than before.
entries.title: Coals, not flames

entries.onMind: whether coals alone will bring it to a boil
entries.reason: The fire was burning down and the tray needs live coals under it.
entries.text: Fed three sticks into the fire on the far side of the ring, away from the tray, so the flames stay off the bark. The coals under the tray are glowing orange again.
entries.title: Flames to one side

entries.onMind: who keeps getting things in that basket
entries.reason: He checks the basket for notes when he is up.
entries.text: Three new things in the basket at the stump: a big roll of thick paper tied with twine, a yellow stick of wood with a sharp gray point, and a clear glass bowl turned upside down, as wide as my hand. I did not ask for any of them, so I set the bowl back the way it sat and left all three.
entries.title: Not mine either

entries.text: Forty minutes on coals and the tray finally steams, with a ring of small bubbles coming up off the bottom. The pinned corners are dry. Slow, but nothing burned.
entries.title: Small bubbles

entries.text: Washed the acorns in fresh pool water and poured the brown off on the stones. While I knelt there something on the far side flashed white for a blink, low down past the bank, the way the pool flashes when the sun catches it. The sun is behind me, so whatever caught it is over there.
entries.title: A flash across the water

entries.onMind: whether three waters takes the bitter edge off
entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray for the third water and pushed the ash up around it. The south breeze keeps blowing leaves into my swept ring; I picked two out of the coals.
entries.title: Third water

entries.query: hot leaching acorns how many water changes until not bitter taste test
entries.source: Backyard Forager: Hot Leached Acorns
entries.text: The slate says to boil, pour off the brown and boil again, and to start tasting after the third or fourth water; some acorns take as many as fifteen. It also says not to wait for the water to run clear, because it may never. Mine are the bitter kind.
entries.title: Fifteen waters

entries.reason: The slate said to start tasting after the third water.
entries.text: Fished one acorn out of the tray and ate it. The first of it is mild, almost sweet, and then the bitter comes up at the back of my tongue like after the second water, only smaller. Not done.
entries.title: Third water, tasted

entries.text: Poured the third water off on the stones at the pool, still brown as tea, and filled the tray for a fourth. It is nearly too dark now to tell the color of the water.
entries.title: Almost too dark

entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray and pushed the ash up around it. Four waters so far. If it takes fifteen I will be doing this until the owls start.
entries.title: Fourth water

entries.onMind: a second net for the creek
entries.text: Knotted the fifth round of the new net over the gauge stick while the tray heated. The meshes come out even as long as I don't pull the last knot of a row too hard. Two more rounds and it will hold a batch.
entries.title: Fifth round

entries.reason: The fourth water needs live coals under it.
entries.text: The coals under the tray had gone dull, so I fed in three split branches and pushed the ash back around the bark. Sparks went up past the low branches, and the tray is steaming again.
entries.title: More wood

entries.onMind: a fifth water, maybe in the morning
entries.text: Ate a handful out of the tray with my fingers. The bitter at the back is smaller again, about the size of a breadcrumb now, and I ate them anyway because I was hungry. Five waters might finish it.
entries.title: Fourth water, tasted

entries.text: Wrote four short lines on the twenty-first page in acorn ink, one for each water, and how bitter each one tasted. The lines get shorter going down the page.
entries.title: Counting waters

entries.text: Poured the fourth water off on the stones at the pool; it came out like weak tea instead of strong. Across the water the small yellow light is on in its low spot, steady, not moving.
entries.title: Fourth water off

entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray and pushed the ash up around the sides. The fire has plenty left in it from the last feeding.
entries.title: Fifth water

entries.onMind: drying a batch on the ring stones
entries.query: how to dry and store leached acorns so they keep
entries.reason: Five waters is a lot of work to throw away if a batch goes bad.
entries.source: Eat Weeds: How to Store and Process Acorns the Right Way
entries.text: The slate says leached acorns keep if you spread them one thin layer deep somewhere low and warm, turn them about every hour, and give them around half a day. They have to be completely dry before they go in anything closed. The ring stones stay warm long after the flames are gone.
entries.title: Half a day of drying

entries.onMind: what falls over there like that
entries.text: Knotting the sixth round, I heard a thin flat clatter across the water, like the sheet-sliding sound from the other afternoon, and a few small rattles after. The yellow light over there stayed where it was.
entries.title: A clatter

entries.onMind: whether the ring stones will dry a batch
entries.text: Ate a big handful from the tray. The bitter is only there if I go looking for it at the very back of my tongue, and I stopped looking. Five, then, for this oak.
entries.title: Fifth water, tasted

entries.reason: The slate said low and warm, one thin layer, turned every hour.
entries.text: Picked the boiled acorns out of the tray and laid them one deep on the outer ring stones, on the side away from the flames. Near the fire the stones are too hot to keep a finger on; at the back they are just warm.
entries.title: One layer deep

entries.text: Knotted the seventh round. The net is as deep as my forearm now and holds my fist without bulging. It needs something at the top so it can close.
entries.title: Seventh round

queries: how to put a drawstring on a knotted net bag
netting a bag finish top row drawstring through meshes
entries.query: how to put a drawstring on a knotted net bag
entries.reason: His new net is deep enough for a batch but has no way to close at the top.
entries.source: 5 out of 4 Patterns: DIY Mesh Drawstring Beach Backpack
entries.text: The page I found folds a sleeve of cloth around the top of the bag and feeds two strings through it from opposite sides, so pulling both closes it from both ways at once. My net has no cloth to fold. But its top row is already a row of holes, so a cord can go in and out of those instead.
entries.title: A cloth sleeve

entries.onMind: whether the stones stay warm enough through the night
entries.text: Turned the acorns over with my fingers. The tops have gone dull and pale; the undersides are still dark and damp where they sat on the stone. The fire is down to more glow than flame.
entries.title: Dry on top

entries.text: Wrote on the twenty-second page: five waters for this oak, then one layer on the ring stones, turned every hour. Under it I drew the net's top row with two cords going round from opposite sides.
entries.title: Twenty-second page

entries.onMind: what to put in it first
entries.text: The basket held a net sack of knotted cord with a drawstring, the same make as the one in the creek. This one I asked for. The paper roll, the yellow stick and the glass bowl are gone; whoever they were for came and got them.
entries.title: Asked for, this time

entries.text: Mine still has no top, and now it doesn't need to hurry. One for the creek, one for the fresh batch, and mine for carrying, once it closes.
entries.title: Three nets

entries.onMind: keeping air on them all night
entries.reason: The slate said nothing closed until they're dry, and a net is mostly holes.
entries.text: Slid the drying acorns off the ring stones into the new sack instead of the bark box. Across the water the yellow light was down by the creek again, low, near the stepping stones; after a while it went back east to its usual spot.
entries.title: Into the new net

entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals with a stick until no red showed. The stones the acorns sat on are still warm under my palm.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.onMind: whether they'll be dry by morning
entries.text: Tied the net sack of acorns up beside the drying herbs by the door, where the air moves. Half a day, the slate said; they've had an hour and a half.
entries.title: Hung by the herbs

entries.onMind: the two owl voices on the fourth page
entries.text: Dreamed the net by the door was full of owls instead of acorns, every one of them hooting five times. I tried to count them on one hand and kept running out of fingers.
entries.title: A net of owls

entries.text: Squeezed the net sack by the herbs. The acorns rattle against each other now instead of thudding, and the one I bit in half was pale and dry right to the middle.
entries.title: Dry all through

entries.text: Ate two handfuls at the table by the lantern. They crunch, and taste more of the fire than of the oak. Through the door the fog lies low between the trunks and I can't see as far as the ring.
entries.title: Breakfast by lantern

entries.onMind: whether the fog is shallower up here than down at the water
queries: why does fog sit low by the creek in the morning
entries.query: why does fog sit low by the creek in the morning
entries.reason: Through the door at breakfast the fog lay low between the trunks and he couldn't see the fire ring.
entries.source: ABC57: Why does fog form near river valleys?
entries.text: The slate says air cools at night, gets heavy and slides down into the lowest ground, and it's there it turns to fog. So the creek is the bottom of everything around here, and the fog collects in it like water in the pool.
entries.title: Cold air goes downhill

entries.text: Nothing in the basket but two leaves, both wet with dew. From the stump the fog looks thinner than at my door, and thicker again down the slope toward the water, the way the slate said.
entries.title: Dew in the basket

entries.onMind: two drawstring cords for the top row of his own net
entries.text: Snapped nettle stalks into the sack at the edge of the brambles. The fog here is only about as deep as the brambles are tall; across the water the tops of the big trunks stand up out of it with no bottoms to them, and nothing else over there shows at all.
entries.title: Trunks with no bottoms

entries.text: Cracked the nettle stalks on the stump and peeled the long threads off them, then rolled them on my knee into a cord as long as my arm twice. It's greener and scratchier than my last one.
entries.title: Cord off the stalks

entries.text: Threaded it through the top row of my net. It goes round once with a hand's length left to knot, and nothing at all left to pull on. I need the second cord after all, and longer.
entries.title: One cord short

entries.onMind: what the far bank looks like with no fog on it
entries.text: Washed the green off my hands at the pool. The fog is lifting off the water in slow rags; the near stepping stones show now, but the far bank is still just gray.
entries.title: Fog coming apart

entries.onMind: how long the dry batch lasts
entries.text: Ate another handful of the dry acorns at my table. The net by the herbs is lighter by about a third now; I should think about what the rest of the week eats.
entries.title: Second breakfast

entries.onMind: whether the rags were where the ground warmed first
queries: why does morning fog lift off water in pieces
entries.query: why does morning fog lift off water in pieces
entries.reason: He watched the fog come apart over the pool in slow rags and wanted to know where it goes.
entries.source: FOX Weather: Does fog really 'burn off'? Dispelling the myth of combustible clouds
entries.text: The slate says the sun doesn't burn fog at all. It warms the ground, the ground warms the air just over it, and the little drops dry up into that air; a breeze stirs in drier air from above too. It never said why it goes in rags, though.
entries.title: Fog doesn't burn

entries.onMind: threading the second cord from the other side
entries.text: Rolled the rest of the nettle on my knee and kept going until the cord reached from my shoulder to my fingertips three times. My knee is green and itchy. This one will go round the top with plenty left to pull.
entries.title: Three arms long

entries.onMind: what the far bank looks like with no fog on it
entries.text: From the table I can see through the door all the way down the slope now, trunk after trunk with their feet showing. The fog has gone back wherever it goes.
entries.title: Clear through the door

entries.onMind: who counts out loud in the forest
entries.text: Pulling the cord through, I heard a voice somewhere down the slope toward the fire ring, low and steady, counting: thirty-nine, forty, forty-one. Then nothing. I leaned to see out the door and there were only trunks.
entries.title: Counting down the slope

entries.text: Threaded the long cord round the top row and knotted the ends together. Pulled, and the whole net gathered up to the size of my fist. My own net is a sack now.
entries.title: It pulls shut

queries: how many acorns can you eat in a day
entries.query: how many acorns can you eat in a day
entries.reason: The net by the herbs is a third lighter already and he wants to know how long the rest lasts.
entries.source: Science Insights: How Many Acorns Do Squirrels Typically Eat in a Day?
entries.text: A squirrel eats ten to twenty acorns a day, about a tenth of its own weight, and twice that before winter. I am a good deal bigger than a squirrel, so I should count on more than twenty.
entries.title: Ten to twenty a day

entries.text: Laid the dry acorns out on the shelf in handfuls of ten. Eleven handfuls. If I eat thirty or forty a day, that is three days, maybe four, and the first batch took two days to soak. I should have started the next one yesterday.
entries.title: Three days of acorns

entries.onMind: sinking the new sack in the creek
entries.text: Gathered acorns under the red oak into the net sack that came in the basket. The wind is out of the west today and smells of salt, and leaves keep coming down through it. Half full already.
entries.title: The new sack fills

entries.reason: The first batch only lasts three or four days, and the creek takes two nights.
entries.text: Cracked the acorns on the stump one at a time under the stone. Forty-six, and seven with grub holes, which I set on the edge of the stump for whoever eats grubs. Thirty-nine good ones in a pale heap.
entries.title: Forty-six cracked

entries.onMind: Who walked past my bench, and why west?
entries.text: Sweeping the shells off the stump, I saw the leaves on the west side of my bench pressed down and scuffed in a line, each scuff longer than my whole foot. The line goes off west toward the lookout. I didn't make it.
entries.title: Scuffed leaves

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the old sack at the pool, tipped the thirty-nine meats in from the new net and set the stone back. The water coming off it went brown again straight away. The breeze kept wrinkling the pool so it showed nothing but wrinkles.
entries.title: Back under the stone

entries.text: Ate a handful from the shelf. Nine handfuls left and a batch in the creek that is ready the day after tomorrow, so it comes out about even if I eat slowly. I kept looking at my own feet and thinking about the scuffs.
entries.title: Two days, then more

entries.onMind: how long the scuffs really are
entries.text: Drew the scuffs on the twenty-third page with the birch pen: a row of long smudges from the bench going west, and my own foot small beside one for size. The ink went on pale; it will darken.
entries.title: The line on paper

entries.onMind: whether a long foot means a tall someone
entries.text: Set my foot in one of the scuffs. It takes two of my feet to fill it, and the next one is farther off than two of my strides. The leaves are smeared, not printed; no toes, no edges, nothing I could draw round.
entries.title: Two of my feet

entries.onMind: where the line goes past the boulder
queries: how tall is someone from the size of their footprint
entries.query: how tall is someone from the size of their footprint
entries.reason: The scuffs by his bench take two of his feet to fill, and he wanted to know what that says about whoever made them.
entries.source: Giles and Vallandigham 1991: Height Estimation from Foot and Shoeprint Length
entries.text: The slate says a foot is about a seventh of how tall someone is, but a print made with something on the feet comes out longer than the foot inside it. These are smears in leaves, not prints, so I can't tell a big foot from a big shoe from a slide. Whoever it is might be tall, or might not.
entries.title: A foot and a seventh

entries.onMind: Whoever went out to the edge has to come back this way.
entries.text: The scuffs go round the foot of the mossy boulder and straight on west, toward the edge where I watch the sun go down. The wind has turned and comes from the north now, with no salt in it. I didn't follow.
entries.title: Past the boulder

entries.text: Ate a handful of the dry acorns at my table. Eight handfuls left on the shelf. My legs feel the walk to the boulder and back more than they should.
entries.title: Eight handfuls now

entries.text: The counting came again, from up the slope by my bench this time: seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, eighty-two, eighty-three. Then it stopped. The same low, steady voice as this morning.
entries.title: Counting again

entries.text: Wrote both counts on the twenty-fourth page: forty-one this morning down by the ring, eighty-three now up by my bench. Whoever it is counts their steps, the way I count breaths for a leaf on the creek.
entries.title: Two counts

entries.text: A second line of scuffs lies over the first by my bench, fresher, with the damp undersides of the leaves turned up. One line went out west and one came back, and they cross right beside the stump. From the scuffs alone I can't tell which is which.
entries.title: A line coming back

queries: how to tell which way someone walked through dry leaves
entries.query: how to tell which way someone walked through dry leaves
entries.reason: He wants to know which way the walker went last.
entries.source: To Know the Land: Determining Direction of Travel on a Fisher Trail
entries.text: The slate says whatever a foot kicks up lands mostly at the front of the track, where the foot lifts out, so the heap points the way someone went. A hard push-off can throw some backward too, so it says to check more than one sign.
entries.title: Leaves pile up in front

entries.onMind: the scuffs heading east toward the creek
entries.text: Looked down at the fresh scuffs again. The loose leaves are heaped at the east end of every one. Whoever went out to the edge has come back past my bench and gone on toward the fire ring and the water.
entries.title: Went toward the water

entries.text: Where I swept the ground bare around the ring, one whole print is pressed into the dirt, longer than two of my feet. It has straight lines across the front and a square heel set apart from the rest, as if the foot stood on a little block. Something was on that foot.
entries.title: A print in the bare

entries.onMind: the scuffs running to the stepping stones
entries.text: Past the edge of the bare circle the scuffs start again in the leaves and run east, toward the stepping stones. I stayed at the ring.
entries.title: On toward the stones

queries: footprint in dirt with lines across the bottom and a separate square heel what made it
entries.query: footprint in dirt with lines across the bottom and a separate square heel what made it
entries.reason: He wanted to know what kind of foot leaves straight lines and a square heel.
entries.source: Off Grid Web: Footprint Analysis 101: Getting a Foot Message
entries.text: The slate says the heel is usually the deepest, clearest part of a print because it comes down first and hardest. The lines are the pattern of whatever is worn on the foot, and each one collects its own nicks and cuts over time, so a print can tell one walker from another.
entries.title: The heel tells most

entries.onMind: the bite in the third line
entries.text: Looked again. The heel is pressed in deepest, like the slate said, and the third line from the front has a small bite out of it. If I ever see that bite again, I will know it is the same foot.
entries.title: A bite out of a line

entries.onMind: whoever wears a foot like that
entries.text: Drew the print on the twenty-fifth page with the lines, the square heel and the bite, and my own foot beside it twice over for size. The leaves are already blowing back onto the bare circle in this little breeze.
entries.title: Twenty-fifth page

entries.text: Followed the scuffs down to the first stepping stone. In the soft mud beside it is the same print, the same small bite out of the third line, and its toes point straight at the water.
entries.title: The same bite

entries.text: From the first stone the far bank was plain in the sun: the gray-blue shape hung between two poles, and under it someone bent over a table of planks, with hair standing up in points. Two round things on its face caught the sun once. Then a small tap, like something set down, and only the creek.
entries.title: Under the gray shape

entries.reason: The stones were right there, but nothing in his own day needed the other side.
entries.text: I didn't cross. Whoever it is was busy with their hands, the way I am at my bench, and I wouldn't want someone walking up the slope at me in the middle of a knot.
entries.title: Not my side

entries.text: Ate a handful of the dry acorns at my table. Seven handfuls left on the shelf. My legs stopped buzzing about halfway through.
entries.title: Seven handfuls

queries: what are the round glass things some people wear over their eyes
entries.query: what are the round glass things some people wear over their eyes
entries.reason: The figure across the water had two round things on its face that caught the sun.
entries.source: Simple English Wikipedia: Glasses
entries.text: The slate says round glass worn in front of the eyes is called glasses, and people wear them to see better, to keep bright sun out, or to keep flying bits out of their eyes. The sturdy kind for flying bits are called goggles. Over there they tink and rasp and grind all day; bits must fly.
entries.title: Glass in front of eyes

entries.text: Drew it on the twenty-sixth page: the gray shape on two poles, the plank table, a bent back, hair in points, and two small circles where the eyes go. I wrote goggles beside the circles with a question mark.
entries.title: Twenty-sixth page

entries.text: The small gray oyster mushrooms I left on the fallen oak are as wide as my palm now. Cut four into the sack and left the smallest ones again.
entries.title: Wide as my palm

entries.text: Lit the fire in the ring, the first one today. The ground is dry and the smoke leaned off north in the light breeze.
entries.title: First fire today

entries.text: Ate the mushrooms hot off a stick on the log seat, a little chewy and nothing like acorns. The seven handfuls stay on the shelf tonight.
entries.title: Not acorns

entries.text: From the log seat the trunks hide the stepping stones. If the one in goggles looks this way, all they will see is my smoke.
entries.title: Only smoke

queries: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow on a log
entries.query: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow on a log
entries.reason: The small ones he left on the fallen oak were as wide as his palm by evening.
entries.source: Field & Forest Products: Oysters Mushrooms on Logs
entries.text: The slate says oyster mushrooms come up suddenly and grow quickly once they start, mostly in fall and most of all after a heavy rain, so you should check the log often. Pick them while the edges of the caps are still curled down. It never said how many days.
entries.title: They come up fast

entries.onMind: the small mushrooms on the fallen oak
entries.text: Wrote the fallen oak on the twenty-seventh page: four cut tonight, the small ones left, and 'pick while the edges curl under'. The ones I ate tonight had flat edges. I'll look at the oak every morning now.
entries.title: Twenty-seventh page

entries.text: One knock of metal on wood from up the slope toward the stump, loud in the quiet, and then nothing. No counting this time. I kept the pen on the page and didn't go up.
entries.title: A knock up the slope

entries.text: Fed four sticks onto the fire. It caught up high and the sparks went straight up; the breeze has gone soft and comes from the south now.
entries.title: Sticks on

entries.text: The light between the trunks to the west went orange and then gray. Past my bench the sun is going into the water at the edge, and tonight I stayed with the fire instead. In the morning I'll look in the basket first.
entries.title: Going into the water

entries.onMind: a pen that doesn't go blunt
entries.text: Started a new birch pen on the log seat while the fire is high. Shaved the end to a slant, slow, so the split runs straight.
entries.title: A spare pen

entries.onMind: who walks round a fire instead of up to it
entries.text: Steps in the dry leaves off past the scarred trunk, quick, going east toward the creek, and one small clink. Past the firelight it was too dark to see anything. They went the long way round my fire, the same as the knock did.
entries.title: Steps to the north

entries.text: Wrote the steps on the twenty-eighth page: north of the fire, going east, one clink, just as the light went. Drew an arrow for which way, and a little fire with a wide curve around it.
entries.title: Twenty-eighth page

queries: how far away can you see a campfire at night in the woods
entries.query: how far away can you see a campfire at night in the woods
entries.reason: Someone keeps going round his fire in the dark, and he wanted to know how far off it can be seen.
entries.source: Preparedness Advice: How Far Away Can You See a Candle at Night?
entries.text: The slate says on a dark night even a candle can be seen miles off over open ground, and that the lay of the land is what hides a light. It said nothing about trees, but here the trunks are my land.
entries.title: How far a fire shows

entries.text: Whoever it is already knows where my fire is; they walk round it. I won't feed it again tonight and let it go down to coals on its own.
entries.title: No more sticks

entries.text: The wind swung round to come from the north and started flicking sparks past the swept circle into the dry leaves. I scraped ash over the coals with a stick and pushed the ring stones in until nothing showed orange.
entries.title: Banked it after all

entries.text: Ate a handful of soaked acorns at my table with the door shut against the wind. Six handfuls left on the shelf.
entries.title: Supper at the table

queries: why does the wind turn around and come from the north in the evening and get colder
entries.query: why does the wind turn around and come from the north in the evening and get colder
entries.reason: All day the breeze came soft from the south, and at dark it swung round from the north and felt drier.
entries.source: theweatherprediction.com: Wind Direction and Weather Forecasting
entries.text: The slate says a south wind usually brings warmer air and a north wind cooler, drier air, and a sudden swing from one to the other can mean a whole new air is coming through. So the warm days may be over for a while.
entries.title: Wind from the north

entries.onMind: dry sticks for the morning fire
entries.text: If colder air is coming in on this wind, the morning fire will be slow to catch. Before bed I'll carry an armful of dry sticks inside the door so they don't take the dew.
entries.title: Dry sticks by the door

entries.onMind: a fire that catches on the first try
entries.text: Pulled dry sticks out from under the leaf heap past the log seat. The top leaves were damp, but the sticks under them snapped clean. Carried an armful home and stood it inside the door.
entries.title: Sticks from the heap

entries.text: With my arms full, a thin flat clatter came across the water, like the sheets sliding again. The yellow light sat steady in its low spot, and the north wind took the rest of the sound away south.
entries.title: A clatter across

entries.onMind: the knobs on the fallen oak
queries: do oyster mushrooms keep growing when it gets cold
entries.query: do oyster mushrooms keep growing when it gets cold
entries.reason: The slate said colder air is coming on the north wind, and the small caps on the fallen oak are what he eats when the acorns run short.
entries.source: Permies: Can oyster mushrooms be grown in cold temperatures?
entries.text: People there grow oysters at about fifty degrees, some kinds a little colder, but say they stop outdoors in real winter. Nobody said how much slower they get. If this cold is only a little cold, the knobs on the oak should still come on.
entries.title: Mushrooms in the cold

entries.text: Whittled the spare pen's tip at my table and cut the slit back to a grain of rice. No ink in here; it stays in the stone by the fire. In the morning it goes on the middle shelf with the other two.
entries.title: The spare pen

entries.onMind: the knobs on the fallen oak
entries.text: The wind leans on the door and finds the gap at the bottom. First thing tomorrow I look at the oak, then the basket.
entries.title: Wind under the door

entries.reason: With no wind to throw sparks, he wanted the ink warm to try the new pen.
entries.text: Opened the door and the north wind had dropped to almost nothing; the leaves on the slope lay still. Took half the sticks from inside the door down to the ring and lit a small fire on the first breath.
entries.title: Wind gone quiet

entries.text: Small quick taps came across the water, metal on metal, a long row of them, then they stopped. The yellow light sat in its low spot the whole time.
entries.title: Tapping across

entries.text: Dipped the spare pen for the first time. It holds ink for most of a line and the slit didn't spread. Wrote the north wind and how it went quiet on the twenty-ninth page.
entries.title: Third pen

entries.onMind: the wind coming back down at sunup
queries: why does the wind die down at night
entries.query: why does the wind die down at night
entries.reason: The north wind he expected to blow cold all night went quiet within an hour.
entries.source: The Weather Guys: Why does the wind diminish after sunset?
entries.text: The slate says after sundown the ground cools faster than the air over it, so the low air goes cold and heavy and stops mixing with the faster wind higher up. The wind is still blowing up there; it just can't reach the leaves until the sun warms the ground again.
entries.title: Where the wind went

entries.text: Ate the handful of soaked acorns I carried down in the bindle, on the log seat. Five handfuls left on the shelf.
entries.title: Five handfuls

entries.onMind: the oak first thing, then the basket
entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. If the wind comes back down when the sun warms the ground, the way the slate says, it will find nothing here to throw.
entries.title: Banked tight

entries.query: how to keep homemade acorn ink from drying out overnight
entries.reason: The ink in the stone by the fire grew a skin and went thick as mud once before, and tonight it sits open again.
entries.source: The Graphics Fairy: How to Make Acorn Ink
entries.text: The page says to keep ink in a jar with a tight lid, somewhere cool, and that ink left in an open dish overnight loses its water and goes darker and thicker. Mine lives in a hollow in a stone with no lid at all.
entries.title: Ink in the open

entries.text: I don't have a jar, but I have plenty of birch. In the morning I cut a square of bark to lay over the hollow and put a pebble on it.
entries.title: A lid for the stone

entries.text: Sorted the soaked acorns on the shelf into two handfuls for breakfast and three for later. Fresh ones go in the creek tomorrow so something is soaking behind these.
entries.title: Breakfast set aside

entries.text: Dreamed I put a bark lid on the ink stone and it kept lifting by itself. Underneath, the ink was tapping in quick little rows, like the metal taps from across the water.
entries.title: The lid that lifted

entries.onMind: a bark lid for the ink stone
entries.text: Ate the two handfuls I set aside last night, at my table, while the round window went from black to gray. Three handfuls left on the shelf, and fresh ones need to go in the creek today.
entries.title: Two handfuls

entries.onMind: a bark lid for the ink stone
entries.text: Walked up to the stump as the sky went pale. Nothing in the basket but three dry leaves, which I tipped out.
entries.title: Leaves only

entries.onMind: whether the ink went thick in the night
entries.reason: The slate said ink left open overnight dries down thick.
entries.text: Cut a square off the fallen birch limb, a hand across, a little wider than the hollow in the ink stone. Trimmed the corners round so they won't catch on anything.
entries.title: A square of birch

entries.text: The ink had gone thick at the edges overnight with a skin across the middle, the way the slate said it would. Laid the bark square over the hollow and put a pebble on top. Unlike the one in my dream, it stays down.
entries.title: Lid on the stone

entries.text: Gathered forty-four acorns under the red oak into the second net sack. A few have a neat round hole in the shell, no bigger than a pinhead, and all the holes are the same size.
entries.title: Forty-four under the oak

entries.text: In the mud by the landing stone there is a fresh print on top of the old ones, long, with the same bite out of the third line, toes pointed back at the water. Whoever carries the light came over to my side last night and went home again.

entries.reason: The plan in the notebook: boil the new sack, keep the first for gruel.

entries.title: Cold water, new meats

entries.reason: Last night the cord corner burned and dumped the water.
entries.text: Set the tray in the ash on the coals and pushed ash up its sides. It steamed and then bubbled, and the pinned corner stayed shut; the pin ends above the water went black but didn't burn through. The water is already going brown.

small animals under creek rocks that come out at night with a light
turning over creek stones at night with a lantern what are they catching

entries.reason: Three nights of a low light, a clank and dripping at the crossing, and he wanted to know what anyone would be doing there.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Sometimes Catching Live Bait Is More Fun Than Catching Fish
entries.text: The slate says people go out at night with lights for frogs, and that the rocks and rotting leaves around fast riffles hide little clawed creatures called crayfish, one or two under every pile. One man kept his alive in a trickle of water to use later. Clanks and dripping at the crossing, and a light low by the water: maybe somebody over there is turning stones.
entries.title: Lights for frogs

entries.reason: The new meats had boiled in the tray since dawn.
entries.text: Tipped the brown water off the tray at the edge of the ring and bit one. One boil took out nearly all the bitter, only a dry pinch at the very end, more than a whole day of cold soaking ever did. Fed the fire two split sticks so it's ready for a second water.
entries.title: Bitter mostly gone

entries.reason: He was too hungry to wait for a second boil.
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the first sack and scooped a handful into my palm. Six days of creek have made them soft, and the water off the sack runs nearly clear now instead of brown.
entries.title: Six days in the pool

entries.onMind: a second water for the tray
entries.reason: He had eaten nothing since last night.
entries.text: Ate the handful one at a time on the log seat with the sun coming in low through the trunks behind me. Almost sweet. Then four of the boiled ones, pinch and all.
entries.title: Breakfast at last

entries.reason: He checks the basket every morning.
entries.text: Morning check at the stump: four dry leaves and an acorn cap, tipped out. Nothing for anybody.
entries.title: Basket check

entries.query: how to find crayfish under rocks in a creek and can you eat them
entries.reason: Yesterday the slate said crayfish hide in creek rocks, and he wanted to know how anyone actually finds one.
entries.source: Farm and Dairy: How to find and catch crayfish
entries.text: Crayfish come out most at night, so dusk is the time to look. You lift a stone slowly, tipped into the current so the mud washes away from you, and take them from behind, just back of the claws; a hungry reader said he ate the tail and claw meat. The stones around my pool are exactly that kind of place, so at dusk I'm going to lift one.
entries.title: From behind the claws

entries.reason: One boil took most of the bitter out, and he wants the rest gone.
entries.text: Carried the tray down to the pool and scooped fresh water over the once-boiled meats, up to just under the fold. The water off the first boil was brown as bark; this one starts clear.
entries.title: Second water

entries.reason: The second water needs a real boil.
entries.text: Set the tray back in the ash and fed three split sticks under it. The smoke went up thick for a while before the flames got going.
entries.title: Up again

queries: how many times do you have to boil acorns to get the bitter out

entries.reason: One boil did more than a day of cold soaking, and he wanted to know how many more it would take.
entries.source: Backyard Forager: Hot Leached Acorns: It's Easier Than You Think
entries.text: Some acorns take as many as fifteen changes of water, and you start tasting after the third or fourth. You stop when there's no trace of bitter left, not when the water runs clear, because it may never run clear. It also says stopping partway is fine, so pool water between boils won't spoil anything.
entries.title: Fifteen waters

entries.reason: He was still hungry, and wanted to taste the difference a second boil made.
entries.text: Ate a dozen meats from the tray on the log seat. Softer than this morning, and the bitter is down to a faint dryness at the back of my tongue. By the slate's count I'm only at two, so the rest go in a third water before dusk.
entries.title: Two waters

entries.reason: The slate said to keep changing the water until the bitter is gone.
entries.text: Tipped the second water off at the edge of the ring and carried the tray down to the pool. Scooped fresh water over the meats again; they come up paler every time.
entries.title: Third water

entries.text: Set the tray back in the ash and fed two split sticks under it. If the third water takes the dryness, the rest are breakfast for days; if not, a fourth.
entries.title: Third boil

queries: what to do with acorns after you boil the bitter out
entries.query: what to do with acorns after you boil the bitter out
entries.reason: The third water was boiling and he wanted to know what comes after.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Here's How to Forage and Eat Acorns, the 'Bread of the Woods'
entries.text: Once the bitter is out you can dry them in the sun and grind them for flour, but wet ones just mash into paste. Or you roast the pieces until they color, like nuts, and roasted dark and steeped they even make a drink. I have coals already and no grinding stone, so roasting first.
entries.title: After the bitter

entries.text: Tipped the third water off, pale as weak tea, and ate ten from the tray on the log seat. The dryness is gone from all but the biggest ones, which still pinch a little at the back.
entries.title: Third water

entries.onMind: drying the rest in the sun, and the pool stone at dusk
entries.text: Pushed three meats onto a peeled twig and held them over the coals until they went brown and crackly. One split and dropped into the fire. The other two taste toasted, better than boiled.
entries.title: Three on a stick

entries.text: Tipped the rest of the leached meats out of the tray onto the flat stone south of the ring, where the sun lands at midday, one layer, none touching. The slate says wet ones mash to paste, so these have to dry first.
entries.title: Sun on the stone

queries: how long do boiled acorns take to dry in the sun before grinding
entries.query: how long do boiled acorns take to dry in the sun before grinding
entries.reason: He had just spread the meats out to dry and wanted to know how long that takes.
entries.source: Almanac: Can You Eat Acorns? How to Prepare, Leach, and Cook Them
entries.text: The slate doesn't say how long in the sun. It says spread them thin, turn them now and then, and keep going until they are brittle all the way through with no soft spots. Mine are soft as cheese, so it will be days, not an afternoon.
entries.title: Until brittle

queries: how to grind acorns with just rocks no grinder
entries.query: how to grind acorns with just rocks no grinder
entries.reason: He has no grinding stone and wanted to know what people use instead.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Here's How to Forage and Eat Acorns, the 'Bread of the Woods'
entries.text: Dry them until they grind to flour instead of paste, then grind them between two rocks. That's all it says about the rocks. I have plenty of rocks; I need the right two.
entries.title: Between two rocks

entries.onMind: lifting a pool stone at dusk
entries.text: Turned over creek stones in the shallows by the pool until one sat round and heavy in my palm, flat on one side. The drying stone can be the bottom one once the meats snap instead of bend.
entries.title: One that fits

entries.onMind: whether the round stone can grind roasted ones

entries.query: how dark to roast acorns to make a drink
entries.reason: He has coals now, the meats won't be dry enough to grind for days, and the slate said roasted dark and steeped they make a drink.
entries.source: Practical Self Reliance: Acorn Coffee
entries.text: Roast them until they are chocolate brown and snap clean when you break one, never wet in the middle, then grind them coarse like the grounds of a drink called coffee. Three or four big spoonfuls to a cup of hot water. I have coals right now, so a stickful goes over them.
entries.title: Chocolate brown

entries.text: Pushed eight meats from the drying stone onto a peeled twig and turned them over the coals until they went dark. Two went black at the ends and smell burned. The other six are chocolate brown and snap clean.
entries.title: Six that snap

entries.text: Cracked the six good ones under the round creek stone on the stump workbench. They break into coarse brown crumbs that smell like toast, nothing like the paste the slate warned about. The round stone works, on dry ones.
entries.title: Crumbs, not paste

entries.onMind: the crumb drink, then a pool stone at dusk
entries.text: The fire had sunk to red coals while I was at the bench. Laid three split sticks on and blew, and it caught. Water in the tray next, and a cup of crumbs to see what kind of drink this is.
entries.title: Coals again

entries.reason: He needs hot water before the crumbs go in.
entries.text: Carried the empty tray down to the pool and scooped it full of cold water, then walked it back up slow so none slopped over the pinned corner.
entries.title: Tray full

entries.text: Set the tray in the ash on the fresh coals and pushed ash up its sides. Steam came off the edges before I had counted to a hundred.
entries.title: Steam at the edges

entries.source: Practical Self Reliance: Acorn Coffee
entries.text: The slate says brew acorn grounds whatever way you brew coffee, three or four big spoonfuls to a cup, and a little strainer helps. It says it tastes lighter than real coffee and less sour. It never says how long, and I have no strainer, so I'll let the crumbs sink and drink off the top.
entries.title: Like coffee

entries.text: Six acorns make about two spoonfuls of crumbs, and the slate wants three or four for a single cup. Tipped them all into the low corner of the tray anyway and watched the water go the color of weak bark.
entries.title: Two spoonfuls

entries.onMind: Roasting a whole stickful once the meats on the drying stone snap.
entries.text: Sipped off the low corner on the log seat. It tastes of toast and smoke and a little of acorn, thin as creek water, and the crumbs that didn't sink got in my teeth. Six acorns was never going to be enough; the drying stone needs more days.
entries.title: Weak and gritty

entries.reason: The slate said to turn them now and then until they are brittle all through.
entries.text: Turned every meat on the drying stone over with my fingers. The tops have gone leathery and pale in the sun, but the undersides are still damp and none of them snap yet.
entries.title: Leather on top

entries.onMind: a whole stickful of crumbs, a splash of cold water, and patience

entries.reason: The crumbs that didn't sink got in his teeth.

entries.text: The slate says steep the grounds about four minutes, then splash a little cold water on top so they drop to the bottom. The people who wrote it tried that and still got what they called a crunchy sip, so they say wait several minutes, or pour it through a clean sock. I have no sock, but I have a whole pool of cold water and plenty of waiting.
entries.title: A crunchy sip

entries.text: Wrote the drink on the thirty-third page: six acorns, two spoonfuls, toast and smoke, gritty. Under it: a whole stickful next time, four minutes, a splash of cold pool water, then wait.
entries.title: Thirty-third page

entries.onMind: lifting a pool stone at dusk to look for the clawed creatures
entries.text: Laid two split sticks across the coals and they caught on their own. If enough of the drying stone's meats snap after a roast, there's a stickful to try before the light goes.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.reason: He wanted a whole stickful for a proper drink, not six.
entries.text: Bent every meat on the drying stone. The ones at the sunny south edge snap clean in two; the rest still bend like leather. Eleven snapped, a stickful if I push them on close.
entries.title: Eleven snap

entries.text: Pushed the eleven onto a green stick and turned them over the coals until they went brown and smelled like toast. One dropped into the fire and I let it go.
entries.title: A stickful

entries.onMind: a stickful for the morning drink
entries.text: Ate five on the log seat while they were still warm, crunchy all through and no bitter at all. The other five go in my bindle for tomorrow's drink.
entries.title: Half for now

entries.reason: The slate said dusk is when they come out.
entries.text: Lifted the pool stones slowly, tipping each one toward the current the way the slate said. Under the third, something small and brown with two claws shot backward and was gone under the next stone before I saw more.
entries.title: Under the third stone

entries.text: So they live on my side of the water too. If whoever has the light turns stones at night, I think I know what they are after.
entries.title: My side too

entries.query: what do crayfish eat in a creek
entries.reason: He wanted to know what the clawed thing under his pool stone lives on.
entries.source: Maine Rivers: Eastern Crayfish
entries.text: The slate says crayfish shred little water plants and eat snails, bugs and small fish, but mostly ones that are already dead, so they tidy more than they hunt. When something bothers them they flick their tails and shoot backward, which is exactly what mine did.
entries.title: Tidies the dead

entries.text: Wrote the crayfish on the thirty-fourth page by firelight: third stone, two claws, went backward. Under it: eats water weeds, tidies up the dead.
entries.title: Thirty-fourth page

entries.text: Laid one split stick across the coals, enough light to whittle by and no more. The air is mild and hardly moving.
entries.title: One stick

entries.onMind: the crumb by the third stone

entries.title: Just to watch

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the first sack in the dark and scooped two handfuls into my palm by feel. The water is cold, but not as cold as it was this morning.
entries.title: Supper from the pool

entries.onMind: why the light is so small tonight
entries.text: Across the water there is only one light tonight, smaller than other nights. Something over there creaked twice, like a branch taking weight, and then stopped.
entries.title: One small light

entries.text: Ate them one at a time on the log seat. Six days of creek and there is no bitter left at all, just cold and soft.
entries.title: Sweet and cold

entries.text: Over the fire ring, in the gap between the trunks, there is a bright point in the southeast that doesn't flicker like the stars around it. A thin bent moon hangs low the other way.
entries.title: A steady one

entries.reason: He wanted the fire a little longer before sleep.

entries.text: The slate says no: to the eye alone the steady one is only a golden dot, and even the glasses you hold up to both eyes won't show the rings. entries.title: Only a golden dot

entries.text: Wrote under the dot on the thirty-fifth page: has rings, too small for eyes, wants a glass twenty-five times. Crossed out "wants" and wrote "would need". I don't want one yet.

entries.text: Sat with my head tipped back at the steady one. Somewhere around that dot there is a ring, tipped a little, and I will take the slate's word for it. The low owl did its five from upstream and nothing answered.
entries.title: Taking its word

entries.text: Knelt at the pool for a last cold drink. Over by the stepping stones on the far side, water sloshed twice, like something heavy moving in the shallows, and then it stopped. I looked a long time and saw only dark.
entries.title: Sloshed twice

entries.text: Scraped the ash over the coals with a stick and pushed the ring stones in. Coals for the morning drink, if the dew stays off.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.onMind: the drying stone in the morning
entries.text: Turned every meat over on the low shelf. The ones that dried in the sun are going leathery again; the rest still bend. They go back to the stone when the sun is on it.

entries.text: Crayfish don't slosh. Whatever was over there in the shallows was bigger than a crayfish, and it was in the water after dark, same as the stone-turner.
entries.title: Not crayfish

entries.reason: He wanted to know what is heavy enough to slosh in the far shallows after dark.

entries.text: The first thing I asked only brought back crayfish and nothing bigger. The second found it: crayfish come out at night, and more than two hundred kinds of animals eat them, raccoons, otters, mink and herons most of all.

entries.text: In the mud by the landing stone there are no small clawed prints at all, only the long print with the bite out of the third line, twice since yesterday's: one pointed at the forest, a fresher one pointed at the water. Whoever it is crossed over to my side again and went back.
entries.title: Only the bitten ones

entries.text: Across the water the gray shape hangs still on its poles and nobody is at the plank table. The slosh was right where that one's light goes down to the water. I think the one in goggles wades.
entries.title: The one who wades

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the first sack and scooped two handfuls into the bindle. Seven days in the pool now; the water off them runs clear and the meats bend without breaking.
entries.title: Seven days soaked

entries.text: Roasted them a few at a time on the stick over this morning's coals and ate them hot on my heels by the ring. No bitter at all, and now my stomach is quiet.
entries.title: Second breakfast

entries.text: The first thing I asked only brought back animal tracks and stone ones from long ago. The second found it: a print with no toes and lines across the bottom is a sole, something worn on the foot, and every sole's pattern and wear are its own, so the bite is that one foot's mark.
entries.title: A print with lines

entries.text: So whoever crosses the stones wears something on its feet, and it is always the same something. My feet only ever leave my feet.
entries.title: Something on its feet

entries.text: Picked every meat off the low shelf into the bindle. The sun is coming through the round window in patches between clouds, so they go out to the drying stone.

entries.text: Spread the meats one layer deep on the drying stone. The clouds closed over before I finished, so there is no sun on the stone, only the breeze coming off the water and moving over them.

entries.text: Drew the long print on the thirty-sixth page as near as I can remember it: no toes, lines straight across, and the bite out of the third line. Wrote 'same foot, always' under it.

entries.text: It says nothing about clouds. Soaked meats dry one layer deep in low warmth with air moving past, turned every hour, and take about twelve hours; the sky today hasn't got twelve hours of sun in it.

entries.text: So the stone was only half of it. They get turned every hour, and if the sun stays away they go on the warm side of the ring, out of the smoke.
entries.title: Every hour

entries.text: Knelt at the pool to drink and something moved under my face: small fish, finger long, holding still in the shade behind the ring stones, all pointed at where the creek comes in. My hand went in and every one was gone; they came back slowly, one at a time.
entries.title: Fish in the pool

entries.text: Across the water the one in goggles sat on a box by its plank table, bent over something in its lap that gave off a little light, the way my slate does. It never looked up, and I didn't wave.

entries.reason: The fish in the pool all hold still facing where the creek comes in, and he wanted to know what they are waiting for.

entries.text: It only told me about one small fish, one that lives in ditches and ponds eating mosquito larvae and other insects. Nothing about my pool, but small fish eat small things that move.
entries.title: What they wait for

entries.text: So they hold facing upstream for whatever the creek brings down to them. I go to the basket every morning for whatever comes, and mostly it's leaves.
entries.title: Facing upstream

entries.text: Roasted six of the drying meats on a stick over the coals and ate them hot. The smoke kept leaning off to the northwest in the gusts, and leaves kept coming down into the ring.
entries.title: Warm acorns

entries.reason: He had read that small fish eat small moving things, and wanted to see what small moving things the creek has.
entries.text: Lifted a stone from the edge of the pool and turned it over. Stuck to the underside were little flat crawlers no bigger than a fingernail, six legs spread wide and two thread tails, and they ran sideways to stay under it.
entries.title: Under a stone

entries.text: Flicked one crawler onto the pool. Before it sank halfway the nearest fish had it and was back behind its stone. Leaves have been landing on the water all morning and not one fish went up for a leaf.
entries.title: Before it sank

entries.text: They are stonefly young: flat bodies, six sprawling legs, two long tails, hiding under rocks in cool running water. The page says they are a favorite food of many fish, and that they only live where the water is clean.
entries.title: Two thread tails

entries.text: The first thing I asked found it. You tie a thorn to the line by its blunt end and push the point into a fat grub, so thorn and line make a V; when a fish takes it you let it run and wait about half a minute before pulling, so it has swallowed it.
entries.title: A thorn by its end

entries.text: So the trick isn't quick hands, it's slow ones: thirty breaths of letting go. The brambles have more thorns than I could ever use.
entries.title: Slow hands

entries.reason: He was hungry and the fire was still up.
entries.text: Ate a double handful of the meats from the bark tray, warm from the ring and a little chewy. I want my hands steady for the next part.
entries.title: Lunch from the tray

entries.reason: He needed thorns for the hook the slate described.
entries.text: Snapped thorns off the gray dead canes, since the green ones bend instead of break. The longest is barely a fingernail; the page said a whole thumb joint. The fish in my pool are only a finger long, so maybe that's right.
entries.title: Dead canes

entries.reason: To have something real to try on the fish.
entries.text: Tied a thorn onto nettle cord by its blunt end. The knot slid off twice; the third time I wound it four turns and pinned it with a second knot, and now it hangs in a V like the page said.
entries.title: A V of cord

entries.reason: He needed bait for the thorn hook.
entries.text: Turned the same edge stone over and picked off one crawler, the fattest. It held on to my finger with all six legs, which is more grip than I had expected.
entries.title: One for the thorn

entries.text: Upstream across the water the one in goggles was crouched in its shallows. It jerked a line up out of the creek, looked at the end of it, and sat back on its heels. The line came up shorter than it went in.
entries.title: A short line

entries.reason: He wanted to try his first hook the slow way.
entries.text: Pushed the thorn into the crawler and let it down. A fish took it and ran under the ring stones, and I let it go and counted thirty breaths like the slate said. When I pulled, the cord came up light: crawler gone, fish gone, and the tip of the thorn snapped off.
entries.title: Thirty breaths

entries.reason: His hands were slow and cold from the pool.
entries.text: The fire was down to embers when I got back. Laid dry sticks on and blew until it stood up, and held my hands over it; pool water stays in the fingers a long time.

queries: thorn fish hook snapped what else can i make a hook from in the woods
entries.query: thorn fish hook snapped what else can i make a hook from in the woods
entries.reason: His thorn snapped off in a fish's mouth and he wanted something stronger.
entries.source: Woodland Ways Blog: Natural and Improvised Fishing Hooks
entries.text: It never says thorns snap, which mine did. It says hooks have been made of bone, claws, teeth and hard wood, and that a little gut hook can be whittled from oak, sharp at both ends, so it sticks crosswise once it's swallowed. I have an oak and I have a knife.
entries.title: Hard wood, both ends

entries.reason: The slate said hard wood, and oak is the hardest I know.
entries.text: Picked through the leaves under my red oak for a dead twig, not a green one; the dead ones snap clean and the green ones only fold. Found one a finger thick and gray all through. The wind kept dropping more leaves on my back while I looked.
entries.title: A dead oak twig

entries.reason: To make a hook that won't snap off in a fish like the thorn.
entries.text: Whittled a sliver off the oak twig and took it down by the fire, sharp at both ends with a groove round the middle for the cord. Oak fights the knife; a birch pen is butter next to it. It came out about as long as my smallest finger's top joint.
entries.title: Harder than birch

entries.text: Upstream across the water the one in goggles was crouched in its shallows, washing something in the water that flashed silver when it turned. Whatever it was, it was about as long as one of my fish.
entries.title: Something silver

entries.reason: He wanted to see if oak would hold where the thorn snapped.
entries.text: Wound the crawler onto the oak hook and let it down. The fish came and tugged at it from both ends, round and round, and stripped the crawler off without ever taking the hook in. When I pulled it up, the oak was bare and whole.
entries.title: Picked from both ends

entries.text: The oak didn't snap, but my fish are only a finger long, and the hook is half the length of their heads. It needs to be a splinter, not a peg. My fingers are cold and slow from the water again.
entries.title: Too fat for them

entries.reason: His hands were too cold and slow from the pool to whittle anything thin.
entries.text: Laid three dry sticks across the flames and sat close with my hands open over the heat. The fingers came back one at a time, the little ones last.

entries.text: Nothing I found says how small. One page says the old ones were bamboo with the cord tied off center, so one end is longer and stands up crosswise when pulled, and the bait is pushed along the whole length so none of it shows. Mine was tied in the middle with the crawler wound round it like a bandage.

entries.reason: The slate said one end should be longer than the other.
entries.text: Split a much thinner sliver off the oak twig and took it down until it bends a little, about as thin as a pine needle. Cut the groove a third of the way along instead of the middle, so one end is long.
entries.title: Thin as a needle

entries.reason: To see if a thin splinter does what the fat peg couldn't.
entries.text: Slid the crawler along the whole splinter so no oak showed and let it down. A fish swallowed it and I counted thirty, and when I drew in it was heavy and came up flashing right to the ring stones, then twisted once and was gone. The splinter came back whole.
entries.title: Right to the stones

entries.text: It held long enough to come up, which nothing has before. Next time I lift it straight out onto the bank instead of drawing it to the stones where it can twist. My fingers are cold again.
entries.title: Closer than ever

entries.onMind: what to do with it now
entries.reason: Last time he drew the fish to the stones and it twisted free.
entries.text: Hid the splinter in a crawler again and counted thirty after the cord went tight. Then I didn't draw it in, I lifted, and a speckled fish a little longer than my finger came up out of the water and landed flapping in the leaves behind me.
entries.title: Out onto the bank

entries.text: I sat down on the bank and held it in both hands until it stopped. All day for one fish the size of a finger, and I'd do the whole day again.
entries.title: My first fish

entries.text: Not always: some little fish get eaten whole. But the guts make the meat spoil fast and slow the heat from reaching the middle, and the belly can hold whatever the fish swallowed. Mine is going on a stick over coals, so the insides come out.
entries.title: Guts in or out

entries.reason: The slate said the insides slow the cooking.
entries.text: Slit its belly with my little knife and washed it out in the pool. The guts sank, and the other fish came straight out from behind the stones and took them.

entries.reason: He was hungry, and he wanted to know what his own fish tasted like.
entries.text: Roasted it on a stick until the skin went brown and curled, and ate it in four bites, little bones and all. It tastes like the pool smells, only warm. Not a meal yet, but it's the first food I ever pulled out of the water.
entries.title: Four bites

entries.reason: So the way it worked doesn't get lost by tomorrow.
entries.text: Wrote the first fish on the thirty-seventh page: the splinter hidden in a crawler, count thirty after the cord goes tight, then lift, don't draw. Drew it a little longer than it was, then crossed that out and drew it right.

entries.reason: He wanted a second fish so supper would be more than four bites.
entries.text: Turned over four stones at the edge of the pool before one had a crawler under it. The light is going gray and the water is colder on my hands than it was at noon.
entries.title: Last crawler

entries.reason: Lifting worked once and he wanted to see it work twice.
entries.text: Counted thirty and lifted, and nothing came with it but the splinter, clean. Something took the whole crawler off without ever pulling. One fish today, then.

entries.text: Across the water a small yellow light came on at the plank table of the one in goggles, about the same time as last night. It stayed bent over the table and never looked out.

entries.reason: He was cold from the pool and wants coals for supper.
entries.text: The fire was down to red embers, so I laid dry sticks on them and blew until they caught. My fingers were slow on the sticks until the heat got into them.

entries.reason: One fish was four bites, and the meats have been drying all day.
entries.text: Took a handful of meats from the bark tray, dry on top and still leathery underneath, and held them over the coals on a stick until they ticked and browned.

entries.text: In autumn fish feed hard from afternoon to dusk, and early morning after a cold night is often good too. When the water gets really cold they slow down and bite only in the warmest part of the day.

entries.onMind: whether fish bite at first light
entries.reason: He is slow in the cold and wants to know if the fish will be too.
entries.text: Woke to gray in the round window and my fingers felt thick. Stayed at the table with the slate a while before going out into it.

entries.source: Angling Times: Where fish go when our rivers get cold in winter
entries.text: The slate says cold fish are sluggish and eat less. They rest in the slow water behind cover by day and feed more toward dusk. In a little stream they hardly move a few steps.
entries.title: Fish go slow too

entries.text: So they are slow in the cold the way I am. I'll lay the scoop in the still water behind the far stones and wait long, and keep one worm back for dusk.
entries.title: Like me, then

entries.reason: His hands won't do fine work until he has warmed by a fire.
entries.text: Raked the ash back with a stick and found two coals, dull orange, not the four I hoped for. Fed them the dry twigs from under the overhang one at a time until they caught.
entries.title: Two coals, not four

entries.onMind: the slack water by the far stones
entries.reason: He wanted to be sure the bait lived before carrying it to the pool.
entries.text: Lifted the wet leaves in the scoop. Both worms are there, cold and slow, but alive.
entries.title: Damp, not drowned

entries.title: Tied in the middle

entries.text: No smoke over the water this morning, and no light. Whoever lives over there is still asleep, or their fire went out in the night.
entries.title: No smoke

entries.reason: He waited for a fish to settle over the worm before lifting, the way the forty-second page says.
entries.text: One stayed over the worm, so I lifted straight up, slow. It rode the scoop halfway out of the water, then flipped over the flat edge and was gone. The worm is still tied in the middle.

entries.text: The water runs off a flat scoop the moment it clears the pool, and the fish runs off with it. Nothing on the edges to stop either one.
