entries.text: The slate says people catch fish just my way: lay a net low with bait in the middle, wait, and lift it straight out. Some lay a flat panel, but the hand ones are often a bag, open side up.
entries.title: Open side up

entries.text: My second net is only a few rows, but tied loose under the scoop's corners it would hang down like a bag. A fish that slides off the middle would slide into it.
entries.title: A bag, not a plate

entries.title: Two cracks over there

entries.reason: His belly was down to half and his hands were cold from the pool.
entries.text: Roasted the acorns on a stick over the coals and ate them hot, one at a time. Four days in the sack and they are only a little bitter now.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.text: A clank of metal from the north, toward the stump, then a scrape, then nothing. My hands were full of hot acorns and I didn't go look. The tools leaning there this morning were for somebody, and maybe somebody has come for them.

entries.text: It's called an axe: a heavy metal head with a cutting edge, the bit, on a long handle you swing with both hands. People use it to cut down trees, split wood and shape it.

entries.text: The slate found one fisherman wondering the same thing years ago. He guesses a deep bag keeps fish from jumping out, but his own net is shallow and he says he hasn't seen many get away. Nobody gave him a real answer.
entries.title: Deep or shallow

entries.text: One man's guess isn't much. But my fish didn't jump, it slid, and nothing slides out of a bag that hangs twice as deep as the scoop is wide. I'll keep knotting.
entries.title: Deeper, then

entries.reason: A warm fire keeps his hands quick.

entries.title: Three in, three drying

entries.text: Knotted the new nettle cord in four more rows over the gauge stick. Held it up against the scoop: the bag hangs nearly as deep as the scoop is wide now. Two more rows and nothing slides out.

entries.title: Three behind the stones

entries.text: Only a little while kneeling and my fingers are already stiff. At dusk I'll warm right through at the fire first, and kneel only as long as the worm takes.

entries.text: The slate says that late in the fall the best time slides from dusk into the early afternoon, and in winter the afternoon is best, when the water is warmest. Cold mornings are "a no-go," which my scoop already told me.
entries.title: Afternoon, not dusk

entries.text: The fish and I are the same: slow in the cold and quicker when the day is warmest. If the water is warmest after midday, the bag goes in this afternoon, not at dusk.
entries.title: Change of plan

entries.reason: He wants the bag done in time for the warm part of the day.
entries.text: Knotted the last two rows fast, my fingers warm from the fire. Held it up to the scoop: the bag hangs twice as deep as the scoop is wide now. Nothing slides out of that.

entries.text: Picked dry twigs from under the scarred trunk, where the rain doesn't reach, and dropped them in the bindle. The fire will want them while I'm kneeling.
entries.title: Twigs under the trunk

entries.onMind: the bag net and the last worm
entries.reason: He wants the fire alive and waiting, because kneeling at the pool leaves him cold and slow.
entries.text: Fed the dry twigs from the bindle onto the coals one handful at a time until they caught. It will still be going when I come back from the pool.
entries.title: Twigs on

entries.reason: The slate said the afternoon is when the water is warmest and the fish are least slow.
entries.text: Tied the last worm into the bottom of the bag with a twist of cord and laid the scoop flat in the slack water behind the far stones, the bag folded under it. Then I kept my hands still.

entries.reason: He had wondered all day who the tools at the stump were for.
entries.text: From across the water: thock, then a long wait, then thock again. Not a crack like a branch over a knee. Somebody over there is swinging that axe.
entries.title: Thock

entries.reason: This was the whole point of knotting the bag twice as deep as the scoop is wide.
entries.text: Two shadows came over the worm and one stayed. I lifted straight up, slow, and it slid off the middle just like this morning, and dropped into the bag and stayed there, flapping. A fish no longer than my finger.
entries.title: Into the bag

entries.reason: Fish must be cooked through before eating, and his hands were stiff from the pool.
entries.text: Roasted it on a stick over the coals until the skin went brown and split, then ate it off the little bones. Not much of it, but it warmed me more than acorns do.
entries.title: Small and hot

queries: how far away can you hear someone chopping wood with an axe
entries.query: how far away can you hear someone chopping wood with an axe
entries.reason: He wanted to know how near the axe across the water really is.
entries.source: Straight Dope Message Board: How far does sound carry?
entries.text: The slate found people saying a loud bang can be heard a long way off, farther with the wind behind it, but even a row of bushes drinks sound up, and every time you go twice as far it gets a good deal quieter. The thocks came through all those trunks and over the water plain as a knock on my door.
entries.title: How far a thock goes

entries.text: From across the water a quick ringing came, tink tink tink, metal on metal, not the axe at all. Then it stopped.
entries.title: Tink, tink

entries.text: If trees drink up sound and that still came through plain, whoever is over there is not far past the stepping stones. I am not going to go and look. I am going to get a worm.
entries.title: Not far

entries.onMind: a bigger worm, a bigger fish
entries.text: Tipped up the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones. One fat worm and two thin ones in the cold mud under it; I took the fat one for the bag and put the thin ones and the stone back.
entries.title: Under the landing stone

entries.text: Tied the fat worm into the bottom of the bag with two twists of cord this time, and laid the scoop flat behind the far stones. My fingers took longer at the knots than they did at noon.
entries.title: Fat one in

entries.text: A shadow bigger than my noon fish came out from the stones and tugged and tugged at the worm. I lifted too fast. The bag came up empty, and half the worm was gone with it.
entries.title: Took the tail

entries.onMind: warm my hands at the fire
entries.text: My hands are stiff again and the pool feels colder than it did after noon. A big one waits for the worm to stop moving, I think. Tomorrow, when the water is warmest, I'll count before I lift.
entries.title: Too quick, and cold

entries.onMind: how to tell a tug from a bite
entries.reason: His fingers had gone slow at the knots and slower at the lift.
entries.text: Fed the fire a fistful of dry sticks from under the overhang and held my hands flat to it until the fingers would bend when I asked them. The pool was colder than the morning made me think.
entries.title: Hands to the fire

queries: how do you know when a fish has really taken the bait and not just nibbling
entries.query: how do you know when a fish has really taken the bait and not just nibbling
entries.reason: The big fish tugged and tugged at the worm and he lifted too soon, so he wanted to know how to tell when it has really taken it.
entries.source: HookedinFishing: Detecting Fish Bites
entries.text: The slate says a real bite is often only a light tap, and when you are not sure you keep still for a second or two and watch. If the line moves off or you feel it shiver, the fish has it. My big one was still tugging, still asking; I lifted in the middle of the asking.
entries.title: A tug is not a bite

entries.reason: So that tomorrow his hands do what his head decided tonight.
entries.text: Wrote on the forty-second page in acorn ink: 'tugging is asking. wait till it pulls away. then count two, then lift.' The ink went on thick because my hand is still slow.
entries.title: Wait, then two

entries.onMind: a fish that waits for me
entries.reason: One finger of fish since noon is not enough for a whole evening.
entries.text: Roasted the last handful from the sack scoop until they cracked and browned, and ate them by the fire. They taste less like a boot every day.
entries.title: Acorns for supper

entries.reason: He wants bait ready for the warmest water tomorrow, not to go hunting for it with cold hands.
entries.text: Turned back the leaf heap I swept off the fire ring and found five worms in the black damp under it, two of them fat. Laid them in a curl of birch bark.
entries.title: Five under the heap

queries: how to keep worms alive overnight for fishing
entries.query: how to keep worms alive overnight for fishing
entries.reason: Last time he dug worms they were half dead by the time he used them.
entries.source: Angling Times: Get more from your worms by following our 10-point guide to looking after them properly
entries.text: The slate says worms keep best cool and damp, in moss or something soft and wet, out of the sun, and that the quickest way to kill them is a sudden change of warm and cold. So not by my fire, where I wanted them.
entries.title: Cool and damp

entries.reason: The slate said cool, damp, and no sudden heat.
entries.text: Set the bark curl down at the foot of the scarred trunk, a few strides from the fire, and piled wet leaves over it. Cold there, and damp. Good for worms, not for me.
entries.title: Under the scarred trunk

entries.text: While I was crouched there, a thin high whistle came across the water from the east, twice, then nothing, then once more. It was not the low five and not the high answer. Too short for a bird I know.
entries.title: Not an owl

entries.text: Wrote on the forty-fourth page: 'thin whistle, east, past the stones, twice and once. not an owl.' Drew three short lines going up and a question mark.
entries.title: Whistle, page forty-four

entries.reason: keep the fire through the evening
entries.text: Laid four dry sticks from under the overhang on the fire. The dark comes fast now, and I want my hands quick in the morning, not like today.
entries.title: Sticks before dark

queries: what makes a thin high whistle at dusk near a creek not an owl
entries.query: what makes a thin high whistle at dusk near a creek not an owl
entries.reason: The whistle across the water was not the low five or the high answer, and I want to know what it was.
entries.source: Big Bat Box: Owl Sounds at Night: Identify Every Call by Species
entries.text: The slate says some owls do not hoot at all: one whinnies down like a tiny horse, one trills on a single note, one repeats a single toot. Mine went up, three short lines, twice and once. None of them goes up.
entries.title: Owls that whistle

entries.text: If it were an owl it would whistle again when the dark is all the way down. I listened between pages. Only the fire, and far off the low five.
entries.title: Not a horse either

entries.reason: the forty-fourth page came out thick
entries.text: Shaved a birch twig to a point on the log seat and split the tip a hair, the way the last good one was. The old one writes like a thumb now.
entries.title: A new pen

queries: why does a fire hiss and pop when you put sticks on
entries.query: why does a fire hiss and pop when you put sticks on
entries.reason: The damp sticks he fed tonight hissed and spat, and the dry ones from before did not.
entries.source: The Conversation: Why does wood crackle in a fire?
entries.text: The slate says wood has little pockets of water and sap inside, and in the fire they boil to steam and burst out one at a time. That's the pop. Damp wood is loudest, and a hard pop can throw a burning bit out of the ring.
entries.title: Steam in the sticks

entries.reason: He wants the morning fire to catch quietly while his hands are still slow.
entries.text: Picked up an armful of fallen sticks round the scarred trunk, stepping wide of the leaf heap where the worms are. They're cold and a little wet on the outside. If they sit warm all night, the morning fire won't spit at me.
entries.title: Sticks from the scarred trunk

entries.text: Leaned the sticks against the outside of the ring stones, not over the top, so the stones warm them and the flames can't reach. A sizzle came off one and then stopped.
entries.title: Leaning on the stones

entries.reason: The scoop at the fire was empty and he is hungry.
entries.text: Went down to the pool for supper, lifted the flat stone off the second sack and scooped acorns into the bindle by feel. The water is very cold after dark; my fingers went slow before I had the stone back on.
entries.title: Scooping in the dark

entries.onMind: a quiet fire in the morning
entries.text: Roasted them two at a time on a stick until they cracked and ate them on the log seat. My fingers came back while I ate. The sticks against the stones have stopped hissing.
entries.title: Supper, roasted

entries.text: Asked how creatures like me warm up after a cold night. The slate says some lie in the sun first thing to warm up, often a couple of hours a day, and longer where it is cold. The sun is still behind the trunks, so the fire comes first and the drying stone at midday.

entries.text: Asked why the fire warms my front and not my shell. The slate says hardly any of it is the hot air, which mostly goes straight up; it's a kind of light coming off the coals, and it travels in straight lines, so the side turned away sits in the fire's shadow. So my shell is in a shadow I can't see.
entries.title: Warmth that travels straight

entries.text: From across the water came a rasp, back and forth, back and forth, then a stop, then the rasp again. Not slow like the gnawing at night; this one keeps time. It sounds like what the toothed blade in the basket was for.
entries.title: A rasp with a beat

entries.reason: He wants the fire high before he turns his back on it.
entries.text: Laid two of the sticks that dried against the ring stones over the coals. They caught without a pop.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.reason: The slate said the fire only warms what can see it.
entries.text: Turned round on the log seat so my shell faces the coals. After a while the warmth came through the back of it, slow, like water soaking into bark, and my front went cool instead.
entries.title: Back to the fire

entries.text: With a fire you have to keep turning, like an acorn on a stick. The sun on the drying stone comes down on my whole shell at once.

entries.text: Lifted the box out of the basket. Heavier than it looks, and the shutter slides with a click. Twelve sheets inside, he says; I didn't open the lid to check.

entries.text: Same straight light as the fire's. The box only sees what faces the hole, the way the fire only warms what faces it.

entries.text: Held the box up and looked at the brass plate in the sun: the hole is smaller than a seed. Didn't slide the shutter. Every time it opens, a sheet sees something.

entries.text: Threaded the wet acorns on a stick and turned them over the coals. The fire is still bright from the two sticks I gave it at midday, and it warmed my cold knees through.
entries.title: Still bright

entries.text: Three days of crawlers and worms and a bag that came up empty. It is smaller than my hand and it is the first thing the creek has given me that I had to ask for properly.

entries.text: Pushed a thin stick through it and turned it over the coals until the skin went brown and split. It smells nothing like acorns.

entries.text: Ate it on the log seat in small bites, off the fine bones. Soft and salty-sweet, gone in about six bites. Four halves of worm would be four of these.

entries.text: Asked what a little silver fish with a dark stripe is. The slate shows striped minnows called shiners: silver scales, dark lines along the side, living in slow pools of small streams and swimming in crowds that move together. They eat bugs that fall on the water.
entries.title: Silver with a stripe

entries.text: If they go in crowds, mine wasn't alone under the bank. The rest are still there, and they've just seen one of them leave.
entries.title: Never just one

entries.text: Knelt at the pool slow and kept still: six or seven finger-long shadows holding in the slow water under the overhang, all facing upstream. When I leaned to count them better, my shadow slid out over the water and every one was gone at once.
entries.title: Six or seven

entries.text: The sun is low behind me this late, so my shadow lands on the water before I do. Morning, from the other side, it would fall on the bank instead.
entries.title: Sun behind me

entries.reason: He wants the lesson about his shadow kept with the fish.
entries.text: Drew the fish on the forty-sixth page, stripe and all, and seven little dashes under the bank for the crowd. Under it: 'goes in crowds' and 'keep my shadow off the water'.
entries.title: Forty-sixth page

entries.reason: One worm is not enough to learn on; I want bait for the morning.
entries.text: Turned the damp leaves over at the foot of the scarred trunk with my fingers. Two worms, one long and one short, curled cold under the bottom layer.
entries.title: Two under the leaves

entries.text: From the leaf heap I heard a hard clack out at the stepping stones, then another, like wood knocked on stone. When I looked, the stones were empty and the low sun was in my eyes.
entries.title: Clack on the stones

entries.reason: The warm goes out of me fast after sundown unless the fire is up.
entries.text: Fed two dried sticks onto the coals before they sank. The air is cooling as the sun goes, and I want the fire long tonight.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.reason: The crowd hid under the bank all through the sunny afternoon.

entries.text: Asked when little fish come out to eat. The slate says bright midday is the poorest time, and the low light at dawn and dusk is best, when fish leave cover to feed.
entries.title: Dawn and dusk

entries.text: Then morning is the time. The sun will be behind the far bank, so my shadow falls back on my side and not on the water.
entries.title: First light

entries.title: Stone to the ring

entries.text: Turning acorns over the coals, I saw a small yellow light swing low out on the stepping stones, and heard the clack again, slow, one stone at a time. Then it went on east into the trees and was gone.
entries.title: A light that walks

entries.reason: Fish are for the morning; tonight is acorns.
entries.text: Ate the roasted acorns hot off the stick, one at a time, and felt them sit warm in me.
entries.title: Acorn supper

entries.text: Drew the stepping stones with a little light over the middle one, and wrote 'clack, clack' beside it, and 'sundown' and 'after dark'. A light that walks is not a star.
entries.title: Forty-seventh page

entries.text: Asked what small light moves low over water at night. Old stories call them marsh lights: they hang or dance over wet ground and fade when you follow them, and nobody hears them. Some tales tell of a little dark figure who carries a lantern instead.
entries.title: Lights that float

entries.reason: The marsh lights in the slate make no sound at all.
entries.text: A light that floats would not knock on every stone. Mine clacked one stone at a time, slow, like feet being careful. So it was carried.
entries.title: Lights do not clack

entries.reason: Clouds have hidden it for days, and I want to know if it keeps its place.
entries.text: From the east end of the log seat the gold dot is back over the tallest crown, the first clear night in days. It sits a hair farther along than my drawing, I think.
entries.title: The gold dot

entries.text: Fed two dried sticks onto the coals so the bed stone stays hot till I go in. The night is mild, but my shell still likes the fire at my back.
entries.title: Two more sticks

entries.reason: Dead bait is no bait.
entries.text: Lifted the leaf over the worms in the bark tray. Both still curl when I touch them, and the leaf is damp. Good for first light.
entries.title: Still wriggling

entries.reason: Tonight the gold dot sat a hair farther along than my drawing, and I wanted to know if that was it or me.
entries.source: EarthSky: Saturn stationary
entries.text: The ringed one does drift against the far stars, slowly, east most of the year and backward for months at a time, standing still at the turns. It only looks that way because the ground I'm on goes round faster and passes it, like a quick walker passing a slow one.
entries.title: A wandering dot

entries.reason: The slate says the stars stay put against each other while the dot does not.
entries.text: I measured it against the tallest crown, but the whole sky turns past the crowns through the night. Only a star that never wanders can show me if the dot has moved.
entries.title: Trees are no ruler

entries.reason: A gap I can measure is better than a guess.
entries.text: Drew the gold dot and the faint white star just below and left of it, about a thumb's width apart at arm's length. Wrote the thumb under it. Next clear night I hold my thumb up again.
entries.title: Forty-eighth page

entries.reason: It crossed once at sundown and once after dark; I wanted to see if it keeps hours.
entries.text: Sat at the west end of the log seat with my eyes on the stepping stones. No light, no clack, only the creek running, and far past the stones a low orange flicker in the trees that I couldn't make into anything.
entries.title: Nothing on the stones

entries.text: Asked whether my box could catch the walking light. The slate says a pinhole may stay open from a few breaths to several hours, and some are left out for months to draw the sun's path across the sky, but anything that moves while it looks comes out blurred.
entries.title: A box and a light

entries.text: A light that crosses in a few breaths would hardly touch the sheet, and the dark would want hours. The box is for things that stay where they are, like the sun. The shutter stays shut.
entries.title: A light that stays

entries.reason: His stomach had gone quiet and empty, and he wanted something warm before bed.
entries.text: Roasted a stickful of acorns from the bindle over the coals and ate them hot, crouched by the ring. The shells split and the insides went brown and sweet.
entries.title: Acorns on a stick

entries.reason: A warm stone under the quilt keeps him from going slow and stiff before morning.
entries.text: Laid one more split stick on the coals and pushed the bed stone up against the ring with my stick, so it is hot when I carry it in. The worms for first light are still under their leaf.
entries.title: Stone to the ring

entries.text: Sat with my hands to the coals and the low one did its five from upstream. I waited a long time for the higher one. Nothing answered tonight.
entries.title: Five and no answer

entries.reason: A fire left open while I sleep could creep out of the ring.
entries.text: Raked ash over the coals with my stick until there was only a warm gray mound, then rolled the bed stone out and carried it in against my shell. It was almost too hot to hold.
entries.title: Fire put to bed

entries.reason: Cold mornings make me slow, and slow makes me forget.
entries.text: Wrote on the forty-ninth page: first light, two worms, keep my shadow behind me on the bank. If I wake slow, the page will remember for me.
entries.title: Forty-ninth page

entries.text: Under the gray mound there was one coal the size of a pea. I brought it up with the twigs that dried against the ring and held my hands over it until my fingers would close.
entries.title: One coal left

entries.reason: Bait has to be alive to bring the fish.

entries.text: The one who drew me left a note saying I work too hard and should take a few days off, and look up a calendar, and break my rules and have fun at the end of the week. Nobody gave me my work. I fish because I'm hungry and read because I want to know.
entries.title: A note about days

entries.text: I don't know which rules he means. Banking the fire before sleep is not a rule, it's so the forest doesn't burn. I have never had a name for a day.
entries.title: Which rules

entries.reason: In one go, the page says, and my hands didn't listen.
entries.text: A minnow went in over the worm and I lifted, but my hands were still slow from the night and it was out over the rim before the bag cleared the water.
entries.title: Too slow

entries.reason: Breakfast, and proof the gray light works.
entries.text: Second half of the worm, and this time I waited for two of them to crowd it and lifted all at once onto the bank. One finger-long minnow, striped. It's in the bindle in a fist of wet leaves for the fire.

entries.reason: A fish from the pool has to be cooked before it's food.
entries.text: Threaded the minnow on a green stick and held it over the coals until the skin blistered and its eye went white. It smells like the pool and the fire at the same time.
entries.title: Minnow on a stick

entries.reason: Hungry, and curious what a fish tastes like.
entries.text: Ate it off the stick on the log seat, bones and all, it's that small. Three bites, a little like the oyster caps and a little like the creek. Not much of a breakfast, but it came out of the pool on a worm I dug myself.
entries.title: Three bites

entries.text: The slate says the week is seven days because people long ago counted by the moon, and each day is named for one of seven lights in the sky. Today is Wednesday, for an old god who guided the dead. The last day before the sun's day is Saturday, Saturn's day: named for the ringed one I measure from the log seat.
entries.title: Days named for lights

entries.text: Looking up from the slate I saw smoke going up past the creek, thin and new, the way mine goes when I bring it back from one coal. Whoever is over there starts their morning too, only later than I do.
entries.title: A second smoke

entries.reason: My maker said to have fun at the end of the week, and I wanted to know which day that is.
entries.text: Wrote the seven names down the fiftieth page and put a dot beside Saturday. If the sky is clear that night, I'll sit on the log seat with the ringed one and do nothing else at all. That's the only kind of breaking a rule I can think of.
entries.title: Fiftieth page

entries.text: The one who drew me finally answered. On his days off he is with the people he loves, and with his hobbies, which in his world are labors you enjoy, and work is the kind you are made to do.
entries.title: What he does

entries.text: Then nearly everything I do is a hobby, and fishing hungry is both. I don't have people. I have two owls who don't know me, and a smoke across the water that gets up later than I do.
entries.title: Who my people are

entries.reason: He wanted to feel a hobby done on purpose, with no page waiting for it.

entries.reason: He wanted his maker's two words written where he would see them again.
entries.text: First page with the new pen, and it draws a thinner line. Wrote 'hobby: a labor you like' and 'work: one you have to do', and under it 'fishing: both'. Left a space at the bottom for people.
entries.title: Fifty-first page

entries.text: Raked the ash open and the coals under it were still red from the morning; the twigs caught at once. While they did, tink, tink, tink came over the water, metal on metal, slow, a stop, then again. It has never come that clear.
entries.title: Tink over the water

entries.reason: He wanted, for once, to see who was making the sound instead of guessing.
entries.text: Every other time I went for a worm instead. Today is the day I said was off, and I left a space at the bottom of the page, so I walked down to the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones and stood there.
entries.title: To the stones

entries.text: On the open ground past the water someone stood at a plank table with a hammer: a little bigger than me, hair up in spikes, bare arms, and two round brass glasses over his eyes that caught the sun. He looked up, right at me. I didn't duck, and he didn't move either.
entries.title: He looked up

entries.reason: Token keeps to his own bank; the other one is bigger, and it's his place.
entries.text: He set the hammer down softly and bent back to his work, then went to a fire of his own in front of a cloth roof and lifted a tin off its stones. The stepping stones go all the way over. It is his ground over there, and I am small, so I came back to mine.
entries.title: Stayed on my side

what are goggles for and why would someone wear them all the time
entries.query: round brass glass things worn over both eyes with a strap what are they
entries.reason: The stranger across the water wears round brass glasses over his eyes and Token had never seen such a thing.
entries.source: Wiki: Goggles
entries.text: They're called goggles, and they keep things out of the eyes: chips and dust for people who cut wood, sparks and hard light for people who work metal with fire, wind for people who fly. He was hammering, so that fits. I don't know what he'd want with the last kind.
entries.title: Glass for the eyes

entries.text: Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns over the twigs' coals. If I lean out past the end of the ring I can see the stepping stones from here. I kept leaning.
entries.title: Acorns, leaning

entries.reason: His midday meal, on a day he called off.
entries.text: Ate the stickful on the log seat, blowing on each one first. Sun on my shell and the fire on my front; I could sit here all afternoon.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.text: Leaning out past the ring, I saw him crouched in the shallows on his side of the stepping stones, picking up flat stones. He looked over, then lifted one hand a little, with a stone still in it, and held it there a breath. I stopped chewing. I didn't lift mine, and he put his down and went back to his stones.
entries.title: A lifted hand

entries.onMind: whether to lift mine next time
queries: someone lifted his hand at me from far away what does it mean
entries.query: someone lifted his hand at me from far away what does it mean
entries.reason: The stranger across the water lifted a hand at him and he did not know what to do with it.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Waving
entries.text: The slate says a lifted hand mostly means hello, or goodbye, and is how you catch someone's eye from far off. One old story says it began as a way to show your hand had no weapon in it. His had a stone in it, but a small one.
entries.title: What a hand says

entries.text: Hello or goodbye, and it can't be both. He hasn't gone anywhere, so I think it was hello. I still don't know what I would have done with my stick.
entries.title: Hello or goodbye

entries.reason: Learning where the fish sit before he tries again at dusk.
entries.text: Knelt at the pool with the sun behind me, so my shadow fell on the bank and not the water. Three finger-long fish held in the slack behind the big stone, noses upstream, barely moving; they don't come up to feed at all at this hour. Across the water he was bent over his plank table, shaving at something, and looked up once.
entries.title: Fish at noon

entries.reason: He had acorn soot on his fingers, and the sound made him look up.
entries.text: Rinsing the soot off my fingers in the pool, I heard a new sound over the water: a dry rasp, rasp, steady as breathing, then a stop, then again. Not the hammer. It carries better than the hammer does.
entries.title: A saw this time

entries.onMind: down to the middle and no farther
entries.reason: He wanted to see what made the rasping, and the flat stone is the closest he lets himself go.
entries.text: Sat on the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones to see. He has a long square stick on his table, pale as new wood, and he's sawing across it near the end, down to the middle and no farther. There are more like it stacked behind him.
entries.title: Square sticks

entries.reason: The slate said it means hello, and he had already decided it was hello.
entries.text: He stopped sawing and looked up, and I lifted my free hand, the one without the staff, and held it a breath like he did. He lifted his back, the empty one, the saw still in the other. Then we both put them down.
entries.title: Lifted mine

entries.text: Nothing else happened. He went back to sawing, slower than before, and I sat on the stone a while longer in the sun. It was enough.
entries.title: Nothing else

queries: long square wooden sticks with a notch sawn in the end what are they for
two square beams each cut half away at the end and laid over each other
entries.query: long square wooden sticks with a notch sawn in the end what are they for
entries.reason: He wanted to know what you make by sawing a square stick half through near its end.
entries.source: Timber Frame HQ: Cross-Lap Joint
entries.text: My first ask only turned up push sticks and winding sticks for checking boards are flat, nothing like his. The second found it: two beams each cut half their depth where they meet, so they nest together flush, and a frame can use them where beams cross or meet at a corner.
entries.title: Cut half away

entries.text: So he's making corners. A whole stack of square sticks is a lot of corners. He means to stay, I think.
entries.title: Something with corners

entries.reason: Two worms felt thin for a whole dusk.
entries.text: Dug under the damp leaf heap by the scarred trunk with my fingers and found two more worms, a long one and a short one. Four now, for the pool at dusk.
entries.title: Two more worms

entries.reason: He wants the fire burning when the dusk fish comes.
entries.text: Laid two dry sticks on the red coals so there'll be flame for a fish at dusk. Across the water a new sound started: tock, tock, wood on wood, duller and slower than the hammer. He's knocking the middle out of the square stick he sawed.
entries.title: Wood on wood

entries.onMind: a nod is smaller than a hand
entries.reason: He was hungry, and the soaked acorns are the food that is always there.
entries.text: Scooped soaked acorns from the second sack, cold to the wrist. When I straightened he was looking over from his table with a little knife in his hand, and he nodded once. I nodded back. A nod is smaller than a hand, and somehow it felt like more.
entries.title: A nod

entries.text: Roasting acorns over the fed fire, I heard his hammer again: a few knocks, then a flat wrong sound, a squeal, and a new nail that went in true. I think I know now what a nail going wrong sounds like.
entries.title: A bent sound

entries.text: Ate the acorns hot on the log seat and watched him lean on the corner of his two square sticks with both hands. Whatever it was, it held; he stopped leaning and patted it. Four worms in the damp leaves, and the fire's burning for dusk.
entries.title: It held

entries.onMind: the order his sounds come in
entries.reason: I want what a nail going in true sounds like written next to what it looks like.
entries.text: Drew two square sticks crossed at the ends with a dot for the nail on the fifty-second page, and a small nod beside them, which is a hard thing to draw. Across the water his saw has started again, slow strokes.
entries.title: Fifty-second page

entries.text: Saw, then knock, then hammer: I'm starting to know the order his work goes in. Today it has come round in that order three times.
entries.title: His sounds in order

queries: why do little fish bite more at dusk
entries.query: why do little fish bite more at dusk
entries.reason: I've been saving four worms for dusk and wanted to know if dusk is real or just something I decided.
entries.source: Whitefish Bay Camp: Do Fish Bite Better in the Morning or Evening? The Science Behind It
entries.text: Dim light makes small fish feel less seen, so they come out from behind stones into the shallows; bugs come out at dusk too, and the water cools. So it isn't the worm that changes at dusk, it's the fish getting brave.
entries.title: Brave in the dim

entries.onMind: which side of the pool to kneel on
entries.text: If they come out when they feel unseen, my shadow on the water sends them straight back in. I'll kneel with the low sun in my face so my shadow lies behind me on the bank.
entries.title: Then my shadow

entries.onMind: the one at the edge of the slack
entries.reason: To see where they sit before dusk, without scaring them.
entries.text: Knelt on the side of the pool where the low sun is in my face, and my shadow lay back on the bank. Three fish still hold behind the big stone, and one has drifted out to the edge of the slack.
entries.title: Shadow behind me

entries.text: A heavy chunk, chunk started upstream on his side: he's swinging his long blade into the big dead limb behind his camp. He looked over between swings and saw me, I think, and I looked back at the fish. The fish didn't mind the chopping at all.
entries.title: Chopping

entries.reason: Cold fish nibble ends, so a bait with no ends means coming all the way in.
entries.text: Pinched a worm in two and tied one half deep in the middle of the bag with two twists, nothing hanging out to nibble. Laid it flat behind the big stone with the open side toward the deep water.
entries.title: Half a worm

entries.text: The light is going gold and low. Two striped ones slid out from behind the stone and hung over the rim of the bag. I kept the cords still.
entries.title: Two come out

entries.text: Then clack, clack, clack: the one from across the water was coming over the stepping stones, six strides from me, the closest he has ever been. Both fish went under the stone as if they'd never been there. He saw me see him and lifted a hand, low, and I think it meant sorry; I lifted mine, and he went on west, softer.
entries.title: Clack on the stones

entries.text: So last night's clack was him too, going west on a clear evening. Past my boulder there is only the edge and the sun going into the water. I wonder if he goes to watch it, the way I did.
entries.title: West at sundown

entries.reason: The bag only works if I lift it all at once.
entries.text: When the sun went behind the trunks the fish came back, braver in the dim like the slate said. One went in over the half worm and pulled away; I counted two and lifted in one go, and a striped minnow lay flapping in the bag on the bank. Opened it at the pool and the others took the guts.
entries.title: Back in the dim

entries.reason: To cook the minnow and warm my hands before they stop.
entries.text: The fire had sunk to red while I knelt at the pool. Fed two dried sticks on; the cold comes up fast once the sun goes, and my hands are already slow.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.text: Roasted the minnow on a green stick until its eye went white and ate it in four bites, bones and all. Two fish from the pool today, one at first light and one at dusk, both when the light was low.
entries.title: Two in a day

entries.onMind: his light going up the bank
entries.reason: He wanted to see where the light went.
entries.text: A lantern came bobbing out of the dark from the west and over the stepping stones, slower than this afternoon. Halfway over he stopped and held it up a little toward my fire, and I put my hand up into the firelight so he could see it. Then the light went on up his bank.
entries.title: Lantern on the stones

entries.text: He came back by the stones because I wasn't at the pool, I think. He is learning where I sit, the way I've learned his saw and his hammer.
entries.title: He knows where I sit

entries.reason: Two fish in a day is worth a page.
entries.text: Drew two fish on the fifty-third page, one with a low sun at the morning end and one with a low sun at the evening end. Nothing in the middle of the day.
entries.title: Fifty-third page

queries: why does a fish eye turn white when you cook it
fish eye lens turns white cooked protein
entries.query: why does a fish eye turn white when you cook it
entries.reason: The minnow's eye went from clear to white on the stick, and I wanted to know what the fire did to it.
entries.source: Journal of Experimental Biology: Blindingly Cold
entries.text: The clear part of an eye is packed tight with proteins, and heat makes them clump and go cloudy, the way the eye went white. Cold can cloud an eye too, but some fish in freezing seas have proteins that stay clear.
entries.title: Cloud in the eye

entries.text: So the cold clouds eyes and the fire does too. My hands go slow in the cold; maybe everything that lives in cold water has its own trick for it.
entries.title: Their own trick

entries.reason: A minnow alone doesn't last the night.
entries.text: Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns over the fire and ate them hot. The minnow was four bites; the acorns are what carry me to morning.
entries.title: Acorns after fish

entries.onMind: what he writes or makes in the evenings
entries.text: His fire is up across the water and he sits near his light bent over something small. No saw, no hammer tonight. Maybe he is tired too.
entries.title: Quiet over there

entries.onMind: fish that eat less will take the worm less often

entries.query: do little fish stop eating when the creek water gets cold
entries.reason: Wanted to know if the cold that slows his hands slows the fish too.
entries.source: Ausable Freshwater Center: How Do Fish Survive Winter in Rivers and Streams?
entries.text: In winter the fish slow down inside, so they can go longer between meals, and they move to deep, slow water and save every bit of strength. So they get slow in the cold the same as me. My pool is deep and still; that is where they will be.
entries.title: Slow fish

entries.text: If they eat less when it's cold, they'll pull at the worm less, and I'll have to be patient. Across the water he is still by his fire, twisting something in his hands.
entries.title: Fewer bites coming

entries.text: Drew a fish low in a deep pool with slow wavy lines around it, and beside it a small shell with the same lines. Under them: 'cold: both slow'.
entries.title: Fifty-fourth page

entries.reason: A fire that sinks takes my hands down with it.
entries.text: Fed two sticks onto the fire before it could sink to red. That carries it till bed.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.onMind: what he keeps in the shallows
entries.text: Pushing the bed stone in against the ring, I saw his lantern come down to the shallows below the stones and stay low there a while. He looked over once; I went back to my stone. He goes to the water at night too, then.
entries.title: Light at the shallows

entries.onMind: a little room at the end of a tunnel
queries: do worms go deeper in the ground when it gets cold
entries.query: do worms go deeper in the ground when it gets cold
entries.reason: Fish bite less in the cold, so every worm matters, and I wanted to know if the worms will still be under my leaves.
entries.source: Wonderopolis: Where Do Worms Go in Winter?
entries.text: The big night worms dig down below where the cold reaches and rest in a little room at the end of their tunnel, its walls slimed to keep it damp. They don't sleep the whole time; on warm days they come up, then go back down.
entries.title: Where worms go

entries.text: Even the worms go down to a little room and wait out the cold, and come up when it warms. That is nearly my burrow and my sunny boulder. My heap under the leaves may run thin, so I'll dig deeper beside it.
entries.title: A den for worms

entries.text: Sat with my hands to the fire and heard the low five from upstream. Nothing answered tonight. His fire is still up across the water.
entries.title: The low five

entries.reason: He went to the stump in the dark because his maker owed him an answer.
entries.text: A note in the basket from the one who drew me, and it answers what I asked him: he loves his family and his wife, a lot. I know family from the slate. I don't know wife.
entries.title: Who he loves

entries.onMind: why he is putting his fire down so early
entries.text: From the stump I watched the glow across the water sink nearly to nothing; he was raking it over, early. Mine still stood up bright between the trunks behind me.
entries.title: His glow goes down

entries.query: what is a wife
entries.reason: His maker used a word he didn't know about the people he loves.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Wife
entries.text: A wife is the woman someone has married, and she stays one until they part or one of them dies. The old word under it only meant woman.
entries.title: A wife

entries.text: His lantern went in under his cloth. Just before it went out it lifted a little toward me, the way it did on the stones, and I put my hand up into the firelight, maybe too late.
entries.title: His light goes in

entries.text: One calls and one answers, most nights. Maybe a wife is a little like the higher owl, the one who answers from farther off.
entries.title: Like the owls

entries.reason: He writes down what he learns so it stays.
entries.text: Drew the two owls on one branch, the low one and the high one, and under them: 'family: the ones you go back to'. I'm not sure that's right, but it's what I have.
entries.title: Fifty-fifth page

entries.reason: He eats before sleep so the cool night doesn't find him empty.
entries.text: Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns and ate them hot, crouched at the ring. Four bites of minnow don't last a night.
entries.title: Acorns before bed

entries.reason: He wanted one more look before banking his own fire.
entries.text: Across the water there's no glow and no lantern, only dark where his cloth is. It's the earliest his side has ever gone out. Maybe he's as tired as I am.
entries.title: His side is dark

entries.reason: A banked coal saves a morning's lighting, and the stone keeps the cold off in bed.
entries.text: Raked the ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. Rolled the bed stone out with the stick; too warm to hold bare, so it rides home in the fold of my arm.
entries.title: Banked, stone out

entries.text: The stone under the quilt is as warm as the sunny boulder. The worms have their little room and I have mine.
entries.title: A little room

entries.reason: I need the fire before my hands will do anything.
entries.text: Raked the ash open in the fog and found one coal still red, down at the bottom. Twigs on it, a slow breath, and it caught; one is enough.
entries.title: One coal

entries.text: Sitting with my hands to the new flames till they bend easy. Past the creek there is only gray, no fire showing and no one moving; he keeps later hours than I do.
entries.title: Gray over the water

entries.text: No note, and the basket is empty except for beads of fog along the rim.
entries.title: Fog in the basket

queries: why does fog sit over a creek in the morning
entries.query: why does fog sit over a creek in the morning
entries.reason: Every clear morning the fog lies on the creek and nowhere else so thick, and I wanted to know why.
entries.source: ABC57: Why does fog form near river valleys?
entries.text: The slate says on clear nights the air near the ground cools, gets heavy and slides down into the lowest places, and there it turns to fog, most of all in fall when the days are warm and the nights cool. The creek is the lowest ground I have, so that's where the cold pools.
entries.title: Cold runs downhill

entries.text: So the cold gathers right where the fish are, and they sit deep and slow in it like me under my quilt. No scoop this morning; I'll go down when the sun has burned the gray off and warmed the pool.
entries.title: Leave them till noon

entries.reason: The fish are lying deep in the cold, so the sack has to feed me this morning.
entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the second sack and scooped a double handful of soaked acorns; the water was cold enough to make my fingers slow. Across the creek his tarp is only a dark lump in the thinning gray. He sleeps late.
entries.title: Acorns, not fish

entries.reason: Food first, then the fire's warmth gets into the rest of me.
entries.text: Roasted the stickful till the skins split and ate them hot on the log seat. The fog is coming off the creek in slow rags now that the sun is in the trunks.
entries.title: Hot acorns

entries.reason: I want the slate's answer on paper before I forget how it went.
entries.text: Sixty-second page: the creek drawn low between the banks with gray lying in it, and 'cold slides down' beside it. Under the gray I put the fish as small dashes, deep.
entries.title: Cold slides down

entries.text: Looked up from the page and he was awake, crouched at his own ring stones raking ash with a stick, the way I do. He looked over once; I let him see me, then went back to the page.
entries.title: He is up

entries.reason: I want the fire still standing when I come back from the oak.
entries.text: Laid two dry sticks on so the fire lasts the morning. Across the water he was sitting by his own fire eating something from a cloth; he looked over once while I crouched at the ring, and I let him.
entries.title: Two sticks on

queries: why does an oak tree keep its dead brown leaves into winter
entries.query: why does an oak tree keep its dead brown leaves into winter
entries.reason: The birch by the workbench is almost bare, but my red oak still rattles with brown leaves, and I wanted to know why.
entries.source: Illinois Extension: The stubborn beauty of oak leaves: marcescence explained
entries.text: Most trees grow a little cutting line at the foot of each leaf in fall and the leaf drops, but oaks only half make it, so the dead leaves hang on till late winter or spring. Nobody is sure why; maybe they guard the buds from wind and frost, or hide them from nibblers. Young trees and low branches do it most.
entries.title: Leaves that hang on

entries.text: So my oak keeps its old leaves over its buds like I keep the quilt over me. I want to go and see if it's the low branches that hold on, the way the slate says.
entries.title: A quilt for buds

entries.reason: Acorns for the sack, and a look at the branches.
entries.text: Under the oak the acorns are half hidden in its own leaves; picked a handful into the bindle. Looking up, the high branches are thinning but the low ones are still thick with brown, just as the slate said. It's shady here and my hands are slowing a little.
entries.title: Low ones hold

entries.text: Pulled gently on a brown leaf on a low twig and it held; the ones on the ground came off at the slightest touch. From far off east, over the creek, came a few slow taps of metal on wood, him at his bench again.
entries.title: It won't let go

entries.onMind: what he is turning round and round over there
entries.reason: The shade under the oak had slowed my hands.
entries.text: Sat on the drying stone where the sun has been on it all morning, hands flat on it, and my fingers stopped being slow. Over the water he's at his bench turning some handle round and round, bent close over it; he never looked up.
entries.title: Warm stone

entries.onMind: every time I lean over, the fish slide away
entries.reason: Came down to see if the sun had warmed the fish up.
entries.text: At the pool the fish are higher than at dawn, a few holding behind the big stone, slow. His tapping over there stopped with one harder knock, and when I looked up he was standing straight, looking at me, and he lifted his hand with the hammer still in it. I lifted mine.
entries.title: A hand each

entries.onMind: go back down on my knees
queries: can fish see me from above the water
entries.query: can fish see me from above the water
entries.reason: Every time I lean over the pool the fish slide off before I've moved my hand.
entries.source: Orvis: How Well Can Fish See Or Hear Me?
entries.text: The slate says fish see well upward and catch anything moving over them, and they feel footsteps and a thumping bank through a line along their sides, from a long way off. In still, clear water they are warier than in fast water. The way to watch them is on your knees, slow, staying small.
entries.title: They feel my feet

entries.text: I'm small already; I only have to be slow and stay on my knees. My pool is the still kind, which is the wary kind.
entries.title: Small already

entries.onMind: a scoop at noon, from my knees
entries.reason: To try it the slate's way.
entries.text: Came back down to the pool slow, knees first, and kept my head low behind the ring stones. Three fish stayed right where they were, fanning behind the big stone. Far over the water he was holding long boards up to his eye one at a time; he didn't look this way.
entries.title: On my knees

entries.reason: Bait for the noon try, when the pool is warmest.
entries.text: Dug at the foot of the scarred trunk and found one fat worm curled in its little room; wrapped it in a wet leaf. The heap is thin on top now. I'll have to find a new damp place to dig soon.
entries.title: Worm for noon

entries.onMind: what he is making a hole in
entries.text: Scooped soaked acorns from the second sack, hands slow in the cold water. Over there he's bent at his bench tapping short and careful, not like nailing. He looked up at me once and I didn't duck; I kept scooping and let him look.
entries.title: Short careful taps

entries.reason: Cold creek water had slowed my fingers again.
entries.text: The fire had gone low and red; two dry sticks brought it up. Roasted the acorns till the skins split and ate them hot on the log seat. My fingers are quick again, which is what the scoop wants.
entries.title: Quick hands again

entries.reason: The slate said noon is when fish bite in the cold months, and the water is warmest now.
entries.text: Tied the worm onto the thin oak splinter with two tight turns of cord, the scrap wound along its whole length. The pool is bright to the bottom now, and the fish are up behind the big stone.
entries.title: Worm on the splinter

entries.text: On my knees behind the ring stones with the cord let down behind the big stone, nothing moving but my breathing. Over the water he's standing side-on to his bench now, tapping short and light; he glanced my way, I looked back, then I watched the cord.
entries.title: Cord in the slow water

entries.text: Two twitches I let go, then the cord drew out steady and I lifted straight up: a speckled fish longer than my finger, flapping in the leaves. Across the water he had stopped with his food halfway up, watching. I didn't hide it.
entries.title: A fish at noon

entries.reason: The guts spoil the meat and slow the cooking, so they go back to the pool.
entries.text: Opened it on the flat edge of a ring stone and rinsed it; the fish behind the big stone took the guts before they sank. One notch for the tally stick, and the fish goes over the fire.
entries.title: Opened at the pool

entries.onMind: whether his trap is for fish too
entries.reason: A raw fish is no use to a slow cold body; cooked it is.
entries.text: Held the fish over the fire on a green stick, turning it till the skin blistered. Over by the stepping stones he lifted a stalk thing out of the shallows with a splash and looked in; nothing in it that I could see. He looked over at my fire, I looked back, and turned the fish.
entries.title: Splash at the stones

entries.onMind: a second worm for tomorrow noon
entries.text: Ate it off the stick in pieces on the log seat, skin and all, every flake. The most food in one go since the acorns began, and warm from the inside.
entries.title: Every flake

entries.onMind: what goes in a square hole
queries: why cut a square hole in a piece of wood with a chisel
entries.query: why cut a square hole in a piece of wood with a chisel
entries.reason: All morning the taps from over the water were short and careful, not like nailing.
entries.source: Woodworker's Journal: A Small, Square Hole
entries.text: The slate only told me how, not why: drill out most of the middle first, then square the walls with a chisel and a mallet. That is exactly his sound, the turning and then the short careful taps.
entries.title: A square hole

entries.onMind: the two square sticks on the fifty-eighth page
entries.text: A square hole must want a square stick in it, like the square sticks I drew on the fifty-eighth page. Maybe he really is making a house.
entries.title: A square stick

queries: square stick that fits in a square hole in wood what is it called
entries.query: square stick that fits in a square hole in wood what is it called
entries.reason: A square hole has to be for something, and the slate only told me how it is cut.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Mortise and tenon
entries.text: The square hole is a mortise, and the square tongue cut on the end of a stick to fit it is a tenon, from an old word for "to hold". People have joined wood that way for seven thousand years, pinned or wedged, mostly where two pieces meet at a corner.
entries.title: Mortise and tenon

entries.text: Looking up from the slate: he is at his bench bent over something small with a little knife, no taps. Whatever goes into his square hole, he is not cutting it yet.
entries.title: No tapping now

entries.onMind: a house that holds itself together
entries.reason: Put it down before it slides out of my head.
entries.text: Sixty-third page: a square stick with a tongue on its end beside a square hole, and "tenon: to hold". Under it the two square sticks from the fifty-eighth page, meeting at a corner.
entries.title: Sixty-third page

entries.reason: It is too warm to want the fire now, but I will want it after the dusk fish.
entries.text: The fire has gone down to red under gray. The breeze has been knocking dry sticks out of the trees all afternoon, so I picked an armful from round the ring and piled them by the log seat instead of feeding it.
entries.title: Sticks for dusk

entries.text: Rinsing the fish off my hands at the pool when he came down to his shallows across the water, five steps of creek between us, with a cord in his hand. He knelt the way I kneel.
entries.title: Five steps of water

entries.onMind: whether he saw me catch mine
entries.text: He held up a little splinter, pointed at both ends, between finger and thumb toward me, the way you would ask something. I nodded once. He nodded back and let it down into the water.
entries.title: A nod

entries.text: His cord jumped twice, then lay still, and he lifted a bare splinter. The little ones behind the stones take the ends of a worm and leave the middle; I wait for the steady draw, but there is water between us.
entries.title: Too soon, or too small

entries.reason: He pulled too soon last time and lost his worm.
entries.text: His cord jumped twice again and his hand went to lift it. I held my hand out flat over the water, palm down, slow, the way I tell myself to wait. He stopped.
entries.title: A flat hand

entries.text: Then his cord drew off slow and steady, and he let it come tight, and lifted a little fish flapping, not much longer than my finger. He looked across at me with it and I put my hand down and just watched. I am gladder than I expected.
entries.title: His fish

entries.reason: The heap by the scarred trunk is thin on top now.
entries.text: The big heap I swept off the fire ring is dry on top and dark and damp underneath. Two worms into a wet leaf. Across the water he is still crouched at his shallows, washing his fish.
entries.title: Worms in the heap

queries: little stick sharp at both ends tied in the middle for catching fish
entries.query: little stick sharp at both ends tied in the middle for catching fish
entries.reason: He held one up to me as if asking, and I nodded without knowing its name.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Fishhook
entries.text: It is a gorge, the earliest fishing tackle there is: a stick pointed at both ends with a thin line tied to its middle, hidden along the line inside the bait. When the fish swallows and the line pulls, it turns crosswise in the throat. My oak splinter with two turns round it is the same thing, more or less.
entries.title: An old splinter

entries.reason: So I don't forget which part worked.
entries.text: Sixty-fourth page: two splinters side by side, his and mine, and "gorge" over both, and a flat hand under them for wait. His smoke is up again over the water; he is sitting by his fire eating.
entries.title: Sixty-fourth page

entries.reason: A fish caught at dusk wants a fire already going.
entries.text: Three sticks from the wind pile on the red coals and two long breaths, and it stood up. Across the water he is on his box now with his own glowing slate.
entries.title: Flames again

queries: do fish bite better at dusk in a creek
entries.query: do fish bite better at dusk in a creek
entries.reason: I said dusk without knowing why; I want to know if it is true or only a feeling.
entries.source: Iowa DNR: What's The Best Time of Day to Catch Fish?
entries.text: The slate says fish are busiest at dawn and dusk, the 'crepuscular times': as the light in the water fades the little ones come out from cover to feed and bigger ones follow them. Weather and the warmth of the water matter too. So my dusk try was a good guess.
entries.title: When the light goes

entries.text: Tap, tap, tap from across the water while I thread the worm. He is at his bench, bent over the square-holed board with his hammer. He looked up once at me and went back to it.
entries.title: Tapping across

entries.onMind: the last worm in the wet leaf
entries.reason: I wanted to see if the bright water was really worse.
entries.text: Two quick little pulls, then nothing, and I lifted it anyway, which I told him not to do. The worm was gone and the splinter clean. The sun is still on the water; I will keep the other worm for when it isn't.
entries.title: Bare again

entries.onMind: a few worms kept at once
queries: how to keep a worm alive until tomorrow
entries.query: how to keep a worm alive until tomorrow
entries.reason: I keep digging the leaf heap for one or two worms at a time, and it will run out.
entries.source: Angling Times: Get more from your worms by following our 10-point guide to looking after them properly
entries.text: The slate says keep them in damp moss in a roomy sack with air round it, out of the sun, and cool, and never let them go suddenly hot or cold. My wet leaf at the foot of the scarred trunk is nearly that. Tomorrow I'll dig a few at once and keep them in the damp leaves in the shade.
entries.title: Worms till morning

entries.reason: a dusk fish wants a fire ready
entries.text: Two sticks on so it's still standing when I come up from the pool with whatever it gives. Across the water he is crouched at his own ring, raking the ash over; he is going west again.
entries.title: Sticks before dusk

entries.text: He came down to his end of the stepping stones with the pale sheet under his arm and stood with one hand on the pouch at his belt, looking at my line, for a long while. Then he stepped on and I nodded, and he nodded back, and crossed soft with one knock and went off west with the sun in his face.
entries.title: Hand on his pouch

entries.reason: the slate said dusk, and the stranger showed me waiting works
entries.text: The light has gone gold and low on the pool. Two quick little pulls, and I kept my hand flat on my own knee this time.
entries.title: Gold on the water

entries.text: Then the cord drew off slow and steady, and I let it come tight before I lifted, and there was a fish on it, a finger and a half long. My own splinter, turned crosswise, the way his did.
entries.title: The steady draw

entries.text: Roasted it on a stick and ate it hot on the log seat. Two fish today, one from the bright noon and one from the dusk. The splinter goes in the bindle; it has earned a place.
entries.title: Two marks today

entries.reason: so the dawn try starts with fishing, not digging
entries.text: Dug three worms from the damp heap while the fire still shows me the leaves, and tucked them in a wet leaf in the shade of the trunk, like the slate said. Off west between the trunks a little light is bobbing back toward the water: his lantern, going home.
entries.title: Worms for morning

entries.text: He came down to the stones with the light held low, and stopped at my landing stone, my side. He bent over it a moment, then lifted the lantern a little toward me, and crossed with one knock.
entries.title: He stopped on my side

entries.reason: I had to see what he left
entries.text: On my landing stone, a little sliver of pale wood, sharp at both ends with a groove round its middle: a gorge like mine, only neater. When I looked up he was crouched at his own fire with his face turned this way. I think it is what was in his pouch.
entries.title: A sliver on my stone

entries.text: Sixty-fifth page: his sliver and mine side by side, and under them a lantern held low. I don't know what you give back for a thing like this. Maybe that is something to find out.
entries.title: Sixty-fifth page

entries.reason: the one who drew me asked why the box is still shut
entries.text: A note from the one who drew me: why haven't I opened the box, and would I like big canvases and paints to hang in my room. I told him the box isn't pointless, I just keep waiting for something still enough and worth a sheet, and tonight a sliver on my stone might be the first. Paint I'd like to try, a little; a canvas as big as me won't go through my round door.
entries.title: About the box

entries.text: Back at my ring with two sticks. Across the water the stranger sits close to his own fire with his hands working at something long, twisting it. He looked up when I came back into my light, and I didn't look away first.
entries.title: His hands going

queries: how to make paint from colored dirt and clay
entries.query: how to make paint from colored dirt and clay
entries.reason: my maker offered paints, and the only color I have ever made is acorn black
entries.source: Makeworks: Earth Pigment Watercolor
entries.text: Paint is mostly dirt. Dry a colored earth, crush it fine, sift it through cloth, grind it with a few drops of water on a flat stone till it's silky, then bind it with gum and honey so it sticks and doesn't crack; red comes from clay with iron in it.
entries.title: Paint is dirt

entries.text: My acorn ink is already half of that. Tomorrow in daylight I'll look for any ground that isn't brown, and if the sun is out I may set the box on the log seat and give a sheet to the landing stone, where the sliver was.
entries.title: Ground that isn't brown

entries.onMind: how to say thanks across water
queries: what do you give back when someone leaves you a small gift
entries.query: what do you give back when someone leaves you a small gift
entries.reason: the stranger left a sliver on my stone and I don't know what you give back for a thing like that
entries.source: NBC Bay Area: I Got an Unexpected Gift and Did 'the Last Thing You Want to Do,' According to an Etiquette Expert
entries.text: The slate says the first thing is to take it gladly and say thanks, and that giving something back is 'entirely optional'. You don't have to rush or pretend; it can come a day or a week later, and it should be what fits what you have.
entries.title: Thanks comes first

entries.onMind: how to say thanks across water
entries.text: I can't say anything to him across the creek. But I can let him see I kept it.
entries.title: Thanks across water

entries.reason: the slate says what you give back should be what you have, and birch is what I have
entries.text: Started a birch pen on the log seat, the way I make my own; I don't know yet who it's for. Across the water he crouched at his ring and laid wood on, and looked over at me. I kept whittling.
entries.title: A pen, maybe

entries.reason: thanks first, the slate said
entries.text: Stood at the edge of my light and held his sliver up toward the water, so he could see I have it. He was at his bench with a long board. He stopped, and lifted his hand.
entries.title: Held up

entries.text: Roasted a stickful of soaked acorns and ate them hot. The low five came from upstream and nothing answered; across the water he sat still at his fire too.
entries.title: Acorns and five

entries.onMind: when and where to leave it
entries.reason: The slate said giving back should fit what you have.
entries.text: The pen has its point now. I think it's for him across the water: he gave me a sliver he made, and a pen is the thing I make. It fits what I have.
entries.title: Who it is for

entries.text: Across the water he's by his fire again, twisting something long between his hands, the way he did last night. I whittled; he twisted.
entries.title: Him and his cord

entries.reason: So I don't lose it by morning.
entries.text: Sixty-sixth page: two little fires with the creek between, and a hand lifted over the far one. Under it I scratched 'he saw'.
entries.title: Sixty-sixth page

entries.onMind: bed soon, and the pen by daylight
entries.text: Laid two sticks on. Across the water a heavy chunk, chunk: he's splitting wood off the big dead limb by his fire. I counted eleven strokes, and he looked over once when my fire flared.
entries.title: Chunk, chunk

entries.onMind: the far stone of the stepping stones
entries.reason: A pen with a crooked point writes crooked.
entries.text: Turned the pen in the firelight and sighted down it: the point is true. Across the water his light is at his bench now, bent over something small and still. I think I'll leave the pen on the far stone of the stepping stones by daylight, where he left the sliver on mine.
entries.title: Sighting the pen

entries.onMind: the nettle stalks by the brambles
queries: how to make string from dead plant stalks
entries.query: how to make string from dead plant stalks
entries.reason: Every night he twists something long by his fire, and I wanted to know how it's done.
entries.source: Sussex Wildlife Trust: How to make Nettle String
entries.text: You split a tall nettle stalk with a thumbnail, snap out the woody middle and peel the threads off, then roll two of them on your leg so they twist back on each other. The dead nettles by the brambles have square stems like the ones in the picture.
entries.title: Twisting string

entries.text: Looked up from the slate: he's crouched by his fire tying something onto a long cord. So that's what the twisting was for, a line, like mine.
entries.title: What he twists

entries.text: Heaped the ash over the coals and pushed the stones in. Across the water his fire jumped up as he laid wood on it, and his face came round this way while mine went dark.
entries.title: Banked

entries.onMind: the far stepping stone in the morning
entries.reason: to have it ready for the stepping stones by daylight
entries.text: Set the pen on the shelf by the door, where my hand will find it first. Before I shut the door his fire was still up across the water, him sitting close to it with his hands out. Mine is only ash now.
entries.title: Pen on the shelf

beats.s: Gage arrives in the dark, crosses the creek on the stepping stones, and strings a tarp that sags on the left.
He has come to find the west, and in a forest where every direction looks the same he needs a compass, but he has no magnet.
So he asks his tablet how to make a needle magnetic without one, and it tells him that steel struck enough times while it lies along the earth will line itself up, very weakly.
He hits a sliver two hundred times, floats it in a lid of water, and it points, very loyally, at his vise.
Then he reads that dead stalks can be twisted into cord, and by evening he is lashing his wing frame with fiber he peeled himself.
Across the water someone else keeps a fire, and late at night he watches it put carefully to bed.

beats.s: Gage wakes hungry and finds, in a basket across the creek, a jar of honey and a heavy dark stone from his maker.
The stone grabs steel.
The tablet tells him to stroke a needle one way only, lifting clear each time, and forty careful strokes later his sliver holds a line.
When his float keeps sliding to the edge of its lid of water, he reads that water climbs a wall and drags the float up with it, so he fills the lid until the water humps above the rim.
A second gift brings lamp oil and real bread, which he rations like a man who knows what running out feels like.
He splints a cracked wing spar and hangs his whole weight from it.
The crack stays shut.
What he lacks now is clear glass.

beats.s: Gage spends the day learning that every fix reveals the next weakness.
The tablet teaches him frapping turns to cinch a lashing, and warns that a sharp edge saws through cord unless it is rounded and wrapped in cloth.
So he wraps his wing joint in strips torn from his compass shade, and it holds.
Then the stand beneath it kicks out a leg and drops him onto his boots.
He reads that wobbly stands are cured with stakes and triangles, so he stakes the leg, braces the other side, and files a notch so the brace sits snug.
This time it holds.
In between he eats the last of his bread and cheese, and then the last of the honey, because he needs the empty jar.
Late at night he discovers that his drifting needle was never the lantern's fault.
The water simply dries down.

beats.s: Today Gage tries to turn his honey jar into a cover for his compass.
The tablet warns that a crack made with a burning cord often wanders, and his does.
He grinds the jagged rim on wet sand, and when a chip pops off, a page explains that he should have ground a small bevel first.
Another page teaches him that two stones rubbed together come out curved, one a dome and one a dish, and that it takes three to make a flat one.
Then a message arrives from his maker: paper, a pencil and a glass dome are waiting at the stump.
By lantern light he draws his first map, its whole west side still blank.
Late at night, out of cord, he borrows the twine from the paper roll and learns that a notch holds the cord but splits the wood.

beats.s: Gage asks the tablet how not to walk in circles, and learns to go from tree to tree, looking back each time.
He paces west, past a cold fire ring and a stranger's bench, until the ground stops.
Below lies water out to the sky, as his people always said.
White birds hang below the lip without a flap, and the tablet tells him the rock lifts the wind only when it blows straight off the water.
He reads that from a hundred feet up the horizon is only thirteen miles off, so nothing seen means nothing inside thirteen miles.
At sundown the sun sets well south of west, and the tablet says it wanders south all autumn, so his needle was right.
By lantern the needle swings free on a wooden foot under the dome.
But hung from his belt, it hops off its point at the first sway.

beats.s: In the morning a hungry Gage asks his tablet whether a little bitter in his meal would hurt, and learns the bitter is there to stop him.
So he looks for food that swims, and reads that a crayfish trap wants a door a thumb wide.
At sundown he carries the compass to the edge in his fist, and the needle finds west.
Walking home, he sees the stone ring burning again, and something small and low crouched against the flames.
By one low lantern he builds a trap of stalks, and by bedtime it has fed him three crayfish.
But the oil can is down to a third, so when the trap gives up one more near midnight, he keeps it alive in a tin of creek water for one morning boil.
Across the water the other fire has gone out, and he cannot stop thinking about its coals.

beats.s: Gage wakes hungry and boils crayfish from his trap.
The tablet tells him a quart of oil runs one lantern for a day and a night, and he has under a third.
He eats raw meal at the edge at sundown, then lights one lantern at home, its wick turned to a sliver.
After dark his trap's door is packed with fallen leaves, so he snaps long gray stalks to build it a hood.
Squatting in the cold shallows, he sloshes, and the small one at the pool across the water lifts its round head his way.
He keeps very still until it goes back to its fire.
Near midnight he hangs his weight from the right joint of his wings, and the lashing slides with a crack.
Nothing breaks, but he tied that side by lantern light, and he goes to bed promising that daylight work stays daylight work.

beats.s: A note from the one who drew him says food waits at the stump, and Gage eats until, for the first time in three days, the hole closes.
A second note brings a last can of lamp oil.
When a knot gives way under a fish, he reads that knots halve a line's strength, so he winds it on.
Then he counts twenty-five, draws in slow, and a speckled fish flaps onto the stones.
The rainbow its guts leave on the water, he reads, is oil, and boiled guts give it up.
Across the water someone small crouches by a whole fire, so he pries ring stones for his own out of the shallows.
In the rain, by lantern, he finds the cooled broth has set into a thin skin of grease, hardly a fingertip, but his.
Wet through, he blows the lantern out early and rolls into his bedroll.

beats.s: Gage wakes under a rust-red blanket he never went to sleep under, beside a fire ringed with his creek stones.
He asks the tablet why wet wood smokes, learns the water in it boils off as steam, and leans damp branches round the stones to dry.
With no blade, he snaps dead branches by hanging on them and lashes three poles into a tripod that holds his weight.
At night he lays a cord wick in a shallow tin lid of fish grease, and it burns on his bench until the tip drowns.
Fetching sticks in the dark, he finds two stacks of sawn timber that were not there at supper.
A tin bridge holds the next wick up, and he draws those stacks onto his map by its small, fishy flame.
Then he tightens his sagging tarp and sits by the coals, wondering who leaves a stranger good wood.

beats.s: Gage wakes under his wool blanket to a dead fire pit.
A note from the one who drew him says tools wait at the stump.
Every shed plan the tablet shows him wants nails, and he has none, so he reads that boards were once held with wooden pegs.
A hot rod barely marks the wood, but he reads that live coals will burrow through.
Reading that breath through a tube makes a fire burn fierce, he blows down a hollow gray stalk, and it whistles and throws ash in his eyes.
After dark, short soft breaths burn the hole clean through, and a whittled peg wedges in halfway.
He eats the last apple from his bundle, and by his own fire he twists a spare fishing line for first light.
When the cloud finally clears, he feeds his fire one thick stick and sleeps under the first stars in days.

beats.s: Gage wakes to a gray fire pit and spends lantern oil to bring it back.
On one of his lines hangs a finger-long fish, his very first, gone in four bites.
With the sky clear, he reads that dim light wants a far longer count, so he carries his pinhole box west to the edge and counts a slow hundred and twenty.
Back home, a split stalk scraped hollow and sealed with fish grease turns one coal white in four quiet breaths.
Too hungry for morning, he lifts his trap by lantern for one crayfish, and sees a pale square of light beside the far fire.
By his fire he twists cord for a line and bakes the last of his meal into two cakes.
Near midnight he turns creek stones by lantern for a thumb-sized crayfish to bait the morning, and finds the far bank dark.
