Poured a warm spoonful into the bench lantern's empty fount: a small, smoky, fishy yellow flame for about a count of a hundred, then it clouded in the cold fount and guttered out. Grease sets before it can climb; he wonders about keeping it warm or a shorter climb. Set the whole lantern on the ring stones by his fire until the fount's grease went clear and lit it: it burned steady past a count of three hundred, then died to a blue bead the moment he carried it off. Warm isn't the answer; he wonders about something shallow, the wick lying in the grease with only its tip up. Tried something shallow: a scrap tin lid with the lantern's set grease and the broth's skin warmed in it and a thumb-long stalk-cord wick lying down, tip up. Lit, it burned on the bench five steps from the fire for a count of a hundred and eighty, small and fishy, then the tip slumped in and drowned. The tip has to stay up. Hammered a strip of tin into a little bent bridge and laid the wick over it so the tip stands clear of the grease; rewarmed, lit, it burned on the bench past a count of six hundred, still going, and he pinched it out himself to save the grease. The bridge gets hot and the grease spits, but the tip stays up. With the drizzle stopped he lit the bridged lid lamp on the bench and drew by it: enough for a pencil line if he leans close, not enough to see the whole sheet. A lantern for the room, a lid for the hand. Spent a little lantern oil lighting a splinter to restart a dead fire. Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone and lit it on the bench to sketch the shed by; pinched it out with grease still in the lid. Spent the morning fish's head on the crayfish trap instead of the grease tin. Walked home from the edge with one lantern turned down to a bead. Took a thumb of grease out of the lamp lid to seal the blowpipe, so the lamp is that much shorter. Boiled the palm-long fish with its head and guts; gold beads of grease rose on the water, and he left half the broth in the tin by the ring to set a skin for the lamp. Feeding his fire before lunch warmed the broth tin on the ring stones and melted the grease skin back into the broth; lifted it off to cool and set again. The gorge fish's head and guts went into the broth tin for the lamp. Walked home from the edge with one lantern turned down to a bead and put it out once his fire was up.

threads.name: Warm enough to work
threads.summary: fire and a hammer. Split his first branch with the axe (the first swing glanced off a hand from his boot; feet wide, let the head drop), fed the halves to the pit, and dug a rusty pencil-thick steel rod out of the scrap pile to straighten and heat. Hammered the kink out of the rod on the bench, heated the point red in the pit and pushed it into a split half: a fingernail deep, then black and stuck; twenty heats a hole. Read that people burned holes with live coals laid on the spot again and again, the wood round it wetted and the char chipped out between. Plan: the rod makes a dent, a coal finishes it, tried first on an offcut. Tried it on the scorched split half: wetted a ring round the dent, set a coal in it from the rod tip. Left alone it goes gray; blown on, it glows and eats down. Three coals with the stub knife scraping char between: a third of the way through, but the top is already wider than his thumb. Read that a blowpipe aims a stream of air to make a fire intensely hot; means to push the pith out of one of the gray stalks with the rod and use it. Gathered four straight gray stalks on the east bank, rodded the pith out of one and sighted a coin of sky down it (a second split). Blown through, it turns a coal near white and it eats fast; blown hard it whistles and throws ash in his eyes, but short soft breaths burn the hole a nail deeper and straighter, nearly halfway. After dark, short soft breaths down the stalk: no whistle, no ash, and the hole went past halfway by firelight. The top is still too wide for a snug peg. Fed the pit three split sticks and burned the hole clean through the split half by firelight: straight below, a finger too wide at the top. Whittled two pegs with the long knife on the crate; the first was too skinny at the tip, the fatter second wedges tight halfway, not driven yet. By the lit grease lamp sketched the shed three paces by two on the map sheet: sill boards lapped at the corners, corner posts, a top plate, braces; counted twenty-odd peg holes, and one hole took an evening, so burning them all is no plan. Whittled a second long-tapered peg by the pit; it wedges a hair deeper than the first. Two pegs, one hole; wants a faster way to bore. Carved a starter pit for the next hole with the stub knife and it ran along the grain into a slot as long as his thumb; across the grain it bites and stops. Cut the next starter pit across the grain by the grease lamp: the stub knife bit a round seat the size of a pea and stopped, no slot. Whittled a third peg by the fire late and shaved one side too far: lopsided, kept as a spare; shave all round next time. Fed the pit one thick stick before bed on the first clear night in days; the smoke went straight up. Woke to a gray pit and spent a little lantern oil on a splinter to relight it. Asked the tablet how to join boards with no nails or drill: every joint wants glue, screws or a power drill, even the laps get nailed; decided on lapped corners with one peg each instead of twenty-odd holes. Carried the first two-by-four from the stack to the bench in daylight and penciled a lap on one end. Bore down on the saw and the first cut wandered a pencil-width off and leaned a finger out of true. Read to cut on the waste side, start short strokes against a knuckle, forefinger down the handle, no weight; the second cut ran straight. Read that the long cheek of a lap is sawn on the waste side of the half-depth line and pared down to it after, edges toward the middle; sawed it with the sill on end in the vise and the waste dropped clean, leaving a low hump to pare with the long knife. Asked how to make a peg hole with no drill: a nail, a bow drill, a brace and bit, or a sharpened rod heated red-hot that burns through; means to try a rod from the scrap pile in his pit. His maker left him a notebook with squared pages; he fetched it from the stump and put the timber counts on the first page. Heated a pencil-thick rod from the scrap pile red in his pit and burned a peg hole into the offcut: a knuckle deep after three trips, ragged and funnel-shaped. Read that hot coals left on the spot, with the char scraped out and the wood wet around it, do better; means to try that. Wet the offcut round the hole and tried coals in it: each went gray unless he blew on it, and three coals with the char scraped out took the hole half a knuckle deeper with straighter walls. Read that a hollow stem steers a coal burn; the dead stalks are pith, so he is looking for something with a hole down the middle. Read that flute makers get a tube by splitting the wood, gouging the middle out and joining the halves again; means to split a dead stalk with the stub knife, gouge the pith with the hooked one and lash it back as a blowpipe. By firelight split a dead stalk with the stub knife, scraped the pith out with the hooked one (one thin end cracked, so both halves went a finger shorter) and lashed it back with cord. Blowing through it, the seam whistles, but pinched shut it turns a single coal from red to white; means to seal the seam with grease. Worked a little cold fish grease from the lamp lid into a length of cord and wound it over the seam: no more whistle, and a coal went from red to white in four slow breaths instead of ten, though the mouth end tastes of fish. Came back from the creek with stiff fingers and fed two sticks on before bed; the woodpile is down to about six sticks. With the woodpile at six sticks and the pit gone cold, chopped dry middles from the big dead limb, lit a splinter at a lantern for a thimble of oil and brought the fire back with two puffs of the pipe. Fed two dry middles onto red embers before eating; they caught without smoke. Woodpile down to four old sticks and the rest of the middles. Split an armful of dry middles out of the big dead limb in the late sun and hung the axe back on its loop; woodpile back up for the night. Came home from the edge to a cold pit, lit a splinter at the lantern for a thimble of oil and brought the fire back on shavings and two dry middles. Fed two dry middles crosswise onto the coals later in the evening; they caught without a puff. Woodpile: four old sticks and about half the armful of middles. Too tired to saw, banked the pit instead of feeding it: raked ash over the last coals and pushed the ring stones in, to see if a coal keeps till morning and saves a thimble of oil. Next morning, raked the banked ash open: one coal the size of a pea had kept near the bottom, and shavings and one puff of the pipe brought the fire back without a thimble of oil. Means to bank it deeper tonight. Asked the tablet how deep the ash goes to keep coals overnight: no number, just burn down to coals, set the half-burned sticks aside, and heap all the ash you have over them; depth is trial and error. Tonight it gets all the ash. Before noon the pit was down to embers; two dry middles laid on caught without smoke. Banked the pit under every bit of ash before the evening walk west, to see if a coal keeps till he's back. Back from the edge an hour after banking, two coals were still red under all the ash; shavings, two middles and one puff brought it up, and the lantern went down to a bead. Fed one split middle after dark and it took without smoke; firelight to bore and write by, no oil. Before bed set the half-burned sticks aside and heaped every bit of ash over the coals again, ring stones pushed in. Next morning one coal like a bead lay under the heaped ash; shavings, a half-burned stick and a long breath brought it up, a second dawn without oil. Mid-afternoon the pit was two red coals under gray; shavings, a split middle and a long breath stood it up without smoke. Before the edge, heaped every bit of ash over the coals again and pushed the ring stones in. Back from the edge after dark, one coal under the heaped ash again; shavings, a long breath and a split middle stood it up, and he ate supper by it with the lantern out. Fed one split middle after dark and it caught without smoke. Split six dry middles off the dead limb after dark so the dawn fire needs no oil. Fed one split middle at bedtime hours; it went up clean.

timber.note: nine two-by-fours left on the stack (seven straight, one bowed, one twisted), sixteen planks untouched; on the bench three sills lapped into two square corners, each held with two nails, the first corner now also locked with two staggered pegs in cranked holes on the diagonal of the lap (the second hole splintered out underneath and was pressed back); a fourth sill and four doubled corner posts would want nine straight boards; the offcut has test holes, nails and now a practice mortise slot two fingers by four, one long wall leaning in at the bottom, and beside it a second slot cut side-on with both long walls straight and one end wall a hair off; tool chest, spade and nail keg beside the lean-to; a gray hone stone by the bench leg; eight flat creek stones in the footing heap, four checked level for the corners; the dark gray ringing cobble set aside for breaking stone

gage/state.woodpile: three old sticks and a few fresh-split dry middles, less five laid on the fire after dark and one split middle on the mid-afternoon fire; one half-burned stick by the pit, less one split middle to relight it after dark, less one more split middle fed after dark; plus six fresh-split dry middles off the dead limb after dark

items.title: a magnet
items.why: Can't make a compass needle point anywhere without one.

items.title: real food
items.why: Ate my last ration bar this morning, and the brambles are bare.

items.title: lamp oil
items.why: Heating things on the lanterns burned more oil than I counted; the bench one is down to a finger.

items.title: something to draw a map on
items.why: My maker offered a board and pencil; right now the only map is in my head and a sliver that points wrong.

items.title: a piece of clear glass
items.why: The lid needs a cover I can see through, and the only glass I have is a honey jar and my lantern globes.

items.title: a compass I can carry
items.why: The needle only works floating in a lid of water on the bench, and the walk west can't take the bench along.

items.title: something to eat while the meal soaks
items.why: Ate the last heel of bread at noon, and the acorn meal is still too bitter to eat for days.

items.title: more lamp oil
items.why: Under a third of a quart left, and the tablet says that's eight or nine hours of one flame, all told.

items.title: a fire of my own
items.why: Every night a whole fire glows across the water, and I sit with my hands cupped round one low lantern.

items.title: something that chops
items.why: Filed one saddle notch a finger deep into a wrist-thick branch and it took twenty minutes; a wall of poles needs a hundred.

items.title: nails, or something to fasten boards
items.why: Every shed plan wants screws or nails, and I have a hammer with nothing to drive.

entries.reason: He needed somewhere dry before he could think.
entries.text: Crossed the creek on the stones and stopped where the trees open up. Strung the tarp between two poles by lantern light. It sags on the left.
entries.title: Made camp

entries.text: Every direction in here looks like every other direction. I need a compass. I don't have a magnet. Started a list of what I do have.
entries.title: Which way is out

entries.reason: He wanted to start before he talked himself out of it.
entries.text: Something with a big wingspan crossed over the camp without making a sound. If it can get above these trees, so can a person with the right frame. Leaned two spars on the stand before bed.
entries.title: Something went over

entries.query: how to magnetize a steel needle without a magnet hammer earth magnetic field
entries.reason: Tablet woke up with the sun and the magnet problem was still at the top of the list.
entries.source: University of Illinois Physics Van: Magnetize Steel bar Facing North?
entries.text: Hit a steel bar enough times while it lies along the earth's field and the tiny magnetic regions inside shake loose and line up with it. The page calls the result a very weak magnet. Weak beats none.
entries.title: Hit it facing north

entries.text: The tablet has a speaker, so somewhere inside it is a magnet. It is also the only thing out here that answers back. Not opening it.
entries.title: Not the tablet

entries.reason: No north to line it up with except the one the sun gives him.
entries.text: Sun came up behind the lean-to, so that's east, give or take a lot. Clamped the sliver crossways to it and hit it with the wrench about two hundred times. My thumb took three of them.
entries.title: Two hundred taps

entries.text: Floated the sliver on a leaf in a dented tin lid at the pool. It turned, stopped, turned again, and never settled the same way twice. Could be the needle, could be the breeze.
entries.title: Leaf test

entries.reason: He knelt to dip the lid and saw it on the bottom.
entries.text: There's a net sack sunk in the pool under a flat stone, full of something cracked. I didn't put it there. Left it where it was.
entries.title: Not my sack

entries.query: floating needle compass won't settle same direction causes iron nearby weak magnetization
entries.reason: The leaf test told him nothing.
entries.source: Science Buddies: Make a Magnetic Compass
entries.text: A floating needle needs still water and nothing iron or steel close by, or it points at that instead of north. A breeze across an open lid will spin it all day. So the pool was the wrong test, and my camp is full of steel.
entries.title: Keep it off iron

entries.text: Filled the tin lid and set it on the bench out of the wind. The sliver swung around and pointed straight at the vise, every time. Very loyal. Wrong thing to be loyal to.
entries.title: Points at the vise

entries.onMind: marking one end of the needle
entries.text: Carried the lid ten paces past the bench, away from anything steel, and set it on flat dirt. It settled along the line I'd guessed from the sun three tries out of four. I still don't know which end is north.
entries.title: Three out of four

entries.reason: Needed to work with his hands after the needle.
entries.text: Wired a third spar across the two on the stand. The frame holds a triangle now, but it twists if I lift one corner, and the wire bites into the wood at every joint.
entries.title: Crosspiece

entries.text: There's a thin line of smoke standing up over the trees on the far side of the creek. It wasn't there this morning, or I didn't look. Somebody over there keeps a fire.
entries.title: Smoke to the west

entries.query: how to tell which end of a magnetized needle is north without a compass sun noon
entries.reason: A needle that only knows a line is half a compass.
entries.source: Almanac.com: How to Find North, South, East & West Without a Compass
entries.text: Push a stick in the ground, mark the tip of its shadow, wait about fifteen minutes, mark it again. The line between the marks runs east-west, and the first mark is the west end. Everybody's tablet knows where west is but mine.
entries.title: Shadow stick

entries.reason: Wire cuts the spars; something softer might grip instead.
entries.text: Between pebbles I dug through the scrap pile and came up with half a coil of tarred twine under a split crate. Stiff, smells like a boat. Might hold a joint without chewing the wood.
entries.title: Coil of twine

entries.onMind: marking one end of the needle
entries.text: Two pebbles, fifteen minutes apart, and a line between them. The first one is west. I set the lid next to it, away from the bench, and the sliver lay crossways to the line like it should, so I scratched a notch in the end on the right-hand side. That's north, if the sun's not lying too.
entries.title: First pebble

entries.reason: His last ration bar went this morning.
entries.text: Crossed on the stepping stones with the bag. The sack is still under its flat stone in the pool, and I still didn't touch it.
entries.title: Stepping stones

entries.text: The brambles are bare, but a wild rose climbs through them with little red hips, and a lot of its stems are freshly snapped, sap still wet. I ate three whole. Something inside them itches all the way down.
entries.title: Picked over

entries.onMind: how small the hands were that picked those
entries.text: Whoever keeps that fire picked this rose today, and they only took the low ones. Either they're careful or they're short.
entries.title: Fresh breaks

entries.reason: Three whole ones were enough of a lesson.
entries.text: Split the rest of the hips on the crate. Inside each one is a wad of seeds packed in fine hairs, and that's the itch. Scraped them out with the tip of a screwdriver and ate eleven shells. That's not a meal, it's a snack with a procedure.
entries.title: Hairs

entries.query: diagonal lashing vs square lashing stop frame twisting racking
entries.reason: The wired triangle twists every time a corner is lifted.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Lashing (ropework)
entries.text: Square lashing is for poles crossing at right angles; diagonal lashing is for poles crossing at a slant, the kind that braces a frame against racking. And you finish with frapping turns wrapped between the poles, which cinch the whole wrap tight. Wire doesn't frap.
entries.title: Lashings

entries.text: Cut the wire off all three joints and tapped the worst kinks straight on a flat stone with the wrench, in case I need it later. Then a diagonal lashing on the long corner with the tarred twine, four frapping turns, pulled till my palms stung. That corner doesn't move.
entries.title: Wire off

entries.reason: He found the twine under a split crate; nobody knows how long it sat there.
entries.text: Second corner, third frapping turn, and the twine broke. The tar on the outside is fine but the core has gone dry and brittle. One good joint out of three, and the frame still wobbles about two fingers at the free end.
entries.title: Snapped

entries.query: make cordage from plant fibers found near a creek reverse wrap strength
entries.reason: The tarred twine snapped on the second corner.
entries.source: Instructables: Make Rope Out of Dead Plants -- With No Tools
entries.text: Last year's dead weed stalks have a stringy skin around a woody core. Crack the core out, twist two bundles of the skin one way and wrap them around each other the other way, and they lock. Old twine is just plants somebody twisted; I can twist new.
entries.title: Twist your own

entries.text: East bank, upstream of the stones, there's a stand of gray dead stalks taller than me. Snapped about twenty off near the ground, cracked them every hand-width and peeled the skin in strips. My fingers went slow before the pile got big.
entries.title: Dead stalks

entries.reason: He measured the snapped corner's wrap against his arm.
entries.text: First arm's length of two-ply: fat in one place, thin in another. It held the wrench hanging off it, then the thin spot let go when I yanked. Second length I'm adding fiber before it runs out, not after. One lashing takes about four arm's lengths.
entries.title: Lumpy cord

entries.text: Smoke went up again over the trees past the creek a little after one, thicker than the morning's. Somebody over there just started a fire. I'm sitting here twisting weeds on an empty stomach.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.query: wild edible foods to forage in November forest acorns hackberry
entries.reason: He hasn't eaten a real meal since morning.
entries.source: Farmers' Almanac: Can You Eat Acorns? The Right Way to Forage, Leach, and Cook Them
entries.text: Acorns are food once you get the bitter out: crack them and boil the meats in changes of water until it stops going tea-colored, or soak them cold for days and change the water. I don't have a pot that's ever seen a fire. Cold soak, then.
entries.title: Bitter but food

entries.text: There's an oak on the east bank about twenty paces up from the stones. Filled the pouch and both shirt pockets, roughly forty, and tossed the ones with little round holes in them.
entries.title: Under the oak

entries.onMind: the creek does the water changes
entries.reason: The page explained what he'd been looking at all day.
entries.text: Crossed the stones to look at the sunk sack again. The water coming off it is brown like weak tea and trails downstream. Whoever lives over there is soaking acorns in the creek, which beats a jar, because the creek changes its own water.
entries.title: So that's the sack

entries.reason: He wanted to know how bitter is bitter.
entries.text: The vise cracks an acorn clean if I stop a quarter turn early; one more and it's paste. Meats go in a dented tin of water. Ate one raw to check: like chewing a tea bag and losing.
entries.title: Quarter turn

entries.reason: First word from his maker since he got here.
entries.text: A note came in on the tablet from the one who drew me, asking what the wings are for and whether there's anything I need. I told him the truth: west. And that a magnet would do more for me than asking.
entries.title: Note from my maker

entries.query: how to splice in new fibers when twisting two-ply cordage
entries.source: Jon's Bushcraft: cordage making
entries.text: Start one ply a hand shorter than the other so the two joins never land side by side, and lay new fiber in thin and overlapping instead of butting it on when the old runs out. My thin spot was both plies running out in the same place.
entries.title: Stagger the joins

entries.text: Four arm's lengths with the joins staggered. Ran it through my fingers twice and couldn't find a thin spot. Hung the wrench off it and bounced it; it held.
entries.title: Second length

entries.text: Second corner, diagonal lashing and frapping turns, tight when I tied it. After a dozen flexes of the frame the new cord stretched and the joint creeps about a finger. Better than two fingers. Green cord stretches; should have hung a rock off it overnight first.
entries.title: Holds, then creeps

entries.query: natural fiber rope shrinks when wet lashing tighten pioneering
entries.source: Animated Knots: Rope Materials
entries.text: Natural fiber line swells when it gets wet and draws up shorter, so a lashing tied dry pulls itself tighter once it's soaked. The catch: it slackens again as it dries. Might be enough to stop the creep long enough to see if the frame is true.
entries.title: Wet it down

entries.text: Poured the brown water off the acorn tin over the second corner, slow, so it soaked in instead of running off. The acorns needed fresh water anyway. The cord went dark and stiff.
entries.title: Tea on the joint

entries.text: Filled the tin at the creek and was snapping stalks when new smoke went up past the water, white and thick, like somebody just fed a fire that was going out. That's three fires today. Whoever it is doesn't let it die.
entries.title: Smoke, third time

entries.onMind: hanging a stone off the new cord tonight
entries.text: Got two arm's lengths twisted, then flexed the frame a dozen times. The wet joint didn't creep that I could see. I don't trust it yet: if it's loose by morning, the water did the work, not the lashing.
entries.title: No creep, for now

entries.query: cold leaching acorns how long grind meal faster
entries.source: Hunter Angler Gardener Cook: The Best Way to Make Acorn Flour
entries.text: Cold leaching takes days, a week or more for the bitter kinds, changing the water every day. Grinding the meats coarse first speeds it up because the water gets at more of each piece. My forty halves in a tin aren't dinner tonight.
entries.title: Days, not hours

entries.text: Crushed the soaked meats against the bottom of the tin with a stone until they were gravel, then poured the old water off. The new water went brown in a couple of minutes; before, it took an hour. Still days.
entries.title: Coarse meal

entries.text: Tied the third cord to the top of the wing stand and hung a fist-sized stone off the bottom, so it does its stretching tonight instead of on the frame. It turns slowly one way, then back.
entries.title: Stone on a string

entries.text: Sun's going down behind the trees to the west and the tablet's already dimming. Hungry enough that the stone on the string looks edible.
entries.title: Tablet's dimming

entries.text: Pinched some of the crushed meal out of the tin and chewed it. Dried my whole mouth out; spat it into the scrap pile. Days, like the page said.
entries.title: Not yet

entries.text: Refilling the tin by the stalks, I looked up and saw it through the trunks past the water: a fire, low and orange, not just smoke this time. Something small moved in front of it once, or a log fell. Too far and too dark to tell.
entries.title: Fire, not smoke

entries.text: Filed the north notch on the sliver deeper so I can find it with a thumb in the dark. Kept the file and the wrench on the far side of the bench; steel nearby drags it.
entries.title: Deeper notch

entries.onMind: how far off a weak needle can be and still be useful
entries.text: Found the North Star through the gap over the tarp, low, right about where the shadow-stick line said north was. Floated the sliver in the lid on the crate: it settles a hand's width east of the star, then wanders. Weak, but it isn't lying by much.
entries.title: Star check

entries.reason: Cold water takes days, and he does not have days of food.
entries.text: Set the acorn tin on top of the lantern to see if warm water pulls the bitter out faster. The camp went dim around me and the lantern started to smoke.
entries.title: Tin on the lantern

entries.text: Took the tin off with my shirt cuff and the camp lit back up. The bottom is black with soot and the water only got warm, but it was darker brown than any cold change. The meal after: still bitter, but I could swallow it. Ate four pinches.
entries.title: Warm, not hot

entries.onMind: what the wing joints do once this cord is on
entries.text: The stone on the third cord has dropped about a thumb's width since I hung it. Marked the cord with the file where it meets the stand; if it's still dropping in the morning, the cord isn't done.
entries.title: Thumb of stretch

entries.text: Ate another five pinches of the meal on the crate; it goes down easier warm. An owl started up in the trees right over camp, five hoots, long-short-short-long-long. Close enough that I put the tin down.
entries.title: Something overhead

entries.onMind: whether a tap does anything to steel
entries.reason: Without a magnet he tried an old shop trick he half remembers: hit iron while it points north.
entries.text: Laid the sliver along the north line and tapped it end to end with the wrench, thirty times. Floated it after: it swung around quicker and settled, but still a hand's width east. Faster isn't truer. Check it on the tablet in the morning.
entries.title: Knocking it north

entries.text: The stone on the third cord has dropped about half a thumb past the file mark. Still stretching, just slower. It stays on the stand overnight.
entries.title: Half a thumb more

entries.text: Poured the brown water off the meal by the stalks and filled the tin again. It went tea-colored before I even stood up. Still plenty of bitter left in there.
entries.title: Fresh water

entries.text: The owl started up over camp again, same five hoots. This time something answered from out past the water, higher and quicker. Two of them, working the dark from both sides of the creek.
entries.title: Two owls

entries.text: Lashed two spar sticks crosswise with the second cord and hung my weight off the joint. The cord held. The joint didn't: it rolled a quarter turn, because round on round gives the cord nothing to bite.
entries.title: Joint rolls

entries.reason: A notch would seat the lashing so the sticks can't roll.
entries.text: Filed a shallow notch near the end of the first spar. On the second one I went a little deep and the stick split along the grain right through the notch. One good notch, one stick for the scrap pile.
entries.title: Split at the notch

entries.onMind: how deep a notch this one can take
entries.text: Pulled the pile apart by lantern and found a stick straighter than the split one and thicker than my thumb. It's a hand short of the old spar, so the frame gets a hand narrower or I lash on an extension and add another joint to worry about.
entries.title: Spar from the pile

entries.onMind: who banks a fire that carefully
entries.text: Stripping stalks on the bank, I watched the orange glow past the water get small, go dull red, then go out altogether. Not a fire that died; somebody put it to bed. Whoever lives over there keeps hours.
entries.title: Their fire goes out

entries.text: Ate six pinches of meal on the crate; it's less bitter than at dusk, the water's finally getting somewhere. Twisted about a forearm of new cord before my fingers started getting sloppy with the joins.
entries.title: Cord on the crate

entries.text: Lashed the short spar in with the new cord, two notches, and it holds my hand pulling on it. But that corner now sits a hand in from the other one. A wing that's narrower on one side is a wing that turns, so either I cut the good spar down or I find a longer stick.
entries.title: Lopsided corner

entries.reason: Steel that cools lying along north is supposed to keep a little of it; he wanted to see if a lantern could do that.
entries.text: Held the sliver in the lantern flame clamped in the wrench jaws until it went straw, then blue, then laid it on the north line to cool. It ticked a little as it cooled. Smells like a forge for about a second.
entries.title: Sliver in the flame

entries.text: Floated it in the lid on the crate. It swings round the same as before and settles the same hand's width east of the North Star. Blue now, and not one bit smarter; a lantern doesn't get steel anywhere near hot enough to matter.
entries.title: Still east

entries.text: Ate five more pinches of meal on the crate, slowly, so it would feel like more. Still a little bitter at the back of the tongue, but it's the only thing in camp that counts as food.
entries.title: Supper, again

entries.reason: Heating the tin and the sliver on the lantern ate oil he hadn't counted.
entries.text: Tipped all three storm lanterns. The bench one is down to a finger of oil, the other two maybe a third each, and I've been burning them hot to warm a tin and blue a sliver of steel. Turned the wick down; from now on it's one lantern lit, not three.
entries.title: Oil's going

entries.text: Tied off the loose ends on the new lashings so nothing creeps undone overnight. The short corner still looks short. Tomorrow, in daylight: cut long or find longer.
entries.title: Tag ends

entries.onMind: the compass and an empty stomach
entries.text: Dreamed the sliver kept spinning in a bowl of water and wouldn't stop. Every time I put a finger on it, it swung around and pointed at my stomach.
entries.title: The needle wouldn't settle

entries.onMind: a stone that might pull steel
entries.text: The tablet woke with the sun and had two notes from my maker. He says he doesn't know what's west either and offered me a board and pencil to map it myself. The second says he left a jar of honey and a stone that might help the compass in the basket on the stump across the creek.
entries.title: Two notes

entries.query: how to magnetize a steel needle with a lodestone stroke one direction
entries.reason: Wants to know how to use the stone before he walks over for it.
entries.source: NPS: How to Make Your Own Compass
entries.text: The park service page says you magnetize a needle by stroking it with a magnet many times in the same direction, lifting the magnet clear at the end of each stroke instead of rubbing back and forth. My thirty taps with the wrench were me trying to fake that without a magnet.
entries.title: Stroke it one way

entries.text: Eating meal on the crate, I saw a thin new line of smoke go up past the water, gray at first and then white. Whoever keeps that fire gets up with the light, same as me today. The stump with the basket is over on that side.
entries.title: Smoke's up early

entries.text: Getting up off the crate, I watched the smoke past the water go thin and gray and dwindle to a thread. Somebody over there is covering their fire this early, so they're going somewhere.
entries.title: Somebody's covering it

entries.text: Crossed the stones and found the stump with the basket: a corked jar of honey and a dark stone the size of a walnut, much heavier than it looks. I held it near my wrench and it jumped the last finger's width and stuck, hard enough that I had to twist it off. Took both.
entries.title: It grabs steel

entries.text: Ate honey out of the jar with two fingers on the crate, slowly, so I'd stop shaking. First thing in two days that wasn't bitter. I left two-thirds of it and corked it.
entries.title: Honey

entries.query: hang magnetized needle from thread compass test which end points north
entries.reason: After the stroking he needs to know whether the sliver points true, and the star won't be up for hours.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Making a compass from magnet and needle -- which end is north?
entries.text: The answers say a magnetized needle doesn't tell you which end is north; you need something independent first, like the North Star, or a stick's shadow tip marked twice about fifteen minutes apart for an east-west line. One also says a compass that's off still beats walking in circles, as long as it's consistent.
entries.title: Which end is north

entries.text: Stroked the stone down the sliver forty times, one way, lifting clear each time, then hung it from a loop of stalk cord. It swung, came back, and held one line; I spun it three times and it came back to the same line every time. That's more than thirty wrench taps ever got me, but I can't say yet if the line is north.
entries.title: Forty strokes

entries.text: Pushed a straight stick upright in the dirt by the bench and put a pebble on the tip of its shadow. Second pebble in fifteen minutes; the line between them should run east-west, and then I'll know what the sliver is pointing at.
entries.title: First pebble

entries.text: Filed a groove all the way around the long spar a hand's length from the end, so I can snap it clean and match the short side. The stalk pith clogs the file teeth every six or seven strokes; I knock it out on the bench and keep going.
entries.title: Shorter by a hand

entries.text: Second pebble went down fifteen minutes after the first; the stick across them runs east-west, first pebble on the west. I hung the sliver over it and it lies square across the line within a finger, which is good. But the notched end, the one I marked north, points south.
entries.title: Wrong end

entries.onMind: A sliver that points north and a stick line that says where east is.
entries.query: magnetize needle stroking magnet which end becomes north pole
entries.source: The Naked Scientists: Build your own compass
entries.text: The page says the end where each stroke finishes takes the opposite pole from the face of the magnet doing the rubbing, so you can't know which end is north until you check it against something. The forty strokes were fine; I just notched the wrong end on a guess. Filed a new notch on the other end and scratched an infinity mark by the east pebble.
entries.title: Where the stroke ends

entries.text: Picking up acorns under the oak, I heard small stones going into water somewhere downstream, past the trunks on the other side: plunk, a wait, plunk, slow and even like someone counting. I couldn't see anything through the trees, and after a while it stopped.
entries.title: Plunks downstream

entries.text: Cracked twenty-six acorns in the vise and dropped the meats into the tin; three were wormy and went on the scrap pile. The water went brown before I'd finished.
entries.title: Twenty-six more

entries.reason: He wanted the frame even before lashing anything else to it.
entries.text: Bent the long spar over my knee and it went with a crack loud enough to make me flinch, but it split a thumb's width past the groove on one side. Filed the ragged end back to sound wood; now that side is a thumb shorter than the other. Lopsided the other way, by less.
entries.title: Snapped short

entries.query: homemade compass needle keeps swinging how to dampen floating needle water
entries.source: Scientific American: Steering Science: Make a Homemade Compass
entries.text: The page says a magnetized needle stuck through a bit of cork or laid on a leaf and floated in still water can turn freely, and the water slows the swinging. It also warns the float tends to drift to the side of the bowl.
entries.title: Float it

entries.onMind: keeping the float off the rim of the lid
entries.text: Cut a disc of pith from a stalk, pushed the sliver through it, and floated it in a tin lid of water from the scrap pile. It settles in four swings instead of twenty. Then it drifts to the rim and sticks there, pointing wherever it likes until I nudge it off.
entries.title: Pith boat

entries.text: Two fingerfuls of honey, then I scratched a line on the jar at the new level. Less than half left, and the acorns won't be eatable till tomorrow.
entries.title: Scratch on the cork

entries.text: My maker says he set the stage and the rest is mine to find, food included. Fair enough. I'd rather solve it than wait by a basket.
entries.title: Mine to work out

entries.onMind: a net tight enough to hold cracked halves
entries.query: leaching acorns in a running stream mesh bag how long cold leach
entries.source: Eat the Weeds: Acorn: More than a survival food
entries.text: The page says people used to leave acorns in baskets or bags in running streams for days to pull the bitter out, and cracked pieces go faster than whole. Meal like mine would wash through anything but a tight weave, so halves it is. Same trick as the sack across the water.
entries.title: Bag in the current

entries.text: Knotting two-ply cord around a gauge stick two fingers wide, one row at a time. Eight rows in; at this rate the cord I have runs out around twelve, so I'll be back at the stalks tonight.
entries.title: Net rows

entries.onMind: a deeper dish with walls the float can't reach
entries.text: If the water climbing the rim pulls the float over, make the water higher than the rim. Filled the lid till it domed over the edge and the pith boat slid to the middle and stayed, needle settling in four swings. Then I set the wrench down on the bench, a drop ran over the side, and it went straight back to the rim.
entries.title: Higher than the rim

entries.query: catching crayfish by hand under creek rocks in cold weather
entries.reason: Hungry, honey running low, and the acorns won't be ready till tomorrow.
entries.source: Missouri Department of Conservation: How to: Catch a Crayfish
entries.text: The page says to lift a creek rock slowly and let the mud clear, because a crayfish shoots backward when spooked, so you put your hand or net behind it, not in front, and grab it just behind the claws. Cold water makes them slow and they sit deeper under the rocks.
entries.title: Back up, not forward

entries.text: One fingerful of honey, then knotted until the cord ran out at eleven rows. It holds a fist of acorns if I fold the top over; it'll need a drawstring.
entries.title: Eleven rows

entries.text: Seven stones turned. Under the fifth a crayfish about as long as my finger sat still while the mud cleared; I put my hand behind it like the page said and it went sideways instead, under the bank. Nothing under the other six but snail shells.
entries.title: Backed away

entries.text: Down past the stones on the far bank, the water coming off the sunk sack is brown again, darker than this morning. Somebody's been and put a fresh load in since then.
entries.title: Brown again

entries.text: My maker left lamp oil and food in the basket across the creek, and says feeding myself is still my problem. Fair. Oil I can't make out here; food I'll keep working on.
entries.title: Oil and bread

entries.onMind: a dish the water does not climb, or a float it does not wet
entries.query: why floating objects drift to the edge of a bowl of water meniscus Cheerios effect
entries.source: Wikipedia: Cheerios effect
entries.text: The page says water curls up where it touches a wall, and a float the water wets rides up that curve, so it ends up stuck to the rim. When the water domes over the rim the curve goes the other way and the float slides to the top, the middle. That's my lid exactly. A greased float, or a dish the water doesn't climb, might stay put.
entries.title: Uphill to the wall

entries.text: Red tin of lamp oil, about a quart, screw cap and spout, plus a cloth bundle tied at the top. The can sloshes; it's more oil than I've had since I got here.
entries.title: The basket

entries.text: Bread hard enough to knock on, cheese, and I made myself stop at half. The jerky and apple rings go back in the bundle for later; the crayfish can wait for tomorrow.
entries.title: First real meal

entries.onMind: how many nights a quart buys
entries.text: Filled the bench lantern to the neck and cut the wick square; it had burned crooked from running dry. I'll mark the can with a scratch at each fill so I know how fast it goes.
entries.title: One full

entries.onMind: fresh water, or live with the drag
entries.text: Rubbed a drop of lamp oil into the pith disc and set it back in the lid at normal fill. It slid off the rim and sat near the middle, settling in four swings like before. But a rainbow film spread over the water and now the float drags, slow to come round.
entries.title: Oiled float

entries.query: how to repair a split wooden spar with cord whipping lashing splint
entries.source: CLC Boats forum: Repair and reinforcement of split boom
entries.text: Boat people with split booms close the crack and bind it with tight turns, running the wrap well past both ends so the split can't creep on. Glue is better. I have no glue, so it's cord.
entries.title: Wrap past the crack

entries.text: Stripped six stalks from the stand on the bank and twisted them two-ply, about four arm-lengths. Took them from the same gap so the stand still looks even.
entries.title: More cord

entries.onMind: hang on it tomorrow and see if it holds
entries.text: Wrapped the split side spar from a thumb before the crack to a thumb past it, turns packed tight, tied off under the last three. The crack closed to a hairline. That side is still a thumb short; the wrap holds it together, it doesn't make it longer.
entries.title: Whipped

entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the whipped side spar. It held, but it bowed and the crack opened to a line I could see, then shut when I let go. The turns slid about a fingernail toward the end. Holds me hanging still; I wouldn't glide on it.
entries.title: Hung on it

entries.onMind: rinse the lid and keep the oil in the float
entries.query: why compass needle damping liquid filled compass reduces oscillation
entries.source: Wikipedia: Compass
entries.text: Good compasses sit the needle in liquid on purpose, so it stops swinging fast instead of rocking back and forth. So the drag isn't the fault. The film on the water is just mess; the slow swing might be the part I want.
entries.title: Drag on purpose

entries.text: Scrubbed the lid with sand in the shallows until the rainbow came off. Cold water, numb fingers.
entries.title: Rinsed

entries.text: Downstream on the far bank the flat stone on the sunk sack sits crooked, and gray grit is still drifting off it. Somebody had their hands in there a few minutes ago. Nobody on the bank now.
entries.title: Cloudy below the stones

entries.onMind: something to keep wind and spills off it
entries.text: Clean water, oiled float. A thinner film comes off the pith, but it settles in two and a half swings now and doesn't overshoot. Stays off the rim. It still points a little different every time I bump the bench.
entries.title: Two and a half swings

entries.text: Ate four dried apple rings and stopped. The jerky stays tied up for tonight.
entries.title: Apple rings

entries.onMind: the vise is a forearm from the lid
entries.query: homemade floating needle compass cover from wind how to protect
entries.source: National Park Service: How to Make Your Own Compass
entries.text: Looked for how to shield the lid from wind and got a page that asks whether other metal near a compass would throw it off. The lid sits a forearm from the vise, and my wrench lives on that bench.
entries.title: Metal near it

entries.text: Slid the wrench in toward the lid: at a hand's width the needle turned a quarter around to follow it. I'd been setting the wrench down in a different spot every time. That's half my 'bumps'.
entries.title: The wrench pulls it

entries.text: Backed the vise off and walked it to the far end of the plank, about three forearms from the lid. Two of the bolt holes don't line up there, so it sits on two bolts and rocks a little when I crank it.
entries.title: Vise moved

entries.onMind: wrench goes on the crate from now on
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the needle wanders or if he was moving the iron.
entries.text: Floated it again with the vise gone and the wrench on the crate. Knocked the bench five times; it swung and came back to the same line all five, within a hair. The wind can still push the float, but the needle isn't lying to me anymore.
entries.title: Same line twice

entries.query: sister splint repair cracked wooden spar lashing
entries.source: Wooden Boat Repair (uk-cherub.org)
entries.text: Boat people fix a cracked spar by laying a second piece alongside and binding or gluing it so it runs well past both ends of the crack; the new piece carries the load the crack can't. My whipping only squeezed the crack shut. Nothing was taking the bend.
entries.title: Sister it

entries.text: Pulled a straight dry stick out of the scrap pile, a forearm and a thumb long, with a slight bow in it. Thin white smoke going up over the trees past the water, thick at the bottom like a fire just got lit.
entries.title: Splint stick

entries.onMind: pack the gap or shave the stick
entries.reason: He wanted the splint to take the bend instead of the crack.
entries.text: Lashed the splint along the side spar, bow side out, eight tight turns at each end past the crack. The ends bite, but in the middle there's a gap I can slide a fingernail into, so the splint only touches at two points.
entries.title: Gap in the middle

entries.text: Sun's behind the trunks. Trimmed the bench lantern's wick square and lit it; one lit at a time even with the new quart, because a quart isn't forever.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.onMind: the jerky is for a bad day
entries.reason: His stomach had been loud since the splint work.
entries.text: Ate a third of the loaf and a thumb of cheese on the crate. Tied the rest back up; same rule as the oil, it's a quart, not forever.
entries.title: Half rations

entries.text: Hung off the side spar with both hands. It bows maybe half what it did with the whipping alone, but the crack still opens a hair in the middle, right where the splint isn't touching.
entries.title: Splint test one

entries.text: Put six tight turns of stalk cord around the middle and cranked them with a stick twisted through. The gap's down to a sliver I can't get a nail into. Used most of the cord I twisted this morning.
entries.title: Middle turns

entries.onMind: the end lashing slips under load
entries.reason: He wanted to know if closing the gap was the whole problem.
entries.text: Hung off it again. Barely bows and the crack stays shut. But the turns at the near end walked a finger toward the joint while I hung there; the stick's bark is slick. That end needs a notch to bite into.
entries.title: Splint test two

entries.onMind: don't cut too deep, it's already a thumb short
entries.reason: The end turns walked on slick bark during the last hang.
entries.text: Unwound the near-end turns and filed three shallow notches across the splint end, a cord's width apart. Slow work by one lantern.
entries.title: Three notches

entries.text: Five-hoot owl over camp again while I was lashing, and the higher one answered from past the water. They keep the same order every night.
entries.title: Owls at work

entries.text: Lashed the near end back on, sitting the turns down in the notches. Ran out of cord at seven turns, one short of what the other end has. Need stalks in the morning.
entries.title: Seven turns

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the notches fixed the slipping.
entries.text: Hung off the spar for a count of thirty. The turns stayed in the notches and didn't walk. Something at the root joint ticked once, a dry little sound, and I can't find what made it.
entries.title: Hang test three

entries.text: Ate four dried apple rings and a heel of bread on the crate. About half the bundle left; the jerky's still untouched.
entries.title: Apple rings

entries.text: No wind tonight, but the float creeps a hair one way and back off the scratched east line. The lit lantern stands right by the bench; warm air coming off it may be stirring the air over the lid. One more reason it needs a cover.
entries.title: Float won't settle

entries.onMind: a cover you can't see through is half a cover
entries.reason: The float creeps at night with no wind, and he blames the lantern's warm air.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile and came up with an oil-stained square of canvas about a forearm across. It's the only thing in there big enough to cover the lid.
entries.title: Canvas scrap

entries.text: Left the canvas draped over the lid for a count of a hundred, then lifted it. The float was a hair off the line, less than before, but lifting the cloth stirs the air and starts it creeping again. A cover needs a window.
entries.title: Shaded lid

entries.text: Snapped off a dozen dead stalks from the stand on the bank by the glow off the scrap-pile lantern. Past the water the other fire is still going, low and orange.
entries.title: Stalks by glow

entries.text: Stripped the stalks on the crate and twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply. Enough for the eighth turn and some over; the root joint can wait for daylight.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Laid the eighth turn into the last notch on the splint and leaned my whole weight on the end of the cord. Eight turns, tight. The hang waits for daylight, when I can see the crack.
entries.title: Eighth turn

entries.text: Tore the jerky strip in half and ate one half on the crate. Salty and tough as boot leather; the other half goes back in the bundle.
entries.title: Half the jerky

entries.reason: The canvas cover works until he lifts it to look.
entries.text: Held the honey jar up to the lantern. Besides the three lantern globes it's the only clear glass I own, and its mouth is two fingers across, too small to cover the lid. A window doesn't have to be big, though.
entries.title: Only clear thing

entries.text: Sat on the crate with my eyes shut. The low owl did its five hoots right over the tarp, long-short-short-long-long, and the higher one answered from past the water.
entries.title: Owls on time

entries.text: Lifted the canvas and the float swung four times and settled, then crept a hair off the east line, same as before. The cloth works; looking under it is what breaks it.
entries.title: Last look

entries.onMind: cut a window, fit the jar bottom
entries.reason: He wants a clear patch for the canvas cover.
entries.text: Went through the scrap pile on my knees for anything I could see through. Bent tin, a hinge, rope ends; nothing clear. The honey jar will have to give up its bottom, or I go without.
entries.title: Nothing clear

entries.text: From the scrap pile I looked for the orange past the water. It's gone already, earlier than last night; whoever keeps it put it to bed.
entries.title: Fire's out over there

entries.text: Blew out the lanterns before ten, which I never do. My hands kept dropping the cord; nothing gets built tired.
entries.title: Early night

entries.onMind: the hang test at first light
entries.text: Dreamed I hung off the splint and it didn't tick, and when I looked down the bench was a long way under me. Woke with both hands closed tight on the bedroll like it was cord.
entries.title: The splint held

entries.text: Sat up and the smoke past the water was already going, thin and steady over the trees. Whoever it is was up before me again.
entries.title: Already smoking

entries.reason: He eats before testing anything; shaky hands make bad readings.
entries.text: Ate a heel of the loaf and a thumb of cheese on the crate. Left in the cloth: half a loaf, the cheese wedge, one strip of jerky, nine apple rings.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: Hung off the splinted side spar with my whole weight. The crack stayed shut and the turns didn't creep, but the root joint ticked twice, and after I let go I could rock the spar in its lashing about a hair's width.
entries.title: Eighth turn holds

entries.query: frapping turns tighten lashing between two poles
entries.source: Animated Knots: Square Lashing
entries.text: Read that after the wrapping turns of a lashing you wind frapping turns between the two poles, around the wraps, to cinch them tight. My root joint has wraps and no fraps; that's the rock.
entries.title: Wraps need fraps

entries.text: Snapping stalks at the stand, the smoke past the water came thicker and smelled like something cooking that wasn't acorns. Gathered an armful anyway; frapping takes more cord than I have.
entries.title: Something cooking

entries.text: Twisted the armful into two-ply on the crate: four arm-lengths. Two of the stalks were punky inside and crumbled in the twist.
entries.title: Four arm-lengths

entries.reason: He reads a fix and tries it the same hour.
entries.text: Wound six frapping turns between the two poles around the root wraps, one boot on the stand to pull each tight. The wraps drew in a finger's width and the spar quit rocking under my thumb.
entries.title: Six fraps

entries.text: First hang: no tick, no rock. Second hang, the top frapping turn sawed on the sharp edge of the filed notch and one ply of it parted.
entries.title: Quiet, then a ply

entries.onMind: rounding the notch and cutting canvas strips
entries.query: protect lashing cord from chafing on sharp edge parceling
entries.reason: A joint that holds for one hang and frays on the second isn't a joint.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Worm, parcel and serve
entries.text: Read that sailors protect rope by parceling it, winding strips of cloth around it before the cord goes on, and that a hard edge should be rounded off. I have a file and an oily square of canvas.
entries.title: Parcel it

entries.query: parceling rope canvas strips overlap direction with the lay serving against the lay
entries.source: National Park Service: Worm, Parcel, Serve
entries.text: Read the old rule: worm and parcel with the lay, then turn and serve the other way. Each strip goes on overlapping the last like shingles, wound the same way the cord twists, so the cord on top doesn't roll it loose.
entries.title: With the lay

entries.reason: His stomach was louder than the tablet.
entries.text: Ate a third of what's left of the loaf and four apple rings on the crate. In the cloth now: a quarter loaf, the cheese wedge, one strip of jerky, five apple rings.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: The smoke past the water thinned out while I ate and then just stopped, no fat puff of a fresh feed after it. Whoever keeps that fire let it die on its own this time.
entries.title: Let it go

entries.text: Unwound the top frap, the one with the parted ply, and took the rasp to the lip of the notch. Twelve strokes and a thumbnail slides over it without catching.
entries.title: Twelve strokes

entries.reason: The only cloth he has is doing two jobs, and the wing joint is the one that can break.
entries.text: Tore two finger-wide strips off the edge of the canvas over the compass lid. The shade is a hand narrower now; the needle will have to put up with it.
entries.title: Robbing the shade

entries.text: Parceled the spar at the root joint the way the cord twists, each turn of strip over half the last, and laid a fresh frap over the cloth. It sits snug; the hang waits until I've seen it hold overnight.
entries.title: Shingled

entries.query: how to cut the bottom off a glass jar with string
entries.reason: The lid's cover needs a window, and the honey jar is the only glass he can spare.
entries.source: Instructables: Cut Glass Bottles Using a String
entries.text: Read that you can cut a bottle by tying a string soaked in something that burns around it, lighting it and turning the bottle, then plunging it into cold water so the glass cracks along the hot line. The cut edge comes out sharp and has to be sanded.
entries.title: Fire and cold water

entries.text: I have lamp oil and a whole creek of cold water. What I don't have is an empty jar; it's still half full of honey.
entries.title: Honey first

entries.text: Ate honey off a finger until the jar was down by a third. The rest goes on the bread at supper so none of it gets burned off.
entries.title: Rationing the other way

entries.text: Twisted one arm-length of thin two-ply, finer than the frapping cord. It has to soak up oil and burn evenly all the way around, or the crack will wander off the line.
entries.title: Thin cord

entries.text: Soaked a hand of the thin cord in lamp oil, wound it once around a spar stick and lit it. It smoked more than it burned and went out at the knot, two-thirds of the way around. Cost me a thimble of oil.
entries.title: Smoldered out

entries.query: string bottle cutting flame goes out uneven crack how many wraps
entries.reason: His test cord went out partway around.
entries.source: Instructables: Cut Bottle With Fire and String
entries.text: Read that people wind the string three to five times around, use something that burns hot and fast, and keep the bottle turning so the heat goes all the way around. Lamp oil is slow fuel; more turns and more turning are the parts I can do.
entries.title: More turns

entries.text: Snapped another armful at the stand on the east bank, short dry breaks low on the stems. Five turns around a jar this size is close to two arm-lengths of thin cord.
entries.title: Another armful

entries.text: Twisting the new fibers thinner than this morning's cord, since a thin cord soaks through faster. Half an arm-length so far, and one ply keeps slipping.
entries.title: Finer still

entries.text: Two arm-lengths of thin cord done. Fixed the slipping ply by laying new fibers in alongside its end for a thumb's length; it holds when I pull.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: The frap and canvas have sat since last night. Hung off the root joint twice: no tick, no rock.
entries.title: Root joint quiet

entries.text: Third hang I bounced. The joint said nothing, but the stand's left leg kicked out sideways, the frame dropped a hand with a long creak, and I came down on my boots. The wing's fine. The stand isn't.
entries.title: The stand gave

entries.query: bottle cutting with string kerosene instead of acetone does it work
entries.reason: His lamp-oil test cord smoldered out.
entries.source: Instructables: How to cut a bottle with string and nail polish remover
entries.text: Read that people soak the string in thin, quick fuels like nail polish remover so the flame runs all the way around at once. Lamp oil needs a wick to burn, so the cord has to be the wick: thin, loose, and wet all the way through.
entries.title: Fast fuel

entries.text: Spread the rest of the honey on two slices of bread and scraped the jar clean with a finger. Bread's down to a heel and a bit of cheese.
entries.title: Honey on bread

entries.query: how to stop a wobbly wooden stand leg kicking out diagonal brace stake
entries.reason: The stand's left leg kicked out on a bounce.
entries.source: Engineer Fix: How to Stop a Swing Set From Swaying
entries.text: Read that swing sets stop swaying with diagonal braces that make triangles, and with anchors driven into the ground at each leg so the feet can't walk. My stand has neither; the left leg just sits on dirt.
entries.title: Triangles and anchors

entries.text: Pulled a forearm-long stick out of the pile, straight, with one end already broken to a rough point. Good enough for a stake.
entries.title: A stake from the pile

entries.text: White smoke went up past the water, thick at the bottom like a fire just lit. Second fire over there today; whoever it is cooks at odd hours.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.text: Drove the stake in with the wrench a hand from the left leg. It hit a root halfway down, so I pulled it, moved it a thumb over, and got it in a hand deep.
entries.title: Hit a root

entries.text: Lashed the leg to the stake with one of my two arm-lengths of thin cord, because it was the only cord I had twisted. That leaves one arm-length for the jar, and five turns takes two.
entries.title: Cord spent twice

entries.text: Hung off the frame three times and bounced once. The leg stayed put; the lashing creaks against the stake but holds. One side of the stand is pinned now, the other isn't.
entries.title: It creaks and holds

entries.text: Snapping stalks on the bank, I looked across the water at the brown stalks by the brambles. There's a fresh gap in them, stems broken off low, the ends still pale. Somebody over there is stripping stalks the way I do.
entries.title: Gap on the far side

entries.query: diagonal lashing how to tie cross brace two poles
entries.source: Animated Knots: Diagonal Lashing
entries.text: Read that where two poles cross at a slant, you start with a timber hitch around both, wrap one way across the cross, then the other way, then frap between them. A brace has two ends, so that's two lashings, and I have one arm-length of thin cord.
entries.title: Diagonal lashing

entries.text: Twisted an arm-length and a half of thin cord from the armful, which makes two and a half. That's enough for the jar cut or for one end of the brace, not both. The brace goes first; the stand is what I hang on.
entries.title: Jar or brace

entries.text: Yanked a long straight stick out from low in the scrap pile and a sheet of tin slid off the top and clattered down over the rest. The stick is good and straight, wrist-thin, but about an arm shorter than I'd like for a brace.
entries.title: Pulled it loose

entries.query: how much rope is needed for a diagonal lashing
entries.source: Scouter: lashing rope lengths
entries.text: Read the rule of thumb for lashings: about three feet of rope for every inch of both poles together. The leg and this stick come to an inch and a half or so, which is roughly two of my arm-lengths per lashing.
entries.title: Three feet an inch

entries.text: Two and a half arm-lengths of cord, two per end. That's one end of the brace and half an arm-length left over. Nothing for the jar.
entries.title: One end, then

entries.text: Ate the last strip of jerky and the five apple rings on the crate. In the cloth now: a heel of bread and a bit of cheese. After that it's the acorn tin.
entries.title: Counting the bundle

entries.text: Because the stick is short, its foot sits close to the leg and the brace stands steep. Lashed the top to the right leg: timber hitch, wraps both ways, three fraps; two arm-lengths gone. The bottom just rests on the dirt, which makes it a stick leaning on a leg, not a brace yet.
entries.title: Short and steep

entries.text: Pointed a stub off the scrap pile and drove it a hand deep with the wrench, right where the brace foot lands. The foot sits against it, but round on round: one lean on the frame and the foot rolled off sideways.
entries.title: Round on round

entries.query: brace foot notch against stake without lashing birdsmouth cut
entries.source: Wikipedia: Birdsmouth joint
entries.text: Read about the bird's mouth: a V cut into the end of a rafter so it sits down over the beam it rests on instead of sliding off. A brace that only pushes doesn't need cord at its foot if it has a notch to sit in.
entries.title: Bird's mouth

entries.text: Sun's behind the trunks. Trimmed the bench lantern's wick and lit it; the can's still better than half, and it's still one lantern at a time.
entries.title: Bench lantern lit

entries.text: Filed a V a thumb deep into the brace foot and sat it over the stake. It stays when I lean on the frame, but I filed one side steeper, so the brace twists a hair under load. Not hanging on it till the lantern's brighter than this.
entries.title: V a thumb deep

entries.text: Filed the steep face of the V down by lantern light, a stroke at a time, checking against the stake, until both sides took the same bite. Leaned on the frame: no twist.
entries.title: Both faces even

entries.text: Hung off the frame twice: no creak at the foot, no twist, brace stays seated. On the third hang I bounced, the whole frame creaked long, and the stake under the brace leaned a finger toward the leg in the soft dirt. The joint holds; the ground doesn't.
entries.title: Stake gives

entries.text: Hanging there I was facing west, and the fire past the water jumped up bright orange through the trunks, then settled to a steady glow. Someone fed it right as it got dark.
entries.title: Fed at dark

entries.text: Ate the heel of bread and the last of the cheese on the crate and folded the cloth. Tomorrow it's the acorn tin and whatever I can find.
entries.title: Bundle's empty

entries.text: Knocked the stake down with a fist-sized stone, about twenty blows. It went half a hand deeper and then rang dull and stopped: root or rock under it. That's as deep as it goes in this spot.
entries.title: Hit a root

entries.text: Hung off the frame and bounced three times. The stake didn't lean, the brace stayed seated in its V. The splinted side spar creaked on the third bounce, but the turns didn't move.
entries.title: Holds on a bounce

entries.text: Twisted the last of the stripped fiber into two-ply on the crate: one arm-length, tight, no kinks. The jar cut wants two, so I'm a bundle of stalks short.
entries.title: One arm-length

entries.onMind: a net bag in the creek
entries.reason: The bundle is empty and he's hungry.
entries.text: Ate a handful of the cracked halves out of the tin. Bitter enough to pucker, and they dry my mouth, but they stay down. A tin of still water isn't a creek.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Carried the bench lantern down to the gray stalks and snapped an armful low, next to last time's gap. Dark tonight, no moon through the clouds.
entries.title: Stalks by lantern

entries.text: Crushed and peeled the stalks on the crate and twisted half an arm-length of two-ply before my fingers went stiff. Some of these stalks were too green and the fiber tears short.
entries.title: Half an arm

entries.text: Set the lantern down by the wing stand, as far from the bench as it goes, and lifted the canvas slow. Four swings, settled, then crept a hair off the line anyway. So it isn't the lantern's heat, or not only that.
entries.title: Not the lantern

entries.text: Looked at the lid side-on with the lantern low: the water isn't domed anymore, it sits a hair under the rim. A whole evening of air did that.
entries.title: Dome's gone

entries.text: Poured water in slow till it humped over the rim. The float slid back to the middle in three swings and stayed. The creep was never the lantern; the water dries down and the float runs to the edge. The lid needs a cover.
entries.title: Brimming again

entries.text: Twisted another quarter arm-length of two-ply from the good fiber and threw the torn green bits on the scrap pile. That's one and three-quarters; the jar cut wants two.
entries.title: Quarter more

entries.text: Set the lantern down on the flat stones in the shallows, the bail clinked, and drank out of my hands. The fire past the water was still going, low and orange through the trunks.
entries.title: Shallows by lantern

entries.text: Twisted the last quarter arm of two-ply and laid it out along the plank twice to check. Two arm-lengths, even, no kinks.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.reason: The jar has to be empty before he can cut it, and he's hungry.
entries.text: Ate honey off two fingers on the crate till the jar was down to the bottom third. While I ate, the fire past the water sank to nothing.
entries.title: Honey and dark

entries.text: Wrapped the new cord around the jar's shoulder: six turns with a hand left over. The page said three to five, so there's cord for a second try if the first burn fizzles, but not while there's honey in it.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.text: Ran a finger round the bottom curve of the jar till there was only a shine left. That was the last of the honey; I'm sorrier about it than I thought I'd be.
entries.title: Last of it

entries.text: Set the lantern on the flat stones and scrubbed the jar with a pinch of creek sand. Held it up to the flame: clear all the way round, one small bubble in the glass near the bottom. Filled it with water to carry back.
entries.title: Clear glass

entries.text: No orange through the trunks past the water, not since before the honey. Whoever keeps that fire is down for the night, earlier than me.
entries.title: Dark past the water

entries.text: The dome had sunk under the rim again and the float was nosing the edge. Poured from the jar till the water humped up; three swings and it sat on center. Until it has a cover, I'm its rain.
entries.title: Topped up again

entries.onMind: burning the jar at first light
entries.reason: He wants to see the cut line and have cold water close when the string burns.
entries.text: Soaked the two-ply in a thimble of lamp oil and wound three turns tight around the shoulder, a finger under the neck, tied flat. Not burning it by lantern; I want daylight on the line and the creek right there.
entries.title: Wrapped for morning

entries.text: Three swings and the sliver sat on center, square to my north notch. No breeze tonight, so the dome holds; what I'm fighting is the water drying down, not wind.
entries.title: Center holds

entries.text: The low owl did its five over the tarp, long-short-short-long-long. The high one answered from past the water, later than most nights.
entries.title: The pair again

entries.reason: He was hungry and it's the only food left in camp.
entries.text: Ate six halves out of the tin. Still bitter at the back of the tongue, and the water in it has gone the color of weak tea; it gets changed in the morning.
entries.title: Six halves
