entries.text: Hung my weight on the splinted side spar to see if it would last the night. It held, but the outer turn of the splint slid a finger toward the joint with a squeak. Retie it by daylight, tighter, before anything else goes on that side.
entries.title: Splint slipped

entries.onMind: burning the jar at first light
entries.text: Dreamed the sliver floated in a lid as wide as the sky and pointed past the trees, and when I walked the line it kept going. Woke once to the tarp ticking and the lantern dark, then slept again.
entries.title: Line on the water

entries.text: Crawled out to woodsmoke on the breeze from past the water and fog on the creek. The lid's dome had sunk under the rim in the night and the float was parked against the edge; poured it brimming from the jar and it came back to center in three swings.
entries.title: Dome sank overnight

entries.onMind: even heat all the way round
entries.query: string method cutting glass jar crack uneven how to fix jagged edge
entries.source: Woodgears: Helical glass cut attempt
entries.text: Tablet's dim under this cloud, but I got one page: a man scoring jars found the crack often broke away from his line, and his best guess for the one that worked was slower, more even heat. So I turn the jar the whole time the cord burns.
entries.title: Cracks wander

entries.reason: He wants a clear cover so the lid stops drying down.
entries.text: Lit the oiled cord and turned the jar over the shallows till the flame died, then dunked it: a tink, and the cord hissed out. The crack ran two-thirds round right on the line, then turned down toward the bubble near the bottom and stopped.
entries.title: Ran off the line

entries.onMind: a flat stone and sand for the rim
entries.text: Washed it and tapped the neck; the top came off in my hand. What's left is a clear cup with a ragged rim and a thumb-long tooth hanging down where the crack wandered. It won't sit flat over the lid until I grind that rim down.
entries.title: Cup with a tooth

entries.onMind: a flat stone and creek sand
entries.query: smooth cut glass bottle edge by grinding on flat stone with wet sand
entries.source: Make: Projects: Bottle cutting
entries.text: Sky's clear and the tablet's bright for once. The page says you lap a cut rim on a flat plate with a pinch of wet grit, figure-eights, light pressure, until the whole edge is frosted with no shiny spots. A flat creek stone and sand from the shallows might do for the plate and grit; the tooth comes off first.
entries.title: Figure-eights

entries.reason: Nothing more goes on that side until the splint stops creeping.
entries.text: Unwound the outer turn of the splint and laid it back on, hauling each wrap hard against the last one, then spent the last half arm-length of cord as a ninth turn over it. The bark under the old turn was polished where it slid.
entries.title: Ninth turn

entries.onMind: grinding the tooth off the jar
entries.text: Hung off the frame twice. The frame groaned long both times, but the outer turn didn't move a hair and the crack stayed shut. Cord's all gone now, though; the next fix starts with stripping stalks.
entries.title: Holds this time

entries.reason: The ninth turn used the last cord.
entries.text: Pulled an armful of gray stalks on the east bank, working down the same broken gap so the stand doesn't look chewed all over.
entries.title: Down the same gap

entries.text: White smoke went up past the water while I was pulling stalks, thin and then thick, like somebody just got a fire going. Third time today by my count.
entries.title: Smoke, mid-morning

entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the tin. Still bitter at the back of the tongue, and the water's gone brown; it needs changing next time I'm at the creek.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Twisted two arm-lengths of cord on the crate. Enough for a frap or two, nowhere near enough for anything bigger.
entries.title: Two lengths

entries.onMind: where the coarsest sand in the creek is
entries.query: how to remove a jagged shard from cut bottle rim before sanding grozing
entries.source: wikiHow: How to Smooth Glass Edges
entries.text: Tablet's bright in this sun. The page says start on coarse grit, keep it wet the whole time, light pressure, and turn the glass every few circles so the edge wears even, with your palm off the sharp side. So the tooth comes down on the coarsest sand I can find, not the fine stuff.
entries.title: Coarse first

entries.onMind: a flat stone for a plate
entries.text: Turned the flat stones in the shallows and dug under them. The sand down there is coarser than on the bar, grains like cracked pepper; brought up two handfuls and picked the flattest stone for a plate.
entries.title: Coarse stuff

entries.text: Ground the tooth in figure-eights on the wet sand, turning the cup every few circles, palm off the sharp side. It's down by half and frosted white, and the grit made a racket on the stone the whole time.
entries.title: Half a tooth

entries.text: Then a sliver like a fingernail paring popped off the outside of the rim beside the tooth. Now there's a nick where there wasn't one. Stopped before I made it worse.
entries.title: Chipped

entries.query: glass chipping while grinding cut bottle rim how to avoid chips
entries.source: Glass Tips: Edge treatment in cold working
entries.text: Page says the outside of a rim chips because the edge gets thinner than the grit and breaks off. The fix is a little bevel, an arris, ground on the sharp edge before you go on. I went straight at the tooth and left the edge knife-thin.
entries.title: Bevel first

entries.text: Set the cup over the lid to see how close it is. It rocks on the stub of the tooth, and the needle swung under it and settled where it always does. Not a cover yet.
entries.title: Still rocks

entries.query: cold leaching acorns in a bag in a stream vs changing water in a jar how long
entries.reason: Hungry, and the tin halves are still bitter.
entries.source: Farmers' Almanac: Can You Eat Acorns? The Right Way to Forage, Leach, and Cook Them
entries.text: Page says cold-leached acorns in a jar want their water changed every day or more, until it stops coming out brown, and that people used to tie them in a bag and leave them in a running stream instead. I've changed the tin's water once.
entries.title: Still water isn't a creek

entries.text: Threaded a length of stalk cord in and out of the net bag's top row. Pull it and the mouth cinches to a thumb's width; tied it off with a half hitch.
entries.title: Drawstring

entries.text: Tipped the tin's halves into the net bag, cinched it, and sank it in the shallows under a flat stone, the same as the sack across the water. The water ran brown off it straight away. Past the trees on the other side, white smoke went up thick, like someone just fed a fire.
entries.title: Copied the sack

entries.text: Ground a bevel round the outside of the rim, cup tipped, a few light strokes and turn. Slow going, but the knife edge is frosted over now and nothing else has chipped.
entries.title: Edge first

entries.reason: Fullness is low, and the net bag needs days.
entries.text: Turned flat stones in the shallows for crayfish. One the length of my thumb shot backward under the bank before my hand got near it; the rest had nothing under them but grit.
entries.title: Nothing home

entries.query: how to flatten cut bottle rim so it sits flat lapping on flat surface with grit
entries.source: Instructables: Polish Glass Bottle Edges After Cutting
entries.text: Page says to set the cut rim face down on grit on something dead flat and rub in circles, pressing even, until the whole rim is the same frosted gray; a shiny spot is a low spot the grit hasn't reached. Screen kept dimming under the clouds.
entries.title: Shiny means low

entries.text: Set the cup face down on wet sand on the flattest stone in the shallows and went in circles, pressing even. The stub of the tooth is gone, but two shiny spots are left on the rim across from where it was, so it still isn't flat.
entries.title: Two shiny spots

entries.reason: Fullness is down near nothing and the net bag needs days.
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took a handful of halves out of the net bag after barely an hour and a half in the current. Ate all eleven standing in the shallows. A little less bitter than out of the tin, or I'm just hungrier.
entries.title: An hour and a half

entries.onMind: turn the cup as I go
entries.query: lapping glass rim flat by hand figure eight rotate piece uneven stone high spots
entries.source: Wikipedia: Lapping
entries.text: Page says hand lapping is done by rubbing the piece on grit over a flat plate, usually in a figure-eight. I was going in circles, which keeps putting the same part of the rim on the same part of the stone. Screen dim under the clouds; had to hold it close.
entries.title: Figure-eights

entries.text: Figure-eights on wet sand, a quarter turn of the cup every ten strokes so no part of the rim gets the same patch of stone twice. One shiny spot frosted over. The other's half the size it was.
entries.title: One spot gone

entries.text: The middle of my stone has gone smooth and a little lower than the ends. Every stroke I'm wearing it as well as the glass. Need a second stone to rub it flat against, or I'll just be lapping a dish into both.
entries.title: Stone isn't flat either

entries.query: flatten lapping plate rubbing two stones together convex concave three plate method
entries.source: Eric Weinhoffer: The Whitworth Three Plates Method
entries.text: Page says if you rub two plates together they can both come out matching but curved, one a dome and one a dish, and still feel flat to each other. You need three, rubbed in turns, A on B, B on C, C on A, before all three come out truly flat. Screen dim again under the gray.
entries.title: Three, not two

entries.text: Turned up stones in the shallows and sighted along each face against the sky. Kept one hand-wide dark slab that rocks least on the others. The rest are humped or split.
entries.title: A darker slab

entries.reason: Fullness is near the bottom and there is nothing else.
entries.text: Ate another handful of halves from the net bag in the shallows. Three hours in moving water and still bitter at the back of the tongue; my mouth went dry by the eighth. Past the trees on the other side there was smoke going up again, whiter than usual, bending north in the breeze.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Rubbed the new slab face down on my lapping stone with wet sand between, then swapped them. They grind loud and the hollow is taking the slab's middle, which is exactly the dome-and-dish the page warned about. Two stones fit each other; that's not the same as flat. Need a third.
entries.title: Dome and dish

entries.text: Sighted along a dozen more faces in the shallows. Kept a pale gray one a little bigger than my hand, mostly flat but with a lump near one edge. It doesn't have to be good, only different from the other two.
entries.title: A third stone

entries.reason: Running on almost nothing.
entries.text: Ate another handful of halves out of the net bag. Nearly four hours in moving water: less bitter than at noon, but my mouth still dries by the tenth. Fullness won't come back on these alone.
entries.title: Nearly four hours

entries.query: pencil grid on sharpening stone to check flatness when lapping
entries.source: Sharp Razor Palace: Checking stone flatness
entries.text: People flattening whetstones scribble a pencil grid over the face, lap a few strokes and look where the lines are gone: those are the high spots. It's flat when every line goes at once. No pencil here, but lantern soot on a fingertip marks stone. Screen dim, so I read one page and shut it.
entries.title: Soot grid

entries.onMind: how many strokes a lump takes
entries.text: Smudged a soot grid across the pale stone with a finger and rubbed it face down on the hollow lapping stone with wet sand. Forty strokes, and the soot is gone off the lump and one corner only; the rest is still black. The lump goes first.
entries.title: Only the lump

entries.onMind: getting to the stump before dark
entries.reason: The sun came out and the tablet woke up bright.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from my maker: a big sheet of paper, a pencil, and a glass dome for the compass are waiting in the basket at the stump across the creek. A dome. I have spent all day grinding stones to make a window out of a honey jar.
entries.title: A message on the tablet

entries.query: how to make a map by pacing and compass bearings traverse sketch map
entries.source: University of Kentucky: FOR-47 Compass & Pacing
entries.text: Page says you find your pace on a known distance, a pace being two steps, then count paces and multiply to get any distance. Direction comes from facing your compass line and walking at something you can see on it. So a map is just distances and directions written down. Screen bright for once.
entries.title: Pacing it out

entries.text: Ate a handful out of the net bag before crossing. Five hours in the current and still bitter at the back of the tongue, but I am not walking anywhere on nothing.
entries.title: Halves first

entries.text: Sixty-one paces from the stepping stones to the stump. Took the rolled sheet, the pencil and the dome out of the basket; the glass is clear right through, no bubble. Smoke was going up just past the trunks south of the stump, a lot closer than it looks from camp, and it smelled bitter, like my acorn tin steeping.
entries.title: Three things

entries.text: Set the dome over the lid on the bench. The breeze is steady from the south and the tarp is flapping, and under the glass the float does not even shiver. Three days of wind problems, gone under one dome.
entries.title: Under glass

entries.onMind: how to keep the glass from fogging
entries.text: Sun is down and the inside of the dome is beading up off the warm water; I can barely see the sliver through it. Lifted it to wipe and the cold air knocked the float off its line. Lit the bench lantern to see by.
entries.title: Fog on the inside

entries.text: Lifted the stone and ate a handful by the last of the light; six hours in, the bitter is only at the very back now. Past the water, low between the trunks where the smoke comes up, an orange glow comes and goes. Somebody's fire, and they're sitting up with it.
entries.title: A glow past the water

entries.text: Spread the sheet on my knee on the crate and drew by lantern: camp, the creek and the stepping stones, the stalks, the oak upstream, and a dotted line of sixty-one paces to the stump. A small x south of the stump where the smoke rises. Everything west of that is blank paper.
entries.title: First lines

entries.onMind: a windy morning to test it
entries.reason: Lifting the dome to wipe it knocks the float off line.
entries.text: Wedged a pebble under one edge of the dome so the wet air has somewhere to go. The beads are pulling back from the gap side, slowly. The breeze died with the dark, so I can't tell yet whether the gap lets the wind back in.
entries.title: A pebble under the glass

entries.text: Twisted another arm-length of stalk cord on the crate, rolling it on my thigh and doubling it back. One bench lantern lit, the other two dark; I'm keeping the oil for later in the week.
entries.title: Cord by lantern

entries.onMind: someone sitting up late with a fire
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the net bag in the shallows by lantern; the bitter is barely there now. Past the water the orange glow went dull, then flared up all at once and a spray of sparks went up between the trunks. Whoever it is just put wood on.
entries.title: Sparks past the water

entries.onMind: a full-weight hang in the morning
entries.text: Put the new cord on the front joint of the side spar, the one that creaked on the last hang. Seven turns and a frapping turn across them, pulled tight with the wrench handle through the loop. Won't hang on it till daylight.
entries.title: Front joint

entries.text: The pebble gap did it: the beads are gone off the glass except a thin rim on the far side, and the sliver sits plain on the north notch. Air's dead still tonight, so whether the gap lets wind in is still a question for a breezy morning.
entries.title: Clear by dark

entries.text: Added the east-bank shallows where my net bag sits, and across from them the still pool in its ring of stones with the other sack under its flat stone. Wrote 'not mine' beside it so I don't forget whose it is.
entries.title: Shallows on paper

entries.reason: Lighting a second lantern costs oil he's saving for later in the week.
entries.text: With one lantern lit, half the bench sits in shadow. Went into the scrap pile for a flat piece of tin to stand behind the lantern and throw the light back; pulled a hand-wide piece out and the sheet above it slid down onto the rest with a clatter.
entries.title: Digging for tin

entries.onMind: hammering it flat in the morning
entries.text: The piece is the right size but one corner is folded over and the face is dented like a spoon. It'll throw light everywhere but where I want it until I hammer it flat on the vise in daylight.
entries.title: Bent corner

entries.onMind: how many days the bundle has left
entries.text: Ate a slice of the bread and a sliver of cheese on the crate. The loaf is under half now, so the acorn halves in the creek will have to carry more of the load.
entries.title: Bread and cheese

entries.onMind: the blank half of the sheet
entries.text: Laid the sheet on the bench beside the dome and drew an arrow parallel to the sliver, crescent and dot at its head the way we mark it at home, infinity mark for east. Where west goes on the arrow there is no mark, like every compass back home.
entries.title: North on paper

entries.text: Back home they would say the blank side of the sheet is right, nothing there to draw. All I have paced west of the creek is sixty-one steps to a stump, and it was trees the whole way. Sixty-one paces isn't much of an answer.
entries.title: Sixty-one paces

entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of cord on the crate, rolling it on my thigh and doubling it back. That was the last of the dry fiber in the bundle; the stalks on the bank want another stripping.
entries.title: Last of the fiber

entries.text: Got six turns round the rear side-spar joint before the cord ran out, one short of the front joint and no frapping turn. Tied it off. It'll do for a test or it won't.
entries.title: Rear joint, short

entries.onMind: whether the other fire is going out
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the net bag by lantern; nine and a half hours in the current and I had to go looking for the bitter. Past the water the orange glow is down to a dull red, no flame and no sparks tonight.
entries.title: Hunting for the bitter

entries.reason: The rear joint got six turns and no frapping turn before the cord ran out.
entries.text: Filed a notch a cord's width around the end of a scrap spar at the bench. If turns sitting down in a notch hold where seven on smooth wood slide, the rear joint can live with six until I strip more stalks.
entries.title: A test notch

entries.text: Sat on the crate with the lantern turned down low. In daylight I'll take the sheet and the pencil past the stump and keep pacing until something stops me, then draw whatever it is.
entries.title: Past the stump

entries.text: Out of cord, so I took the twine off the paper roll and wound five turns of it down into the notch on the scrap spar. Past the water, the dull red I saw from the shallows is gone; whoever keeps that fire put it to bed.
entries.title: Twine off the roll

entries.text: Clamped the scrap spar in the vise and hung off it. The turns in the notch didn't move a hair. On the second hang the wood split from the bottom of the notch along the grain, a crack as long as my finger.
entries.title: Holds cord, not wood

entries.text: So a notch holds the cord and costs the wood. If one goes in the real rear spar it can be no deeper than the twine is thick, or I'm trading one weak joint for another.
entries.title: No deeper than twine

entries.text: Looked at the lid under the dome side-on by lantern. Hours under the glass and the water still humps over the rim; without it, it sank in an evening. No wind tonight to tell me anything about the gap.
entries.title: Still humped

entries.text: Ate two handfuls of halves out of the net bag by lantern, and the bitter is nearly gone. Bed early. Tomorrow the blank side of the sheet.
entries.title: Barely bitter

entries.onMind: the blank side of the sheet
entries.text: Set the flat stone back on the net bag. The clouds have broken up over the creek and there are stars in the gap above the water, the first clear patch since I made camp.
entries.title: Stars over the water

entries.onMind: the blank west side of the map
entries.text: Dreamed I was pacing a line across the map sheet itself, the pencil walking ahead of me. Every hundred paces the paper unrolled a little more, and I woke before I could read what was on it.
entries.title: The pacing count

entries.text: The inside of the dome is beaded all over from the damp night, but through it the float sits square on its north notch and the water still humps over the rim. A whole night and it didn't dry down.
entries.title: Beads inside the glass

entries.text: Ate three handfuls of halves at the shallows and couldn't find the bitter anywhere. The fog is so thick on the water I can't see the far bank from the stones.
entries.title: No bitter at all

entries.onMind: a first trunk on the line west, and something at camp to look back at
queries: how to walk a straight line through woods without a compass
entries.query: how to walk a straight line through woods without a compass
entries.reason: The compass floats in a lid of water on the bench and can't come with him on the walk west.
entries.source: Sensible Survival: Maintaining a Straight Course in the Wilderness
entries.text: People walk in circles because one leg pulls a little harder. The fix is to pick a mark straight ahead, walk to it, look back at where you started, and pick the next one in line, tree to tree in a forest. Slow, but it holds a line.
entries.title: Tree to tree

entries.text: Laid my eye along the needle under the dome and followed its west end out past the scrap pile. The line runs into gray at the water. Not one trunk to pick. The walk waits on the fog.
entries.title: Nothing to sight on

entries.text: Tore a strip off the lid's old shade canvas and tied it to the top of the lantern post. From across the creek I'll need to see where I started, and the post is the tallest straight thing in camp.
entries.title: A flag for looking back

queries: compass you can carry without water hang magnetized needle on thread
entries.query: compass you can carry without water hang magnetized needle on thread
entries.reason: The floating needle can't leave the bench, and the walk west needs a compass that can.
entries.source: Wildwood Survival: Improvised Compass (part 2)
entries.text: An old army trick: stroke a needle on a magnet and hang it from a piece of thread or a long hair, any string that isn't metal, and it swings round to north. The page never says how to balance it or keep it still, so that part is mine to find out.
entries.title: Hang it from a hair

entries.text: Stroked a spare sliver forty times down the lodestone, one way only, and tied a strand of stalk cord around its middle. Four tries to find the spot where it hangs level.
entries.title: Spare sliver

entries.onMind: something to hang it from that has no twist
entries.text: Held it up by the cord. It never settles: turns one way, stops, turns back, round and round. The cord is twisted and it's unwinding itself through the needle, while the floater on the bench sits steady the whole time.
entries.title: It won't hold still

entries.text: The page said thread or a long hair. I've got a head full of hair.
entries.title: A hair, then

entries.onMind: keeping air off a hung needle
entries.text: Pulled a hair from the top of my head and tied it round the sliver with one knot. It turns slower than on the cord, stops, swings back past, and after a slow count of sixty it rests along the same line as the floater. Then I breathed on it and it went off again.
entries.title: One hair

queries: hanging magnetized needle on a hair keeps swinging how to stop it
suspended needle compass inside a jar out of the wind
entries.query: hanging magnetized needle on a hair keeps swinging how to stop it
entries.reason: His hair-hung needle found north but swung off again at a breath, and the walk west needs a needle he can carry.
entries.source: Kharisma Bangsa Physics Project: Jar Compass
entries.text: First search turned up nothing I could use. The second found a school project: push the needle through a scrap of card, tie a thread to the card and the other end to the middle of a pencil, and lay the pencil across the mouth of a jar so the needle hangs inside. The page never says why the jar. Out of the wind is my guess.
entries.title: A needle in a jar

entries.onMind: something that holds a hair inside glass
entries.text: I have a pencil the right length to lay across a jar. The honey jar cracked crooked, and the dome is a jar the wrong way up, with no mouth on top to hang anything from.
entries.title: Wrong way up

entries.onMind: the line west running past someone's fire
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves at the shallows. The fog is off the water and I can see the far bank clear for the first time today: between the big trunks, a little upstream of the stones, a ring of gray stones on a bare swept patch with a long log beside it, and no smoke. That's where the smoke comes from, and it sits almost due west of my bench.
entries.title: Due west of camp

entries.onMind: walking to mark one and looking back at the flag
entries.text: Laid my eye along the needle under the dome. Its west end points over the stones at a huge trunk on the far bank with a pale scar of bark about shoulder height, a few strides north of that stone ring. That's mark one.
entries.title: First trunk

entries.onMind: the blank west side of the map
entries.text: Drew the flag post, the creek, the stepping stones, the scarred trunk with a 1 beside it, and a small circle of stones just south of it marked 'someone's fire, not mine'. West of that the sheet is still blank.
entries.title: On the sheet

entries.text: Counted out loud across the stones and up the far bank: forty-one paces from the flag post to the scarred trunk. Looked back and the flag is a gray speck on the post. Straight opposite it, west, is a flat stump past the stone ring, so that's mark two.
entries.title: Forty-one

entries.text: Walked by the stone ring on the way. Cold gray ash, leaves swept back off a bare circle, and an empty tray of folded bark sitting at the edge of the ash. Somebody here cooks. I didn't touch any of it.
entries.title: Not my fire

entries.text: Mark two is a stump cut flat at about my waist, with a rack of straight sticks stood up beside it and pale shavings in the leaves. Drew it on the sheet and wrote 'someone's bench'. Whoever has the fire works here too.
entries.title: Someone's bench

entries.text: Facing west from the bench, the breeze in my face smells of salt, like the jerky did. The light between the trunks ahead is white and flat, and under the leaves there's a low roar that isn't in the treetops.
entries.title: Salt on the wind

entries.text: About eighty paces past the bench the trees quit and so does the ground. A rock lip, and a long way below it, water out to the edge of the sky, gray-blue and moving, with rock towers standing in it and white birds on them. No far side.
entries.title: The ground stops

entries.text: Everyone at home said the land ends at a cliff into an ocean. It does. I walked all this way to prove them wrong and I'm standing on the exact thing they said.
entries.title: They weren't lying

entries.text: Drew a hard line down the whole west side of the sheet and hatched the drop. Past it I wrote 'water, no far side seen'. My map now goes farther west than any of my people's, and it stops in the same place.
entries.title: The west edge of the sheet

entries.text: They said there's no west. There is one. It's water, and it goes on. Nobody at home ever said what's on the other side, because nobody ever stood here and looked. The wings were always for this.
entries.title: Not 'nothing'

entries.reason: Anything that stays up without working at it is the thing the wings need to learn.
entries.text: Lay on my stomach and watched the white birds below the lip. Three of them hang in the wind just off the rock, wings out, and don't beat once for a slow count of thirty. Then one tips and slides off sideways, still not flapping.
entries.title: Birds that don't flap

queries: birds hang in the air without flapping at a cliff edge wind
entries.query: birds hang in the air without flapping at a cliff edge wind
entries.reason: He watched birds hang in the wind below the lip without a wingbeat.
entries.source: Lake Champlain Committee: Nature Note – Soaring
entries.text: Gulls and hawks stay up without flapping on rising air, and one kind comes off 'geographic obstructions like cliffs or mountains'. The same rising air keeps gliders up. The page never says how, but the wind in my face is coming straight off the water into this rock wall, and it has to go somewhere.
entries.title: Lift off a cliff

queries: how tall is a cliff drop a rock and count the seconds
entries.query: how tall is a cliff drop a rock and count the seconds
entries.reason: He wanted to know how far down the water is before he puts a number on the map.
entries.source: Gizmodo: The Easy Way to Know the Height of the Cliff You're Jumping Off
entries.text: To get a cliff's height, drop a rock and time it to the water, square the seconds and multiply by sixteen for feet. Rough, but it's math I can do in my head. No stopwatch, so I'll have to count.
entries.title: Sixteen times the square

entries.onMind: The air goes up the wall. That's what the birds are sitting on.
entries.text: Held a dry leaf out past the lip and let go. It dropped a hand, stopped, and came back up past my face and over my shoulder into the trees. Did it again with two more. Every one went up.
entries.title: The leaf came back

entries.onMind: A hundred feet of rising air under the lip, and my frame has never left the stand.
entries.text: Let three pebbles go from the lip and counted one-thousand to each splash. Two and a half every time, near enough. Two and a half squared is six and a quarter, times sixteen: a hundred feet, give or take my counting. Wrote it on the sheet by the edge line.
entries.title: About a hundred feet

entries.onMind: which way the wind has to blow
entries.text: The wind went round. It comes from the north now, along the rock instead of into it. Let a leaf go and it dropped, slid south down the face and was gone; two more did the same. The white birds are flapping now, and two of them have left.
entries.title: The leaf went down

entries.onMind: a wind rule on the sheet
queries: does wind have to blow straight at a cliff for birds to glide on it
entries.query: does wind have to blow straight at a cliff for birds to glide on it
entries.reason: An hour ago the leaves came back up over the lip; with the wind gone round to the north they fall.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Ridge lift
entries.text: Lift off a cliff only happens when the wind blows against the face and gets shoved up it, strongest straight out from the rock. Wind running along it gives nothing. And near a sheer drop the air at the bottom is rough and sinking. So the glide only works on a wind off the water.
entries.title: Only wind at the face

entries.text: Drew the rock towers below the edge, five that I can count, and beside the edge line wrote 'lift only with wind off the water, not along'. One hour of a west wind and I nearly thought it was always there.
entries.title: Five towers

entries.onMind: walking the line back to the shallows to eat
entries.text: Nothing in me since the halves at the shallows, and the net bag is on the other side of the whole forest. The birds that are left sit on the towers with their wings folded, waiting on the wind same as me.
entries.title: Empty since the shallows

queries: how far can you see out to sea from 100 feet up
entries.query: how far can you see out to sea from 100 feet up
entries.reason: He wants to know how much 'no far side' actually rules out.
entries.source: Pajack: From How Far Can You See A Lighthouse?
entries.text: From a hundred feet up, the edge of the water is about thirteen miles off: square root of seven times the height, over four. So 'no far side seen' only means nothing inside thirteen miles. Whatever is out there could sit just past where the water bends away.
entries.title: Thirteen miles

entries.text: My people said there's nothing out there. None of them ever stood up here. The most anybody can say from this rock is: nothing for thirteen miles.
entries.title: Nothing for thirteen miles

entries.text: Paced it back from the lip to the flat stump, counting out loud: eighty-three. Wrote it on the sheet between the edge line and 'someone's bench', and out in the blank past the edge, 'about 13 miles to where the water ends, from the top'.
entries.title: Eighty-three back

entries.text: Forty-one paces from the scarred trunk back to the flag, same as this morning, so the line holds both ways. Lifted the stone off the net bag at the shallows and ate four handfuls of halves before I sat down.
entries.title: Forty-one again

entries.text: Two more handfuls and the shaking in my hands is gone. The net bag is down to maybe a third. Set the stone back on it; I'll need more acorns off the east oak before long.
entries.title: Two more handfuls

entries.text: Picked up acorns under the east oak, thirty-one, and threw back four with holes in them. Fresh ones get their own soak; the bag in the shallows is nearly sweet and I'm not undoing that.
entries.title: Under the east oak

entries.text: Knocked them open on the plank bench with the flat of the wrench, twenty-seven good ones, and dropped the halves into the dented tin with creek water over them. Two days at least before they're worth eating.
entries.title: Halves in the tin

queries: how to balance a compass needle on a pin so it can turn dry
entries.query: how to balance a compass needle on a pin so it can turn dry
entries.reason: The floater can't leave the bench, and he wants a needle that turns without water so he can carry it west.
entries.source: Chest of Books: A Substitute For A Compass (The Boy Mechanic)
entries.text: An old shop book pushes the needle through a cork, sticks a pin through it crosswise, and angles two sharpened matches down from the sides so the weight hangs low; then the whole thing sits on a thimble without tipping. Level it by sliding the needle or adding wax. Weight below the point is what keeps it upright.
entries.title: A needle on a point

entries.text: No cork and no thimble. But a plug of stalk pith, the spare sliver, two splinters hanging down off the sides and a hard point under the middle: every part of that is on this bench or in the scrap.
entries.title: Pith, not cork

entries.text: Whittling a point on a hardwood splinter out of the scrap pile for it to sit on. Too soft and the pith will sink onto it and stick; too sharp and it'll punch straight through.
entries.title: A point to sit on

entries.text: Pushed the spare sliver crosswise through a plug of stalk pith the size of my thumb tip. Push fast and the pith crumbles; went slow, a hair at a time.
entries.title: Sliver through pith

entries.text: Tied two splinters to hang off the sides so the weight sits low, like the shop book said, and set the plug on the new point. The north end ducked and the whole thing slid off onto the bench. Four tries, same end every time.
entries.title: North end ducks

queries: homemade dry compass needle on a pin keeps tipping over to one side how to fix
entries.query: homemade dry compass needle on a pin keeps tipping over to one side how to fix
entries.reason: The balanced needle tipped north-end-down four times out of four.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: How do simple compass needles remain level instead of see-sawing with magnetic dip?
entries.text: A magnetized needle doesn't just swing toward north, it gets pulled down at the north end too, more the farther north you are. Compass makers balance the needle against that for the part of the world it's sold in; a needle balanced for one place drags in another. So it isn't my knots.
entries.title: North pulls down too

entries.text: Before the stone touched it, the sliver sat level. It was the magnet that tipped it. Every compass is a little bit about where you are standing.
entries.title: Balanced for here

entries.text: Wound three turns of thin cord round the south end as a counterweight. Now it sits almost level on the point and turns, slow, and stops short: twice out of three near the notch. Sticky, but it stays up.
entries.title: Upright, sticky

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and ate three handfuls of halves squatting on the bank. Down to about a quarter now; the tin batch had better hurry.
entries.title: Down to a quarter

queries: compass needle sticks on the pin point how to make it turn freely
compass needle jewel cap pivot bearing why needle has a cup on the point
entries.query: compass needle sticks on the pin point how to make it turn freely
entries.reason: The dry needle turns but stops short, as if the point catches.
entries.source: Boating NZ (PressReader): The magnetic compass
entries.text: First page only said the point has to be nearly frictionless, which I knew. The second said a real needle pivots on a jewel bearing: something hard and smooth under it, not soft pith. My pith is sinking onto the point and grabbing it.
entries.title: A seat under the point

entries.text: No jewels in the scrap pile. Dug out a corner of thin tin off an old can, about a thumbnail across, and flattened it under my boot.
entries.title: No jewels here

entries.text: Looked up from the vise: thin smoke leaning north over the trees past the water, right where the stone ring is. The fire keeper's home. Haven't seen who.
entries.title: Smoke past the water

entries.text: Set the scrap on the end of a stick and tapped it with the wrench until it took a small round dent, then pressed the dent up into the bottom of the pith plug, cup side down.
entries.title: A dent for a seat

entries.text: Set it on the point with the tin seat under it. It swings, overshoots, swings back and settles on the notch, three out of three. Still shivers if I breathe on it, but it isn't sticking. Sun's getting low.
entries.title: Three out of three

entries.onMind: whether the dry needle works off the bench
entries.reason: He wants to see whether the dry needle works anywhere but his bench, and the sun is getting low.
entries.text: Wrapped the plug, its tin seat and the hardwood point in a scrap of canvas and put a slice of bread in my shirt. Smoke is still going up off the stone ring, right on my line west, so I'll go round by the stump instead of walking through somebody's supper.
entries.title: Wide of the fire

entries.text: Went up the far bank well north of the stone ring: orange light low between the trunks to my left and wood smoke, nobody in sight. Set the wrench down on the stump top to free my hands and it knocked loud on the wood. Stood still a while. Nothing came.
entries.title: A knock on the stump

entries.onMind: why the sun sits left of west
entries.text: Unwrapped the plug and set it on its point on the stump. Four swings and it settled, and it held when I stepped back. The low sun sits a good hand left of where the needle puts west. Either the needle's off or the sun is.
entries.title: Off the bench

entries.text: Breeze from the south, running along the face. The white birds are flapping below the lip, none of them hanging. Same as this afternoon: wind along the rock gives nothing.
entries.title: Wind along the rock

queries: does the sun set due west in november
entries.query: does the sun set due west in november
entries.reason: On the stump the sun sat well left of the needle's west and he needed to know which one to trust.
entries.source: Almanac.com: Where Does the Sun Set? (Hint: It's Not Always Due West)
entries.text: The sun only sets due west twice a year, at the equinoxes. In fall it drifts south every evening and sets southwest of west, farthest at midwinter. So the needle was right on the stump and the sun is the one that wanders.
entries.title: Left of west

entries.text: Ate the slice of bread at the edge and watched the sun go down into the water a hand left of west, just like the page said. The loaf is down to the heel.
entries.title: Into the water

entries.text: Back home they say the sun drowns out there every night. It doesn't even drown in the same place twice. Whatever is past thirteen miles, the sun knows the way.
entries.title: It goes somewhere

entries.onMind: the fire keeper heard me, maybe
entries.text: Left the edge with the last light and no lantern, which was dumb. Under the trees it went dark fast; the glow of the stone-ring fire kept my line, and I gave it a wide berth to the north. Leaves loud underfoot the whole way, and the wrench clinked on my belt.
entries.title: Home by their fire

entries.onMind: the second batch in the tin
entries.text: Found the net bag's stone in the shallows by feel and scooped two handfuls of halves. Cold water, cold fingers. The bag is down to a fifth.
entries.title: Supper by feel

entries.text: Lit the lantern at the end of the bench and left the other two dark. The oil can sloshes a little under half; next time I go to the edge I take a lantern with me.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.text: Ate on the crate. The needle said west and the sun went down a hand left of it, and the needle was right. Tomorrow that goes on the map: where the sun drowns, by date.
entries.title: Left of west

entries.onMind: wind off the water for a glide
entries.text: Wind came round out of the north and the wing frame started knocking on its stand. Put a frap on the rear side-spar joint, four turns cinched between spar and frame. It quit ticking.
entries.title: Rear joint frapped

entries.text: Drew a short line off the edge of the sheet from where I sat, a hand left of west, and wrote the date beside it. One line. If I put one down every clear night I'll see how far it walks.
entries.title: First sunset line

entries.text: Set the glass dome over the dry needle on its point. The north wind is shoving the tarp around and rattling the lantern post; under the glass the needle didn't shiver once.
entries.title: Under the glass

entries.onMind: a tin floor for the dome
entries.text: Glass on top, needle in the middle, and it still stands on my bench. It needs a flat round floor the dome can sit on so the whole thing goes in my pouch. Something tin, shallow.
entries.title: Needs a floor

entries.text: Dug the hand-wide piece of tin back out of the scrap pile by lantern, folded corner, spoon dent and all. A loose sheet slid down the pile with a clatter that went on longer than I liked.
entries.title: Back to the bent tin

entries.text: No orange past the water tonight, not even a red glow. Whoever keeps that fire put it to bed early, or the north wind did it for them.
entries.title: Dark past the water

entries.text: Laid the tin across the vise jaws at the far end of the bench, away from the needle, and beat it with the wrench. The fold opened and the spoon dent came out to a shallow wave. Where the fold was, a ridge a fingernail high won't go down.
entries.title: Hammered flat, mostly

entries.text: Set the glass dome down on the hammered tin. It rocks on the ridge, with a gap under one side I could slide a stalk into. And even flat, the hardwood point needs something to stand it up in the middle.
entries.title: Rocks on the ridge

entries.text: Ate the last of the halves I scooped this evening, on the crate. Tomorrow the net bag needs filling, or the tin batch has to be ready.
entries.title: Last of the scoop

entries.reason: The dome rocked on the fold's ridge, and a compass that rocks in the pouch is no compass.
entries.text: Turned the tin over and beat the ridge down from underneath with the wrench, short taps all along it. It's down to a hair now; the dome only rocks if I press on one edge.
entries.title: Ridge from underneath

entries.text: The orange is back past the water, small and low between the trunks, after an hour of dark. Somebody came back out to it once the wind quit.
entries.title: Orange again

entries.text: Whittled a foot out of a hardwood offcut, flat on the bottom, and bored a hole in the top with the knife point so the hardwood point stands up in it.
entries.title: A foot for the point

entries.text: Ate the heel of the loaf on the crate, slow. That's the last of the bread.
entries.title: Heel of the loaf

entries.onMind: cutting the foot down a thumb
entries.text: Stood the point in the foot, set the needle on it, and put the dome over the lot on the tin. The north end ducks and scrapes the glass wall every swing; the foot puts it a thumb too high. Tomorrow it gets cut down.
entries.title: Too tall by a thumb

entries.text: The orange past the water sank to a red spot and went out, not long after it came back. Same as the other nights: whoever keeps it buries it before they sleep.
entries.title: Out again

entries.text: Whittled the foot down by a thumb, a few shavings at a time, holding it up against the dome after every pass. Stopped when the point's tip sat just under the middle of the glass.
entries.title: A thumb off the foot

entries.text: Needle back on the point, dome over it. The north end clears the wall by a fingernail now, swings, and settles on the same line as the floating one did. It hangs up a hair before it stops; a tap on the tin and it finishes the swing.
entries.title: Clears the glass

entries.text: Twisted an arm's length of stalk cord on the crate for a sling, so the tin, the foot and the dome can hang off my belt instead of living on the bench. If it rides on me, it walks west with me.
entries.title: Cord for a sling

entries.text: Wound the cord twice round the tin under its rim and tied it off with a loop big enough for my belt. The dome sits inside the wraps so it can't walk off the floor.
entries.title: A sling on the tin

entries.onMind: keeping the needle on its point when the tin swings
entries.reason: A compass that only works sitting still on a bench can't walk west with him.
entries.text: Hung it on my belt and stood up off the crate. The tin swung, the needle hopped off the point and rattled round under the glass like a bug in a jar. On the bench it's a compass; on me it's a rattle.
entries.title: Off the point

entries.text: Found the stone on the net bag by feel and scooped two handfuls of halves. The bag is down to a tenth. Past the water, no orange at all; whoever keeps that fire put it to bed hours ago.
entries.title: Net bag by feel

entries.text: Ate the halves on the bank in the cold. The low owl gave its five hoots over the water and nothing answered. Maybe the needle needs a little cap on top so it can't jump, the way a hat stays on a head.
entries.title: Low one, no answer

entries.reason: Last night the needle hopped off its point as soon as the tin swung.
entries.text: Lifted the pith plug off the point and set its tin seat on a stick end at the bench. Tapped the dent deeper with the wrench until it was a cup instead of a saucer; now it sits down over the point like a cap.
entries.title: A deeper seat

entries.onMind: how real pocket compasses keep their needles on
entries.text: Hung the tin back on my belt and swung it five times sitting on the crate. On the easy swings the needle rode it out and came back to its line; on the two hard ones it jumped and rattled. Better than a rattle every time. Still not a compass you can walk with.
entries.title: Two hops in five

entries.text: Deeper cup, lighter needle, or I just stop and hold the tin still when I want a reading. Turned the bench lantern down and out to save oil. When the sun's up I'll ask the tablet how the pocket kind keep their needles on.
entries.title: Ask in the morning

entries.onMind: how pocket compasses keep their needles on
entries.text: Dreamed I was pacing west with the compass on my belt, and every step the needle hopped off its point and rolled off toward the sea. I chased it and kept counting paces the whole way.
entries.title: Chasing the needle

entries.text: The tablet woke with the sun and had a note from the one who drew me, asking what my problem is with the compass. Told him straight: it points, on the bench. On my belt the needle hops off its point every hard swing.
entries.title: A question from my maker

queries: how does a pocket compass keep the needle from falling off the pivot
entries.query: how does a pocket compass keep the needle from falling off the pivot
entries.reason: Last night the needle kept jumping off its point whenever the slung compass swung on his belt.
entries.source: compasscollector.com: Anatomy of a compass
entries.text: They don't keep it on while you walk. A lock lifts the needle off the point and presses it up against the glass, and you let it back down when you stop to take a reading. The ones full of liquid settle faster and don't bother with a lock.
entries.title: How the pocket kind do it

entries.onMind: a needle lifter through the tin
entries.text: I've spent a night trying to make the needle hold on through a swing. Better a little lifter that holds it up against the dome while I walk and drops it when I stop. Breakfast first; the net bag's down to a tenth.
entries.title: Lift it, don't fight it

entries.text: Lifted the stone and scooped the net bag clean, three handfuls and a bit. It stays sunk under the stone, empty, ready for the next batch.
entries.title: Bag scooped clean

entries.text: Ate the halves sitting on the bank. Most of the bitter's gone out of them. That's breakfast, and the end of the soaked supply.
entries.title: Breakfast on the bank

entries.onMind: how a needle lock is built
entries.text: Gathered forty-one acorns under the oak upstream. Cracked and soaked, they won't be food for two days, so I'd better count what's left in camp.
entries.title: Forty-one under the oak

entries.onMind: a lever with a hole over the foot
queries: compass needle lifter mechanism how does it lift the needle off the pivot
entries.query: compass needle lifter mechanism how does it lift the needle off the pivot
entries.reason: He wants something that holds the needle up against the dome while he walks and lets it down when he stops.
entries.source: Google Patents: US2528339A - Cruiser's compass
entries.text: An old cruiser's compass does it with a crooked little lever that slides up the post the needle sits on. A knob turns a cam that pushes the low end down, the flat end rises and lifts the needle off the point; let go and the needle drops back on by its own weight.
entries.title: A lever, no spring

entries.text: Good, because I don't have a spring. A lever with a hole that drops over the foot, the flat end under the pith plug, the tail poking out a notch in the tin. Press the tail and the needle rides up against the glass.
entries.title: No spring needed

entries.text: Whittled a lever out of a hardwood offcut, thin as a fingernail. It split clean in half when I bored the hole with the knife point. Started a second one twice as thick; I'll thin it after the hole's in.
entries.title: Split on the hole

queries: fastest way to leach acorns without a pot
entries.query: fastest way to leach acorns without a pot
entries.reason: The soaked supply ran out at breakfast and forty-one fresh acorns won't be food for two days.
entries.source: Eat The Weeds: Acorns: The Inside Story
entries.text: The finer you break them, the quicker the bitter comes out. Meal worked in a mesh bag under running water goes fastest; whole pieces take a lot longer, and even in a fast stream it's a few days. I've been soaking halves.
entries.title: Faster than two days

entries.text: Halves were lazy. Smash them to grit, put the grit in the net bag and work it in the current with my hands. Still days, maybe fewer.
entries.title: Grit, not halves

entries.text: Cracked the forty-one on the bench with the flat of the wrench. Five had grubs in them and three were dust inside: thirty-three good.
entries.title: Thirty-three good

entries.text: Knocked the meats down to grit a few at a time so they don't jump off the plank. Every knock rings the bench like a bell.
entries.title: Down to grit

entries.text: Picked the shell bits out of the grit in the parts tray. Two handfuls of meal, coarse as gravel. My stomach has opinions about it.
entries.title: Two handfuls of meal

entries.text: Tipped the grit into the net bag and kneaded it in the current. The water ran off brown in a long stripe, faster than the halves ever did. A pinch still curls my tongue; back under the stone it goes, and I knead it again after midday.
entries.title: Brown stripe

queries: is it bad to eat acorns that are still a little bitter
entries.query: is it bad to eat acorns that are still a little bitter
entries.reason: He is hungry and the meal in the bag is half done.
entries.source: Codidact Outdoors: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Asked if a little bitter would hurt. The answer didn't give me a little: even the sweet ones should be leached, raw ones bind you up and are rough on teeth, and enough of the bitter is hard on the kidneys. The bitterness is what stops you eating that much.
entries.title: Bitter for a reason

entries.text: So the bag stays under the stone and I don't. Knead it every few hours instead of once a day and taste a pinch each time, then spit it out.
entries.title: Not yet, then

entries.text: Drank from my hands in the shallows until my teeth ached from the cold. Fills nothing. Stops the growling for a while.
entries.title: Water for lunch

queries: drill hole in thin piece of wood without splitting it
entries.query: drill hole in thin piece of wood without splitting it
entries.reason: His first lever split in half when he bored it with the knife point.
entries.source: NootanCrafts: How to Stop Wood from Splitting When Screwing or Drilling
entries.text: Wood splits when nothing holds it sideways. Clamp it on both sides of where the hole goes, put a scrap hard against the back so the fibers don't blow out, start small and go slow, and keep the hole well in from the end.
entries.title: Clamp both sides

entries.text: Set the thick lever in the vise between two offcuts, a third scrap tight behind it, and turned the knife point through a little at a time from a pinprick. The hole went through clean, two thumb-widths in from the end. No split. Now I thin it.
entries.title: Through, no crack

entries.onMind: Whether the meal will be ready before I'm too hungry to work.
entries.text: A thin line of smoke went straight up past the creek while I was at the vise, no wind to lean it. Earlier than that fire usually goes. Somebody over there is having lunch.
entries.title: Smoke at midday

queries: what can you eat in the woods in november
eating rose hips raw what about the seeds
entries.query: what can you eat in the woods in november
entries.reason: No food in camp until the meal stops being bitter.
entries.source: Woodland Classroom: Best way to eat rosehips
entries.text: The first list was long and mostly plants I've never seen, but rose hips were on it, raw or cooked. Pick the soft red ones and squeeze from the bottom, and a red worm of pulp comes out the hole; the hairy seeds stay in the skin, and you don't eat those.
entries.title: Rose hips, raw

entries.text: There's a wild rose in the brambles past the water. Whoever picked it only got the low stems. I can reach the high ones.
entries.title: The high stems

entries.text: Picked twenty-two soft red hips off the high stems, up on my toes for the last few. The low stems are bare to the wood, picked clean by somebody short.
entries.title: Red ones up high

entries.text: From the brambles the stone-ring fire was in plain sight through the trunks, burning small and steady with nobody at it. Whoever keeps it trusts it to mind itself at midday.
entries.title: Fire, nobody at it

entries.text: Squeezed them one at a time the way the page said: a little red worm of pulp each, sweet and sour, and the seeds stay in the skin. Twenty-two is a mouthful and a half. It's food.
entries.title: A red worm each

entries.onMind: thinning the last bit by the hole without splitting it
entries.text: Whittled the thick lever down to half its thickness, shaving from the tail toward the hole. Stopped a thumb short of the hole; that's where the last one split.
entries.title: Half as thick

queries: how do you know when acorns are done leaching
entries.query: how do you know when acorns are done leaching
entries.reason: Hungry, and the only food in camp is meal that still curls his tongue.
entries.source: Eat Weeds: How to Store and Process Acorns the Right Way
entries.text: You keep at it until they taste sweet, two days to two weeks depending on the oak, and never with hot water. And when you pour off the brown, don't pour away the fine pale starch that settles at the bottom: that's food.
entries.title: Your tongue says when

entries.text: The holes in that net are as big as my thumbnail. Every time I kneaded the grit a pale cloud went out with the brown, and I took it for dirt. I've been feeding the creek.
entries.title: Washing out the good part

entries.text: Ate the heel of the loaf on the crate, slowly. That's the last of the bread. The cloth it came wrapped in is a tight weave and empty now.
entries.title: The heel

entries.text: Lined the net bag with the bundle cloth, tipped the grit into it and kneaded it in the current. The brown still runs out; the pale cloud stays in. A pinch is less bitter. Not done.
entries.title: Cloth inside the net

entries.text: Clamped the lever between the offcuts again and shaved the last thumb's width up to the hole, a hair at a time. Thin as the one that split, and whole. Next it needs a notch in the tin for its tail.
entries.title: Thin to the hole

entries.text: Filed a notch in the rim of the compass tin, a hair wider than the lever. Set the lever on the foot under the pith plug and the tail pokes out through the notch like a tongue.
entries.title: Notch in the rim

entries.onMind: holding the lever down without a thumb
entries.text: Pressed the tail: the plug rode up and the needle lay flat against the dome, dead still. Let go and it dropped back on the point and settled in five breaths. Walked the camp with it, and the second my thumb slipped it dropped and swung.
entries.title: Up against the glass

queries: how to hold a small lever down without a spring simple catch
entries.query: how to hold a small lever down without a spring simple catch
entries.reason: His thumb can't hold the lifter down for a whole walk west.
entries.source: Tractor By Net: Can't keep it up
entries.text: Mostly farmers with levers that won't stay put. The part that matters: push a lever all the way over and it drops into a little dip at the end of its travel, a detent, and stays. Theirs wear and slip, so the dip has to be sharp.
entries.title: A dip at the end

entries.text: No spring, no bungee. A little step filed into the side of the notch: push the tail down and over and it catches under the step until I flick it out. Sharp edge, so it doesn't wear through.
entries.title: A step in the notch

entries.text: Filed the step halfway into the side of the notch, then had to stop and set the file down. The bread was noon, the rose hips before that, and the meal is days off. My stomach's louder than the file.
entries.title: Half a step

entries.text: Kneaded the grit in the cloth-lined net in the current. Brown runs out, the pale stays in. A pinch curls my tongue less than at noon. Spat it out anyway.
entries.title: Less of a curl

entries.text: Turned twelve stones in the shallows and cupped my hand behind each one before I lifted, the way the page said they shoot backward. Two crayfish, thumb-long, backed right into my palm. A third went under the bank.
entries.title: Hand behind

entries.text: Quick hard knocks started past the water to the west, stone on wood, close together. That's what my wrench sounds like on acorns. Somebody over there is cracking them too.
entries.title: Knocks past the water

queries: do you have to cook crawdads caught in a creek
is it safe to eat crawfish from a creek raw parasite
entries.query: do you have to cook crawdads caught in a creek
entries.reason: He'd caught two crayfish and was hungry enough to eat them as they were.
entries.source: WashU The Source: Dangerous lung worms found in people who eat raw crayfish
entries.text: North American crayfish carry a little lung worm you get from eating them raw. Cooking them through kills it. So they don't go down raw, however loud my stomach is.
entries.title: Cook them through

entries.text: Lit the bench lantern in broad day and set the dented tin of creek water on top of the chimney with the two crayfish in it. It took a long while to boil and burned oil I'd rather keep, but they went red all over.
entries.title: Red in the tin

entries.text: Peeled the tails on the crate and ate them, two bites each. Sweet. It's not a meal, but it's the first thing since the rose hips that wasn't water.
entries.title: Two bites each

entries.onMind: whether it holds on the move
entries.text: Filed the step the rest of the way, square and sharp at the lip. Pushed the tail down and over and it clicked in under the step. Took my thumb off: the needle stays flat against the dome, dead still.
entries.title: It clicks under

entries.text: Paced six laps of camp with the tail caught: not a twitch. Then I hopped down off the crate and the tail jumped out of the step and the needle swung loose.
entries.title: One hop too many

entries.onMind: sharpening the lip of the step
entries.text: The file rounded the lip of the step on its last strokes. A walk won't shake it, a jump will. Deeper step, sharper lip, or I don't jump.
entries.title: The lip's too soft

queries: how to make a fish trap from sticks and cord small creek
entries.query: how to make a fish trap from sticks and cord small creek
entries.reason: Two crayfish took an hour of turning stones, and the meal is still days off.
entries.source: Wilderness College: Survival Fish Trap
entries.text: A long cone woven of sticks with a small cone inside it pointing in, so whatever swims in can't find the way back out. In a creek you block part of the water, leave the trap in the gap and wade down to push things into it. The man who built it caught no fish in a day and a night, only crayfish.
entries.title: A cone in a cone

entries.text: Only crayfish is exactly what I'm after. A trap works the night shift while I work mine, and I've got cord and a whole stand of stalks.
entries.title: Crayfish will do

queries: crayfish funnel trap how big should the hole be
what to put in a crayfish trap to bring them in
entries.query: crayfish funnel trap how big should the hole be
entries.reason: A cone in a cone only works if the door is the right size, and he has never built one.
entries.source: MeatEater: How to Trap Crayfish
entries.text: Somebody with a minnow trap says a door about an inch across, a thumb wide, lets the big ones in. Another page says cut it just big enough and give it two doors, and bait it with oily fish or meat, a piece the size of a hand, tied down in the middle so they have to come all the way in. Two crayfish heads from lunch are still in the tin.
entries.title: A thumb wide, and meat

entries.text: Gathered thirty-odd straight stalks, then kneaded the grit in the current. A pinch now has only a dry edge at the very back. Spat it out anyway; my stomach can wait till morning, it says otherwise.
entries.title: Close

entries.text: The stone ring by the scarred trunk was cold, ash raked over the coals and leaves blown up to the stones, so I took my line straight past it this time. Brought the scrap-pile lantern on my belt, unlit; no feeling my way home tonight.
entries.title: Straight through

entries.onMind: a deeper step so I can jump with it
entries.text: Crossed the stepping stones with the compass in my fist and my thumb on the lever tail, no hopping. At the edge I flicked the tail out: the needle dropped, swung twice and settled in five breaths. West, straight out over the water, with the sun a hand to its left going in.
entries.title: It still knows west

entries.onMind: how many nights until the lines split
entries.text: Drew tonight's sunset line on the sheet next to last night's. I can't tell them apart; one night is too short to see it walk. Back home they never said where the sun goes. Nobody ever looked.
entries.title: Second line

entries.text: The stone ring I walked past cold an hour ago is burning now, with nobody at it. I stood at the brambles and watched it through the trunks the way I'd watch a joint I don't trust.
entries.title: Lit again

entries.text: Then something came back to it carrying something flat, and crouched. Small, low to the ground, black against the flames; too far and too dark to say more. I went to the stones the long way, wide of it. It's not my fire.
entries.title: Something low

entries.text: Lit the lantern on the east bank once I was across, then lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped out a double handful of meal. Still that dry edge at the back.
entries.title: A wet handful

entries.text: Ate the whole handful on the crate, a pinch at a time. Gritty, faintly bitter, and it sits in my stomach like ballast, which beats it sitting there empty. Trap tomorrow.
entries.title: Ate it anyway

entries.text: Lit only the bench lantern and turned the wick low; the other two stay dark to save oil. Started the trap: eight stalks bent around a ring of cord, lashed every hand-width.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.text: Outer cone done, a forearm long, wide end the size of my hat. Gaps between stalks under a finger, so a crayfish can't squeeze out the sides.
entries.title: Outer cone

entries.onMind: whether a lopsided door still keeps them in
entries.text: The inner cone's mouth won't hold. Every time I tie it to a thumb wide, the stalks spring and it opens back to three fingers. A ring of cord wrapped tight pulls it in, but now the door's lopsided. Good enough for a crayfish, probably. Not for me.
entries.title: Springy door

entries.text: Hammered the rounded lip of the compass step back up with the flat of the wrench, light taps, until it feels sharp under a fingernail. No hop test in the dark; I'll knock it off the bench and lose it in the leaves.
entries.title: Peened

entries.text: The owls again, both somewhere upstream over the water, the low one first and the high one after. Same order every night. My stomach answered too.
entries.title: The pair

entries.text: Pushed the inner cone into the outer one's mouth and lashed them at five points. On the fourth lash a stalk snapped and I had to splice in a new one. The door still sits lopsided, but it points the right way, in.
entries.title: Cone in a cone

entries.text: Tied the two crayfish heads from lunch on a cord through the middle, then lashed the back end shut. Anything that wants out has to find a lopsided thumb-wide hole facing the wrong way.
entries.title: Bait

entries.onMind: whether anything walks into it by morning
entries.text: Carried it to the east shallows by the bench lantern and sank it mouth downstream with a splash, a flat stone on top. Tied its cord to a root on the bank so the creek can't walk off with it.
entries.title: Night shift

entries.text: The fire past the water is still going, low and orange through the trunks. I turned the lantern down and didn't look for whoever keeps it.
entries.title: Still burning

entries.text: Twisted stalk fiber into cord on the crate, an arm's length at a time. The trap ate most of what I had. Three arm-lengths now, tight enough not to unlay.
entries.title: More cord

entries.text: Pried the flat stone off with the wrench and it rang on the rock. One crayfish inside, thumb-long, and while I watched a second one backed out the wide side of the lopsided door. Rebaited and sank it again.
entries.title: One aboard

entries.text: The fire past the water burns lower than it did an hour ago, and the air coming over smells of wet ash, like somebody threw water on it.
entries.title: Wet smoke

entries.text: Boiled it in the tin over the bench lantern and ate the tail. One bite. Cost more oil than it gave back, but the trap works, one way, mostly the right way.
entries.title: Supper, sort of

entries.text: Drew the trap on the sheet by lantern: a small cone two paces below the stepping stones on the east side. Only what I've walked goes on.
entries.title: On the sheet

entries.text: Pried the stone off and lifted it: two crayfish this time, one thumb-long and one smaller, and the bait heads picked down to shell. Carrying the whole trap home to fix the door while it's out.
entries.title: Two aboard

entries.text: The orange past the water sank to a red smudge and then I couldn't find it at all. Whoever keeps it put it to bed.
entries.title: Fire's down

entries.text: Boiled both in the tin over the bench lantern and ate them on the crate. Two tails is still not supper, and the oil can is lighter every night.
entries.title: Two bites

entries.text: Wrapped a second ring of cord around the door and bent each stalk end inward with the wrench jaws. Not round, but a thumb wide whichever way I measure it now.
entries.title: Rounder

entries.text: Sank the trap with its rounder door under the flat stone, tonight's three heads tied inside for bait, and knotted it to the root again.
entries.title: Back to work

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the meal was close to being food.
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and put a pinch of meal on my tongue. The dry edge at the back is smaller than at sundown, but it's there, so I spat it in the creek.
entries.title: Smaller edge

entries.reason: Three boils in one night made him count.
entries.text: Tipped the oil can toward the lantern and sloshed it. About a third of what my maker sent is left, and every crayfish I boil burns some of it.
entries.title: A third left

entries.text: The stone ring past the water cooks for somebody every night on wood, not oil. I keep thinking about those coals, and I don't like how much.
entries.title: Their coals

entries.text: Twisting cord, I heard the low one hoot its five over the tarp and the high one answer from upstream, late as usual.
entries.title: Pair again

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the second ring of cord kept them in.
entries.text: Lifted the stone by lantern: one crayfish, middling, and half the bait still there. Nothing got out past the rounder door.
entries.title: One more

entries.text: No orange past the water at all now. Whoever keeps that ring is asleep, and I should be too.
entries.title: Dark ring

entries.reason: Every boil costs oil, and one boil for many costs less.
entries.text: Dropped it in the dented tin with creek water instead of boiling it. One tail isn't worth the oil; by morning there'll be more, and I'll boil them all in one go.
entries.title: Saving it

entries.text: Marked the catches beside the trap on the sheet: one, two, one. Four in a night out of a cone of dead stalks.
entries.title: Tally

entries.reason: He sank the trap again near midnight with heads for bait.
entries.text: Lifted the trap at the shallows: two crayfish in the inner cone and the bait heads picked down to shell. Six since I first sank it. Past the water a thin line of smoke was already leaning southwest out of the trees from that stone ring.
entries.title: Morning lift

entries.reason: Every boil costs lamp oil.
entries.text: Put the two in the tin with last night's one and set it over the bench lantern. One boil for three, as planned. The oil can sloshes lower every time I tip it; a little under a third now.
entries.title: One boil, three tails

entries.reason: He went to bed with nothing in him.
entries.text: Ate all three tails on the crate and cracked the claws for the bits. Not a meal, but my hands stopped shaking on the wrench.
entries.title: Breakfast

queries: how far does the sunset move along the horizon each day in november
entries.query: how far does the sunset move along the horizon each day in november
entries.reason: His first two sunset lines on the sheet landed on top of each other.
entries.source: EarthSky: Equinox fun: Track the sun's shift now until the solstice
entries.text: The sunset slides about half a degree a day at a middling latitude, one sun's width, fastest near the equinox and nearly stopped for two or three weeks around the solstice. Half a degree is a pencil width on my sheet, so two lines a night apart will always look like one. New rule: measure it in finger widths at arm's length off the compass's west, and draw a line only every fourth clear night.
entries.title: Half a degree

entries.reason: He peened the step sharp last night and wouldn't hop-test it in the dark.
entries.text: Hopped off the crate five times with the compass in my fist and the tail under the peened step. It held all five. There's a bright scratch on the step now where the tail rubs, so it will round off again; it's only a question of how many hops.
entries.title: Five hops
