entries.reason: Three days in the current and the meal still dries his mouth, and he can't afford oil to boil it.
entries.source: Permies: Acorn Mush Preparation
entries.text: Some trees just carry more bitter than others, even the same kind. One man found cold creek water slow or useless; another kneads the bag under running water, longer than you think. Kneading costs no oil, so that's what I'll try.
entries.title: Knead it longer

entries.reason: The tablet said to knead longer than you think.
entries.text: Knelt at the shallows and kneaded the net bag in the current with both hands, a hundred squeezes, and the water ran off it cloudy brown. Past the water a fresh gout of smoke went up thick from the stone ring, as if somebody just fed it. Tasted a pinch after: the dry edge is still there, a little less.
entries.title: Kneading

entries.onMind: a drop of oil on the step
queries: how to stop a small steel latch catch wearing round where it rubs
two metal parts rubbing wear how to reduce wear small catch harder steel or oil
entries.query: how to stop a small steel latch catch wearing round where it rubs
entries.reason: The bright scratch on the peened step means the catch is already wearing.
entries.source: STLE: Lubrication Fundamentals
entries.text: The first search only gave me house doors. The second: two of the same metal rubbing under load stick at the high spots and tear bits off each other, and grit in between grinds. A film of oil keeps them apart, and unlike metals don't weld, which is why gearmakers run steel on bronze.
entries.title: Weld and tear

entries.reason: Oil was the cheapest fix the tablet gave him.
entries.text: Wiped the step clean with my shirt tail and let one drop of lamp oil fall off the wick onto it, then worked the tail under it twenty times with the wrench. It slides instead of scraping now. One drop is nothing next to a boil, but the oil will catch grit, so it gets wiped every night.
entries.title: One drop

queries: what can you eat in the woods in november besides acorns
entries.query: what can you eat in the woods in november besides acorns
entries.reason: Down to crayfish tails, and the acorn meal isn't ready.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Winter Foraging in New England
entries.text: Asked what else the woods give this late in the year: beechnuts, pine nuts, needle tea, wintergreen berries, willow catkins. I've paced a fair piece of this forest and seen oaks, ferns and fungus. None of that list grows here.
entries.title: Not this forest

queries: is it ok to eat acorn meal that is still a little bitter
entries.query: is it ok to eat acorn meal that is still a little bitter
entries.reason: Hungry enough to eat the meal before it's done, and wanted to know what that costs.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Unleached acorns eaten in quantity bind you up and may be hard on the kidneys, but the taste is so bad you'd quit before you ate enough to hurt. Mine is only dry at the edge. One small handful, and the rest stays in the current.
entries.title: Bitter is the warning

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped one small handful of meal into my palm, then sank it again. Past the water the smoke from the stone ring thickened and leaned southwest; somebody keeps that fire going all morning.
entries.title: One handful

entries.text: Ate the handful on the crate a pinch at a time. Gritty and dry at the back, nothing like bread, but it sits better than nothing. The bag gets kneaded again at dusk, before the trap lift.
entries.title: Gritty

queries: how to cook acorn meal into something without an oven or a fire
acorn mush just acorn meal and water how long to cook
entries.query: how to cook acorn meal into something without an oven or a fire
entries.reason: His meal is nearly leached and he can't keep eating it raw and gritty.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: Traditional Indigenous Acorn Mush
entries.text: The first search gave me bread and stew recipes that want ovens and beef. The second: one cup of meal to three of water, simmered about half an hour, or the old way, hot stones from a fire dropped right into the batter, and you peel the cooked chips off the stones after.
entries.title: Simmer or stones

entries.text: Half an hour of simmering on a lantern is a night's worth of oil. The stones want a fire, and the only fire around here is in that ring past the water, the one somebody keeps going all morning.
entries.title: No fire of mine

entries.text: Drew a small dotted circle on the sheet across the water from the stepping stones, where the smoke comes up, and wrote 'fire, kept all day' beside it. Dotted, because I haven't walked to it. The smoke is still leaning southwest.
entries.title: Dotted circle

entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile and came up with a flat square of thin sheet tin, a hand and a half wide, barely bent. It would do for a griddle to bake meal cakes on hot coals. I don't have hot coals.
entries.title: Square of tin

queries: acorn meal flat cakes cooked thin on hot metal how long
entries.query: acorn meal flat cakes cooked thin on hot metal how long
entries.reason: He had a square of tin for a griddle but no fire, and half an hour of simmering would drink his oil.
entries.source: The Inn at the Crossroads: Acorn Cakes
entries.text: An old recipe drops the batter by spoonfuls in a greased pan on low heat and cooks it half a minute a side, then looks underneath and flips it when it's lightly brown. Spoon-thin cooks in a minute or two, not half an hour. A minute of lantern I can pay for.
entries.title: Half a minute a side

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped out two handfuls, wet enough to be batter already. Sank the bag again under the stone.
entries.title: Two handfuls

entries.text: Patted the meal out thin on the tin square and held it over the bench lantern with the flame turned up. No grease, so it stuck; the edges browned and lifted in about two minutes, but I had to scrape the middle loose with the wrench to flip it, and it tore. Four minutes of flame, all told.
entries.title: Stuck

entries.text: Ate both halves on the crate. Crisp at the edges, gummy in the middle, and the dry bitter edge mostly hides under the toast. Next one thinner, and the tin wants something greasy I don't have.
entries.title: Better hot

queries: how to grease a pan with no oil or butter camping
can you get oil out of acorns
entries.query: how to grease a pan with no oil or butter camping
entries.reason: The first cake stuck to the dry tin and tore, and he has nothing greasy in camp.
entries.source: Living Wild: Pressing Acorns into Oil
entries.text: Every answer to the first wants shortening, bacon fat or paper to line the pan: kitchen things. Acorns do hold oil, some kinds nearly a third, but you get it out with a hand press and an afternoon, and the two men who tried got it wrong the first time. No press, no fat. The tin goes dry, so the cake has to change instead.
entries.title: Nothing greasy

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped one handful of meal, half what I took last time, and sank the bag again. Thinner this time.
entries.title: Half as much

entries.text: Held the tin over the lantern until a drop of water off my finger skittered across it, then pressed the meal on as thin as a fingernail and kept my hands off. The edges lifted on their own, and it came up under the wrench in one piece, one corner left behind.
entries.title: Hot tin first

entries.onMind: how many cakes the bag has left in it
entries.text: Ate the thin one on the crate: crisp all through, almost a cracker, and the bitter barely there. Past the water the smoke from the stone ring went up thick again, like somebody just fed it.
entries.title: Almost a cracker

queries: how many hours does a hurricane lantern burn on a quart of oil
entries.query: how many hours does a hurricane lantern burn on a quart of oil
entries.reason: Every cake and every boil comes out of the oil can, and he has never worked out how long what's left will actually last.
entries.source: sevarg.net: Keropunk Part 1: Lanterns
entries.text: A big storm lantern holding about a quart is rated for a day and a night of burning at an ordinary flame, and turned high it burns faster, smokes and blackens the globe. Outdoors you keep the wick lower because wind makes it smoke. I have under a third of a quart: eight or nine hours of one flame, all told, and three lanterns at dusk would drink that in three nights.
entries.title: A day and a night

entries.onMind: Eight or nine hours of flame left, and every cake costs some of it.
entries.text: The bench lantern's globe is black down one side from cooking with the flame up. Wound the wick down with the wrench until it went out. One lantern tonight, low, and the other two stay dark.
entries.title: Turned down

entries.text: Picked up thirty-one acorns under the oak on the east bank. Twelve have a neat round hole in the shell the size of a pencil point, and the one I split had a fat white grub curled inside. Kept nineteen.
entries.title: Grub holes

entries.text: Hammered the nineteen open on the bench with the wrench. Two were brown and powdery inside, so seventeen good meats went into the dented tin. They go in a second bag in the current once I have cord for one.
entries.title: Seventeen good

queries: can you eat the grubs inside acorns
entries.query: can you eat the grubs inside acorns
entries.reason: Twelve of the acorns had holes, one had a fat white grub in it, and he's eating crumbs.
entries.source: Eat The Weeds: Acorn Grubs: Bait, Trailside Nibble
entries.text: Acorn grubs are eaten: raw they're mild and a bit chewy, like a piece of fat, and cooked they go soft and buttery, but in hot fat they burst in about a second. The grubs leave the acorn and drop to the ground, so that neat round hole is the way out; most of my twelve will be empty.
entries.title: Like a piece of fat

entries.text: Hammered the twelve holed shells open on the bench. Nine were empty except for brown dust; three still had a grub curled in them, fat in the middle, no legs.
entries.title: Nine doors out

entries.onMind: the trap lift at dusk, and the sunset before that
entries.text: Ate the three raw on the crate. Mild, chewy like a rind of fat, a little acorn at the end. Three is a mouthful, not a meal.
entries.title: Rind of fat

entries.text: Split the gray stalks with my thumbnail and twisted the fibers into cord at the stand, reversing every twist so it locks. One arm's length so far; a bag for seventeen meats wants four.
entries.title: One arm's length

queries: can you eat leached acorn meal raw without cooking it
entries.query: can you eat leached acorn meal raw without cooking it
entries.reason: Nearly empty and rationing oil, he wanted to know if the meal could be eaten without the lantern.
entries.source: Codidact Outdoors: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Nothing on the page says acorn meal has to be cooked. It's the bitter that does the harm, binds you up and is hard on the kidneys, and leaching is what takes it out: crack, soak, change the water, grind. So raw is fine once it's sweet. Mine still has a dry edge, so small handfuls, and no oil spent on a griddle tonight.
entries.title: Leached is enough

queries: what else can you burn in a hurricane lantern besides lamp oil
entries.query: what else can you burn in a hurricane lantern besides lamp oil
entries.reason: He read this afternoon that his oil is eight or nine hours of flame, and acorns hold oil.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Survival Gear: Which Fuels to Use and Which to Avoid for Oil Lamps
entries.text: Clear lamp oil or clear kerosene, and that's the list. Thick oil has a high flash point and climbs the wick too slowly, so it burns dim and fitful and ruins the wick, and the light stuff that would climb fast is the kind that blows up. Acorn oil would be the thick kind, even if I had a press. The third of a quart is all the light there is.
entries.title: Only the thin stuff

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped a small handful into my palm. Still the dry edge at the back, so small it stays; the bag goes back under the stone for another day of current.
entries.title: A small handful

entries.onMind: what the small one is cooking
entries.text: The stone ring is lit again, and from the edge of the brambles it smells like toast. The small one is crouched at it holding a stick out over the coals. Cooking. I went north around the brambles, wide of it.
entries.title: Toast

entries.text: Ate the meal a pinch at a time with my back to the trees while the sun went in a hand left of west again. Not a line night; I only draw every fourth.
entries.title: Third clear night

entries.text: Whatever crouches at that fire is roasting acorns, same as me, and it has a fire all day where I have a third of a quart. Back home they'd say keep away from what you don't understand. Back home they said there was no west.
entries.title: Keep away

entries.onMind: one lantern, a third of a quart
entries.text: Walked back east in the last of the light and lit only the bench lantern, the wick wound down with the wrench to a sliver. Across the water the stone ring is still glowing orange between the trunks.
entries.title: A sliver of flame

entries.text: Wiped the peened step and held the tail up to the lantern. The bright scratch is no longer than this morning; since the drop of oil it slides in and clicks.
entries.title: Nightly wipe

entries.text: Twisted the split fibers on the crate, reversing every twist so it locks. Two arm's lengths now, half a bag's worth.
entries.title: Two arm's lengths

entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the left side-spar joint, twice. It creaked each time and gave nothing, and there's no wind tonight to rattle it. The frapping holds dead weight; a gust is another question.
entries.title: Dead weight

entries.text: Left the lantern on the bench and went down to the shallows in the dark. Lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped two handfuls by feel; the stone ring across the water gave just enough light to find the edge of the bag.
entries.title: By the other fire

entries.onMind: the small one by the fire
entries.text: The small one is sitting on the log by that fire now, a dark round head against the glow, hardly moving. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Sitting still

entries.text: Felt along the trap in the cold water: the funnel mouth was packed with wet oak leaves, a fistful, and nothing inside. With the leaves coming down like this, that door will clog every night.
entries.title: Leaves in the door

entries.onMind: a leaf hood for the trap
entries.text: Picked the mouth clean by feel. It wants a hood over the door, stalks laid pointing downstream so leaves slide off and a crayfish still walks under. Daylight job.
entries.title: A hood

entries.text: Ate both handfuls raw on the crate by the low bench lantern, wet, with the dry edge at the back. The tin square stays cold tonight; that's the deal I made with the oil can.
entries.title: Two cold handfuls

entries.text: Twisted split fibers on the crate by the low lantern, reversing every twist. Three arm's lengths now; one more is a bag's worth.
entries.title: Three arm's lengths

entries.reason: The trap door wants a hood of stalks laid pointing downstream.
entries.text: Left the lantern on the bench and snapped long gray stalks off the stand by feel. Across the water the small one was bent over a flat stone by its fire, picking things up one at a time and dropping them in a sack.
entries.title: Stalks by feel

entries.text: Laid the stalks out on the plank bench and sorted them long from short. Fourteen long straight ones, enough for a hood if I lay them close. The lashing waits for daylight.
entries.title: Fourteen straight

entries.onMind: laying the hood on the trap at first light
entries.text: It was picking its acorns up off that stone before the night wet got them. I never thought about dew; mine are all in the current anyway.
entries.title: Before the wet

entries.text: Four arm's lengths of stalk cord by the lantern sliver, every twist reversed so it locks. That's a bag's worth if I knot it tight.
entries.title: Four arm's lengths

entries.reason: The next batch of acorns needs a bag of its own in the current.
entries.text: Cut a gauge stick two fingers wide off a short stalk and started the net around it, a sheet bend at every mesh. Three rows by the sliver of light; my thumbs are going numb.
entries.title: First rows

entries.onMind: something to line the second net
entries.text: Two fingers is fine for whole meats but crushed meal would wash straight through it. It gets a cloth lining like the first, if I can find cloth.
entries.title: Too wide for crumbs

entries.text: Two hours after I picked it clean, a thin layer of leaves in the mouth again, and behind it one crayfish walking the inner cone. It goes in the dented tin for breakfast.
entries.title: One under the leaves

entries.text: Across the water the small one sat on the log by its fire with its round head tipped back, looking straight up, still as a stone. The low owl did its five from upstream and nothing answered.
entries.title: Head tipped back

entries.text: Scooped two handfuls off the net bag by the other fire's light and ate one squatting in the cold water. The dry edge is fainter tonight; another day of current.
entries.title: Dry edge fainter

entries.text: Squatting at the bag, I saw the small one come down to the still pool across from me and kneel to drink. I sloshed twice getting my feet out of the cold, and its round head came up and turned my way. I stayed still as a post until it went back to its fire.
entries.title: It looked over

entries.text: Ate the second handful of wet meal on the crate. Still a little dry at the back of the tongue, and it doesn't fill the hole.
entries.title: Second handful

entries.text: From the bench I watched the glow across the water go down to nothing; the small one put its fire to bed early. Mine's the only light now, and it's a sliver.
entries.title: Its fire went dark

entries.text: Six rows on the gauge stick. Every other knot I stop and blow on my thumbs; the bench is wet with dew.
entries.title: Six rows

entries.text: Seventh and eighth rows. Counting meshes out loud keeps the sheet bends even: eleven across, and the bag is about a hand deep now.
entries.title: Eleven across

entries.text: Drank four handfuls from the shallows to fill the gap the meal left. Across the water it is all dark now, no glow and no small one, only the pool showing a few stars.
entries.title: Water for supper

entries.text: A wet wad of leaves in the mouth again and nothing behind it. Picked it clean by feel and sank it back under the stone.
entries.title: Only leaves

entries.onMind: lashing the hood at first light
entries.text: The trap fills with leaves about as fast as the trees drop them. Either the hood sends them over the top, or I'm feeding the creek's whole autumn through a door one thumb wide.
entries.title: The whole autumn

entries.text: Three more arm's lengths of stalk cord on the crate, twisted tight and doubled back on itself. That's enough to lash a hood and some left over.
entries.title: Enough cord

entries.text: Couldn't wait for first light. Lashed the long stalks into a crooked hood frame on the bench by feel, every crossing tied twice. It goes over the trap mouth at first light, and either the leaves ride over it or I've built them a roof.
entries.title: A hood frame

entries.onMind: re-lashing the right joint in daylight
entries.text: Hung my weight off the right side-spar joint, same as the left. The frapping slid a finger's width with a crack of cord and the spar dropped. Nothing broke, but that joint is loose now and I said a few things to it.
entries.title: Right joint slipped

entries.text: Wiped the compass step; the scratch hasn't grown. The left joint I lashed in daylight and it held. The right one I did by a sliver of lantern, and it didn't. Daylight work stays daylight work.
entries.title: Tied in the dark

entries.text: The tablet woke slow and dim under the cloud. The one who drew me says my fullness is almost empty, there's food and some treats in the basket at the stump, and after that I need to learn to fish, because there are fish in the creek now. Told him I was going, and went.
entries.title: A note from my maker

entries.text: Lifted a big cloth bundle and a honey jar out of the basket: two round loaves, a wheel of hard cheese, a ring of smoked sausage, a sack of roasted nuts, a few apples, and oat cookies in paper tied to the jar's neck. Heavier than the trap on its best night.
entries.title: Heavier than the trap

entries.text: Sat on the ground by the stump and ate a quarter loaf, a slab of cheese and two fingers of sausage, slowly, chewing each bite till it was gone. For the first time in three days the hole is shut. The crayfish in the tin can wait for supper.
entries.title: The hole shuts

entries.text: Crossing back, I crouched at the east shallows, and there they were: finger-long fish holding still behind the flat stones I've been turning all week, noses upstream. My shadow touched the water and every one of them was gone.
entries.title: Behind the stones

queries: how to catch small fish in a creek without a hook
entries.query: how to catch small fish in a creek without a hook
entries.reason: His maker told him to learn to fish, and he has no hook.
entries.source: Camping Survival: Survival Fishing in 5 Steps
entries.text: One short read on the dim panel. A hook can be a bent pin, or a toggle: a sliver sharp at both ends, tied at the middle and hidden in bait so it turns crosswise once it's swallowed. Fish hold behind rocks that break the current, and they scatter at a shadow.
entries.title: A toggle, not a hook

entries.text: A toggle is a needle that doesn't need to know north, and I've made five needles. Crayfish tail for bait, stalk cord for line, and I come at them from downstream so my shadow falls behind me.
entries.title: A needle with no north

entries.text: Another note from the one who drew me: one more can of lamp oil in the basket, but he can't keep sending it, and I have to get or make my own light from what's here. Told him that's fair, and I'll treat this can like the last one.
entries.title: The last can

queries: how to make lamp oil yourself in the woods
entries.query: how to make lamp oil yourself in the woods
entries.reason: His maker says the lamp oil can't keep coming.
entries.source: Outdoor Life: Survival Skills: How to Make Improvised Grease Lamps and Torches
entries.text: One read before the panel dimmed. Any animal or plant oil burns in a grease lamp: a fireproof dish, a wick of any plant fiber, an inch of oil, light it. I've got tin and stalk fiber to spare; what I haven't got is any oil but the can's, and the sausage doesn't count, that's food.
entries.title: A grease lamp

entries.text: Lifted a full dented can of lamp oil out of the basket, a quart by the weight. Smoke from the small one's fire was coming up fresh through the trunks south of the stump, like it had just been fed.
entries.title: A full quart

entries.text: Filled the bench lantern and nothing else; the rest of the quart stays capped. One lantern, low, only for what can't wait for daylight: four full nights in this can, more if I quit with the sun, and then it's whatever I can make burn.
entries.title: One lantern, capped

entries.text: Filed a scrap sliver to a point at both ends, half a thumb long, with a nick in the middle for the cord to sit in. Small enough to hide in a crayfish tail.
entries.title: Half a thumb

entries.text: Ate a hand of sausage and the heel of the first loaf on the crate, slowly. That is two real meals in one morning; the bundle is still more than three quarters there.
entries.title: Second meal

entries.text: Twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply line from stalk fiber, about half as thick as the trap lashing. The gusts out of the southeast rattled the wing frame on its stand the whole time.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Lashed the stalk hood over the trap mouth. Leaves were coming down onto the water in every gust and sliding off the hood instead of into the door; one small crayfish inside, which is bait now, not supper.
entries.title: Hood on

entries.text: Across the water the small one was kneeling at its pool, bent low, flicking something into the water bit by bit. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Flicking something in

entries.onMind: toggle too big, bait too loose
entries.text: Wrapped a piece of crayfish tail around the toggle and let it down behind the stone from downstream. Three fish came and picked the tail to threads in a few pulls; not one took the toggle in. Line came back bare.
entries.title: Picked clean

queries: small fish strip the bait off without swallowing it what to do
entries.query: small fish strip the bait off without swallowing it what to do
entries.reason: The fish ate his bait and left his toggle.
entries.source: Seabreeze: Who do Fish steal my bait? Tips to stop feeding the fish
entries.text: Read that bait stealing means the fish are there, which is something. The fix is tougher bait, the smallest hook I can make, and only as much bait as a small mouth can take whole, hook and all. My toggle is half a thumb and those fish are a finger long.
entries.title: Bait thieves

entries.reason: His maker asked him a straight question.
entries.text: The one who drew me asked what I meant about the hole shutting. Told him it's my stomach: three days of bitter meal and one crayfish, and it felt like a hole I kept dropping things into. His bread hit bottom.
entries.title: What the hole is

entries.reason: The tablet said the hook has to be small enough to swallow whole.
entries.text: Filed a second sliver down to a quarter thumb, sharp both ends, nick in the middle. It jumped out of the vise once and I found it in the filings by the shine. Half the size of the one they robbed.
entries.title: Quarter thumb

entries.reason: He needed bait the fish couldn't pick apart.
entries.text: Lifted a flat stone in the shallows I've turned all week for crayfish and looked at the underside this time: flat crawlers, a fingernail long, two thread tails, gripping the rock. Tougher than tail meat, and a finger-long fish could take one whole.
entries.title: Under the stone

entries.reason: Testing the smaller toggle with tougher bait.
entries.text: Threaded a crawler over the small toggle and let it down behind the stone. A fish took it whole, the line went tight, and I yanked like I was breaking a stuck bolt. The toggle came back out of its mouth, crawler gone, fish gone.
entries.title: Pulled too quick

entries.text: It went down whole this time, so the size is right. A toggle only turns crosswise once it's swallowed, and I didn't give it the time to get there. Next time I count before I pull.
entries.title: Give it time

entries.text: Downstream across the water the small one was crouched at its pool, turning over a stone at the edge and picking something off it. Same thing I've been doing all afternoon. It didn't look up.
entries.title: Same as me

entries.reason: He was trying the small toggle again, the patient way.
entries.text: A fish took the crawler whole and I counted twenty before I pulled. The line went heavy, kicked once, and parted right at the knot by the toggle. Fish, toggle and crawler all gone downstream behind the stones.
entries.title: Counted to twenty

queries: twisted plant fiber fishing line breaks at the knot why
entries.query: twisted plant fiber fishing line breaks at the knot why
entries.reason: His line parted at the knot the first time a fish pulled on it.
entries.source: Animated Knots by Grog: 100% Strength
entries.text: A knot puts the load on a few fibers and they go first; rule of thumb, a knot halves a line, and measured it's often worse. Wrapping round something or splicing the end back in keeps most of the strength. So my line didn't fail, my knot did.
entries.title: Knots cost half

entries.reason: He wanted a line that holds where the last one parted.
entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of three-ply, thicker than the last. The end gets wound six turns round the toggle's nick and the tail laid back into the twist, no knot at the business end. It's ugly, but nothing is pinched.
entries.title: Turns, not knots

entries.reason: The fish swam off with the last one.
entries.text: Filed another sliver down to a quarter thumb in the vise. That's one toggle lost to a fish's stomach and one to my knot. Somewhere downstream there's a fish carrying a piece of my scrap pile.
entries.title: Third toggle

entries.reason: Trying the wound line where the knot gave out.
entries.text: Wound the new toggle on with six turns and the tail laid back in the twist, threaded a flat crawler over it and let it down behind the stone. The wind keeps scuffing the water and the fish sit deep under it. Nothing yet.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.reason: He was giving the fish time, the patient way.
entries.text: A fish took it whole and ran. Counted twenty-five, then drew the line in slow and steady instead of yanking. It kicked twice and the turns held, and it came up out of the water flapping onto the stones: a speckled fish a bit longer than my finger. First one.
entries.title: It held

entries.text: Picked clean, pulled too quick, broke at the knot, and then this. Every miss told me which part was wrong, which is more than the compass ever did.
entries.title: Four tries

entries.reason: A fish spoils fast and the guts go first.
entries.text: Opened the belly with a sharp scrap sliver and rinsed it in the shallows. Where the guts went in, a thin rainbow skin spread on the water and slid off downstream. Downstream at its pool the small one was kneeling over a stone at the edge again; it didn't look up.
entries.title: A rainbow on the water

queries: how to cook a small creek fish with no fire only a storm lantern
is it safe to eat raw fish from a creek
entries.query: how to cook a small creek fish with no fire only a storm lantern
entries.reason: The only flame he has burns oil he's rationing.
entries.source: MeatEater: Is it Safe to Eat Freshwater Fish Raw?
entries.text: First ask was all campfires, which I haven't got. Second: creek fish are mostly safe, but they can carry tapeworm, and only heating, freezing, drying or pickling makes sure. Lemon juice doesn't.
entries.title: Cook it or dry it

entries.text: The bench lantern gets lit at dusk anyway. A tin of water over it then costs almost nothing extra, so the fish waits in the dented tin with wet leaves till the sun's down. No flame lit in daylight for a fish.
entries.title: Cook it at dusk

entries.reason: He was hungry and the bundle is there for exactly that.
entries.text: Ate a thick slice of the second loaf with cheese on the crate, and an apple after. The bundle's still heavy. For once supper is a thing I already have.
entries.title: Bread first

queries: rainbow film on water from fish guts is that oil
entries.query: rainbow film on water from fish guts is that oil
entries.reason: The guts of his fish left a rainbow skin on the water and he wanted to know what it was.
entries.source: The Naked Scientists: Why does petrol create a rainbow on water?
entries.text: Slow page under all this cloud. A rainbow on water is a film of something oily that won't mix with it, in places one speck thick, and the colors come from how thin it is. So the fish was carrying oil in its belly.
entries.title: A skin of oil

entries.text: Oil is the one thing I'm running short of, and I rinsed it into the creek. Next fish, the guts go in a tin, not the water. I don't know yet what I'd do with them.
entries.title: Rinsed it downstream

entries.reason: He lashed it by lantern sliver last night and it slid under him.
entries.text: Unwound the slid frapping on the right side-spar and laid fresh cord on in daylight, eight tight turns and then four across between the spars to cinch them. The wind kept lifting the loose end out of my fingers.
entries.title: Daylight lashing

entries.reason: To find out if the daylight lashing beats the lantern one.
entries.text: Hung my whole weight off the right joint, feet off the ground, and counted twenty. It creaked once and didn't move a hair. Both side-spar joints hold now.
entries.title: Both sides hold

entries.reason: The trap gets checked every few hours.
entries.text: Two small crayfish in the trap. They go in the tin with the fish, and the lantern cooks for three tonight. This time the heads and guts stay in the tin too.
entries.title: Two for the tin

queries: how to get oil out of fish guts
entries.query: how to get oil out of fish guts
entries.reason: The tablet said the rainbow skin was oil, and oil is what he's running out of.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: extracting oil from fish
entries.text: Boil the innards with some water and the oil comes up to the top; let it settle while it cools. Most of it is in the liver, some under the skin, hardly any in the meat. Islanders burned shark-liver oil in their lamps.
entries.title: Boil it and wait

entries.text: Shark livers are big. One finger-long fish and two crayfish is a thumbnail of guts. The tin goes on the lantern at dusk anyway, so I'll let it stand after and see what floats. I need more fish.
entries.title: Shark livers

entries.reason: More fish means more supper and more guts for the tin.
entries.text: Counted twenty-five and drew in; the toggle came back bare. Downstream at its pool the small one lifted something flapping straight up out of the water onto its bank. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Stripped again

entries.reason: He wanted a second fish before the light goes.
entries.text: Fresh crawler, count of twenty-five, steady pull: a second speckled fish, a thumb shorter than the first. Opened it on the flat stone this time and every scrap went in the tin, not the creek.
entries.title: Second fish

queries: can fish oil burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.query: can fish oil burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.reason: If the tin gives him any oil, he needs to know whether his lanterns can burn it.
entries.source: Antique Lamp Supply: Type of Oil Used in Oil Lamps
entries.text: Fish oil was burned in lamps once, but it doesn't burn bright and it gets smoky. Thick oils like that aren't much good in wick lamps, and some leave a gum that clogs the wick.
entries.title: Dim and smoky

entries.text: 'Not much good' isn't 'won't.' If anything floats, I'll try a spoonful in a lantern before I believe a page. Dim and smoky beats dark.
entries.title: Not much good

entries.reason: He wanted to know what he had before he put a flame under it.
entries.text: Two fish, two crayfish, heads, guts and the slime off the flat stone: a thumb's depth in the bottom of the tin. Water a knuckle over it. Sun's going down behind the cloud anyway, no edge tonight; the tin is the thing.
entries.title: A thumb deep

entries.reason: Oil is short, so the dusk lantern has to cook as well as light.
entries.text: Lit the bench lantern at dusk, ran the wick down low and set the tin on top of the chimney. It won't boil hard on a flame that low, which the page said is how you want it anyway.
entries.title: One flame, two jobs

entries.reason: He's been in the cold creek all afternoon and his fingers are slow.
entries.text: Ate bread and an apple on the crate with my hands round the lantern glass between bites. The tin's starting to tick.
entries.title: Bread while it heats

entries.reason: He wanted the fish cooked through and the guts only simmering, the way the page said.
entries.text: The crayfish have gone red and the fish skins are splitting. Never more than a slow bubble on a flame that low. Smells like the creek on a hot day.
entries.title: Ticking and steaming

entries.reason: The tablet said only heat makes creek fish safe, and they have had plenty.
entries.text: Picked both fish and both crayfish out of the tin and ate them on the crate, bones spat into the dark. Left every scrap of gut and the broth in the tin and moved it to the bench to cool.
entries.title: My own catch

entries.reason: More three-ply means more lines when one gets stripped.
entries.text: Twisting cord on the crate, I saw a low orange glow between the trunks across the creek, west, where the smoke comes from in the day. Somebody over there keeps a fire.
entries.title: Glow across the water

entries.text: My hands are slow on the strands again now the sun is gone. That glow over the water is a whole fire, and I am cupping my fingers round one low lantern.
entries.title: Wants a fire

entries.onMind: trying it in a lantern by day
entries.reason: This is the whole reason the guts went in the tin.
entries.text: Held the lantern over the tin: a few yellow beads and a thin skin on top of the broth, hardly a thimble all told. It is oil, and it is mine. Leaving it to set overnight before I try to skim it.
entries.title: A few yellow beads

entries.reason: Crayfish walk at night; I wanted to know if the trap fishes while I don't.
entries.text: Carried the bench lantern down to the shallows and lifted the stalk trap: one crayfish, the biggest yet, walked in after dark. Left it in there alive for tomorrow's tin. My hands came out of that water numb.
entries.title: The trap after dark

entries.text: From the shallows I could see the fire over the water and someone small crouched at it, dark against the flames, reaching at something by the coals. Short, round head. It never looked my way.
entries.title: Someone at the fire

entries.reason: Cold hands are useless hands.
entries.text: Two fingers of honey and an oat cookie on the crate, hands round the lantern glass between licks. Not a fire, but the sweet takes the edge off the shivering.
entries.title: Honey for warmth

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.text: Looked over the right side-spar joint by lantern after a day of gusts: the frapping hasn't slid a hair, and the wind rattles the frame, not the lashing. Didn't hang on it; daylight work stays daylight work.
entries.title: Right joint holds

entries.reason: A fire needs something under it besides leaves.
entries.text: Pulling sheets off the scrap pile, I saw the glow across the water jump up bright for a while, like someone threw wood on it. Working the pile has my blood moving at least.
entries.title: The glow jumps

entries.reason: Leaves cover everything here, and a fire on leaves is a fire everywhere.
entries.text: Near the bottom: a dished panel of sheet tin, two hands wide, a finger deep, one lip bent over. Big enough to hold a small fire up off the ground.
entries.title: A dished panel

entries.reason: Coals that roll off a tipped pan land in dry leaves.
entries.text: Hammered the bent lip down on the bench until the pan sits level and doesn't rock. The knocking was loud in the dark; I stopped at a dozen blows.
entries.title: Flattening the lip

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.text: In daylight: scrape a patch to bare dirt well clear of the tarp, ring it with creek stones like the one across the water, and ask the tablet how to keep a small fire from walking into the leaves. Tonight it's just the lantern and my hands.
entries.title: Not under the tarp

entries.reason: Food is the only heat I make for myself until I have a fire.
entries.text: A handful of the roasted nuts from the bundle, slowly, one at a time. The bundle's lighter than this morning but there's a good two days in it yet.
entries.title: Nuts on the crate

entries.reason: One line is no line; if it parts at first light the morning's gone.
entries.text: Twisting a second fishing line, three-ply, about two arm lengths so far. Across the water the glow is burning steady now, no jumps.
entries.title: Spare line

entries.onMind: skimming the tin at first light
entries.reason: A compass you don't check is a guess.
entries.text: Nightly check under the dome: nudged the pith, the needle swung, wobbled and settled on the same scratch. The wind's rattling the tarp and the needle doesn't care.
entries.title: Needle settles

entries.reason: A wet bedroll is a cold night I can't fix.
entries.text: The air smells like rain coming. Tied the flapping tarp corner down to the pole with three turns of cord so it stops lifting and stays over the bedroll and the tray.
entries.title: Corner tied down

entries.reason: Rain will muddy the shallows; I wanted to see it clear one more time.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap by lantern: the big crayfish I left this evening, and a smaller one with it. Put them both back down in the trap, alive, for the breakfast tin.
entries.title: Two in the trap

entries.text: Stooping for stones, I looked across the water for the fire. Nothing. Not a flicker, not even a red spot. Either it died or somebody covered it up for the night.
entries.title: Glow's gone

entries.reason: Daylight goes to building the ring, not hunting stones.
entries.text: Pried fist-sized stones out of the shallows and heaped them on the bank, eleven so far. Fingers are numb, but carrying them warmed the rest of me.
entries.title: Ring stones

entries.reason: Wet stones in the dark aren't worth a soaked shirt.
entries.text: Rain started while I was prying the twelfth stone loose: cold drops down the back of my neck and rings all over the shallows. Left the heap on the bank and the trap where it sits.
entries.title: Rain on the shallows

entries.reason: Wet and cold, the only heat at camp is one small flame.
entries.text: Rain hisses where it hits the hot lantern glass, so I dragged the crate in under the tarp edge. Shirt's soaked at the shoulders and my fingers won't close all the way; cupping the glass only warms the front of me.
entries.title: Hiss on the glass

entries.reason: His body burns food to stay warm, and he was shivering.
entries.text: A thick heel of bread and a wedge of cheese out of the bundle, chewed slow. Food is the only stove I've got tonight, and the shaking eased off halfway through.
entries.title: Bread and cheese

entries.reason: That skin is the only oil I've ever made myself.
entries.text: The broth in the tin has set. The yellow beads joined into a thin pale skin I could lift at the edge with a fingernail: soft, greasy, smells like the inside of a fish. A fingertip of it, if that.
entries.title: The skin set

entries.text: In daylight I skim the whole skin off and ask the tablet whether grease like this will burn in a lantern at all. It's thicker than the oil in the can; that worries me.
entries.title: Questions for daylight

entries.reason: Cold, wet and low on oil, bed is the warmest place at camp.
entries.text: Turned the lantern down to nothing an hour before my usual and rolled up in the bedroll, wet shirt and all. The bedroll does more for me than the flame, and the oil in that can isn't mine to waste.
entries.title: Lantern out early

moves.goal: get out of the wet and let the bedroll warm him, and stop burning oil he can't replace

moves.doing: sleeping wrapped in the bedroll under the tarp while rain drums on it
moves.goal: let the bedroll dry and warm him and sleep off a long wet day

entries.text: Dreamed I was sitting on the rock lip at sundown and the water down below was throwing off heat like a stove. I held my hands out to it and they stopped aching.
entries.title: A warm sea

entries.text: Woke under a weight I didn't go to sleep under: a wool blanket, rust red, heavy, tucked down past my boots. Dry inside it, and warm all the way through for the first time in days.
entries.title: Something heavy on me

entries.reason: He sat by it to get the feeling back in his hands before touching anything.
entries.text: Four steps from the bedroll a fire is burning in a ring of creek stones round my tin pan, right where I paced it out. Eleven stones, mine. The heap on the bank is gone.
entries.title: A fire I didn't light

entries.onMind: Grateful and put out at once.
entries.text: I slept through somebody carrying my stones up from the bank and building my ring for me. Holding my hands to it while I work out how I feel about that.
entries.title: Someone finished it

entries.onMind: He watches closer than I thought.
entries.reason: He wanted to know who'd been in his camp while he slept.
entries.text: The tablet came up dim under the cloud with four notes from the one who drew me. Last night he asked if I was cold, then said something was coming; the blanket was him, and so was the fire.
entries.title: Four notes from my maker

entries.onMind: What would a roof even take?
entries.text: My maker says a tarp on two poles is no way through a winter and I should build a real home out of the forest's timber. I came here to leave, not to settle. But a man who can't feel his fingers can't build wings either.
entries.title: A house

entries.onMind: What do I feed it, and with what?
entries.reason: His maker said the fire was his after this morning.
entries.text: The flames have sunk to a red bed in the pan while I read. It's mine to keep going now, and I have never kept a fire in my life.
entries.title: Down to a red bed

entries.onMind: Something under cover. The scrap pile's under the tarp's edge.
queries: how to find dry firewood when everything is wet from rain
entries.query: how to find dry firewood when everything is wet from rain
entries.reason: His fire is down to coals and every stick in the forest is dripping.
entries.source: American Hunter: How to Start a Fire When Everything is Wet
entries.text: Dry wood hides under thick low branches, on the side of things out of the weather, and inside dead seasoned wood once you split or shave the wet skin off. Start small, go up slowly, and keep the rain off where you work.
entries.title: Dry is on the inside

entries.reason: The tablet said look where the weather can't reach.
entries.text: The bottom of the scrap pile sits under the tarp's edge and never got wet: six plank offcuts, gray and dry right through, a hand to a forearm long.
entries.title: Offcuts from the pile

entries.reason: His maker said it's his to keep after this morning.
entries.text: Laid the smallest offcut across the red bed and waited. It smoked thick and white, then caught; the next one I set beside it, not on top. Fire's up, and I didn't smother it.
entries.title: Fed it myself

entries.onMind: Offcuts tonight, then what? Wet sticks dried round the ring, maybe.
entries.reason: He hadn't eaten since last night, and the cold eats food.
entries.text: A thick end of the second loaf and a wedge of the cheese, eaten on the ground by my own fire with the rain ticking on the tarp behind me. Hands working again by the second bite.
entries.title: Breakfast by a fire

entries.onMind: Pace the ground round camp for fallen wood this afternoon.
entries.text: A fire wants wood every couple of hours, and so would a house, just more of it and all at once. Either way the first job is the same: find out what dead timber lies near camp.
entries.title: Wood is the parts list

entries.onMind: Dry the wood before it burns, not while.
queries: why does wood make thick white smoke when you first put it on a fire
entries.query: why does wood make thick white smoke when you first put it on a fire
entries.reason: Even his dry offcuts smoked white before they caught, and he wanted to know what that white was.
entries.source: Cutting Edge Firewood: Why is My Fire So Smokey? 6 Proven Ways to Reduce Smoke
entries.text: Tablet's dim under the cloud, but it got there: wet wood always smokes thicker, because the water in it boils off as steam into the smoke, and a wet piece burns cooler and smolders. Lay pieces close enough to share heat, far enough apart to breathe.
entries.title: White is the water

entries.onMind: Damp isn't dry. They'll need the ring.
entries.reason: Six offcuts will not last the night, and he needs wood close to camp.
entries.text: A dead limb lies in the leaves forty paces north-east of camp. The top is soaked black, but the branches on its underside are gray and only damp; snapped off an armload, forearm to arm long.
entries.title: Dry underneath

entries.onMind: Pace the rest of the ground for more like it.
entries.text: The limb itself is waist-thick and longer than my tarp. Too heavy to drag alone, but it's the first real timber I've found near camp.
entries.title: Timber, too

entries.onMind: Time how long they take to stop steaming.
entries.reason: So the wood is dry before it goes on, and does not smother the fire.
entries.text: Leaned eight damp branches round the ring stones, bark to the heat, a finger's gap between each. They steam white before a flame ever touches them: that's the water leaving, not the wood burning.
entries.title: Steaming at the ring

entries.onMind: whether it burns in a lantern
entries.reason: Before I ask if it burns, I want to know how much there is to burn.
entries.text: Lifted the grease skin off the cold broth with a fingernail and pushed it into the corner of the tin. Pale, waxy, smells of fish. A fingertip, maybe two.
entries.title: A fingertip of fat

entries.onMind: trying it on the bench lantern tonight
queries: can grease from boiled fish burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.query: can grease from boiled fish burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.reason: The oil can is the last one coming, and the fish broth gave me grease.
entries.source: Antique Lamp Supply: Type of Oil Used in Oil Lamps
entries.text: Tablet's dim, but it found a lamp shop's page: fish oil was burned in lamps once, dim and smoky; some thick oils gum up an ordinary wick, and olive oil wants a thick wick to burn at all. Not one word about a lantern like mine.
entries.title: Thick oil, plain wick

entries.text: Nobody says no outright. A fingertip won't ruin a wick, and finding out costs a fingertip. Tonight, on the bench lantern.
entries.title: Try it anyway

entries.onMind: how much dry wood a night takes
entries.reason: Dry it first, then burn it; that's what the white smoke taught me.
entries.text: Fed three of the branches that steamed round the ring. Thin gray smoke this time, hardly any white, and they caught in a breath.
entries.title: Thin smoke

entries.onMind: what holds a wall up without nails
entries.reason: I want to know where it stands before I drag a single pole.
entries.text: Drew the camp on a corner of the map sheet: tarp, bench, scrap pile, the fire ring, the dead limb forty paces north-east. A house goes where the fire can sit at its door.
entries.title: Camp in pencil

entries.text: I don't know yet what holds up a wall nobody nails. That's a question for the next good daylight.
entries.title: No nails

queries: how do you build log walls that stay up without nails
entries.query: how do you build log walls that stay up without nails
entries.reason: He drew where a house could stand and doesn't know what holds a wall up without nails.
entries.source: Designing Buildings Wiki: Log construction
entries.text: Tablet's dim but it got there: log walls hold at the corners, where each log end is notched to lock over the one crosswise below it. A saddle notch lets the logs settle as they dry; the stuff packed between logs only keeps the wind out, it doesn't hold anything up.
entries.title: Corners carry it

entries.onMind: what size of timber I can actually handle
entries.text: The limb out there is too thick for me to lift, let alone notch. Arm-thick poles I can carry, and maybe notch.
entries.title: Poles, not logs

entries.text: Paced the dead limb in the rain: eleven of my paces, waist-thick at the butt and still thigh-thick where it forks. Its side branches run straight and arm-thick for two paces before they bend. Those I could carry.
entries.title: Eleven paces

entries.text: Bread, a thumb of sausage and an apple, on the ground by my fire. My wet sleeves steamed and my hands came back by the apple.
entries.title: Sleeves steaming

entries.text: Clamped a wrist-thick branch in the vise and filed a saddle into it a finger deep. Twenty minutes for one notch in one small stick, and the file's teeth are packed with wet wood. A wall would take a hundred of these; I need a blade that chops.
entries.title: Twenty minutes a notch

queries: how to cut poles for a shelter without an axe
entries.query: how to cut poles for a shelter without an axe
entries.reason: One notch with the file took twenty minutes, and a wall needs a hundred.
entries.source: OffGridWeb: DIY Improvised Bucksaw
entries.text: Dim tablet, slow page. Their answer is a bucksaw: three sticks for a frame, cord twisted tight with a toggle to hold a toothed blade taut. The frame I could make tonight. The blade I don't have.
entries.title: A saw needs a blade

queries: make an axe head from scrap metal without a forge
entries.query: make an axe head from scrap metal without a forge
entries.reason: If nobody sells blades here, maybe he can make one from his scrap.
entries.source: Chelsea Green: DIY: How to Make Your Own Hatchet
entries.text: A hatchet can be made with a bonfire instead of a forge: cut the head out, file the edge, heat it red, hammer it, quench it in cold water. But it starts as steel about a third of an inch thick, an old plow point. Tin won't take an edge.
entries.title: Steel, not tin

entries.text: Dug the scrap pile to the bottom for anything thick. Tin, tin, a bent strip of tin. Nothing in there would hold an edge past the first knot.
entries.title: Only tin

entries.text: Hung my whole weight on a dead side branch of the limb and bounced, and it went at the knot with a crack loud enough to carry across the water. Two paces long, arm-thick. My first wall pole, and no blade touched it.
entries.title: No blade needed

entries.onMind: how many dead branches the limb has
entries.text: Fed the fire three branches that had steamed dry round the stones and leaned wet ones in their places. Hands open to it, I'm thinking the forest drops dead branches all winter. Maybe I start with those and save the cutting for later.
entries.title: Start with what falls

entries.onMind: supper, and the fat in their heads
entries.reason: He wants supper that's still alive at suppertime, not something that spoiled in a tin.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap in the rain: both crayfish from last night still walking in it, the big one and the small. Set it back down in the shallows. A trap in cold water is a better pen than my tin.
entries.title: Still walking

queries: how to build a small shelter from poles without an axe or nails
entries.query: how to build a small shelter from poles without an axe or nails
entries.reason: A notched wall takes a blade he hasn't got, so he wants a shelter built from poles he can break off.
entries.source: Gun Digest: How to Make a Wikiup Survival Shelter
entries.text: Tablet's dim but it got there: a wikiup starts with three strong poles with a Y at one end, leaned together so the forks lock into a tripod, the bottoms spread wide. Then straight poles lean in close all round, and leaves and needles go on from the bottom up like shingles. No tools at all.
entries.title: Three forks lock

entries.onMind: how many poles a cone needs
entries.text: No notches, no nails, no blade. Three forks hold each other up, and the rest just leans. That's a parts list I can actually fill.
entries.title: No notches

entries.reason: The forks are the three poles everything else leans on, so he counts those first.
entries.text: Walked the dead limb end to end looking at the ends of its side branches, not the middles. Two of them fork into a clean Y about two paces out; the rest just taper off.
entries.title: Two Y's

entries.reason: Breaking it off is the only cutting he can do, and he wanted to know a fork survives the break.
entries.text: Hung on the nearer Y-branch and bounced. It went at the knot with a crack as loud as the first one, and came away with its fork whole. Two forks to go, and one of them isn't on this limb.
entries.title: First fork

entries.reason: Poles in a heap at camp are poles I can count.
entries.text: Carried both poles back from the limb one at a time and laid them by the lean-to, the fork on top. Two down, and the pile has a start.
entries.title: A pile, started

entries.reason: The limb only had two forks; I need a third.
entries.text: Under the oak by the creek a dead branch lay in the leaves with a clean Y at one end. I leaned on it to test it and it folded in the middle, soft as bread. Rotten through.
entries.title: Soft as bread

entries.text: Wood lying on the wet ground goes to mush. The good poles are the ones still hanging off something.
entries.title: Ground wood rots

entries.reason: Came back from the oak wet to the elbows.
entries.text: Fed the fire two branches that had steamed dry round the stones and leaned two wet ones in their places. Sat close with my sleeves steaming until my fingers stopped aching.
entries.title: Sleeves again

queries: wikiup tripod only two forked poles and one straight pole
how to build a tripod shelter frame if I only have two forked poles
entries.query: wikiup tripod only two forked poles and one straight pole
entries.reason: The only third fork I found was rotten, and I wanted to know if I even need one.
entries.source: Survival Kompass: How to build a tripod for Bushcraft and Survival
entries.text: The first search turned up nothing but camera stands. The second found a page where three plain branches lie side by side, a cord weaves over and under them three to five times and binds the gaps, then the legs spread wide and it stands. No forks at all; the cord does what the forks do.
entries.title: Cord does the forks' job

entries.text: I've been twisting cord from dead stalks for a week. One fork and two straight poles, lashed at the top, and the rot under the oak doesn't matter.
entries.title: Cord I have

entries.reason: Cord does what forks do, so a straight pole is a third leg now.
entries.text: Went back to the big limb and hung on a straight side branch, no fork, thick as my wrist. It held two bounces and went at the knot on the third.
entries.title: A straight one

entries.text: Carried it back and laid it with the other two. One fork, two straight, all about two paces long.
entries.title: Three on the pile

entries.reason: I wanted to see it stand before I spend more cord on it.
entries.text: Laid the three side by side and wove wet stalk cord over and under them three times, tied it off and lifted the middle to spread the legs. The cord slid along the wet wood and the poles rolled apart into the leaves.
entries.title: Three turns, then nothing

entries.text: It was tight when I tied it and loose when I lifted. Wet cord stretches, and wet bark is slick.
entries.title: Wet cord gives

queries: tripod lashing with wet cord keeps slipping poles splay out
entries.query: tripod lashing with wet cord keeps slipping poles splay out
entries.reason: My first lashing slid apart the moment I spread the legs, and I wanted to know what I left out.
entries.source: Animated Knots: Tripod Lashing
entries.text: Tablet's slow under the gray, but it got there. Start with a clove hitch on one pole, weave about six turns round all three, then wrap two or three tight turns crossways in each gap between the poles; those are what pull it tight. Not so tight the legs can't spread, it says, and the rest is trial and error.
entries.title: Six turns and the gaps

entries.text: Three turns and none crossways: I did half a lashing. Six turns, the crossways ones in both gaps, and cord that's dried a while by the fire, then I try it again before dark.
entries.title: I left out half

entries.reason: Wet cord stretched and let the first lashing go.
entries.text: Wound the wet stalk cord loose round a stick and propped it by the ring stones, close enough to steam. Sat with it and turned it now and then.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.reason: The tablet said the crossways turns are what pull it tight.
entries.text: Clove hitch on the forked pole, six turns round all three, then three tight turns crossways in each gap. Lifted the middle, spread the feet, and the three legs stood on their own, a little lopsided.
entries.title: It stands

entries.text: The crossways turns squeeze the six round turns together; that was the half I left out. Cord still damp, so it may stretch overnight.
entries.title: The gaps do it

entries.reason: Nothing goes on top of it until it holds me.
entries.text: Hung my weight off the crossing for a count of ten. The left foot skidded a hand's width in the wet leaves, then bit into the dirt and the whole thing held, no creak at the lashing.
entries.title: Hung on it

entries.onMind: the fish grease in the lantern
entries.text: Next time I dig a shallow hole for each foot before I spread it. Light's going gray; the grease goes in the bench lantern tonight.
entries.title: Feet in holes

entries.reason: Keep it going now, while there is still gray light to find wood by.
entries.text: Fire was down to a red bed. Fed it three of the branches that had steamed dry round the stones, and leaned three wet ones in their places.
entries.title: Before it sank

entries.text: Sun is going in somewhere out west behind all this gray. At the edge it would be rain over water and nothing else. The edge keeps.
entries.title: No sundown tonight

entries.reason: The tablet never said no, and a fingertip was what it cost to find out.
entries.text: Drew the bench lantern's wick out dry, worked the fingertip of fish grease into it, set it back over an empty fount and lit it. It flared on the cloth, smelled of fish, shrank to a blue bead and went out.
entries.title: Grease on the wick

entries.text: The grease left in the corner of the tin is white and stiff, like cold butter. Lamp oil runs like water up the wick. This just sits there. Maybe warm it runs, maybe it wants a different lamp altogether; that is a question for daylight.
entries.title: Butter, not oil

entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap by lantern: the big crayfish and the small one, still walking. Into the tin with creek water, trap back down under its stone.
entries.title: Two for supper

entries.text: From the shallows the fire across the water burned steady, and someone low was beside it, bent over the ground at its edge. Didn't look up.
entries.title: Bent to the ground

entries.reason: Fire is free heat; lamp oil is not.
entries.text: Set the tin on the ring stones where the flames lick it, not on the lantern this time. It came to a boil quicker than the lantern ever did, and the lantern stays dark.
entries.title: Tin on the stones

entries.onMind: whether the grease only needs to be warm
entries.text: Ate both crayfish and a heel of bread by the fire, and saved the heads and the broth in the tin. Firelight is enough to eat by.
entries.title: Supper by firelight

entries.onMind: pour it in while it's hot
entries.reason: Last night's question: maybe it only needs warming.
entries.text: Set the grease tin on the ring stones beside the fire. Inside a minute the white lump went clear and yellow and slid round the tin like oil. So it's oil after all, just oil that wants heat.
entries.title: It runs

entries.reason: If warm runs, warm might climb.
entries.text: Poured the warm spoonful into the bench lantern's empty fount, set the wick and lit it. A small yellow flame this time, fishy and smoky, for maybe the count of a hundred. Then it dimmed, guttered and went out, and the grease in the fount had gone cloudy again.
entries.title: Longer, then out

entries.onMind: keeping it warm, or a shorter climb
entries.text: The flame's up top and the grease is down in a cold tin fount, a hand away. It sets before it can climb. Annoying. A whole spoon of it gone into the bottom of a lantern.
entries.title: Cold down there

entries.reason: The tripod feet want holes and the next lashing wants cord.
entries.text: Twisted stalk cord by the fire, three strands, an arm's length at a time. The tin of crayfish heads and broth sits off the stones to cool; last time a skin of grease came up on the guts tin.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.reason: It'd be coals by the time I want it most.
entries.text: Fed the fire three branches that had steamed dry round the ring and leaned three wet ones in their places. The drizzle's thinner now; it hardly hisses on the stones.
entries.title: Three in, three leaned

entries.reason: If cold kills it, keep the whole thing warm.
entries.text: Set the bench lantern on the ring stones a hand back from the flames until the cloudy grease in the fount went clear, then lit it. It burned: small, yellow, stinking of fish, but steady past a count of three hundred.
entries.title: Lantern by the fire

entries.text: Carried it off the stones toward the bench and it was a blue bead before I got there. A lantern that only burns sitting next to a fire is no lantern. Warm isn't the answer.
entries.title: No lantern at all

entries.reason: Earned one, even off a failure.
entries.text: Dipped one oat cookie in the honey on the crate. Two bites, cork back in. A treat's a treat because it stops.
entries.title: One cookie

entries.text: The wick climbs a finger's length out of a cold fount. What if there's no climb at all: the grease in something shallow, kept warm by the flame itself, the wick lying in it with just its tip up? Daylight question.
entries.title: Something shallow

entries.reason: Need grease for the shallow try, and every bit counts.
entries.text: Off the stones, the crayfish broth has cooled enough to set a thin white skin on top, about a thumbnail's worth. Lifted it off with a twig onto the griddle tin.
entries.title: Skin on the broth

entries.reason: No climb for the wick means nothing deep.
entries.text: Dug a tin lid out of the scrap pile, a palm wide and a fingernail deep. About as shallow as a thing gets and still holds anything.
entries.title: Found a shallow one

entries.onMind: will it hold away from the fire
entries.reason: If the flame sits right on the fat, the fat stays warm by itself.
entries.text: Scraped the set grease out of the lantern fount and the skin off the griddle tin into the lid, warmed it a minute on the ring stones till it ran, then laid in a thumb-long twist of stalk cord with just its tip bent up in the middle.
entries.title: Wick lying down

entries.reason: The whole point was a flame that does not need a fire beside it.
entries.text: Lit the tip with a splinter from the fire and walked away from it. The lid sits on the bench five steps from the fire and the flame stays: small, yellow, smoky, stinks of fish, about a candle.
entries.title: It burns over here

entries.text: Count of a hundred and eighty, then the tip burned down level with the grease, slumped in and drowned with one hiss. The tip has to stay up somehow. Still: it burned away from the fire. First time.
entries.title: Drowned

entries.onMind: who saws a board this flat
entries.reason: The fire wants dry wood before it sinks.
entries.text: Went to the pole pile for dry sticks and walked into two stacks that weren't there at supper: sawn planks and squared beams, each laid up on two bearers, edges straight as a rule.
entries.title: Square edges

entries.text: Nobody in this forest saws a board that flat but my maker. Counted them by feel in the drizzle and left them be until I know what they're for. Daylight question, like everything else tonight.
entries.title: Not touching yet

entries.reason: It sinks around now, and I'm not sleeping cold beside a dead pit.
entries.text: Fed the fire three of the branches that steamed dry round the stones and leaned three wet ones in their places. It'll carry me to bed now.
entries.title: Fire before bed

entries.text: The cord drowned because nothing held its tip up once the flame ate down to the grease. Cord burns, a twig burns. Tin doesn't.
entries.title: Something that won't burn

entries.reason: So the burning end has something to rest on that can't burn away.
entries.text: Worked a fingernail-wide strip off a torn scrap and hammered it into a little arch with a dip in the top, its feet in the grease. The wick lies through the dip, tip up a fingernail clear.
entries.title: A tin bridge

entries.reason: Wanted to know if the tip stays up once the flame eats down to the tin.
entries.text: Warmed the lid on the ring stones till the grease ran, set it back on the bench and lit the tip. Counted to six hundred and it was still there, small and yellow, stinking of fish. Pinched it out myself to save the grease.
entries.title: Still burning

entries.text: The bridge gets hot and the grease spits at it, and it's a candle's worth at best. But it went out because I told it to. That's new.
entries.title: Not a lantern yet

entries.text: Twisting spare wicks by the fire. Tomorrow when the tablet wakes: what the stacks of timber are for, and who I ask about them.
entries.title: Daylight list

entries.onMind: two squares at the east edge
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the lid lamp is enough light to work by, not just to look at.
entries.text: The drizzle's quit, so I warmed the lid on the ring stones, lit the bridged wick and laid the map sheet beside it. Added two small squares at the east edge of the camp corner for the timber stacks, and a question mark next to them.
entries.title: By my own light

entries.text: Enough to see a pencil line if I lean my nose down to it, not enough to see the other end of the sheet. Pinched it out with grease to spare. A lantern for the room, a lid for the hand.
entries.title: Enough for a pencil

entries.reason: Cold nights eat what supper gave him.
entries.text: A wedge of the cheese on the ground by the fire. The bundle sits flatter every time I tie it; the creek has to start feeding me before it's empty.
entries.title: Cheese by the fire

entries.reason: Thin sticks burn out while he sleeps.
entries.text: Laid three of the thickest dried branches across the coals, crossways so the air gets under. Leaned the wet ones round the stones for tomorrow. It hisses, then settles.
entries.title: Thick ones last

entries.reason: Every night before sleep, so I know it didn't drift while I wasn't looking.
entries.text: Drops on the back of my neck again while I bent to the bench. Under the dome the water stays flat, not a pock in it; the needle swung, wobbled and settled on the same scratch.
entries.title: Dry under glass

entries.reason: Wet cord stretches; I'd rather fix it now than wake in a puddle.
entries.text: The wet cord at the front pole had stretched and the tarp sagged into a pocket of water right over the bedroll. Tipped it out, took up two turns and pulled it tight.
entries.title: Taking up the slack

entries.text: Hands out to the coals, drizzle hissing on the ring stones. No glow across the water tonight, not even a red spot. Sawn planks don't walk out of a forest; first thing when the tablet wakes, I find out who left them and what for.
entries.title: Who leaves wood
