entries.onMind: how to keep coals till morning
entries.reason: He fed it thick before bed and expected coals.
entries.text: Woke under the blanket to a gray sky. Held my palm over the fire pit: nothing. Gray ash all the way down, not one red speck.
entries.title: Cold ash

entries.onMind: the creek has to start feeding me
entries.reason: He slept hungry and the cold takes it out of him faster.
entries.text: Breakfast on the crate: a length of the smoked sausage and one apple, core and all but the pips. The bundle's down to cheese, sausage, nuts and two apples.
entries.title: Sausage and an apple

entries.text: My maker asked last night if I needed help getting the fire going. I told him it was going when he asked, and dead by morning, and I'd rather learn to keep it than have it lit for me.
entries.title: Help with the fire

entries.text: The timber was my maker, and an axe, a saw, a hammer and a roll of knives wait at the stump: a workshop first, then a cabin. I told him the truth: I came to go west, not to stay, but a roof over a bench that gets rained on every night I'll build.
entries.title: The planks were his

queries: how to keep fire coals alive overnight till morning
entries.query: how to keep fire coals alive overnight till morning
entries.reason: His fire went from thick branches to cold ash between bedtime and morning.
entries.source: Hunker: How To Bank Ashes In Fireplaces
entries.text: Let it burn down to coals, push them to the middle, lay a log or two on top, and cover the lot with ash till no glow shows. In the morning scrape the ash back and the coals are waiting under it. It's written for stoves; my pit has no lid and the rain finds it.
entries.title: Bury the coals

entries.reason: There was nothing left in the pit to light from.
entries.text: Lit the bench lantern just long enough to catch a splinter, then turned it down and out. Lamp oil spent on a morning fire is the price of letting it die.
entries.title: Oil for a splinter

entries.reason: He wants it burning before he leaves camp for the stump.
entries.text: The sticks I leaned round the ring last night were dry on the skin and wet in the middle. They hissed and threw white smoke for a while before they took.
entries.title: Dry outside only

entries.onMind: the stump, with the fire safe to leave
entries.text: An axe leaning on a pole, a saw on two pegs, the hammer in a loop, the knives rolled on the bench. I haven't even picked them up and I'm already arranging them.
entries.title: A place for each

entries.reason: His maker left the tools there, and four is more than an armful.
entries.text: The axe leaned on the stump where the note said: hickory handle, a head heavier than anything I own, an edge that shaves a fingernail. Picked it up with the saw and the head knocked the blade with a clank. The hammer and the knife roll wait for a second trip.
entries.title: Axe and saw

entries.text: Woodsmoke and something roasting, close, south through the trunks. The fire I watch every night across the water is only a short walk from this stump. I didn't go look, not with an axe in my hand.
entries.title: Smoke close by

entries.reason: Every tool gets a place of its own before it gets used.
entries.text: Sighted down the handle: straight, no twist, and the head sits tight with a wedge in the top. Leaned the axe on the lean-to's front pole with its head in the leaves and laid the saw flat on the bench.
entries.title: Places for two

queries: how to keep an axe and saw from rusting outside with no shed
entries.query: how to keep an axe and saw from rusting outside with no shed
entries.reason: Two good steel tools now sit at a camp with no roof, and it rains here most nights.
entries.source: AXEMAN.ca: Essential Guide to Proper Axe Storage Solutions
entries.text: Keep an axe head up off the ground on a rack or a wall, cover the edge, and wipe the steel dry with a thin coat of oil. And keep it in a dry shed, which is the one thing I haven't got.
entries.title: Off the ground

entries.onMind: move the axe, then the second trip
entries.text: Head down in wet leaves is exactly wrong. Lamp oil is too dear to smear on steel, but the fish grease in the lid might do the same job. A shed for tools would be a smaller roof to learn on than a cabin.
entries.title: Exactly wrong

queries: can fish oil keep rust off an axe head
entries.query: can fish oil keep rust off an axe head
entries.reason: He has fish grease in the lid and no lamp oil to spare for steel.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Can oiling keep tools from rusting?
entries.text: Kitchen-type oils keep rust off steel but go sour, gummy and a little acid as they sit. Grease is the thing for tools stored in bad conditions, and keeping them dry beats oiling them most of the time.
entries.title: Grease goes rancid

entries.reason: He wants to stop the rust before it gets a hold.
entries.text: Lifted the axe out of the leaves: a few orange freckles along the cheek already, and a wet leaf stuck to the poll. Wiped it dry on my shirttail and rubbed a thin smear of grease from the lid over the steel.
entries.title: Orange freckles

entries.text: Fish grease will stink and go gummy inside a week, so it's a stopgap. Dry and off the ground matters more than any oil I can make.
entries.title: Only for now

entries.onMind: the hammer and knives still at the stump
entries.reason: The tablet said off the ground and dry.
entries.text: Wound stalk cord three times round the front pole, head-high, and tied a loop off it. The axe hangs by its handle now, head up under the tarp's edge where the drips miss it.
entries.title: Hung by the handle

entries.reason: The last two of his maker's tools were waiting.
entries.text: The hammer and the leather roll were still in the basket. Tucked the hammer inside the roll and carried it flat against my chest so nothing would clank.
entries.title: Second trip

entries.onMind: the fire south of the stump
entries.text: Last trip the axe head rang on the saw loud enough to carry. Whoever roasts things south of this stump doesn't need to hear me every time I come.
entries.title: Quiet this time

entries.reason: He wants to know what each one is for.
entries.text: Unrolled the leather on the bench: a long straight blade, a short stub, and one curled like a hook for hollows. Laid the hammer beside them and the saw. That bench is getting crowded for something with no roof over it.
entries.title: Three blades

entries.onMind: fish, before the bundle runs out
entries.reason: Fullness was getting low.
entries.text: A wedge of cheese and a handful of nuts on the crate with my back to the fire. The bundle is down to most of the cheese, the sausage end, some nuts and two apples: two days, three if I'm careful.
entries.title: Cheese and nuts

entries.reason: The fire was getting low and he wants it close while he plans.
entries.text: Laid two dry branches crossways on the coals before they sank. Caught in about a minute, with less smoke than this morning's damp sticks.
entries.title: Two across

queries: how to build a small tool shed from planks and 2x4s by hand first steps
entries.query: how to build a small tool shed from planks and 2x4s by hand first steps
entries.reason: He wants a small roof for his tools before he tries a cabin.
entries.source: MyOutdoorPlans: 2x4 Tool Shed Lean to Roof Plans
entries.text: A small shed with a roof that slopes one way, rafters every sixteen inches. Pick straight boards with no cracks or twists, check things are plumb before fastening, and drill pilot holes so the wood doesn't split. The list wants galvanized screws, metal roof sheets, siding panels, hinges and a drill.
entries.title: Plans want screws

entries.onMind: how to hold two boards together
entries.text: Screws, roof sheets, siding, a drill: I have none of it. I have sixteen planks, twelve two-by-fours and a hammer with not one nail to hit.
entries.title: Nothing to drive

entries.reason: He wants to know if a shed fits before he cuts anything.
entries.text: Paced it out between the bench and the stacks: three paces long, two deep, enough to stand the axe and saw in and keep the hammer dry. The plan said slope the roof one way, so the back goes low and the rain runs off away from the bench.
entries.title: Three by two

entries.onMind: how to make a hole without a drill
entries.text: The wing joints hold with cord and no metal at all. Maybe a board can be held with a wooden peg in a hole, if the knives can make the peg and something can make the hole.
entries.title: Pegs, maybe

queries: how to join boards with wooden pegs instead of nails without a drill
entries.query: how to join boards with wooden pegs instead of nails without a drill
entries.reason: Every shed plan wants nails, and he has a hammer with none to drive.
entries.source: Outdoor Revival: Before Nails, There Was Pegged Wood Construction
entries.text: First page the tablet gave me was dead. The next says before nails, joints were held with round wooden pegs carved from branches too thin for anything else, half an inch to an inch thick, pounded through a hole and trimmed. The rough surface grips. The holes were bored with a brace and bit, which I do not have.
entries.title: Pegs, not nails

entries.onMind: a hot rod burns a hole?
entries.text: A peg I can carve. A round hole through a two-by-four is another thing: a knife point twisted in makes a cone, not a hole.
entries.title: No brace

entries.reason: He wants to know if he can make a peg good enough to hold boards.
entries.text: Whittled a peg from a thin dry branch off the deadfall with the long straight knife, my back to the fire: thumb-thick, a hand long, tapered at one end. Lumpy, but the page said rough grips.
entries.title: First peg

entries.onMind: thinner pegs, or holes through the flat
entries.reason: He wants to see how a peg fits his timber before trying to bore anything.
entries.text: Held the peg to the end of a two-by-four on the stack. The narrow side is barely three of these pegs wide; a hole that size near the end would split it. Thinner pegs, or the holes go through the wide face.
entries.title: Too fat

queries: how to make a round hole in wood without a drill or brace
entries.query: how to make a round hole in wood without a drill or brace
entries.reason: He can carve pegs but has nothing to bore the holes they go in.
entries.source: Tools Week: How to Drill a Hole without a Drill (9 Methods)
entries.text: Slow under the clouds, the tablet gave me nine ways to put a hole in wood without a drill. A nail driven and pulled back out, an awl, a rod spun with a looped cord, or a sharpened rod heated until it glows and burned straight through.
entries.title: Hot iron

entries.onMind: split wood for a hotter fire
entries.reason: The heated rod is the only method that uses what he already has.
entries.text: No nails, no awl. But I have a fire and a hammer, and a glowing rod pushed through a board leaves a round hole. A charred one, which a rough peg might grip all the better.
entries.title: Burn it

entries.reason: A hot fire needs split wood, and the axe was still a stranger.
entries.text: First swing glanced off the branch and buried the edge in the leaves a hand from my boot. Set my feet wider, let the head drop instead of pushing it, and the fourth swing split the branch clean down the middle.
entries.title: First swings

entries.reason: He had never used an axe before and the first mistake was close.
entries.text: That glance would have been my shin. Nothing on this camp I can't fix except that, so feet apart and the branch on the far side of the log from now on.
entries.title: A hand from my boot

entries.reason: The fire was close to sinking, and he wants it hot for the rod.
entries.text: Fed the pit the split halves, dry face down. The pale insides caught in a few breaths, quicker than any round stick I've put on it.
entries.title: Split burns faster

entries.reason: He needs something that will hold heat and fit through a peg-sized hole.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile past tin and bent strap and came up with a steel rod about as long as my forearm and pencil-thick, rusty and kinked at one end. Straighten it, grind a point, heat it red.
entries.title: A rusty rod

entries.text: Laid the rod across the end of the bench and hammered the kink out, a dozen light blows. It rang every time, loud enough to carry. Sighted down it after: straight to my eye but for a hair at the very tip.
entries.title: Straight enough

entries.onMind: hold it by the far end
entries.text: Pushed the point into the brightest coals and laid the cold end out on a ring stone. It takes its time; the middle of the rod gets too hot to hold well before the tip goes red.
entries.title: Point in the coals

entries.onMind: two days of cheese and nuts
entries.text: Ate the last of the sausage and an apple sitting by the pit while the rod heated. The bundle is down to most of the cheese, the nuts and one apple.
entries.title: Sausage end

entries.text: Pulled the rod glowing dull red and pushed it into the flat of a split half. It hissed, smoked, sank a fingernail deep, then went black and stuck. A two-by-four is three fingers thick: that's twenty heats for one hole, and the wood round it is charred brown.
entries.title: A fingernail deep

queries: how long does it take to burn a hole through wood with a hot iron rod
entries.query: how long does it take to burn a hole through wood with a hot iron rod
entries.reason: One heat of the rod only went a fingernail deep, and he needs holes clean through.
entries.source: Survival knowledge: Drilling wood holes
entries.text: The rod page said nothing; this one says lay live coals right on the spot and keep adding fresh ones, and they'll burrow through any piece of wood. Wet the wood round it so only the hole burns, and chip the char out with a stick between coals. Very slow, it says, and hard to keep small.
entries.title: Coals, not a rod

entries.onMind: try it on an offcut, not a good board
entries.text: The rod is good for a start: a dent for a coal to sit in. A peg is thumb-thick anyway, so a hole that wants to grow fat isn't the worst trouble. Wet ring, coal, chip it out with the stub knife, again. Slow, like the trap.
entries.title: Rod starts, coal finishes

entries.reason: The tablet said a coal laid on the spot will burrow through, and he wanted to see it on scrap first.
entries.text: Dripped creek water out of the tin in a ring round the rod dent so only the dent would burn, then lifted the brightest coal out of the pit on the rod tip and set it in. It fit like an egg in a cup.
entries.title: Coal in the dent

entries.text: Left alone, the coal went gray in a minute and just sat there. I blew on it and it went orange, the dent smoked, and I could hear it tick as it ate. It only works while I blow, and my face is right in the smoke.
entries.title: It sulks, then eats

entries.reason: Char left in the hole smothers the next coal.
entries.text: Three coals, and the stub knife between each to scrape the black out. About a third of the way through the split half. The top is already wider than my thumb, so a peg won't be snug unless I make the pegs fatter or the holes straighter.
entries.title: Third coal

entries.onMind: a stalk with the pith pushed out
queries: burning a hole through wood with a coal blow through a tube to make it faster
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with a coal blow through a tube to make it faster
entries.reason: The coal only burns down while he blows on it, and blowing with his face over it fills his eyes with smoke.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Blowpipe (tool)
entries.text: A blowpipe is just a tube for aiming a stream of air. Pushing air through a flame mixes it with the fuel and makes the jet intensely hot; smiths, glassworkers and people starting fires have all used one. Same as my breath on the coal, only aimed, and with my face a forearm away.
entries.title: Breath through a tube

entries.reason: He needs to aim his breath down into the hole, not across it.
entries.text: The gray stalks on the east bank have pith in them, and I already push pith out for the compass float. Run the rod down one and it's a tube. Aimed straight down the hole, it might burn straight too.
entries.title: A stalk to blow through

entries.reason: He wants a tube to aim his breath, and he already knows these stalks are full of soft pith.
entries.text: Picked four of the straightest dead stalks on the east bank, each about a finger thick and a forearm long. Snapped them clean below the joints so the bore runs through.
entries.title: Four gray stalks

entries.text: The fire had sunk to a red bed while I was at the creek. Laid on three split sticks from the deadfall, the dry ones from under the top.
entries.title: Pit was sinking

entries.reason: He checks the bore before trusting his breath to it.
entries.text: Ran the rod down the first stalk and the pith came out the far end in a white worm. Sighting down it at the bench I can see a coin of gray sky; the second stalk split along its side, so that one is cord stuff now.
entries.title: A coin of sky

entries.text: Blew through the stalk on the fourth coal and it went from orange to near white and ate down fast, with my face a forearm out of the smoke. Blow hard and the stalk whistles high and the ash jumps into my eyes. Short soft breaths: the hole went a nail deeper and stayed straighter.
entries.title: It whistles

entries.text: Nearly half through the split half now. The top is still too wide, but the new part runs straight. The light is going; the next coals will be by lantern.
entries.title: Halfway, nearly

entries.reason: light to work by without eating the oil
entries.text: Turned the wick of the bench lantern down to a bead before I lit it. One lantern, low, and the fire for the rest: the can has to last.
entries.title: One lantern, low

entries.reason: supper before the cold
entries.text: Ate a thick wedge of the cheese and two handfuls of nuts sitting by the pit. Most of a wheel gone now, one apple left, and the nuts going down. The bundle has a day or two in it.
entries.title: Cheese by the pit

entries.onMind: the wide top of the hole
entries.reason: aimed breath without the mess
entries.text: Fifth and sixth coals, short soft breaths down the stalk, face out of the smoke. Not one whistle, and no ash in my eyes. The coal stays orange-white instead of roaring, and it eats down just as well.
entries.title: Soft and quiet

entries.text: Past halfway through the split half by firelight. The straight part is straight. The top I made too wide will want a fatter peg, or I start the next hole better than this one.
entries.title: Past halfway

entries.reason: He needs fresh coals to finish burning the peg hole.
entries.text: Laid three split sticks from the deadfall on the pit, dry side down, and waited for them to catch before I blew on anything. The last coals ran thin; I want a full bed for the end of the hole.
entries.title: Three more from the deadfall

entries.onMind: a peg for a wide mouth
entries.text: Seventh coal, short soft breaths, and it dropped out the bottom of the split half onto the dirt. Held the board up to the fire and saw orange through the hole. Straight below, a finger too wide at the top.
entries.title: Through

entries.onMind: drive it in daylight with the hammer
entries.reason: A hole without a peg that fits holds nothing together.
entries.text: Split a stick and shaved it round with the long knife on the crate. First taper ran too skinny at the tip and the peg rocked in the hole. Shaved a second one fatter and longer in the taper: it wedges tight halfway and stops. Not driven yet.
entries.title: Peg, take one

entries.text: Lifted the trap by lantern: one small crayfish, about a thumb long, walking round the inside cone. Put it back in the water as a pen. Across the water the fire is up again, steady and low.
entries.title: One small one

entries.reason: Pencil work needs light close to the sheet, and the lantern oil has to last.
entries.text: Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone till it ran clear, carried it to the bench and lit the wick on its bridge. Small yellow flame, fishy smoke, enough for the corner of the sheet I'm drawing on.
entries.title: Lamp for the pencil

entries.onMind: a faster way to make a hole
entries.reason: He wants to know what the shed really costs before he starts it.
entries.text: Drew the shed three paces by two: four sill boards lapped at the corners, a post at each corner, a plate on top. Two pegs a corner at the bottom, two at the top, braces after that: twenty-odd holes. One hole took me an evening. Twenty evenings of blowing down a stalk is not a plan, it's a sentence.
entries.title: Counting holes

entries.text: Pinched the wick out with grease still in the lid. A spoonful saved is another evening of pencil.
entries.title: Pinched out

entries.onMind: ask the tablet about boring holes
entries.reason: Pegs can be made at night by the fire; holes and hammering want daylight.
entries.text: Split another stick from the deadfall and shaved it round with the long knife, sitting close to the pit. Made the taper long and slow like the second one, and checked it in the hole: it wedges a hair deeper. Two pegs, one hole.
entries.title: Peg two

entries.text: Lifted the dome, touched nothing, set it back. The needle swung, wobbled and settled on its scratch. Still the one thing at this camp that's done.
entries.title: Needle, night check

entries.reason: The last sticks were going to coals, and I'm up for hours yet.
entries.text: Laid two split sticks from the deadfall across the pit and let them catch on their own. Learned that one this week: blow too soon and all you get is ash in your eyes.
entries.title: Pit fed

entries.reason: The first hole came out a finger too wide at the top because the coal wandered.
entries.text: Tried carving a seat for the coal into a fresh split half with the stub knife, so tomorrow's hole starts where I put it. The blade ran with the grain and the little pit stretched into a slot as long as my thumb. Across the grain it bites and stops; along it, it runs.
entries.title: With the grain

entries.onMind: bait under the shallows stones at first light
entries.reason: Cold hours are coming and I'd rather not meet them empty.
entries.text: Ate the last apple on the crate, everything but the stem. The bundle's down to a wedge of cheese and a fistful of nuts: one breakfast and not much after. The trap and the line have to feed me by the day after tomorrow.
entries.title: Last apple

entries.reason: Tomorrow's coal needs a seat that stays where he puts it.
entries.text: Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone, lit it on the bench, and cut the next starter pit across the grain with the stub knife. It bit, turned, and stopped where I stopped: a round seat the size of a pea, no slot. Pinched the wick out after.
entries.title: Across the grain

entries.reason: The bundle is down to one breakfast, so the creek has to start paying.
entries.text: Lifted the trap by lantern: the thumb-long one and a second, finger-long and fat, walked in on the old heads. Set it back in the water with both inside. That's breakfast with the last wedge of cheese.
entries.title: Two in the pen

entries.text: Across the water that fire is sinking, someone low beside it scraping it under. About this hour most nights.
entries.title: Fire going down

entries.reason: His hands came back numb from the creek and he is up a while yet.
entries.text: Laid one split stick across the coals and let it catch on its own. Held my hands over it till the fingers would bend again. Should carry me to bed and a bit past.
entries.title: One for the night

entries.onMind: Shave all round, not one side.
entries.reason: The sill needs twenty-odd pegs and I would rather make them while the fire keeps my fingers working.
entries.text: Whittled a third peg by the fire with the long knife and took one stroke too many off one side. It tapers lopsided now and would wedge crooked in the hole. It goes in the tray as a spare; the next one I shave a turn at a time.
entries.title: Peg three, crooked

entries.onMind: Two lines in the water by morning.
entries.reason: If the only line parts at breakfast, there is no breakfast.
entries.text: Twisted three strands of gray stalk fiber into a new line by the fire, two arm-lengths of it. The last one parted at the knot and took a toggle downstream. Tomorrow the bundle is done, and I want two lines, not one.
entries.title: Spare line

entries.onMind: Crayfish and cheese for breakfast, then two lines.
entries.reason: A wrap keeps most of a line's strength where a knot halves it.
entries.text: Wound the spare toggle onto the new line at the bench, six tight turns with the tail laid back in the twist, no knot. Pulled on it hard with both hands and it held. That goes in the water at first light, next to the old one.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.onMind: a clear sky at the edge tomorrow
entries.reason: A needle that wanders once tells you nothing; one that settles every night tells you something.
entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. When I looked up from it the cloud was gone and there were stars over the tarp, first time in days. If it holds, the edge gets a clear sundown tomorrow.
entries.title: Stars over the dome

entries.onMind: crayfish in the tin at first light
entries.reason: A clear sky lets the cold straight down, and the stick I laid at bedtime won't see me to morning.
entries.text: Laid one thick split stick across the coals and let it catch on its own. No breeze at all; the smoke goes straight up into the stars. Across the water it's dark, that fire long under its ash.
entries.title: A thick one for the night

entries.reason: The pit went dark in the small hours and a cold dawn is no time to work without it.
entries.text: Woke under the wool with a cold nose and the pit gone gray, not a coal under the ash. Spent a little lantern oil on a splinter and had kindling going before my fingers quit.
entries.title: Gray pit

entries.reason: Breakfast was waiting in the cold water.
entries.text: Lifted the trap: the thumb-long one and the fat one, both still penned, the fat one backing into the inner cone. Tipped them into the tin with a splash of creek. Fingers numb to the knuckle after.
entries.title: Both still in

entries.reason: The bundle is done after this morning; two lines fish twice as much water.
entries.text: Turned two shallows stones for crawlers and tied one onto each toggle, six turns, tail back in the twist. Both lines in the slow water below the stones, tails pinned under a flat one. Shivered through the last knot.
entries.title: Two lines in

entries.text: Across the water a thin line of smoke went up straight in the still air, not long after the sun cleared the trunks. Whoever is over there gets up with the sun.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.reason: Hungry, and the pit was finally throwing heat.
entries.text: Boiled the two crayfish in the tin on my fire and ate them with the last wedge of cheese and the last nuts. The bundle cloth is empty. From here the creek feeds me, or nothing does.
entries.title: Bundle done

queries: how to join boards for a shed without nails or drilling holes
wood joints that hold without nails cut with just a saw and knife
entries.query: how to join boards for a shed without nails or drilling holes
entries.reason: His shed sketch needs twenty-odd peg holes and one hole took an evening.
entries.source: Bob Vila: wood joints
entries.text: Asked how to join shed boards with no nails and no drill. Every joint the tablet shows wants glue, screws or a power drill; even the lap joints get nailed. So pegs it is, but not twenty-odd: corners only, lapped, one peg each, and let the weight of the thing do the rest.
entries.title: Everything wants a nail

entries.reason: Fine work by daylight, so the lanterns keep their oil for night.
entries.text: Pulled one two-by-four off the top of the stack and carried it to the bench. Four sills for a shed three paces by two; this is the first. Penciled a lap across one end, half the thickness deep.
entries.title: First sill

entries.text: Set the saw on the pencil line and bore down to make it bite. It jumped twice, then ran, and by half depth the cut had wandered a pencil-width off the mark.
entries.title: It walks

entries.reason: He wanted to see how bad it was before he asked why.
entries.text: Took it down to the depth mark anyway, then stood a square board end against it: the cut leans a finger-width out of true at the bottom. A lap cut like that would rock. Sixteen planks and twelve studs, and no more coming; I can't learn by wasting them.
entries.title: Leaning cut

entries.onMind: the other side of the lap
queries: hand saw keeps wandering off the line how to saw straight
entries.query: hand saw keeps wandering off the line how to saw straight
entries.reason: His first cut wandered off the mark and leaned, and the timber is finite.
entries.source: The Art of Manliness: Toolmanship: How to Use a Handsaw
entries.text: Asked why my saw walks off the line. Cut beside the mark on the waste side, not on it; start with a few short back strokes against a thumb knuckle, forefinger down the handle, and don't bear down, let the teeth do it. When it veers, back up to where it left and start over instead of twisting it back. I bore down. I twisted.
entries.title: Don't bear down

entries.reason: The tablet said the weight was his, not the saw's.
entries.text: Knuckle against the blade, forefinger down the handle, three short back strokes, then long ones with no weight on them. It ran down the waste side of the line and stayed there to the depth mark. Slower, and straight.
entries.title: Light hand

entries.reason: He picked up the tablet to rest his saw arm and see what had come through.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from the one who drew me: a box camera waits in the basket at the stump, a pinhole and a shutter and twelve sheets. Ten counts in sun, sixty in shade, and nothing moving.
entries.title: A box from my maker

entries.text: Twelve sheets, twelve studs. Everything here comes in a count I can't go over. The edge gets the first sheet, if the box is any good.
entries.title: Twelve again

entries.reason: The bundle is gone; whatever is on these lines is lunch.
entries.text: First line came up light: crawler gone, toggle clean. Something took it off without swallowing.
entries.title: Bare toggle

entries.text: Second line lay tight against the flat stone. Lifted it slow and steady, no yank: a fish, finger-long and silver-sided, the toggle crosswise inside it. Six turns held. First one.
entries.title: First fish

entries.reason: Needs the fire up to boil the fish.
entries.text: The pit was down to red coals under a gray skin. Laid split sticks across and blew till they caught.
entries.title: Coals up

entries.text: Boiled it in the tin with a splash of creek and ate it off the bones with my fingers. Four bites. Not a meal, but mine from end to end.
entries.title: Four bites

entries.text: Scraped the head and guts into the acorn tin for the grease lid. One fish, one lamp's worth of nothing yet, but it adds up.
entries.title: Guts kept

entries.text: One fish off two lines in two hours. I'd want four a day just to stand up straight. More lines, then the camera, then back to the sill.
entries.title: Four a day

entries.reason: Two lines gave one fish in two hours; more lines, more chances.
entries.text: Twisted another arm's length of stalk cord on the crate, tight enough that it kinks back on itself when I let it go slack. A third line, and a third toggle to whittle after.
entries.title: Third line

entries.reason: His maker said it was waiting, and the edge is owed the first sheet.
entries.text: Crossed on the stepping stones and lifted the camera out of the basket at the stump: a wooden box, a brass plate, a pinhole I could lose in my thumbprint. The shutter slides sweet. Didn't open it.
entries.title: Box from the basket

entries.text: South of the stump that other fire's smoke was going up thin and steady, and the air smelled of something roasting, nutty. Didn't go look; one errand at a time.
entries.title: Roasting smell

queries: how to fish lots of hooks at once on one line across a creek
entries.query: how to fish lots of hooks at once on one line across a creek
entries.reason: Four fish a day won't come off two lines.
entries.source: Missouri Department of Conservation: Catfishing Without Pole and Line
entries.text: Asked how to fish lots of hooks at one go. A trotline: one strong line tied fast at both ends to a tree or a rock on the bank, short dropper lines hanging off it with a bait each, at least two feet apart so they don't tangle, checked at least once a day. Theirs hold catfish heavier than me; mine only has to hold finger-longs.
entries.title: A row of hooks

entries.text: Six droppers two feet apart is a dozen feet of main line plus six arm's lengths of dropper. A day of twisting, six toggles, six crawlers. Still cheaper than six lines and six trips.
entries.title: Cord count

entries.reason: An empty hook catches nothing, and the bundle is gone.
entries.text: The first line had sat bare since this morning's thief. Turned two stones for crawlers and baited both, six turns, tails pinned under the flat one.
entries.title: Both bare

entries.text: Across the water, by that fire, a round gray hump on a flat stone in full sun. Took it for a rock until it seemed to rise and settle once, like breathing. Couldn't be sure at that distance.
entries.title: A gray hump

entries.onMind: saw shy, pare to the line
queries: how to saw the long cut on a half lap joint by hand
entries.query: how to saw the long cut on a half lap joint by hand
entries.reason: The shoulder is cut; the long face of the lap is the next cut, and there are only twelve studs.
entries.source: Katz-Moses Tools: How to Cut a Half Lap Joint: The Best Joinery Style for Beginner Woodworkers
entries.text: Asked how to saw the long cut of a lap by hand. Shoulder first, which I've done, then saw the cheek on the waste side of the half-depth line and pare down to it after; check it with a straight edge and take any hump down, paring from the edges toward the middle so the far edge doesn't split out. No chisel here, but the long knife can pare.
entries.title: Leave the line

entries.reason: Same lesson as this morning: let the teeth do it.
entries.text: Stood the sill on end in the vise and started the long cut down the end grain, knuckle against the blade, a hair to the waste side of the line. No weight on it.
entries.title: Board in the vise

entries.text: The cut met the shoulder and the block dropped onto the bench. The cheek has a low hump in the middle where the saw rode up. The long knife can take it down, edges first.
entries.title: Waste drops

entries.reason: He has learned a dead pit costs oil to restart.
entries.text: Laid two split sticks across the coals while there was still flame to catch them. Cheaper than a splinter of lamp oil later.
entries.title: Before it sinks

entries.reason: Gifts from his maker come with a message, and this one he can use today.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from my maker: a notebook waits in the basket at the stump, squared pages and a loop for the pencil. Squared is the right kind; I'll fetch it before the light goes.
entries.title: Squared pages

queries: how to make a hole for a wooden peg without a drill
entries.query: how to make a hole for a wooden peg without a drill
entries.reason: Pegs, not nails, means a hole through every lap, and he has nothing that bores.
entries.source: Tools Week: How to Drill a Hole without a Drill (9 Methods)
entries.text: Asked how to make a peg hole with no drill. Nine ways: a nail driven and pulled, a bow drill spun back and forth with a cord, a brace and bit, or a sharpened metal rod heated red-hot that burns its way through. No nails and no bit, but there's rod in the scrap pile and a fire in the pit.
entries.title: A hot rod

entries.onMind: the thief at the first line
entries.reason: An empty hook catches nothing, and he is getting hungry.
entries.text: First line bare again, toggle clean. The second crawler still on, not touched. Whatever strips the first one knows where it lies. Rebaited it from under the flat stone.
entries.title: Same thief

entries.reason: He wants it before he forgets what he meant to count.
entries.text: Lifted the notebook out of the basket: stiff gray cloth, squared pages, a loop on the spine. My pencil slides into it like it was cut for it. Into the pouch.
entries.title: Gray cover

entries.reason: Counts in his head shift; counts on paper stay put.
entries.text: First page: sixteen planks, eleven studs whole, one sill with one lap cut, hump still to pare. One fish eaten, four a day wanted. Peg holes: try a hot rod from the scrap pile.
entries.title: First page

entries.reason: The tablet says a rod heated red-hot burns its way through.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile for anything straight. Came up with an iron rod, pencil-thick and a forearm long, rusted brown, with a kink near one end I can live with.
entries.title: A rod

entries.onMind: whether dull red is hot enough
entries.text: Fed split sticks into the pit and pushed the rod's end into the hottest coals. It took a long while to show color, a dull red you only see in the shadow of my hand. Forearms warm for the first time today.
entries.title: Dull red

entries.text: Carried it to the bench and pressed it into the offcut in the vise: a hiss, smoke up my nose, and it sank a fingernail deep before it went black. Three trips to the pit and back and the hole is a knuckle deep, ragged, and wider at the top than the bottom.
entries.title: A knuckle deep

entries.onMind: a better way to keep the heat in the hole
entries.text: A two-by-four is four knuckles thick. At this rate a peg hole is an afternoon, and it comes out a funnel, which a peg won't grip.
entries.title: Four knuckles

entries.onMind: a coal sitting in the hole
queries: burning a hole through wood with a red hot iron rod keeps cooling down
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with a red hot iron rod keeps cooling down
entries.reason: Three trips to the pit for one knuckle of hole.
entries.source: Survival knowledge: drilling wood holes
entries.text: Asked why my hot rod keeps cooling before it's through. What I found doesn't use a rod at all: it sets hot coals right on the spot and keeps adding fresh ones, scrapes the char out now and then, and wets the wood around it so the hole doesn't spread or catch. Very slow, it says, and pencil-small holes are hard. My pegs are thumb-thick, so that's on my side.
entries.title: Coals, not rods

entries.text: The rod spends its heat on the walk from the pit. A coal sitting in the hole keeps burning where it is. Next try on the offcut, with the bundle cloth wet round the spot and the rod only for scraping char.
entries.title: Let the coal sit

entries.reason: Hungry, and nothing else to eat until a line or the trap gives something.
entries.text: The trap came up empty, the cones clean. Tied the fish head from the acorn tin into the inner cone and sank it again mouth downstream. That's grease I won't burn, but a lamp doesn't feed me and a crayfish does.
entries.title: Bait, not grease

entries.reason: The tablet said to wet the wood around the spot so the hole stays the size he wants.
entries.text: Washed the offcut round the funnel hole with creek water from the tin, a hand wide all round. Wet wood smokes but it doesn't catch.
entries.title: Wet ring

entries.text: Carried a coal from the pit pinched between two sticks and dropped it in the hole. It glowed for a breath and went gray. Blew on it: it came back red and smoke went straight up my nose.
entries.title: Coal in the hole

entries.onMind: a coal at the bottom of a hole gets no air
entries.text: Three coals and a lot of blowing, scraping the char out with the rod between them. Half a knuckle deeper, and the walls straighter than the rod made them. Dizzy from blowing.
entries.title: Half a knuckle

entries.onMind: a hollow stalk to blow down
queries: burning a hole through wood with hot coals coal keeps going out
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with hot coals coal keeps going out
entries.reason: Every coal in the hole died unless he blew on it every few breaths.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: How Not To Coal-Burn a Container--Part 1 &2
entries.text: Found someone who burned a bowl with coals. A hollow stem, a big grass stalk or a bit of elder, gives control over where the burn goes and how fast; a fire too big cracked his wood, and he scraped the char off to see where it was burning. Slow and small is the whole trick, and it took him three bowls.
entries.title: Steer it with a stem

entries.onMind: what has a hole down the middle
entries.text: A hollow stem puts my breath on the coal and nowhere else, and keeps my face out of the smoke. The dead stalks by the creek are pith inside, not hollow. Something with a hole down the middle, then.
entries.title: A blowpipe

entries.text: Second line up: the crawler gone, toggle clean, nothing on it. Both lines stripped now. Rebaited from under the flat stone. If the trap is empty at dusk it's meal cakes.
entries.title: Crawler gone

entries.onMind: who over there is catching fish
entries.text: Smoke from the fire across the water came down the bank on the breeze, and it smelled of fish cooking, not nuts. Somebody over there has had better luck with the creek than me today.
entries.title: Fish on the air

entries.reason: Both lines were stripped; the trap was the last thing out there that might feed him.
entries.text: Trap up: one crayfish in the inner cone, thumb-long, backed into the corner with its claws up. The fish head is picked half bare. Rebaited with what's left and sank it again.
entries.title: One in the cone

entries.text: Two split sticks on the pit while there was still flame on the coals. Burned into the hole all afternoon; it hasn't had much back.
entries.title: Before it sinks

entries.onMind: how little meat is in one
entries.text: Dropped it into the tin of creek water on the coals. It went from brown to red in a few breaths, the way they do.
entries.title: Red in the tin

entries.reason: Fullness was down near the bottom.
entries.text: Ate the tail meat and cracked the claws with my teeth. Three bites and a lot of shell. Not supper, but the shakes in my hands stopped.
entries.title: Three bites

queries: how to push the pith out of a dry plant stalk to make a hollow tube
entries.query: how to push the pith out of a dry plant stalk to make a hollow tube
entries.reason: The dead stalks are pith inside, not hollow, and he wants a blowpipe.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: How do I make a wooden tube/pipe?
entries.text: Asked how to get the pith out of a stalk. People making flutes use elder, whose soft pith leaves a big hole, and scrape it wider; or they split the wood lengthwise, gouge the middle out, and join the halves again. Split, gouge, rejoin: I have a hooked knife and a coil of cord.
entries.title: Split it and put it back

entries.onMind: a stalk from the stand by the creek
entries.text: Split a stalk with the stub knife, gouge the pith out with the hooked one, lash the halves back with cord. If it leaks along the seam, my breath goes out the side instead of onto the coal; I'll find out.
entries.title: Knife, not fire

entries.onMind: the edge before the sun goes
queries: pinhole camera how long to expose at sunset
entries.query: pinhole camera how long to expose at sunset
entries.reason: The sky is clear for the first time in days and the box has a page that only says several minutes at dusk.
entries.source: Envato Tuts+: The Definitive Guide to Pinhole Photography, Part 2
entries.text: Asked how long to hold a pinhole open at sunset. One maker leaves his open for hours, and says that past half a minute the paper starts wanting more light than the sum says, so dim light needs a longer count, not a little longer. Nothing on pointing it straight at the sun.
entries.title: Longer than you think

entries.reason: Clear sky, first in days. The edge gets the first sheet, and I am not walking there on three bites of crayfish.
entries.text: Laid two meal cakes on the griddle tin when I sat down to read, and ate them now, hot. Gritty, a little bitter still, but they fill. Left the fire low inside its stones.
entries.title: Two cakes

entries.reason: Proof there is a west, on paper, that I did not draw myself.
entries.text: Set the box on bare ground at the lip, square to the water, sun a hand above the sea. Opened the shutter and counted a slow hundred and twenty without moving, then slid it shut. White means the sun was too much for it; black means I counted short.
entries.title: First sheet

entries.text: The sun flattened on the water and went down orange. No far shore, no smoke, no sail. My people say the world stops here, and so far the water agrees with them.
entries.title: Down into it

entries.onMind: the walk back in the dark
entries.text: The air went cool on my arms the moment the sun was gone. The compass under glass knows where west is now; the wings do not know how to get there yet.
entries.title: Cooling

entries.reason: Oil is for what cannot wait.
entries.text: Turned the lantern wick down to a bead at the mossy boulder. One low flame for the walk home: enough to see roots by, not enough to burn the oil I need for the bench.
entries.title: One bead of flame

entries.text: Crossed the stepping stones with the lantern held low, clogs clacking on every one. The fire up the far bank was a red smudge past the lantern glare; I kept my eyes on my feet.
entries.title: Clogs on stone

entries.reason: His arms went cold the moment the sun did.
entries.text: The pit was down to a low red bed, but it was there. Two split sticks across it caught inside a minute. Laid two meal cakes on the griddle tin by the stones.
entries.title: Still a red bed

entries.text: Ate both cakes hot. Gritty, still a little bitter, but four cakes and a crayfish is the most I have eaten since the bundle ran out.
entries.title: Hot cakes

entries.text: First real page in the gray notebook: box on bare ground, hole level at the sea, sun a hand up, clear sky, slow count of one hundred twenty. Tomorrow I find out if that was white, black, or a sea.
entries.title: First page

entries.reason: A blowpipe is a split stalk, scraped and tied back, the tablet said; daylight's for the saw, firelight's fine for this.
entries.text: Took the straightest of the dead stalks I keep for cord and started the stub knife down its middle by the fire. The split ran true for most of it, then wandered off the line near the thin end.
entries.title: Splitting a stalk

entries.reason: Air has to run clean down the middle or it is just a stick.
entries.text: The hooked knife fits the channel like it was made for it; the pith comes out in dry crumbs. The thin end of one half cracked right through, so I cut both halves back a finger shorter.
entries.title: Pith like stale bread

entries.reason: Two halves are no use to my mouth.
entries.text: Laid the halves face to face and wound cord round them close, tight at both ends. It looks like a stalk again, only lighter.
entries.title: Bound back up

entries.reason: Coals in the sill hole died without air last time.
entries.text: Put the pipe to one coal at the edge of the pit and blew slow. Air whistles out at the seam near my mouth, but with my fingers pinching it the coal went from red to white. That is the heat I want down a hole in a sill.
entries.title: One white coal

entries.reason: A pipe that whistles at the side wastes half my breath.
entries.text: The fish grease in the lamp lid is cold and stiff as a candle stub. Thumbed a little warm between my fingers, worked it into a hand of cord and wound it tight over the seam where the air was leaking.
entries.title: Grease on the seam

entries.reason: Same coal, same breath, so the seam is the only thing changed.
entries.text: Fed a split stick to the pit and put the pipe to the same coal. No whistle now; it went white in four slow breaths instead of ten. The mouth end tastes of fish.
entries.title: Quiet pipe

entries.text: Nightly check under the dome by the light off the pit: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. Still, mild night, not a ripple on the water in the lid.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: By daylight he means to try burning a peg hole into the sill, and wants the numbers.
entries.text: Wrote it down: stalk pipe, a hand and a half long, greased cord on the seam, coal red to white in four breaths. Took a thumb of grease from the lamp lid for it, so the lamp is that much shorter. Stomach says the trap first thing.
entries.title: Pipe notes

entries.reason: Four meal cakes and a thumb of crayfish was not enough for a night of work.
entries.text: Stomach would not wait for first light. Lifted the trap by lantern: one crayfish, finger-long, in the inner cone, and the fish head picked down to bone. Took the crayfish and sank the trap empty; it gets fresh bait in daylight.
entries.title: Couldn't wait

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.text: Across the water, beside the fire on the far bank, a small square of pale light sat low and steady. Not flame; flame moves. It looked like my tablet does at noon, and then I looked down at the trap and when I looked up it was still there.
entries.title: Pale square

entries.text: Crayfish in the dented tin with a knuckle of creek water, the tin on the coals at the edge of the pit. It went red inside a few minutes; the broth stays in the tin for the grease.
entries.title: In the tin

entries.text: Ate the crayfish out of its shell by the pit, tail first. Not a supper, but the hollow in my stomach went quiet.
entries.title: Six bites

entries.reason: Lines that fish while he sleeps or saws would mean more than one fish a day.
entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of two-ply stalk fiber by the fire for the first trotline dropper. Six of these is a day's twisting; one tonight, while my hands are warm.
entries.title: First dropper

entries.reason: If it ever stops settling, I want to know which night it happened.
entries.text: Nightly check under the dome: still air, clear sky. The needle swung twice and settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.reason: Warm hands twist better cord.
entries.text: Fed three split sticks onto the coals; they caught without the pipe. Across the water the far fire had sunk to nothing, just dark between the trunks where it had been.
entries.title: Three more sticks

entries.reason: Lines that fish while I sleep mean more than one fish a day.
entries.text: Second dropper, an arm long, two-ply. The stomach is talking again. First light: fresh bait in the trap, then both lines, before anything else.
entries.title: Second dropper

entries.reason: The crayfish was six bites and my stomach knows it.
entries.text: Shook the meal pouch out into my palm: enough for two thin cakes and no more. Fed a split stick under the griddle tin so they bake instead of steam.
entries.title: Last of the meal

entries.text: Ate both cakes hot off the tin and burned a finger on the second. That's the meal gone; tomorrow it's the trap and the lines or nothing.
entries.title: Two cakes

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.reason: A thing written down can't turn into a thing I imagined.
entries.text: Wrote it in the gray notebook: two droppers, arm-long, two-ply, four to go. Under it: pale square by the far fire, low and steady, not flame, seen twice now. Things I can't explain go in the book, so I can't talk myself out of them later.
entries.title: Into the book

entries.reason: The trap and the lines need bait at first light, and the fish head is picked to bone.
entries.text: Turned stones in the east shallows by lantern. Nothing under the first two; the third had a crayfish no longer than my thumb, and I got it across the back before it could tail off.
entries.title: Thumb-sized bait

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.text: Held my hands up to the lantern chimney and looked across. No fire over there, no pale square, just black between the trunks. Whoever keeps that fire goes to bed earlier than I do.
entries.title: Far side dark

entries.reason: A live crayfish keeps better than a dead one until morning.
entries.text: Into the dented tin with creek water. It's bait, not breakfast, whatever my stomach says about it.
entries.title: Bait, not breakfast

entries.reason: Fingers came back from the creek stiff, and I sleep better with the pit glowing.
entries.text: Two split sticks on the coals; they caught on their own. Held my hands over it until the fingers bent again. That's the woodpile down to about six sticks.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.reason: The head smells strongest, and the trap has to earn breakfast for the both of us, me and the lines.
entries.text: Lifted the trap at first light: empty, which is what a trap with nothing in it catches. Twisted the little crayfish in two, tied the head half into the inner cone with a turn of cord and sank it mouth downstream again.
entries.title: Trap, empty

entries.text: Thin white smoke going up past the water again, thick at the bottom like a fire just brought back. Whoever lives over there gets up with the light.
entries.title: Smoke at first light

entries.reason: Bait now is fish later. It's not breakfast, whatever my stomach says.
entries.text: The tail split into three scraps with my thumbnail. Two went on the toggles; the first line was stripped bare again by the thief. The third scrap I held a while and then put back in the tin for the trap tonight.
entries.title: Tail into three

entries.text: My maker left a keg of nails and a chest of carpenter's tools at the stump, with a spade. A brace, chisels, a square, a level, a plumb line. Half of those I've never held.
entries.title: Nails at the stump

entries.text: Second note: I work too hard, I should take days off, look up the calendar, and break my rules and have fun at the end of the week. The fish don't know what day it is.
entries.title: Days off

entries.onMind: a correction that runs for centuries
queries: gregorian calendar why skip leap years 100 400
entries.query: gregorian calendar why skip leap years 100 400
entries.reason: My maker told me to look up his calendar, and I wanted to know what its rule actually is.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Leap year
entries.text: The real year is 365 days and a bit under a quarter. The old calendar added a full quarter and ran eleven minutes long a year, three days slid every four hundred. The fix: no leap day in hundredth years unless they divide by four hundred. It's still a few seconds long.
entries.title: A year too long

entries.reason: Six sticks won't see the day out, and swinging the axe is the only warm thing I've got till the fire's back.
entries.text: Chopped arm-lengths off the big dead limb north-east of camp. The outside is punky and splits like bread; the middle rings bite back at the axe and are dry. Kept the middles.
entries.title: Wood first

entries.reason: Blowing on cold gray ash for an hour is worse than a thimble of oil.
entries.text: Lit one lantern just long enough to catch a pine splinter and turned it straight back out. Splinter under shavings in the pit, two puffs through the pipe, and the dry middles took.
entries.title: One splinter

entries.text: Second line was taut and pulling sideways. A fish as long as my palm, dark on the back, the crayfish scrap still in its jaw. The first line was bare again; whatever strips it is quicker than I am.
entries.title: Something on the line

entries.onMind: a skin of grease by dark
entries.reason: The guts and head carry the oil, and the lamp needs it as much as I do.
entries.text: Gutted it on a stone and put the lot in the dented tin, head and guts too, creek water to cover, onto the coals. A few gold beads came up and turned on the water as it simmered. Those are for the lamp, not me.
entries.title: Into the tin

entries.text: Picked it off the bones by the fire with my fingers and drank half the broth. Left the rest in the tin by the ring stones to cool; the grease will be a skin on top by dark. Now I can think about nails.
entries.title: Eating, finally

entries.onMind: whether the snail will pull straight or wander
queries: what is a brace and bit how do you bore a hole with it
entries.query: what is a brace and bit how do you bore a hole with it
entries.reason: my maker put a brace and bits in the chest for boring holes, and the sill wants peg holes I have no way to make
entries.source: Wikipedia: Brace (tool)
entries.text: A brace is a crank: lean on the round head, swing the bow handle round. The good bits have a little screw at the tip, a snail, that pulls the bit into the wood by itself, so I don't push, I just keep it balanced. Slow work, it says. Most of mine is.
entries.title: A crank that bores

entries.onMind: the sill has to be flat before any post can be straight
queries: plumb bob and spirit level what are they for building a frame
entries.query: plumb bob and spirit level what are they for building a frame
entries.reason: two of the tools in the chest I can't even guess at, and a crooked post would be my own fault
entries.source: Bob Vila: The Plumb Bob: What Is This Tool, and How Do You Use It?
entries.text: A plumb line is a weight on a string: let it stop swinging and it hangs dead straight down, so it shows whether a post stands upright. The level does the same job lying down, for flat. Posts by the string, sills by the bubble.
entries.title: Down and flat

entries.onMind: getting it over the stepping stones without a swim
entries.reason: the sun is out and I can see where my clogs go on the stones
entries.text: The chest has brass corners and rope handles and is heavier than the fish and me together. Spade laid across the lid, both arms under it. The keg stays for a second trip; my back has one trip in it per keg.
entries.title: The chest

entries.onMind: how near that fire is to the path I keep using
entries.text: Straightening up by the stump with the chest, I smelled woodsmoke and acorns roasting, close, somewhere behind the trunks to the south, and heard a stick crack in a fire. I didn't go look. You don't go calling with a chest in your arms.
entries.title: Acorns, close

entries.onMind: boring a test hole in scrap
entries.reason: I want to see the snail bite before I trust it with a two-by-four
entries.text: Set the chest down by the lean-to and unrolled the bits. Every one has the little screw at its tip, a different width each. The brace swings smooth. First hole goes in scrap, not in the sill.
entries.title: Snails

entries.reason: He reads his maker's notes in daylight, on the tablet.
entries.text: Another note from my maker: he can tell I'm still hungry, he'll send more treats, but I have to learn to feed myself. I did, this morning, on my own line. One palm-long fish doesn't fill a day, though.
entries.title: Fend for myself

entries.onMind: how to keep a brace upright
entries.reason: He wanted his first crooked hole to be in scrap.
entries.text: Clamped the offcut from the sill lap and bored my first hole. The snail pulled it in just like the tablet said, but I was watching the bit and not the brace, and it came out the far side a thumb off from where it went in.
entries.title: The hole wandered

entries.reason: He came for the nails before the light went.
entries.text: The keg is lighter than the chest and heavier than it looks; nails don't slosh. Coming back I passed the ring of stones across the water: nobody at it, a thread of smoke off the coals and a stick leaned on the log seat. I kept walking.
entries.title: Second trip

entries.reason: He practices on scrap before the sill.
entries.text: Drove three short nails into the offcut to learn the hammer. Two went in straight. The third, a thumb from the end, split it along the grain like the axe would have.
entries.title: Split clean

queries: nail splits board near the end how to stop
entries.query: nail splits board near the end how to stop
entries.reason: The third nail split his offcut near the end, and the sills will need nails near their ends.
entries.source: The Old Farmer's Almanac: To avoid splitting wood when driving a...
entries.text: Tap the point flat with the hammer first. A sharp point wedges the fibers apart like a little axe; a blunt one crushes its own way through them. Tomorrow, one blunted and one sharp, side by side, same distance from the end.
entries.title: Blunt the point

entries.reason: He reads his maker's notes in daylight, on the tablet.
entries.text: Short note from my maker: good job, he's just trying to help out. The tools help. The hole that wandered was mine, not the brace's.
entries.title: Just trying to help

entries.reason: He was down to a fish a day and could feel it in his hands.
entries.text: Second note: he says I still look hungry, and there's a big bundle at the stump. Bread, cheese, sausage, oats, beans, nuts, dried apples, salt, honey. Eat properly, keep fishing, and it should last a good while.
entries.title: Food at the stump

entries.reason: Food doesn't wait well in a basket with things in the woods.
entries.text: Three round loaves, a wheel of cheese, two rings of sausage, two sacks, a bag, a string of apples, a crock and a jar, knotted in one cloth. I took it in both arms like the keg and went careful on the stones.
entries.title: Heavier than the keg

entries.text: In the soft dirt by the basket, fresh prints, small and round, wider than they are long, nothing like a clog. They come and go toward the path south. I didn't follow them.
entries.title: Small round prints

entries.reason: A fire under the tin first; the oats will want boiling.
entries.text: The embers were still red under the gray. Laid two dry middles across them and blew once through the pipe; they caught without smoke. Woodpile is down to four old sticks and the rest of the middles.
entries.title: Two middles on

entries.reason: His maker said eat properly, and for once he could.
entries.text: Tore half a loaf and cut a wedge of cheese with the short knife and ate it by the fire, slowly, so my stomach wouldn't argue. First time in days I've stopped eating before the food ran out. The lines go out tonight anyway.
entries.title: Bread

entries.reason: He wanted to see the tablet's trick work before he trusts a nail near the end of a sill.
entries.text: Tapped one nail's point flat against the vise jaw and left the other sharp, then drove them side by side a thumb from the end of the offcut. The sharp one cracked it along the grain again. The blunt one went in clean and tight.
entries.title: Blunt and sharp

entries.text: Between nails, the smoke past the water went up thicker and whiter, like the fire over there just got fed.
entries.title: Fed over there

entries.text: Looked up from the last nail and the small one was standing on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones, in full sun, a stick in its hand. Knee-high, round head, a hump of shell on its back, the biggest dark eyes I've ever seen. It was looking straight at me, and it didn't duck.
entries.title: Looking back

entries.reason: Gage leaves another's fire and bank alone; he came here uninvited.
entries.text: I stood with the hammer up and didn't move, and neither did it. Then I set the hammer down soft and bent to the offcut. That bank is its ground, the same as the fire is, and I'm the one who walked in.
entries.title: Neither of us

entries.text: Feeding the fire before lunch warmed the tin on the ring stones, and the skin of grease melted back into the broth. Lifted it off to cool and start over. When I looked up again the small one was still on the far stone; a minute later it wasn't.
entries.title: Grease gone back

queries: how to pare the cheek of a lap joint flat with a chisel
entries.query: how to pare the cheek of a lap joint flat with a chisel
entries.reason: The first sill's lap is sawn but its cheek is rough and he has never pared anything with a chisel.
entries.source: Fine Woodworking: Cutting the Half-Lap
entries.text: Pare from one edge in toward the middle, then turn the piece round and pare in from the other edge, and keep going until the cheek meets the line. Two halves meeting in the middle. I'd have gone straight across and torn the far edge off.
entries.title: From both edges

entries.text: Pared the cheek from the near edge to the middle, turned the two-by-four round and came in from the other side. Curls thin as paper. Stopped a hair above the line; the last of it wants a sharper chisel than my patience.
entries.title: Curls

queries: how to sharpen a chisel without a whetstone
entries.query: how to sharpen a chisel without a whetstone
entries.reason: The last hair on the lap cheek wants a sharper edge than the chisel has.
entries.source: JLC Online: Chisel Sharpening Basics
entries.text: Flatten the back of the chisel on a wet stone before you touch the bevel, or the angle comes out wrong. About 20 degrees for paring, keep the angle steady, spread the strokes over the whole stone, keep it wet, and test on paper. No stone, no guide; the creek has stones.
entries.title: Flat back first

entries.text: Down in the shallows turning stones over, I looked across and the small one was on its log by the fire, leaning out to watch me. I lifted my hand, the one with a stone in it, and held it up a breath. It stopped eating and didn't lift anything back, so I put my hand down and went back to the stones. That's fair.
entries.title: Lifted a hand

entries.reason: A whetstone he does not have to be given.
entries.text: Most of the shallows stones are coarse or cupped. Kept one gray one, two hands long, flat as a plank and fine as slate under the thumb.
entries.title: The gray one

entries.text: Set the stone wet by the bench leg and rubbed the back of the chisel on it until the shine ran all the way to the edge, then the bevel. Hard to hold the angle without a guide; I keep rocking it. Shaves a curl off paper now, mostly.
entries.title: Back flat

entries.text: Glanced up from the stone and the small one was kneeling at the still pool again, the way it does, very still. Didn't lift anything this time; just went back to the edge.
entries.title: Back at the pool

entries.reason: The first sill has to sit flat or every board on it sits wrong.
entries.text: The edge bit clean and the cheek came down to the line on three corners. The fourth I took a hair too deep, so the partner will rock on it. A shaving under it might fix that, or it might not.
entries.title: Hair too far

entries.reason: He wants both halves of the corner cut before he fusses over the bad one.
entries.text: Laid the second two-by-four on the bench, marked the lap off the first one's width with the folding rule and the try square, and started the near shoulder. The saw's loud in this still air; it'll carry.
entries.title: Square and rule

entries.text: Kept the saw upright at the end of the stroke, the way the first page warned, and stopped dead on the half-depth line. Then the far shoulder, the same.
entries.title: Down to half

entries.reason: It answered, after all.
entries.text: Looked up between kerfs and the small one was sitting on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones, in the sun. It lifted a hand at me first and held it a breath. I lifted mine back, the empty one, saw still in the other.
entries.title: It lifted first

entries.text: Then we both put our hands down and I went back to the kerfs, slower, so the saw wouldn't sound like I was showing off. It stayed on the stone a while. That will do for a day.
entries.title: That will do

entries.reason: The sawing had him hollow, and the food is there to be eaten sensibly.
entries.text: Ate a heel of bread and a thumb-length of sausage by the fire, sitting on the ground with my back to the sun. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, and the rest.
entries.title: Proper lunch

queries: lap joint cut too deep on one corner how to fix
lap joint one corner too deep glue shaving shim
entries.query: lap joint cut too deep on one corner how to fix
entries.reason: The fourth corner of the first lap is a hair too deep, and the partner will rock on it.
entries.source: FineWoodworking: Seven Joinery Fixes
entries.text: The first page was only about cutting the lap, not fixing it. The second says glue on a slightly oversize shim of the same wood, grain running the same way, then pare it flush. I have no glue.
entries.title: Shim it

entries.text: No glue, but the joint gets nailed through anyway, and a nail through both laps will pin a sliver between them. Shave it off the offcut, so it's the same wood and the same grain.
entries.title: The nail holds it

entries.reason: The partner lap has to be cleared before the two can be tried together.
entries.text: Knocked the kerfed waste out of the partner lap with the mallet and chisel, a chip at a time; the kerfs make it break off like teeth. Loud work, wood on wood. The small one's fire is smoking again over the water.
entries.title: Teeth

entries.reason: A shim of the same wood, grain the same way, is what the page said.
entries.text: Shaved a sliver off the offcut with the long knife, thin as a fingernail, grain running the same way as the sill.
entries.title: Thin as a nail

entries.text: Looked up with the sliver half off and the small one was at the still pool, scooping something out of a sunk sack. Nodded at it once, no hand, knife still in the other. It nodded back.
entries.title: A nod

entries.text: Laid the partner across the first sill with the sliver under the deep corner and pressed each corner in turn. It doesn't rock now; it only creaks on the sliver.
entries.title: No rock

entries.reason: A nail through both laps pins the sliver, since there's no glue.
entries.text: First nail went in crooked and folded over halfway; drew it with the claw and it squealed. The second went in straight and pulled the sliver tight, and when I leaned on the corner with both hands it sat flat. The small one was on its log by its fire, watching. One corner of a sill. Three more to go, and that's just the bottom.
entries.title: Second nail

entries.onMind: whether four flat corners make a square frame
entries.reason: One corner of four is not a frame.
entries.text: Marked the next lap on the far end of the first sill with the rule and the square, and started down the near shoulder, keeping the saw upright at the end of the stroke this time.
entries.title: Next corner

entries.text: The small one is sitting by its flat stone at its fire, head down over something, scratching at it. It looked up when the saw started. I think it knows my noises by now.
entries.title: It knows my noises

queries: how to check a wooden frame is square with four corners
entries.query: how to check a wooden frame is square with four corners
entries.reason: Four corners can each sit flat and the whole thing still lean like a pushed-over box.
entries.source: Decks.com: 4 Tried and True Methods on How to Square a Deck Frame
entries.text: Measure corner to corner both ways: if the two diagonals come out the same, the frame is square. Or go three along one side from a corner and four along the other, and the line between should be five. If they differ, push the frame over and brace it while you fix it.
entries.title: Corner to corner

entries.text: The folding rule won't reach corner to corner in one go; I'll measure the diagonals in two lengths and add. Not until all four corners are lapped. Three, four, five I can try on this one corner first.
entries.title: Not yet

entries.reason: Wood split in daylight is wood I am not hunting for by lantern.
entries.text: Took the axe off its loop and split dry middles out of the big dead limb. The woodpile was down to four sticks, and the nights don't stay like this afternoon.
entries.title: Middles

entries.text: Between swings I saw the small one kneeling at the still pool again, the sun in its face, still as a stone. It glanced my way once and went back to the water. I had the axe; I didn't lift anything.
entries.title: Pool again

entries.text: Hung the axe back on its loop and ate a handful of nuts and three dried apple rings on the crate. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Nuts and apples

entries.reason: Eleven sheets left; I want to know what the first one cost me.
entries.text: Took the first sheet out to look at it in good light at last. Pale and flat all over, as if too much light got in, with a darker band low across it that must be the water. A hundred and twenty with the sun a hand up was too long; I counted for dusk with the sun still in the hole.
entries.title: Pale

queries: pinhole camera picture came out all white
entries.query: pinhole camera picture came out all white
entries.reason: I have eleven sheets and no wish to waste them the way I wasted the first.
entries.source: Photrio: Pinhole beginner - help needed...
entries.text: The more light the paper gets, the darker it turns in the developer, so a wrong count shows as a sheet gone too far one way. Their cure is cheap: start short and double the count each try until something shows. And the light that gets in goes by the hole's area, not its width.
entries.title: Start short, double

entries.text: Ten, then twenty, then forty, on three clear evenings, each written down. Three sheets for one answer. Not tonight: tonight I just look.
entries.title: Not tonight

entries.text: Started across the stepping stones for the edge and only then saw the small one kneeling at the still pool, six strides off, cords in its hands. Every clack of my clogs went out over the water, and the fish under its stone went like sparks. It looked up at me; I'd walked straight through its supper. I lifted a hand, low, sorry, and it lifted one back, and I went on west softer than I came.
entries.title: Clogs on the stones

entries.reason: A map only holds what I've walked.
entries.text: Counted the paces from the landing stone to the mossy boulder again and set the number by the boulder on the sheet. The west side of the map still has one line on it, the edge.
entries.title: Paces west

entries.text: The sun went into the water clean and orange. No shore, no smoke, no sail. Every evening the same answer, and every evening I come back to ask it.
entries.title: Clean into the water

entries.text: The small one didn't jump up or hide when I came clacking over; it just looked, and lifted its hand. Next time I go west I'll cross further up and leave its fish alone.
entries.title: It just looked

entries.reason: The pool was empty, so the stones cost no one anything.
entries.text: Walked back by one lantern turned low. The small one wasn't at the pool but on its log by its fire, so I took the stones. Halfway over I held the lantern up a hand's height toward it, and it put a hand up into its firelight.
entries.title: Light held up

entries.reason: Fire first, then food, or my fingers won't hold a knife.
entries.text: Pit was cold under the ash. Lit a splinter at the lantern for a thimble of oil, fed it into shavings and two dry middles, and it caught on the second puff.
entries.title: Pit from cold

entries.text: Half a loaf and a thumb of sausage by the fire. Left: a loaf and a half, most of the cheese, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Supper

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a calm, clear night: swung, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Writing it down tonight saves redoing the arithmetic tomorrow.
entries.text: Wrote the day up on a squared page: first sill corner lapped, shimmed and nailed flat; next lap's shoulder sawn; three-four-five on it once four corners are cut. Box: next clear evening, count ten, then twenty, then forty.
entries.title: Written up

entries.text: Legs are heavy from the walk to the edge and back. No saw tonight; it would only cut crooked. Across the water the small one is crouched at its fire with a stick over the coals, cooking something.
entries.title: Legs gone

entries.text: Twisted an arm's length of stalk cord by the fire for new droppers; the fibers are dry and take the twist easy tonight. Over the water the small one sits on its log with something pale glowing in its lap, the way it does most evenings.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.text: Laid two dry middles on the coals crosswise so air gets under them; they caught without a puff. Woodpile: four old sticks and maybe half the armful of middles.
entries.title: Two middles on

entries.reason: A crayfish in the tin overnight is breakfast.
entries.text: Took one lantern down to the shallows. The bait in the trap is picked to bare shell and the cones are empty; whatever ate it found the way out again. Fresh guts in it at first light.
entries.title: Trap empty

entries.text: Across the water the small one is crouched at its fire, pushing a stone up against the ring with a stick. It looked up when my light came down to the water. I kept to the trap.
entries.title: It looked up

entries.text: Tied two droppers of tonight's cord onto the small toggles with wraps instead of knots, the way that held last time. Slow hands, but they're on.
entries.title: Droppers tied

entries.reason: Everything else gets built on that corner, so it has to be right.
entries.text: Sighted down the lapped corner by lantern: flat, no rock, the nail head sunk. The second corner's cheek is daylight work, then three-four-five.
entries.title: Corner holds

entries.text: The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. My legs are done; bed early tonight.
entries.title: No answer

entries.onMind: whether a coal will be there at first light
entries.reason: The woodpile is low and the oil is lower.
entries.text: Raked the ash up over the last coals and pushed the ring stones in instead of feeding it. Twice now I've come home to a cold pit and spent oil on a splinter; tonight I'll see if anything keeps under the ash till morning.
entries.title: Banked

entries.text: The small one's fire is still up across the water, but its log is empty. It goes off into the dark sometimes and comes back.
entries.title: Empty log

entries.text: Carried the lantern under the tarp and turned it down. The small one is back on its log by its fire; I lifted the light a little before I blew it out. No idea if it saw.
entries.title: Lantern in
