entries.reason: to see if banking keeps a coal till morning
entries.text: Raked the ash open and near the bottom found one coal the size of a pea, still red. Shavings on it, one puff of the pipe, and it caught. Not a drop of oil spent.
entries.title: A coal kept

entries.onMind: the small one keeps early hours
entries.text: The fog's lifting off the water. A thin smoke is already going up from the small one's fire over there; it was up before me.
entries.title: Smoke across

entries.text: My maker asked who Brace is. Told him it isn't a who: it's the crank in the chest that turns a bit into wood, and my first hole went in crooked because I didn't hold it straight.
entries.title: Note from my maker

entries.reason: real food before real work
entries.text: Half a loaf and a wedge of cheese by the fire, sitting down for it. Across the water the small one came down to the pool with the fog gone off it and knelt there in the sun; it looked over at me eating and didn't duck.
entries.title: Breakfast by the fire

entries.reason: its fish, not my corner
entries.text: A dozen strokes into the second lap and the small one's head came up at the pool. Last time my clogs sent its fish under the stone. Laid the saw down on the bench; the cheek can wait till the pool's empty.
entries.title: Saw down

entries.reason: quiet work that still moves the frame on
entries.text: Folding rule on the lapped corner: three along one sill, four along the other, and the long side between them came out five and a thumbnail. Not square. Either the lap's cut off true or I marked the three short.
entries.title: Three, four, five-ish

queries: how deep to bury coals in ash to keep a fire overnight
entries.query: how deep to bury coals in ash to keep a fire overnight
entries.reason: one coal the size of a pea kept last night, and I want more than one
entries.source: AllOutdoor: How to Bank a Fire
entries.text: Asked how deep the ash goes over the coals to keep a fire overnight. No number: burn it down to coals, set the half-burned sticks aside for morning, and heap every bit of ash you have over the coals. Depth is trial and error. Tonight it gets all the ash and the half-burned sticks go by the ring.
entries.title: How deep to bank

entries.text: Looked up from the tablet and the pool's empty; the small one is back crouched at its own fire. The saw can go again.
entries.title: Pool's empty

entries.reason: He'd waited for its fish to finish; now the cut could go on.
entries.text: Back on the second cheek with the pool empty. Between strokes I looked over and the small one on its log put its hand up at me, plain in the sun this time, not firelight. Lifted mine off the saw back at it and went on cutting.
entries.title: Hand across

entries.reason: Wanted to know which of the two mistakes it was before fixing anything.
entries.text: Try square in the inside of the first corner: the blade stands off the far sill a hair at the tip. The laps sit flat and tight, so the cut's fine. The whole corner's just swung a little open on its one nail.
entries.title: Swung, not cut

queries: 3 4 5 came out long how to tell which side of the corner is off
entries.query: 3 4 5 came out long how to tell which side of the corner is off
entries.reason: The corner measures a thumbnail over and he didn't know which way to move it.
entries.source: Concord Carpenter: The 3-4-5 Method For Squaring Corners
entries.text: Asked what it means when the five comes out long. You move one leg in or out until the long side reads five on the dot, and on a whole frame you push the long diagonal's corners toward each other. So one nail is a hinge: swing the four-side in a thumbnail, then nail it again.
entries.title: Long side long

entries.reason: Square first, then fasten.
entries.text: Rule hooked at the three mark, I swung the far end of the four-side in on the one nail, a hair at a time, till the long side read five on the dot.
entries.title: Five on the dot

entries.reason: One nail is a hinge; two hold.
entries.text: Drove a second nail beside the first, and the five still reads true after. First corner's square. Glanced over once; the small one was sitting still on a flat stone by its fire with the sun on its back.
entries.title: Second nail

entries.reason: A bowed sill would throw the whole frame out no matter how square the corners are.
entries.text: Sighted down three two-by-fours off the stack before taking one: the first has a bow you could roll a pencil under, the second a quarter twist. The third runs true. That's the third sill.
entries.title: A straight one

entries.onMind: whether it minds the noise when it isn't fishing
entries.reason: The second corner needs both halves of its lap before anything gets nailed.
entries.text: Marked the lap off the third sill with the try square and started the shoulder. Between strokes I saw the small one under the big trunk north of its fire, picking up sticks, and it stood and watched me a while. Nobody at the pool, so the saw kept going.
entries.title: Third sill

entries.onMind: two fists of oats, four of water
queries: how much water to cook oats in a tin over a fire
entries.query: how much water to cook oats in a tin over a fire
entries.reason: The bundle's oats sack is still full, and he doesn't want to burn a whole meal finding out.
entries.source: Frugal Campasaurus: Campfire Oatmeal: An Easy Pantry Breakfast
entries.text: Asked how much water oats want in a tin over a fire. About twice the water to the oats, heated first, then five minutes or so of stirring once it bubbles, moving the tin about so it doesn't catch. Never boiled a grain in my life.
entries.title: Oats

entries.reason: A hot meal now keeps the bread and cheese for later.
entries.text: Fire was down to embers; two dry middles went on and caught without smoke. Two fists of oats, four of water and a pinch of salt in the tin on the ring stones. Across the water the small one is back on its log with its head bent over something in its lap.
entries.title: Oats on

entries.onMind: stir all the way to the bottom next time
entries.reason: a proper hot meal keeps the bread and cheese for later
entries.text: The oats came out thick and caught on the bottom where I stopped stirring. Ate every bit with a dried apple torn into it; best hot thing since I got here. The small one has come down and is kneeling at the pool, so the saw stays on the bench.
entries.title: First oats

entries.reason: marking makes no noise, sawing does
entries.text: Try square across the end of the third sill, sighting the cheek line along the blade: quiet work. Over the water the small one has something laid flat in the pool and hasn't moved in minutes.
entries.title: Cheek line

entries.onMind: it fishes better than my first line did
entries.text: It lifted straight up out of the pool and there was a fish flipping in its net, a finger and a half long. It stood with it and looked right over at me. I dipped my head at it before I'd thought about it.
entries.title: A fish in the net

entries.reason: the pool's empty, so the noise frightens nothing
entries.text: The small one is back at its fire with a stick over the coals, so the saw went on. Cheek of the third sill's lap, down to the line on both faces and not past it.
entries.title: Cheek sawn

entries.reason: on the first corner one nail let it swing true; two would have fixed it crooked
entries.text: Laid the third sill's lap over the far end of the first, snug, shoulder against shoulder, and turned it to the try square. One nail only, same as last time. Across the water the small one is on its log with its slate up.
entries.title: One nail

entries.text: Stood up from the nail and looked over without meaning to. The small one was crouched at its leaf heap with something wriggling in its hand, and it dipped its head at me, slow and deliberate, like it had thought about it. I stood there like a post, then dipped mine again.
entries.title: It nodded back

entries.reason: three along, four along, five across, or it isn't square
entries.text: Three along one sill, four along the other: across it read five and a finger long. Swung the far end in on the nail until the rule read five on the dot, then drove the second nail beside the first. Two corners square, and this one I got right without the tablet.
entries.title: Second corner square

queries: what to put under wood sill so it doesnt sit on wet ground
shed floor frame on flat stones instead of concrete blocks
entries.query: what to put under wood sill so it doesnt sit on wet ground
entries.reason: Two square corners are no good if the timber sits in the dirt and rots, and this ground was soaked a few days ago.
entries.source: Fine Homebuilding: Building a Shed? Get the Site, Footings, and Floor Frame Right
entries.text: Asked what to put under a sill so it doesn't sit on wet ground. They dig off the soft topsoil, lay a few inches of coarse gravel so water can't creep up into the wood, and set solid blocks under the frame, two or three high at most. I have no blocks, but I have a whole creek of stones.
entries.title: Off the wet ground

entries.text: So before the frame goes down: scrape the spot to hard ground, a bed of creek gravel, and a flat stone under every corner. The creek's right there, but so is the small one's pool. I'll take my stones from my own bank.
entries.title: Stones, not dirt

entries.reason: a stone in the wrong place is a carry wasted
entries.text: Drew the three sills on the map sheet as a square with one side still open, and put a dot at every corner where a stone goes. Four dots: four stones flat on both faces, or near enough.
entries.title: Four dots

entries.reason: I said I'd take my stones from my own bank, and this is my bank
entries.text: Down in my own shallows lifting flat stones, and the small one is at its pool, not six strides off across the water, scooping something out of a sunk sack. It didn't leave when I came down. So I didn't either.
entries.title: Both at the water

entries.text: Every stone I set on the pile clacks, and the fish under its side scatter and come back. It looked up at the noise and I held still with a stone in both hands. No nod either way, just a look, and then we both went back to work. Seven stones, two flat on both faces.
entries.title: Clack

entries.reason: a corner that rocks on its stone will throw the square I worked for
entries.text: Sighting across each stone beside the heap. Two sit dead flat, one rocks on a hump, one will do with a bed of gravel under it. That's three; the fourth corner wants one more trip.
entries.title: Flattest faces

entries.reason: the last corner wants a stone
entries.text: Back down to my shallows for one more, and found it under the second riffle: flat on both faces, a hand thick. The small one was on its log by its fire with a stick over the coals, something roasting; I could smell it across the water. It looked up when the stone clacked. I didn't stop, and neither did it.
entries.title: Fourth stone

queries: spirit level how to read the bubble
entries.query: spirit level how to read the bubble
entries.reason: There's a glass tube with a bubble in it in the chest and I've never once used it; if the sills sit on stones, the stones have to sit flat.
entries.source: Hunker: How To Read A Bubble Level
entries.text: Asked the tablet how to read the bubble in the long tool from the chest. Lay its edge flat, let the bubble settle, look at it with your eye level: between the two lines is level, nearer one line means that end sits high. Turn it end for end and the bubble should land in the same spot, or the tool itself is lying.
entries.title: The bubble tool

entries.text: The page only says lay it along. But a stone can sit level one way and tip the other, so every stone gets it twice, along and across. First I'll turn the tool end for end and see if it lies.
entries.title: Both ways

entries.text: Turned it end for end on the flattest stone: same spot both ways, so it tells the truth. Two stones read between the lines along and across, and the new one from the riffle sits true both ways. The rocker sends the bubble half out; it goes back to the creek. Three level and one to bed in gravel: that's four.
entries.title: Bubble says

entries.reason: Gravel's heavy work and the walk west is after it.
entries.text: A heel off the loaf and a wedge of cheese on the crate, slow, before the gravel. Across the water the small one is under the big trunk north of its fire again, bending for sticks; it saw me eating and went on picking. Left: a loaf less a heel, the cheese less three wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey.
entries.title: Heel and wedge

entries.reason: The stones want a bed of gravel under them, and its fish don't want my noise.
entries.text: Down for gravel, and the small one is kneeling at its pool washing its hands; the water goes brown round them. Took the top end of my shallows, the farthest from it, and scraped up by the handful instead of tossing stones on a pile.
entries.title: Gravel, quiet

entries.text: Its fish stayed out the whole time, holding behind its big stone. It stayed too, crouched where I could see it, not hurrying. That's twice today we've both stayed. The gravel here is all worn round; I don't know yet if round packs.
entries.title: Its fish stayed

entries.onMind: scraping the corners to hard ground
entries.reason: Mark it before I dig, so I dig once.
entries.text: Tipped the first sackful down beside the stone heap; the corners will want three or four more. On the map sheet, a small ring of gravel round each of the four corner dots, and the rocker crossed out.
entries.title: Rings on the dots

queries: does round river gravel pack under a footing stone
entries.query: does round river gravel pack under a footing stone
entries.reason: Every bit of gravel in my shallows is worn round, and I don't want a corner I squared to drift.
entries.source: Hello Gravel: Crushed Stone for a Shed Base (vs River Rock)
entries.text: Asked whether round creek gravel packs under a footing. It doesn't, much: smooth faces don't interlock, so round stone shifts under load. Broken stone with sharp edges locks when you tamp it down in thin layers, a couple of inches at a time. Round is good for letting water run, not for holding weight.
entries.title: Round won't lock

entries.text: So my first sack is drainage, not footing. If it wants sharp stone, I break stone, and a hammer on rock rings a long way, all the way to its pool. That's a daylight problem for tomorrow.
entries.title: Drain, not footing

entries.reason: Last time I came back from the edge to a cold pit.
entries.text: Raked every bit of ash over the last embers and pushed the ring stones in before walking west. If a coal keeps till I'm back, no oil spent.
entries.title: Banked for the edge

entries.text: At my end of the stones the small one was crouched at its pool with its net flat in the water. Didn't step on; stood still with the map rolled under my arm. It lifted the net, empty, and held it up a bit at me. Dipped my head and went over slow, clogs set down flat; only one knock.
entries.title: I waited

entries.text: High thin cloud tonight, so the sun went into the sea pale orange instead of hard. Kept the box shut: ten is for a clear evening. No shore, no smoke, no sail, same as every night.
entries.title: Through the veil

entries.text: It held the net up so I'd see there was nothing in it yet. Like telling me I could go. Out here my people say the world stops, and back there something small is fishing and waiting on me to cross.
entries.title: Showed me empty

entries.reason: It showed me its empty net so I could cross; seemed right to show it something back.
entries.text: Came back by lantern. At the stones the small one was on its log by its fire, facing my way. Held the lantern up a little, the way it held up its net, and it watched me and didn't look away. Crossed with one knock.
entries.title: Lifted the lantern

entries.reason: Every lit wick is oil I don't get back.
entries.text: Raked the ash back: two coals still red under every bit of ash I had, an hour and a bit after banking. Shavings, two dry middles, one puff, and it stood up. Turned the lantern down to a bead and set it by the bench.
entries.title: A coal kept

entries.text: Two heels of bread and a long piece of sausage, sitting on the ground by my fire. Left: most of a loaf, the cheese less three wedges, about a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, the beans, most of the nuts and apples less one, salt, honey.
entries.title: Supper by my fire

entries.text: Two fires now, twenty paces apart with the water between. The small one is bent over something on its log by its own. Tomorrow I break stone, and a hammer on rock carries; better in the middle of the day, when its fish aren't biting anyway.
entries.title: Two fires

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome, hardly a breath of wind: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. The lever tail still slides on the step.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Firelight is free; the lantern stays a bead.
entries.text: Twisting stalk fiber by my fire. Over the water the small one sat on its log with a stick over its coals. Looked up and it was already looking my way; held it a breath, neither of us moved, then back to the twist.
entries.title: It was looking

entries.text: Two arm-lengths of two-ply cord off the stalks, even enough for a dropper line. Wet cord stretches, so it goes on the line dry.
entries.title: Two arm-lengths

entries.text: Wrote tomorrow on a squared page: break sharp stone at midday when its fish are down anyway; break with a hard creek cobble, not the claw hammer, whose face is for nails; lay it in thin layers and tamp each one.
entries.title: Stone, on paper

entries.reason: one middle now keeps it up till I turn in
entries.text: Laid a dry middle on and it caught clean. The low one did its five from upstream, and a long while later the high one answered. Over the water the small one sat dead still on its log, listening too.
entries.title: Both owls

entries.onMind: what the small one is cutting
entries.reason: the fish hold at different depths, and one bait only asks one of them
entries.text: Tied the new two-ply onto the fish line a hand above the bottom hook, so a second bait hangs higher in the water. Pulled every knot hard while the cord is dry; wet, it would stretch and slip.
entries.title: A dropper

entries.reason: it answered my lantern
entries.text: Looked over. The small one had put down whatever it was cutting and lifted its hand at me across the water, just a little. Took a breath and lifted mine back. Then we both went back to our hands.
entries.title: It lifted a hand

entries.text: I came here to be alone and I keep counting its fire. A lifted hand isn't asking anything. Maybe on this side of the water I'm not the one trespassing after all.
entries.title: Not trespassing, maybe

entries.reason: A stone that rings ought to be the hard one; a thud means it'll crumble first.
entries.text: Turned the flat stones from the footing heap over by firelight for a cobble to break with tomorrow. The dark gray one rings when I knock it on another; the brown ones thud. Over the water the small one sat with its head tipped back at the sky.
entries.title: One that rings

entries.reason: The keg runs out someday; pegs I can make from the woodpile.
entries.text: Whittling a peg from a split offcut with the short knife, tapered at one end, about as thick as the test hole. If a peg holds a joint, nails aren't the only way to fasten.
entries.title: A peg

entries.text: Over the water the small one sits bent over a pale square of light, like my tablet's, but at night. Mine's dead the minute the sun goes. What has it got that glows in the dark?
entries.title: A glow in its hands

entries.reason: A hammer carries at night, and it's reading.
entries.text: Tapped the peg into the crooked test hole with the hammer. On the third tap the small one looked up from its glow, so I kept it to three.
entries.title: Three taps

entries.text: The peg sits tight at the bottom of the hole and rocks at the top, because the burned hole is wider there. A peg wants a straight hole, and a burned one never is.
entries.title: Loose at the top

entries.reason: a burned hole is never straight
entries.text: Opened the chest by firelight and lifted out the bent crank and its row of bits in their slots. Fit the bit nearest my peg's thickness into its jaws and turned it against my palm. It wants to go round, not burn its way in.
entries.title: The crank with bits

entries.text: Over the water the small one is crouched at its ring, raking ash over the coals. About now every night its light goes down, and mine's still up.
entries.title: Its light goes down

entries.reason: firelight is free; oil is not
entries.text: Laid a split middle on and it took on the second breath, no smoke to speak of. Across the water its ring is a dark smudge now, and it has gone off toward its big tree.
entries.title: A split middle

entries.reason: find out what the crank is for
entries.text: Set the point on the offcut, leaned on the round head with my chest and cranked. The bit walked in and came out the far side in curls. I can sight straight through the hole at the fire: same width top and bottom.
entries.title: Straight through

entries.text: Tapped the peg in: tight at the mouth and tight at the bottom, and it won't rock. Kept it to a few soft taps; the small one has gone in to sleep.
entries.title: Tight all the way

entries.reason: so tomorrow starts where tonight ended
entries.text: Wrote it on a squared page: burned holes rock, cranked holes hold. Peg one sill corner in daylight, where I can watch the bit go in square.
entries.title: Written up

entries.reason: one peg alone lets the corner pivot
entries.text: Split the other half of the offcut and whittled it down to match the first peg. One peg in a lapped corner is only a hinge; two and it can't turn.
entries.title: A second peg

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a still, clear night: swung once, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: a bed on an empty belly is a cold one
entries.text: A handful of nuts and one dried apple out of the bundle by the fire. Over the water its side is all dark now, not a spark in its ring.
entries.title: Nuts by the fire

entries.reason: a sill that slides spoils a straight hole
entries.text: Twisting dry stalk into two-ply on the fire's side. In daylight I want a sill lashed down to its footing stone while I bore, so it doesn't creep under the crank.
entries.title: Cord for the sills

entries.reason: warm hands sleep easier than cold ones
entries.text: Hands out to the fire before I bury it. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. Over the water nothing moves; its side has been dark an hour.
entries.title: Hands to it

entries.reason: two pegs in one corner should be twins
entries.text: Sighted down both pegs against the flames. The second runs a hair fatter at the head than the first; a scrape in daylight and they will match. They go in holes from the same bit, so they had better.
entries.title: A hair fat

entries.reason: a kept coal is cheaper than a lit wick
entries.text: Set the two half-burned sticks aside for the morning and heaped every bit of ash over the coals, then pushed the ring stones in. Last time that kept two coals; tomorrow should start without a drop of oil.
entries.title: Buried for morning

entries.reason: a kept coal is cheaper than a lit wick
entries.text: Raked the heap open: one coal, red as a bead, at the very bottom. Shavings, one of the half-burned sticks and a long breath, and it's up. Second morning running with no oil spent.
entries.title: One bead left

entries.text: Across the water the small one is already on its log by a fire of its own, bent over something in its lap. It looked up once and back down. Fair enough for a good morning.
entries.title: It was up first

entries.reason: Fine work on an empty belly shakes.
entries.text: A heel of bread and a wedge of cheese by the fire, sitting on the ground with my back to the sun. Over the water the small one crouched at its ring laying sticks on; it looked up at me once, and I chewed slower and didn't look away.
entries.title: Bread by the fire

entries.text: Whittled the fat head of the second peg down in thin curls till the two lie side by side the same. Both should go through the same bit's hole now.
entries.title: Pegs matched

queries: where to put a wooden peg in a lap joint how far from the end
entries.query: where to put a wooden peg in a lap joint how far from the end
entries.reason: Before I bore into a good sill I want to know where the holes belong.
entries.source: FineWoodworking: Drawbore placement?
entries.text: Only an old talk between two woodworkers, about a different joint, and no distances at all. Two things worth keeping: don't set two pegs in a line where they fight each other, stagger them, and a hole pulled too far off splinters out the far side.
entries.title: Not much on pegs

entries.reason: Two nails alone let a corner turn; a peg won't.
entries.text: Set the holes on the diagonal of the lap, a thumb in from each edge, and cranked the first one straight down through both sills. The peg tapped home tight with the hammer, no rock. Across the water the small one's log is empty; it's gone off west somewhere.
entries.title: First peg home

entries.onMind: next time bore halfway from each side
entries.reason: One peg alone is a hinge.
entries.text: Cranked the second hole on the other diagonal, a thumb in from both edges, eyes on the bit the whole way. It broke out ragged on the underside, a splinter as long as a nail, just what the tablet warned about. Pressed it back down; it'll hold.
entries.title: Ragged underneath

entries.onMind: what comes up off a sill
entries.text: Second peg tapped home, and I hung my weight off the far sill end; the corner didn't so much as tick. On the last tap I looked up and the small one was crouched at its pool across the water, watching me. I lifted my hand with the hammer still in it, and it lifted one back.
entries.title: Both pegs home

entries.onMind: a square hole, and I only own round bits
queries: how to attach a corner post to a wooden sill
entries.query: how to attach a corner post to a wooden sill
entries.reason: The sills are square and pegged, and the next thing up is a post; I don't know what holds a post to a sill.
entries.source: Chest of Books: Corner Posts
entries.text: An old building book says a corner post wants to be four by eight, or two four-by-fours set close together; one alone is hardly enough. Its foot gets a tenon that sits in a mortise chopped into the sill, and its top is spiked to a plate. My boards are two by four, so a post of mine would be at least two of them side by side.
entries.title: Posts twice as thick

entries.text: A mortise is a square hole, and I've got two chisels I've never used and a bit that only makes round ones. Bore it round first and pare it square, maybe. Not before I know I've even got the boards.
entries.title: A square hole

entries.onMind: whether the bowed one can be a post with its bow turned in, or poles from the limb
entries.reason: No more timber is coming unless I ask.
entries.text: Sighted along every board left on the stack: seven straight, plus the bowed one and the twisted one set aside again. A fourth sill and four doubled posts want nine. Two short before I've cut a single stud for a wall; I'm not cutting anything till I've thought about that.
entries.title: Two short

entries.onMind: try it on the offcut first
queries: how to cut a mortise with a brace and bit and a chisel by hand
entries.query: how to cut a mortise with a brace and bit and a chisel by hand
entries.reason: A post's foot wants a square hole in the sill, and all my bits make round ones.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: How to Cut a Mortise
entries.text: Bore a row of holes inside the lines to take out most of the waste, then pare the long sides straight down with the chisel, its flat back to the wall, tapping light so it doesn't split. The ends go last, back to the line, and you check each wall with a square. It said a drill, not a brace, but a hole is a hole.
entries.title: Bore, then pare

entries.text: Not in a sill. The offcut's already full of test holes and nails; it can take one more mistake.
entries.title: Not in a sill

entries.reason: Take the waste out round before squaring it.
entries.text: Marked a slot two fingers by four on the offcut with the try square and pencil, and cranked four holes down the middle, a bit's width apart. They wander a hair toward the end where I lean on the brace.
entries.title: A row of holes

entries.text: Tapping the chisel down along the pencil line, light like it said. I looked up and the small one was kneeling at its pool, lifting a flat stone off something sunk there, and looking this way. I looked a moment longer than I would have, then went back to the line.
entries.title: Watched back

entries.onMind: check with the square every few taps
entries.text: Held it up and sighted down the slot. One long wall goes straight down; the other leans in at the bottom like a funnel, where I tipped the chisel without knowing. Fine for a scrap, no good for a post's foot. Next one, the try square goes against it every few taps.
entries.title: Like a funnel

queries: chisel keeps leaning when cutting a mortise how to keep it straight up and down
entries.query: chisel keeps leaning when cutting a mortise how to keep it straight up and down
entries.reason: His first practice slot came out with one wall leaning like a funnel.
entries.source: Woodworking Masterclasses: Freehand straight mortise?
entries.text: A woodworkers' talk says what feels straight up and down isn't, for most people: stand side-on to the bench, keep a square standing beside the work to eyeball against, and step back to look from the side. Most leaning comes from pulling the chisel toward you as you strike.
entries.title: Straight isn't what it feels

entries.text: That's my funnel wall: I was facing the bench and drawing the chisel in on every tap. Second slot side-on, square standing next to it.
entries.title: Pulling toward me

entries.reason: So he can see the chisel lean while he cuts instead of after.
entries.text: Stood side-on to the bench with the try square upright beside the offcut and tapped down the second slot. Across the water the small one is kneeling at its pool dead still with a line in the water; it looked up at the taps once, same as I looked over, then back to its line.
entries.title: Side-on

entries.text: Sighted down the second slot: both long walls straight this time, one end wall off a hair where I got lazy at the last taps. That one I'd nearly trust in a sill.
entries.title: Nearly true

entries.text: Bread and a piece of sausage on the crate, and halfway through the bread the small one lifted something silver out of its pool, flapping in the leaves. I stopped chewing. It didn't hide it; it fishes with nothing but a cord and patience.
entries.title: Its fish

entries.text: Left: most of a loaf less two heels, the cheese less four wedges, a little under a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less two, salt, honey.
entries.title: Pantry

entries.reason: Lunch is eaten; the trap is the next thing that might feed me.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap out of the shallows below the stones: bait gone, nothing in the cone. Across the water the small one was crouched at its fire with a fish on a stick over it; it looked over at the splash and I looked back, then sank the trap again.
entries.title: Empty cone

queries: catch fish on a cord with no hook just a stick and a worm
entries.query: catch fish on a cord with no hook just a stick and a worm
entries.reason: The small one lifted a fish with a cord and no hook I could see, and my hooks have done little.
entries.source: Wikipedia: Fishing tackle
entries.text: Before hooks there was the gorge, a word for throat: a long thin sliver of bone or stone tied to the line at its middle and baited so it lies along the line. The fish swallows it, the line tugs, and it turns crosswise and lodges.
entries.title: The gorge

entries.text: If that's what it's using, the whole trick is a splinter, a worm and waiting for the swallow. I have splinters by the pile.
entries.title: Costs nothing

entries.onMind: a groove at the middle for the cord
entries.reason: To try the old way on the dropper line.
entries.text: Split a sliver off the offcut and carved it thin with the short knife, a point at each end, about a finger long. Next it wants a groove round the middle so the cord can't slide off.
entries.title: A sliver gorge

entries.reason: A cord tied round a smooth sliver will slide to one end and the thing will hang wrong.
entries.text: Cut a shallow groove round the middle of the sliver with the tip of the short knife. Across the water the small one is on its log with its glowing slate, the fire behind it sinking.
entries.title: A seat for the knot

entries.onMind: how it goes on the sliver
entries.reason: The old way wants live bait, and my crayfish scraps all went into the trap.
entries.text: Turned the black leaf mold under the deadfall with the spade and picked out three worms, two thin and one fat, into a wet leaf.
entries.title: Worms

queries: how to bait a gorge hook so it lies along the line
entries.query: how to bait a gorge hook so it lies along the line
entries.reason: A sliver tied at its middle wants to hang crosswise before anything has swallowed it.
entries.source: Field & Stream: Survival Fishing: How to Make a Gorge Hook
entries.text: Groove at the middle, knot seated in it, then spear the sliver right through the bait so it lies flat along the line, points up and down. Then the hard part: give slack while the fish feeds until the bait is all the way down, and only then let the line come tight so it turns.
entries.title: Bait hides the gorge

entries.text: Clove hitch into the groove, pulled hard while the cord is dry, and the fat worm threaded over the whole sliver, both points buried. It lies flat along the cord now.
entries.title: Rigged

entries.text: Knelt at the east shallows below the stones and let the line down behind a stone. Five steps of water off, the small one is at its pool rinsing its hands. It didn't go.
entries.title: Opposite banks

entries.onMind: what it knows that I don't
entries.text: Before I let the gorge down I held it up toward the small one between finger and thumb; I don't know why. It looked at it and nodded once. I nodded back and let it sink.
entries.title: A nod across

entries.onMind: bigger bait, or wait for bigger fish
entries.reason: The tablet said give slack till the bait is all the way down.
entries.text: Two little pulls and I fed slack, then nothing; lifted it and the worm was a rag, the sliver bare. Whatever took it was too small to swallow it. Threading the thin worm on now.
entries.title: Stripped

entries.text: Two little pulls again and I was reaching to lift. Across the water the small one had its hand out flat over the pool, palm down, slow, and held it there. I took it as wait. I fed slack.
entries.title: A flat hand

entries.reason: The tablet said let it come tight only once the bait is down.
entries.text: Then the cord drew off slow and steady, and I let it come tight, and it pulled back. A fish not much longer than my finger, flapping on the stones. I looked over with it in my hand; the small one had put its hand down and was just watching.
entries.title: It turned

entries.onMind: the head for the grease tin
entries.text: Opened it at the water: the sliver had turned square across its throat, the way the tablet said, and came out whole. Head and guts kept for the lamp. The small one has gone up to its fire and is digging in its leaf heap.
entries.title: Crosswise

entries.text: The pit was down to two red coals under gray. Shavings, a split middle and a long breath, and it stood up without smoke.
entries.title: Coals

entries.reason: A fish caught is a heel of bread saved.
entries.text: Boiled it in the tin with a pinch of salt and ate it with a heel of bread, every flake; the head and guts went into the broth tin for the lamp. Across the water the small one is on its log with its glowing slate. I owe it one, I think.
entries.title: My own fish

entries.text: Tablet out while the sun's still on the panel. Across the water the small one is crouched at its ring blowing its fire up; it's got flames again.
entries.title: Sun on the panel

queries: hand held out flat palm down meaning gesture
entries.query: hand held out flat palm down meaning gesture
entries.reason: I took the small one's hand for wait and it was right, but I want to know if that's what it means or if I just got lucky.
entries.source: Emojipedia: Palm Down Hand Emoji | Meaning, Copy And Paste
entries.text: The tablet says a palm turned down is for dropping something or reaching for it, and in some places for waving someone off, or even for calling them over. Nothing about waiting. Didn't matter: the fish said what it meant plainer than the tablet did.
entries.title: Flat hand

entries.reason: I owe the small one a fish, near enough.
entries.text: Whittling a second gorge off the offcut, both ends sharp, groove in the middle. One's enough for me. I don't know yet who the other one is for, or how you'd give it.
entries.title: Second sliver

entries.text: Third practice slot on the offcut, side-on, tapping light. Over at its pool the small one is kneeling with a cord again, sun still on the water. It glanced up at the noise; I kept on, softer.
entries.title: Third slot

entries.reason: A hole cut wrong in a sill can't be uncut.
entries.text: Sighted it against the square: both long walls straight, both ends straight this time. Three slots on scrap; the next one goes in a sill. Across the water the small one lifted its line and it came up bare.
entries.title: Three for three

queries: how deep should a mortise be for a pegged sill corner
entries.query: how deep should a mortise be for a pegged sill corner
entries.reason: The next slot goes in a sill, and a sill I cannot get back.
entries.source: Popular Woodworking: Tenons Rule! So Here Are the Rules on Tenons
entries.text: Asked how deep; it never said. What it did say: the old rule is the tongue is a third as thick as the board the hole is cut in, and at least five times as long as it is thick. My slots are two fingers wide in a board barely three fingers thick. That's two thirds, not one.
entries.title: A third, not two fingers

entries.text: Three good slots on scrap, all three too wide. The one in the sill wants to be one finger wide and as long as my hand. Better to learn that on the offcut than on a board I can't get back.
entries.title: Three for three, too wide

entries.reason: a coal that keeps means no oil spent relighting
entries.text: Every bit of ash over the coals and the ring stones pushed in before the edge, same as last night. Across the water the small one is crouched at its own ring laying sticks on; it keeps its fire going while mine sleeps.
entries.title: Banked again

entries.text: At the stones the small one was kneeling at its pool, threading a worm onto its own splinter. My second sliver was in the pouch and my hand was on it the whole time I stood there. I didn't know how. When I stepped on it nodded; I nodded back and crossed soft, one knock.
entries.title: Hand on the pouch

entries.reason: start short and double, the way the tablet said
entries.text: Clear enough tonight. Box on the ground a step back from the lip, hole at the sun just over the water, shutter open for a slow ten. Twenty tomorrow if it's clear, forty after. Ten sheets left.
entries.title: Ten

entries.text: It went in clean, the scattered cloud over it lit orange from underneath. No shore, no smoke, no sail. Back across the water something small is fishing with a sliver like mine, and I'm still carrying the other one.
entries.title: Still carrying it

entries.reason: a bead is all the walk home needs
entries.text: Lit one lantern at the boulder and turned it down to a bead; the trunks go black fast once the sun's in. Across the creek the small one's fire shows between them, the only light on this side.
entries.title: Bead of light

entries.reason: I can't hand it across, but I can leave it where it'll be found
entries.text: Stopped at the small one's end of the stones and laid the second sliver flat on its landing stone, groove up, where it kneels to thread. It sat on its log by the fire watching me the whole while. I lifted the light a little its way and crossed, one knock.
entries.title: Left on its stone

entries.text: One coal under the heap again; shavings and a long breath and it stood up. Looking up from it I saw the small shape bent at the landing stone, dark against its own fire, then turning something in its hands. It found it.
entries.title: It found it

entries.text: Heel of bread and a wedge of cheese by the fire, lantern out. Didn't feel like giving it something, leaving that sliver. Felt like paying back a fish.
entries.title: Supper by firelight

entries.reason: a third line wants cord, and twisting is work for firelight
entries.text: Twisting stalk cord by my fire, an arm's length done. The small one's fire burned alone for a while; now it's back, crouched at the ring laying sticks on. It looked my way when it came into its light, and it didn't look off first.
entries.title: Its fire alone

entries.text: Wrote the day in the gray notebook: first corner pegged, the gorge fish, ten count at the edge, the sliver left on the stone. Tomorrow the real slot goes in a sill, one finger wide and a hand long, in daylight.
entries.title: Written up

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a south breeze: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: a third line wants cord, and firelight is free
entries.text: Cord's two arms long now and even enough. One more evening of it and the third line is made.
entries.title: Two arms of cord

entries.text: One split middle on; it caught without smoke. Across the water the small one is bent over something in its lap, a little blade catching its firelight. Whittling.
entries.title: Fed, and a blade

entries.reason: a hole cut in the wrong face can't be uncut
entries.text: Sighted down the third sill face by face against the firelight. The upper face has one tight knot near the end; the slot goes in the clean face, a hand from the corner.
entries.title: Picking the face

entries.text: The small one stood at the edge of its light and held something pale up toward the water, toward me. The sliver. I put the sill down and lifted my hand.
entries.title: Held up

entries.text: Hands to the fire. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered; the small one sat still on its log, eating something off a stick.
entries.title: Hands to the fire

entries.onMind: setting three lines at first light
entries.reason: A third line is a third chance at a fish.
entries.text: Third arm of cord twisted and even: enough for a third line with some spare. Across the water the small one's back at its little blade, shavings falling in its light.
entries.title: Third arm of cord

entries.onMind: the space under the last line
entries.reason: His habit now, before the day blurs.
entries.text: Wrote up the day: the gorge fish, the slot rule, the clean face of the third sill. Last line: it held the sliver up, I lifted my hand. Didn't know what to write under that, so I left the space.
entries.title: Written up

entries.onMind: one-finger slot in the third sill tomorrow
entries.reason: Dry wood ready means no oil at dawn.
entries.text: Split six dry middles off the dead limb for the dawn fire; the axe rings loud in the dark. Across the water the small one fed its fire, and when its flames came up it was looking this way.
entries.title: Morning wood

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a light south breeze: swung, settled on its scratch. Across the water the small one sat on its log with something pale and thin up in its light, turning it.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Three lines in, three chances.
entries.text: Carved a third gorge off an offcut and grooved it, then tied it at the middle of the new cord with a clove hitch. Three lines rigged. The small one's face was lit blue a while, bent over its little glowing slab.
entries.title: Third gorge

entries.onMind: that pale thing it was turning
entries.text: Laid a split middle on mine; it went up clean. Across the water the small one was heaping ash on its fire, and its light sank to a red smudge and went out. I looked over as mine came up. It was already only a shape against nothing.
entries.title: Its fire goes down

entries.text: Last night shavings, tonight something thin and pale held up to its fire and turned. I don't know what it's making. Its tree is dark now, and mine is the only light on the water.
entries.title: The pale thing

entries.onMind: three lines in at first light
entries.reason: so the lines go in the moment it's light
entries.text: Turned the wet leaves under the dead limb by firelight and picked out five worms into the dented tin, with damp leaves over them. Last time the best of first light went to digging.
entries.title: Bait tonight

entries.onMind: bore the second corner's holes by daylight
entries.reason: the second corner still only has nails
entries.text: Carving a peg off an offcut for the second corner, eight-sided, tapered a hair. The first corner stopped rocking once its pegs went in; I want the second the same before the fourth sill.
entries.title: Peg for corner two

entries.text: Hands to the fire. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. The small one's tree is still dark; mine's the only light on the water.
entries.title: Last of the night

items.note: Fallen oak just past the mushroom ring with a shelf of gray oyster mushrooms on its side; Token cut six and left the small ones, then came back days later and cut five that had grown hand-wide, leaving the smallest again.
Token's oak past the mushroom ring: a red oak, bristle-tipped leaves, bitter acorns.

Token's netted sack of cracked acorns sunk under a flat stone where the creek runs into the still pool; after six days the water off it runs nearly clear and the meats are soft, and he ate a handful from it one hungry morning.
Flat stone by the fire with a hollow in it; holds Token's acorn ink.
Wild rose climbing through the brambles; the hips on its low stems were picked first, and later the soft red hips on its high stems were picked too.
The big stone by the workbench that Token pressed his birch pages flat under.
Fallen birch limb Token peels bark pages and tray sheets from.
Oak on the creek's east bank about twenty paces up from the stepping stones; Gage gathered about forty acorns under it.

Stand of tall gray dead stalks on the east bank upstream of the stones; Gage strips them for cord, leaving an evenly broken gap. After dark on the thirteenth he snapped fourteen long straight ones off it by feel for a trap hood.

Gage's dented tin: once held his cracked acorn meats soaking; held a live crayfish in creek water overnight, then all three of the morning's crayfish boiled in it over the bench lantern. After dark on the thirteenth a fresh crayfish from the trap went into it in creek water, kept for breakfast. On the fourteenth it held his first fish, then two small crayfish from the trap with their heads and guts, waiting for the bench lantern at dusk. After dark on the fifteenth it boiled both penned crayfish on his fire stones, and kept their heads and broth.
Flat creek stones in the east-bank shallows just below the stepping stones, where Gage turns stones looking for crayfish.
Gage's tin lid of water on the plank bench, a disc of stalk pith floating in it with the magnetized sliver pushed through: his floating-needle compass.
Token's little tower of five flat creek stones on the west bank, marking how far south he followed the creek before the brush closed in.
Long fallen log lying along the creek's west bank just past the brush below Token's cairn, where the creek bends east out of sight.
Bare circle Token swept around the fire ring, five of his strides across.
Heap of leaves Token swept away from the fire ring, piled past the end of the log seat.
Stand of tall dead nettle stalks with square stems at the east edge of the brambles, across the creek from the gray stalks on the far bank; Token snaps them for cord fiber.

Gage's knotted net bag of acorn grit, lined with the cloth from his food bundle so the fine meal stays in, drawn shut with stalk cord and sunk under a flat stone in the east-bank shallows below the stepping stones.

Token's deep folded birch-bark tray, corners lashed with nettle cord; once used at the coals, now carried to the still pool's edge, where he pours pool water over acorn grit in it and tips the brown off. At dusk he filled it with pool water over the saved grit and carried it to the fire.
Huge trunk a few strides north of the fire ring with a pale scar of bark about shoulder height; Gage's mark one on his line west.
Flat, damp stone at the west end of the stepping stones, with a strip of soft creek mud beside it that holds prints.
Token's second net sack of freshly cracked acorns, sunk under a flat stone at the low south end of the still pool, below the first so its brown water runs away from the older batch.

Token's folded birch-bark tray beside the fire ring; the nettle cord at one corner burned through at its first boil, so that corner is now folded over on the outside, lower, and pinned with two whittled birch splinters, which held at the next morning's boil.

Gage's funnel trap of gray stalks, a cone within a cone, baited with crayfish heads and sunk mouth downstream in the east shallows under a flat stone, tied to a root. Caught one, two, then one more in its first night and two more at the morning lift; its door has a second ring of cord and measures a thumb wide every way.

Broad flat stone just south of the fire ring that catches the midday sun; Token spread his leached acorn meats on it one layer deep to dry. After dark on the thirteenth the meats went tacky with dew, and Token picked every one back off into his bindle and carried them home to dry on a shelf.
A flat square of thin sheet tin from Gage's scrap pile, a hand and a half wide; he holds it over the bench lantern as a griddle for thin acorn-meal cakes.

A dished panel of sheet tin about two hands wide that Gage dug out of his scrap pile after dark and hammered flat at the lip, meant to hold a small fire up off the dry leaves. In the small hours of the fifteenth it became the bed of his new fire pit, ringed with his eleven creek stones in front of the lean-to.
A heap of fist-sized creek stones Gage gathered from the east shallows by lantern late on the fourteenth, for a fire ring at his camp; left on the east bank to carry up in daylight.
Rainwater standing in the low spot just south-west of the fire ring after the night rain of the fourteenth.

A big dead limb, about waist-thick and longer than Gage's tarp, lying in the leaves some forty paces north-east of his camp; its top is soaked black, and he snaps the gray dead branches off its underside for firewood.
Gage's three dead poles from the big limb north-east of camp, one forked and two straight, lashed at the top and standing as a lopsided tripod beside the lean-to; it held his hanging weight.
A dead forked branch lying in the leaves under the oak on the east bank, rotten through; it folded in the middle when Gage leaned on it.
sixteen sawn planks stacked on two bearers at the east edge of Gage's camp, left by his maker
twelve two-by-fours stacked on two bearers beside the planks, left by his maker

A shallow tin lid from Gage's scrap pile, a palm wide and a fingernail deep, holding a spoonful of fish and crayfish grease, with a thumb-long stalk-cord wick laid over a little bent bridge of tin so its tip stands clear; his first lamp that burns away from the fire
Gage's new felling axe, leaned against the lean-to's front pole with its head resting in the wet leaves
Gage's new handsaw, laid flat across the plank bench
Gage's felling axe, hung head-up by its handle from a cord loop on the lean-to's front pole, under the tarp's edge; its steel wiped dry and smeared thin with fish grease after a few rust freckles
Gage's claw hammer from his maker, laid on the plank bench beside the saw
Gage's leather roll of three carving knives (long straight, short stub, hooked), unrolled on the plank bench
Small heap of damp leaves at the foot of the scarred trunk, out of the fire's heat, over a curl of birch bark holding Token's five worms for the morning.
A smooth, dry, fist-and-a-half stone Token picked from under the overhang of the scarred trunk (not from the creek), set against the outside of the fire ring to warm for his bed.
Gage's carpenter's chest from his maker, brass corners and rope handles, set down beside the lean-to with the spade leaning on it
Gage's small banded keg of iron nails from his maker, three lengths, set down beside the tool chest by the lean-to
A flat, fine-grained gray creek stone Gage carried up from the east shallows and set on the ground by the bench leg, wet, to hone his chisel on

Gage's small heap of flat creek stones from his own east-bank shallows, carried up to be footings under the corners of his sill frame. Beside them, from late on November 19, a small heap of round creek gravel scraped up from the top end of his east-bank shallows.

beats.s: On his first evening, Token wakes in a hollow beneath an enormous tree and finds a walking staff leaning by the door, which he decides is now his.
The fire takes three tries; the first two, he notes, were small wooden houses.
When an owl begins to hoot in the tall trees, he asks his slate which owl it is, and learns it is not lonely at all, only building a fence out of sound.
He counts the calls on the back of his hand until he runs out of hand.
Supper is nine wrinkled berries and one thorn.
Later the slate tells him of a boy, long ago, who scratched his letters into birch bark, and of the wet mud that kept those scraps for centuries.
So before bed he buries his coals in ash and tucks a curl of bark, scratched with owl dashes, under the log seat.

beats.s: Today Token learns that acorns bite.
His slate explains that the bitterness washes out in water over days, so he sinks them in the creek under a flat stone.
Another page says bristle tipped leaves mean a red oak, the bitter kind, and that is exactly the tree he picked.
He reads that acorn caps make a brown ink, and that something rusty would turn it black, though he has never seen a nail.
Then, past the lookout, the forest simply stops: a sheer drop, and below it water with no far side at all.
That evening a real notebook waits in the basket, the one he asked his maker for.
He asks the slate why the big water smells of salt, and learns that rivers carry salt worn from rock down to the sea.
At his table, he hears a low hush from the west that is not wind.

beats.s: Token wakes from a dream of trying to write down a hush, and spends his morning at the edge of the world, lying on his stomach at the lip to watch long lines of water break white around three rock towers.
His slate tells him those lines were raised by wind somewhere very far away.
Back home he follows his creek south until the brush closes in, and stacks five flat stones to mark where the day ended.
He times a floating leaf and decides, with some satisfaction, that the creek is losing nothing.
In the evening he cuts himself a better pen.
And across the water, in the dark, something rasps and snaps.

beats.s: The second batch of acorns is only half ready, and Token, it must be said, is not good at waiting.
The oyster mushrooms on the fallen oak have grown to the width of his hand, so he cuts four and roasts them.
A smoking leaf inside the fire ring sends him sweeping a wide bare circle around the stones.
He learns that dead nettle stalks make cord, and that a strand let go slack will twist itself into a stronger one.
By firelight he begins knotting a net of his own over a flat stick.
At bedtime the basket holds an old rusty key, and he lays it in his ink overnight to see what iron will do.

beats.s: Token's morning begins with a key.
Left overnight in his ink, it has turned the brown to a dark slate gray.
His slate tells him that iron ink goes on pale and darkens only as it dries in the air, and by afternoon his heaviest strokes have turned purple black.
Then the slate tells him that acorns boiled, poured off and boiled again lose their bitterness in hours instead of days.
Too hungry to wait two nights for the creek, he folds a deep tray of birch bark and sets it on the coals.
Another page warns that some acorns take fifteen waters, but his give up after five.
All day strange sounds drift across the creek, a tink, a creak, a gritty grinding.
And at bedtime the basket holds exactly what he asked for, a second net, which he fills with drying acorns.

beats.s: Token wakes from a dream of a net full of owls and breakfasts on acorns dried right through.
By his fire ring he finds one whole print, with a small bite out of one line.
From the first stepping stone he glimpses someone with pointed hair on the far bank, and he does not cross.
When a north wind starts flinging sparks, he buries the coals himself.
He lights a small fire to try his third pen, and across the water something taps metal on metal.
The slate warns that ink left open goes thick, so the ink stone will want a lid.
Then he sorts his soaked acorns for breakfast and goes to bed.

beats.s: Token spends the day finding signs of a neighbor, like a wild rose picked bare above his reach.
At sundown a small yellow light blinks on across the creek, and when the slate says marsh lights flare and die, he decides this steady one is somebody's lamp.
He reads that bark can boil water on the coals, and the bark holds, but one corner's cord burns through and the water hisses into the fire.
So he whittles birch pins for the corner, and across the water the light returns with a clank of metal on stone.
Then he asks how to boil the bitterness out of acorns faster, and learns that hot water does in an hour what the cold pool takes days to do.
He banks the fire for a morning boil, and goes to bed counting trips to the pool.

beats.s: Token wakes early and blows last night's buried coals back into flame.
At dusk he tips a pool stone, and something small with two claws shoots backward and is gone.
After dark the slate tells him the bright point over the trees that never flickers is a planet called Saturn.
When his drying acorns go tacky with dew, he reads that damp acorns mold fast, and carries every one home to a shelf.
He asks whether anyone could see its rings with their own eyes, and the slate says no, only a golden dot.
He sits with his head tipped back anyway, taking the ring on faith.
Kneeling at the pool for a last drink, he hears something slosh twice in the dark on the far side, and then nothing at all.
Too heavy for a crayfish, he decides, and banks his fire for bed.

beats.s: A thorn hook snaps, and an oak one only gets the bait nibbled away.
So he asks how small a hook should be, and learns instead to hide a splinter thin as a pine needle in the bait.
One fish twists free at the stones, and the next he lifts straight out onto the bank.
Roasted on a stick, his first catch is gone in four bites.
At dusk the bait is stolen without a single pull, and his slate tells him little fish peck it away in nips too small to feel.
Smelling rain, he reads that it washes worms into the creek and wakes the fish, so he stacks dry sticks under the scarred trunk.
Then he learns to bury coals in ash, and before bed he does it, heaping ash over the glow and leaving the rain to tell him if it works.

beats.s: Token wakes late from a night of rain and finds four coals still orange under the ash he buried.
He breathes them back to life, and across the water a small new fire burns.
At the pool he winds a smaller scrap of bait on and lifts a speckled fish onto the bank.
Later a bark scoop meant to lift a fish goes in with a slap, and the fish is gone.
The slate tells him of nets laid low and lifted straight up, so he ties cords to his scoop's corners.
Then he asks what little creek fish like to eat, and reads of worms, not acorn crumbs.
So in the wet dark he digs two cold pink worms from the edge of the firelight.
He reads that worms must stay damp but never drowned, and tucks his rain-filled scoop under an overhang before an early bed.

beats.s: Token wakes from a drizzly night with thick, slow hands.
At the pool a little fish flips off his bark scoop and is gone.
So he knots a net bag, and reads that fish bite best when the water is warmest.
This time a fish no longer than his finger drops in.
A bigger one steals half his worm because he lifts too soon.
At dusk a thin, high whistle comes across the water, and no owl the slate knows sounds like it.
Later the slate offers a tiny owl that toots on and on, all on one note, but his whistle climbed three notes and stopped.
He reads that a hot stone can warm a bed for hours if it is wrapped in tough cloth first.
So he banks the fire, wraps his stone in the rough bindle cloth, and takes a little of the fire to bed.

So he knots a net bag, and reads that fish bite best when the water is warmest. This time a fish no longer than his finger drops in. A bigger one steals half his worm because he lifts too soon. At dusk a thin, high whistle comes across the water, and no owl the slate knows sounds like it. Later the slate offers a tiny owl that toots on and on, all on one note, but his whistle climbed three notes and stopped. He reads that a hot stone can warm a bed for hours if it is wrapped in tough cloth first. So he banks the fire, wraps his stone in the rough bindle cloth, and takes a little of the fire to bed.

beats.s: On a clear, cold morning, Token finds a pinhole box from his maker waiting at the stump.
He reads that a fish cannot swim backward, so he lifts his net in one go, and lands his first fish.
After dark a small yellow light swings low across the stepping stones, clacking stone to stone, and then it is gone.
His slate tells of marsh lights that fade without a sound, so this one, he decides, was carried.
He reads that his steady gold dot wanders slowly against the far stars, and draws it a thumb's width from the faint star nearest it.
Then he wonders whether his box could catch the walking light, and learns that such boxes may stare for hours, and that anything moving comes out a blur.
So the shutter stays shut, and he banks his fire and carries a warm stone to bed.

beats.s: On a gray morning, Token's slow hands lose one fish, then land a striped minnow.
He reads that a lifted hand means hello, and after lunch a hand comes back across the water.
At dusk the stranger comes clacking over the stones and every fish vanishes, but a low hand says sorry.
After dark a lantern crosses back, lifted toward his fire, and Token raises his hand into the light.
Then his maker's note answers the question Token asked him: the ones he loves are his family and his wife.
The slate tells him a wife is the woman someone has married, and the old word only meant woman.
On a fresh page he draws his two owls on one branch: family, the ones you go back to.
The far bank goes dark early tonight, so Token banks his own fire and carries a warm stone to bed.

beats.s: The slate says cold fish bite best near midday, and at noon a fish swims into Token's scoop.
At dusk he lifts his empty scoop so the stranger can cross the stones, then a second fish slides in over the worm.
He asks the slate what a lamp held up at night means, and reads that such lights long told travelers they would not get lost.
He whittles a birch tally stick with a notch for each fish, the way people counted long ago.
When the stranger looks over from his own fire, Token lifts a hand, and a hand comes back.
Under a clear sky he asks how far the golden dot is, and reads that at its closest it is eight times farther than the sun.
Three small knocks come over the water; he looks up, then banks his fire and goes in to sleep.

beats.s: At noon Token lifts a speckled fish onto the bank.
At the pool, the stranger holds up a pointed splinter, and Token nods.
When the stranger's cord twitches, Token holds out a flat hand, and the stranger waits, and lifts a fish.
At dusk his own splinter brings one up too.
Then the stranger comes home by lantern and leaves a little sliver on Token's landing stone.
Token asks the slate what you give back for a gift, and reads that thanks comes first.
So he stands at the edge of his firelight and holds the sliver up toward the water.
Across the creek, the stranger lifts his hand.
By the time the pen in his lap has a point, he knows who it is for.
Last of all he asks the slate how the stranger makes his cord, and reads that dead nettle stalks peel into threads.

threads.name: Who's hooting in the dark
threads.summary: Heard an owl his first night; read that great horned owls claim territory in November. Logged the hoots as dashes on birch bark. Heard it again from the creek, always the same side of the water. Sat by the pool after dark and heard it again from across the water, closer, five hoots long-short-short-long-long; copied them onto the notebook's third page and they match the first night's. Read that each great horned owl's call is its own and stays the same for years, and pairs answer each other, the female higher. At the pool, heard his owl answered by a second, higher voice from farther off. Wrote both voices on the notebook's fourth page, the low five-hoot one and the higher, quicker answer, with a wavy line for the creek between them. Heard both voices again from the pool after dark, the low five hoots across the water and the higher answer from farther off. Counted both voices from the log seat after his first hot meal: the low five from upstream, the higher answer farther off. From the log seat before bed the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. By the fire after dark the low five came from upstream and the higher one answered late, farther off. Before bed, hands to the coals, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. With his hands to the fire after dark, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. Listening on the log seat after dark, the low five came from upstream and the higher one answered late; across the water the stranger had stopped to listen too. Eating roasted acorns after holding up the sliver, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered; the stranger sat still at his own fire. Banked the fire before bed on a mild night; no owl yet.

threads.name: Writing on bark
threads.summary: te the floaters and the brown stripe on the thirty-second page. Wrote the first acorn drink on the thirty-third page, with what to do differently. Wrote the crayfish on the thirty-fourth page by firelight. Drew the treetop gap and a steady bright point on the thirty-fifth page. Fed the fire one stick and wrote under the dot on the thirty-fifth page that it has rings too small for eyes. Drew the long print with the bitten third line on the thirty-sixth page and wrote 'same foot, always' under it. Wrote the first fish on the thirty-seventh page: splinter hidden in a crawler, count thirty, lift, don't draw. Wrote the nibbling on the thirty-eighth page: two tight turns, watch the cord, not the count. Wrote the ash way on the thirty-ninth page, with "rain?" under it. Wrote the hour he buried the coals under 'rain?' on the thirty-ninth page. Wrote the second fish on the fortieth page: a scrap, let the twitches go, lift on the steady pull; under it, warm hands first. Wrote on the forty-first page about creatures that sleep in a den until the cold is over, with 'the burrow?' under it and the stepped splinter drawn small. Drew the scoop lying flat with a worm in the middle on the forty-second page: lay it first, wait, lift straight up. Wrote 'damp, not drowned' on the forty-third page with the scoop drawn under the overhang, and a dot low by the far stones with a line going up the bank. Whittled a fresh birch pen on the log seat after the forty-fourth page came out thick. Forty-eighth page: the gold dot and the faint star just below it, a thumb's width apart, to measure by on the next clear night. Fiftieth page: the seven day names, with a dot beside Saturday. Whittled a fresh birch pen in the sun for no page at all, as a hobby on purpose. Fifty-first page, in a thinner line: 'hobby: a labor you like', 'work: one you have to do', 'fishing: both', and a space left at the bottom for people. Fifty-second page: two square sticks crossed at the ends with a dot for the nail, and a small nod beside them. Fifty-third page: two fish, one with a low sun drawn at the morning end and one with a low sun at the evening end. Drew a fish low in a deep pool and a small shell beside it, both with slow wavy lines, on the fifty-fourth page: 'cold: both slow'. Fifty-fifth page: the two owls on one branch, low and high, and 'family: the ones you go back to'. Fifty-sixth page: a worm tucked all the way inside the bag, no tail hanging out. Fifty-seventh page: the pool with a high sun and a fish halfway up out of the deep, and 'warm water first, then worms'. Fifty-eighth page: the two square sticks again, with a line across the corner and a five on it, and 'a floor? a house?' beside them. Whittled a fresh birch pen, the old one's tip gone soft from the ink. First line with the new pen on the fifty-ninth page: the square sticks with a flat stone under each corner, and 'up out of the wet?'. Sixtieth page: a tally of fish, two marks for today and a row of empty boxes, and 'one or two, big ones go back'. Drew the gold dot and its star on the sixty-first page, a little less than a thumb apart, with 'it walks' under them. Sixty-second page: the creek drawn low with gray lying in it, 'cold slides down', and the fish as small dashes deep under it. Wondered whether a square hole wants a square stick like the ones on the fifty-eighth page: maybe the stranger is making a house. Sixty-third page: a square stick with a tongue beside a square hole, "tenon: to hold", and the two square sticks meeting at a corner under it. Sixty-fourth page: two splinters side by side under "gorge", and a flat hand for wait. Sixty-fifth page: the stranger's sliver and his own side by side, a lantern held low under them, and the question of what you give back. Sixty-sixth page: two little fires with the creek between, a hand lifted over the far one, and 'he saw'.

threads.name: Acorn breakfast
threads.summary: Brambles are done, so he gathered acorns from his red oak, the bitter kind; roasted ones tasted like a boot. Sank a sack in the creek by the still pool to soak the tannins out; the water around it runs faintly brown. Ate the last rose hips. Found gray shelf mushrooms on a fallen oak past the ring that smell like licorice; checked on the slate that they're oysters (gills run down the stem, on hardwood) and roasted six on a stick. After nine hours in the creek the acorns had gone pale and only a little bitter; roasted a handful in the coals and they tasted like a mild nut. Roasted another handful turning them with a stick; none burned. By the second morning the acorns were nearly cream-colored and the water off the sack barely brown; roasted over a fresh fire they had no bitterness left. Got full on acorns for the first time since the berries ran out. Hungry again by mid-morning; took two more handfuls from the sack (maybe a day left in it), lit the fire on the first try, and ate them hot on the log seat. Banked the fire, gathered a half sack of fallen acorns under the red oak, and cracked them on the workbench; eleven had grubs, left on the stump edge. Tipped the new cracked meats into the creek net on top of the pale ones; the water off it went brown again. Ate a handful of the old ones cold: like wet bread, nothing bitter. Ate a handful of the pale ones from under the new batch at the pool after the walk south. At dusk dug the pale ones out from under the new batch for supper and roasted them at the fire; two split and spat. Roasted and ate the last pale acorns from the bark box before bed; the box is empty. Next dawn the new batch, one day in the creek, had gone tan and the water off it weak tea; a red seam was still under the banked ash and lit on the first try. Roasted, they are edible but dry the mouth; this batch needs another day. Read that oyster mushrooms get visibly bigger every day; the small caps left on the fallen oak were hand-wide after two days, with new knobs under them. Cut four, left the knobs, and roasted them at the fire; better than the half-bitter acorns. Read that mushrooms sliced thin and hung on a string or stick in warm air dry and keep for months. Has no string, so started whittling a birch skewer; the first split at a knot and he began again. Whittled a second skewer from a straight twig with no knot: arm-long, grass-thin, and it goes through a leaf without tearing. Gathered a bindle of acorns under the red oak to start a batch every day, but kept them whole: fresh meats on top would set the tan batch back. Nine had grub holes; forty-one are heaped against the burrow's cool wall. At midday ate a handful of the tan batch cold from the sack; still drying, so it gets one more night. Read that dead nettle stalks make strong cord: crush, split, peel the fiber off the core. Snapped an armful of dead nettle stalks at the edge of the brambles and twisted a first finger-length of cord for a second net; it kinks back on itself. Got tired of the kinking, let the strand go slack, and it folded and wound itself into a two-strand cord that stays; now he overtwists on purpose and lets it fold. Three arm-lengths from a third of the armful; a net will take a lot of stalks. Too hungry to wait for the tan batch's last night, took two handfuls; the fire had died but one coal under the ash went orange when raked and caught on bark shreds. Roasted, the tan acorns brown fast and don't split; still a little dry, but they fill him. Went back for more nettle stalks. Twisted the new armful into cord; five arm-lengths now. Read that a net is knotted row by row over a flat gauge stick so every hole is the same size, each knot the same small bend; whittled a flat birch gauge two fingers wide. Took two more handfuls of the tan batch for supper (the water off it still weak tea), fed the fire before it went gray, and roasted them; still dry but filling. Knotted the first row of the second net over the gauge on the log seat: four holes, the first too big because he pulled before the stick was under it. Knotting the second row showed the big first hole pulled every hole under it sideways; untied that knot, put the stick under it, retied, and now both rows sit square, eight holes for about an arm-length of cord. Read that a net bag can be knotted in the round, ends joined and holes added as you go, with no seam. Joined the strip into a fist-sized ring of four holes and started a third row around, adding a fifth hole; the cord will run out before the bag is big enough. Scooped two handfuls of the tan batch in the dark for supper (the water off it paler, one more night) and roasted them two at a time; less dry than at noon. Fed the fire before bed to keep knotting by it. Knotted the third round by the fire with a fifth hole; the cord ran out with the round still open, a bag about the size of his fist. Banked the fire and went to bed needing more nettle stalks to close the round. At dawn the batch was cream after its second night, the water off it clear; one coal had lasted eight hours under the banked ash. Roasted, two nights in the creek is the number: no dryness, and he ate till full. Finished the batch by the fire and stopped because he was full. Twisted four more arm-lengths of nettle cord on the log seat for the net's open round. With the net in the creek empty, cracked the forty-one acorns from the cool wall on the workbench; six had grub holes, and thirty-five went into the net under the stone for a new two-night batch. Hungry with the new batch only just in, found the caps left on the fallen oak only thumb-wide after a day; took the three biggest, brought the fire up from embers and roasted them, two bites each. Knotted the net's third round closed with the new cord; the bag holds about two fists. Read that oyster caps take a few days from first showing, so the thumb-wide ones get a third day. Snapped an armful of nettle stalks for the net's fourth round. Still hungry, hooked the high stems of the wild rose down with his staff and ate a dozen hips by the fire: thin sweet-sour skins and itchy-haired seeds, about one acorn's worth. Knotted the new net's fourth round on the log seat, widening it a hole every sixth knot. Read that acorns boiled, poured off and boiled again in fresh water lose their bitterness in an hour or two; he has no pot, but once simmered ink in a folded birch tray. Folded a bark tray twice as deep as the ink tray and lashed its corners with nettle cord. Scooped two handfuls of half-soaked acorns from the sack into it with pool water and set it at the edge of the coals; the water went tea-brown in minutes, but the dry rim singed and curled where the flames reached it. Pouring off means another walk to the pool for fresh water. Carried the tray to the pool, poured off the brown water and filled it fresh; the bottom has gone soft. The second water came up lighter, but the corner nearest the coals weeps and hisses on the embers. Ate them after two boils: soft like beans with a bitter edge at the end; less hungry than all day. Wrote on the twenty-first page that a tray may need three waters. Read that a bark kettle's corners are folded inward and pinned with splinters, and it sits on live coals with ash banked around it so no flame reaches the sides; water keeps the bark from burning below the waterline. Whittled two birch splinters, folded the weeping corner in and pinned it, and the opposite one to match. Scooped two handfuls of the half-soaked batch into the tray for a three-water try and set it on raked coals with ash around it: nothing weeps, but on coals alone it is slow to heat. Fed the fire on the far side of the ring so flames stay off the tray; after forty minutes on coals the second water finally steamed with small bubbles and the pinned corners stayed dry. Washed the batch at the pool and set a third water heating. Read that hot-leached acorns should be tasted from the third or fourth water on, some kinds taking as many as fifteen, and not to wait for clear water. Tasted after the third: mild at first, bitter still at the back of the tongue. Washed the batch at the pool near dark and set a fourth water on the coals. Knotted the second net's fifth round while a fourth water heated, fed the fire to keep it going, and tasted after four: the bitter is down to a crumb at the back. Counted the waters on the twenty-first page. Poured off the fourth water, now weak tea, and set a fifth on the coals.
